There are reports in veterinary medicine describing CI-AKI/CA-AKI. The largest study included 86 dogs who received mostly nonionic monomers (92 total doses). 59 Seven of the dogs (7.6%) had an increase in serum creatinine ( > 0.5 mg/dL) within 1 week, two of which developed clinical azotemia. These ﬁ ndings are suggestive of CI-AKI, but other possible contributory factors (e.g., hypotension) were identi ﬁ ed. Two dogs and a cat had suspected CI-AKI following CT angiography and transarterial embolization ( w 24 hours apart) using a nonionic, low-osmolar medium. 60 Potential risk factors in those cases included Interna- tional Renal Interest Society (IRIS) stage 1 chronic kid- ney disease, older age, and compensated cardiac disease. Suspected CI-AKI developed in a dog 24 hours post excretory urography using an ionic contrast me- dium. 61 In healthy beagles receiving IV iohexol 6 to 8 weeks apart, there was a subclinical decrease (17%) in glomerular ﬁ ltration rate (GFR) after the second injection. 62 Two studies in dogs and cats found a borderline to mild increase in urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPC) within 1 week following IV contrast medium administration, but the clinical relevance of this is unknown. 63 64 These studies suggest that while CI-AKI is uncommon in animals, consideration should be given to monitoring patients for AKI post contrast medium administration, especially in those with pre-existing renal disease or other potential risk factors. The primary method to decrease the risk of CI-AKI in patients with renal impairment is IV ﬂ uids. 35 Also, nonionic contrast media should be used in any patient with evidence of impaired renal function, given their lower nephrotoxicity pro ﬁ le. Contrast studies should not be performed on dehydrated patients, regardless of pre-existing renal status. Cessation of any potentially nephrotoxic drugs should be considered, 56 although this has not been a proven contributor to CI-AKI. 35 Treatment of suspected CI-AKI in human beings primarily involves IV ﬂ uid therapy. NEGA TIVE CO NTRAST MED IA Negative contrast media absorb x-ray photons less than soft tissue, thereby decreasing the opacity or attenuation of organs containing them. The most common negative contrast media are room air, CO 2 and NO 2 . Both CO 2 and NO 2 are more water soluble than room air, so there is less concern for fatal air embolism, which has been reported after pneumo- cystography. 71 72 Negative contrast media are most used for gastrointestinal and urinary tract imaging, either alone or in double-contrast studies. MAGN ETIC RES ONANC E IMAG ING CONTRA ST MED IA General Information The primary contrast media used in MRI contain the rare earth metal gadolinium (Gd 3 þ). Gadolinium-based contrast media (GBCM) are paramagnetic, whereby they shorten T1 and T2 relaxation times. Clinically, it is their effect on T1-weighted images that is important, where both normal and abnormal structures may have increased signal (hyperintensity) on post- contrast images as compared to precontrast images ( Fig. 5.7 ). Gadolinium in its free form is toxic, so chelating agents are added to minimize this toxicity. GBCM can be divided into categories, based on the type of ligand (linear or macrocyclic) and ionicity (ionic, nonionic) ( Table 5.2 ). Linear ligands partially wrap around the Gd 3 þion, whereas macrocyclic li- gands fully surround the ion in a cage-like structure, which gives the macrocyclic contrast media higher stability. 73 74 Higher stability equates to less dissociation and therefore less release of free Gd 3 þions into the vasculature and tissues. Ionicity affects osmolality, but this does not have a clinically relevant impact at the standard clinical dose (unlike with water soluble iodinated contrast media), because the total molar amount is lower (1 Gd 3 þion vs. 3 iodine ions per molecule). 75 The ability of gadolinium contrast media to shorten the relaxation time is called relaxivity, which depends on the ligand and other factors such as the protein-binding of the contrast medium, magnetic ﬁ eld strength, and temperature. 73 76 Higher- relaxivity contrast media are more effective in shortening the T1 relaxation time, which allows for a lower contrast medium dose without sacri ﬁ cing image quality. For example, the newest macrocyclic GBCM (gadopiclenol) can be used at a lower dose in human beings (0.05 mmol/kg vs. the typical dose of 0.1 mmol/kg for other contrast media), without negatively impacting image quality. 77 GBCMs distribute in the bloodstream and extracellular space with subsequent rapid renal excretion. A few contrast media with higher protein binding are partially excreted by the hep- atobiliary system (organ speci ﬁ c contrast media), which means they can serve a dual purpose, with routine early postcontrast (vascular, extracellular tissue phases) and delayed postcontrast (hepatocellular phase) imaging. 76 78 80 GBCMs are typically given IV but intra-articular and intrathecal use has been described in animals. 81 83 Note that while arthrography with GBCMs is commonly performed in human beings, intrathecal use is not approved. Interestingly, the atomic number (Z ¼64) of gadolinium renders it radiopaque and GBCMs have been evaluated as an alternative to iodinated media since in standard doses gadolin- ium is less nephrotoxic. 84 However, since the molar concen- trations of iodinated media and GBCMs are different, the x-ray attenuation of iodinated contrast media is about three times that of gadolinium contrast media, and as such, GBCMs are less effective at altering radiographic opacity. Ultrasound contrast media are microbubbles of inert gener- ally insoluble gas stabilized by an outer shell ( Table 5.3 ). The microbubbles are smaller than red blood cells (1 7 um) and therefore can pass through pulmonary capillaries without concern for air embolism. 95 The shell provides microbubble stability, but the microbubbles are eventually destroyed. The primary route of administration is intravenous, although other applications have been described. Most of the ultrasound contrast media are blood pool only, meaning that the micro- bubbles remain in the blood vessels. After microbubble rupture, the gas content is eliminated through the lungs, and the shell components are ﬁ ltered by the kidneys and eliminated by the liver. 95 Due to the acoustic impedance of gas, these microbubbles produce marked sound wave scattering and this is the hallmark of CEUS. The behavior of the bubbles is dependent on several parameters, including resonance frequency of the ultrasound beam, focal zone settings, acoustic power, and the inherent properties of the contrast media. Of these, acoustic power is the most important factor affecting microbubble behavior. The power, generally expressed as the mechanical index (MI), is affected by the output of the ultrasound machine, the trans- mitted frequency, and the attenuation of the ultrasound beam with depth. 96 At very low MI values, the microbubbles will remain relatively static and provide only some scatter. As the MI increases ( w < 0.2), the sound waves will cause the micro- bubbles to oscillate in a linear fashion. These linear echoes are similar to the ultrasound appearance of the adjacent tissue and make differentiation dif ﬁ cult, meaning that normal grayscale or Doppler imaging can be of minimal use. With slightly higher MI ( w 0.2 0.5), the microbubbles will oscillate in a nonlinear fashion and will begin to emit harmonics of the resonance frequency. Adjacent tissue will generally not resonate harmon- ically, and it is this fact that allows differentiation of the echoes of the microbubbles from the echoes of the tissue. With even further increased MI ( > 0.5), the microbubbles can oscillate and expand beyond their limits and can be quickly destroyed. This can provide a transient strong nonlinear echo. Donald E. Thrall WHAT IS A RADIOGR APH? A radiograph is an image of the distribution of x-rays * that emerge from the patient. When struck by the primary x-ray beam, which is spatially uniform, there is differential absorp- tion of x-rays by the different tissues in the body. This creates nonuniformity in the distribution of x-rays leaving the patient. The character of the nonuniformity is speci ﬁ c to the makeup of the tissue ( Fig. 6.1 ). In normal subjects, the distribution of x- rays exiting the patient has a repeatable pattern, which is recognized as the normal appearance. When looking at radio- graphs of diseased patients, the examiner is looking for alter- ations in the distribution of the exiting x-rays that have been created by disease, and also by normal variations in anatomy. Artifacts will also in ﬂ uence the appearance of the ﬁ nal image. With experience, normal appearance and the effects of artifacts are recognized with more con ﬁ dence, and different appear- ances of the distribution of exiting x-rays come to be associated with certain diseases. Many sources of normal radiographic anatomy are available to assist with interpretation, including this text, other published material, 1 and online. 2 HOW X- RAY EXPOSU RE IS REPRES ENTED IN THE IMAG E Crucial to proper interpretation of radiographs, and in com- prehending radiology reports, is an understanding of the fundamental relationship of x-ray exposure with the degree of blackness or whiteness in the image. Areas of the radiograph that are black or dark gray are highly exposed regions where many x-rays pass through the patient and strike the imaging plate. Areas of the radiograph that are white or light gray are less-exposed regions where more x-rays were absorbed by the patient and fewer pass through and fewer strike the plate. Descriptions of blackness and whiteness in a radiograph are described in terms or lucency vs. opacity, respectively. Unfor- tunately, multiple synonyms are used to describe lucency and opacity ( Table 6.1 ). The term density or radiographic density has also been used to describe ﬁ lm blackness and whiteness, i.e., dense ¼white. However, use of density has fallen out of favor and descriptions based on opacity are preferred. RADIOG RAPHIC INTERPRET ATION The ability of x-rays to allow us to “ see ” inside of the body is taken for granted, perhaps because there are many other so- phisticated technical advances that are commonplace. the patient to create a radiograph remains a mainstay of diag- nostic medicine in both general and specialty practices. Maxi- mizing the potential value of this relatively simple technique still requires constant and ardent attention to detail. Many factors in ﬂ uence the accuracy of radiographic inter- pretation. The interpreter must have access to information pertaining to the patient. 3 This includes the signalment, medical history, and the physical abnormalities that are present. The history provided by the owner is often helpful in guiding radiographic interpretation, but the history may also be misleading. Recognizing that radiographic ﬁ ndings may not al- ways agree with the history is a critical step in formulating a correct radiographic assessment ( Fig. 6.2 ). The physical examination is also very important regarding the identi ﬁ cation of the region(s) that should be radiographed and in formulating a preliminary list of rule-outs. Radiographs should never be a substitute for a good physical examination. Also, one might expect radiographs to provide a de ﬁ nitive diagnosis, but more often they lead to a ranking of differential diagnoses, and provide direction for further patient evaluation with other tests or additional imaging. When obtaining radiographs, it is critical that accurate positioning and proper radiographic technique be used. When compared to ﬁ lm (analog) imaging systems, the extreme exposure latitude that characterizes digital imaging has reduced the number of errors that occur as a result of incorrect kVp and/or mAs settings. However, overexposure and underexpo- sure are still problems, along with poor positioning and lack of proper views. When an owner agrees to have radiographs of their animal made, a contract has been established between the client and veterinarian and implicit in that is the production of adequate images. Unfortunately, many substandard radiographs of animal patients are produced each day. Submission of poor images to a teleradiology service for interpretation by a specialist cannot compensate for errors in radiographic acquisition. Positioning is not discussed in detail in this book, but the standard views recommended for various areas are outlined in other chapters. One aspect of positioning is important to mention here. It has become common for practices to include the whole body of cats and small dogs in one image, i.e., cat-o- gram and dog-o-gram, respectively. This should be avoided as the anatomy at the cranial and caudal edge of the image will be distorted because these regions are struck by very diverging x- rays. Also, a single radiographic exposure technique will not be optimal for the very different makeup of the thorax vs. abdomen. There is no reason to avoid getting individual studies of both the thorax and abdomen in all patients. Once suitable radiographs of the patient have been pro- duced, interpretation should be done in a quiet, relatively iso- lated, environment. This seems obvious, but taking the time to make sure the viewing environment is suitable will pay off with increased accuracy. Concentration and thoroughness are the major determinants of accurate interpretation. Many of us never receive any instruction in actually how to examine a radiograph. Some people develop a highly accurate examination method whereas others are never able to accom- plish this. Everyone will look at radiographs differently. Some look from the periphery to the center, others from the center to the periphery and some haphazardly. Regardless of the exami- nation method, the most important aspect of viewing is to make sure that the entire image is examined. Not ﬁ nding a lesion is often linked to not looking rather than not seeing. Having a checklist of the regions/structures to be examined will also help in making sure that the entire image is examined. Exam- ples of checklists are included in Chapters 9 17 28 , and 38 In addition to examining the overall “ real estate ” of the im- age, there is an ancillary examination method that can be useful in evaluating juvenile bone disease. This is called targeted viewing . Certain bone diseases have a propensity for certain areas of the skeleton, e.g., osteochondrosis in the caudal hu- meral head, metaphyseal osteopathy/hypertrophic osteodys- trophy (HOD) in the distal radius and ulna, and canine panosteitis in the diaphysis of long bones. Therefore, if during the clinical examination of a young, lame dog, a speci ﬁ c disease is suspected, the commonly affected area should be examined closely in the radiograph. This targeted viewing is ancillary to the general overview and will reduce the incidence of subtle lesions being overlooked. For example, an abdominal radiograph with the patient lying on the left side is referred to as a left lateral rather than the more correct right-left lateral. Oblique views are also named by designating the points of entrance and exit ( Fig. 6.4 ). Angles of obliquity can be speci ﬁ ed by inserting the number of degrees of obliquity between the directional terms involved. For example, if the dorsolateral palmaromedial oblique (DLPaMO) view in Fig. 6.4 was made by positioning the x-ray tube 60 degrees laterally with respect to dorsal, the designation would be D60LPaMO. Standardizing the orientation of images for viewing is also important. The brain learns what to expect a certain part to look like when oriented a certain way. Therefore, images should be oriented on the monitor in a predetermined orien- tation, not randomly. The following has become the standard for image orientation:  Lateral views of any part are oriented with the cranial (rostral) aspect of the animal pointing to the interpreter s left.  Ventrodorsal or dorsoventral radiographs of the head, neck, or trunk are oriented with the cranial (rostral) part of the animal pointing up and with the left side of the ani- mal to the interpreter s right.  Lateromedial or mediolateral radiographs of the extrem- ities, including oblique projections, are oriented with the proximal aspect of the limb pointing up and the cranial or dorsal aspect of the limb to the interpreter s left.  Caudocranial (plantarodorsal, palmarodorsal) or craniocau- dal (dorsopalmar, dorsoplantar) radiographs of the extrem- ities are oriented with the proximal end of the extremity at the top. No convention exists regarding whether the medial or lateral side of the extremity is oriented to the in- terpreter s right or left. RADIOG RAPH IC CONTRA ST An individual structure will not be visible in a radiograph unless there is another structure of a different radiographic opacity that is in contact with it to provide contrast . Examples are liver margin visible due to adjacent fat, bone margin visible due to adjacent muscle, and pulmonary vessel margin visible due to adjacent air in the alveoli. Images can have varying degrees of contrast. A high-contrast image is one that has mostly blacks and whites and few gray shades, whereas a low-contrast image is one that has many gray shades and few blacks and whites ( Fig. 6.8 ). To some extent, this depends on the relative values of kVp vs. mAs, but in digital imaging systems the contrast of the image is affected mainly by the processing algorithm the com- puter applies to the image data (see Fig. 6.8 ). DESCRIB ING ABNOR MALITIE S Abnormalities identi ﬁ ed in a radiograph must be described in some format and then communicated. This might be in the form of communication with the owner, documenting the ﬁ ndings in the medical record, or in a formal radiographic report. The Roentgen sign approach has withstood the test of time as a method for describing radiographic abnormalities. This approach is used throughout this book, in most radiology teaching environments, and by most radiology specialists. The Roentgen sign approach involves describing abnormal radio- graphic changes using one or more of six terms ( Box 6.1 ), and represents a simple and understandable way to communicate abnormal radiographic ﬁ ndings. Once the Roentgen signs have been compiled, they are considered along with the clinical in- formation to arrive at a list of possible causes, or diseases. This list of possibilities is termed a gamut . The mnemonic DAM- NITV is an aid to compiling the most reasonable gamuts, and to decrease the chance that an important possibility is not considered. DAMNITV stands for degenerative, anomalous, metabolic, neoplastic, infectious (in ﬂ ammatory, immune), traumatic, and vascular origins of disease. RADIOG RAPHIC GEOMETR Y A radiographic image is a two-dimensional representation of a three-dimensional object. One effect of this is a loss of depth perception ( Fig. 6.12 ). Depth perception is improved by acquiring two radiographs at 90 degrees to each other. Such radiographs are termed orthogonal radiographs and can be used to mentally reconstruct the third dimension ( Fig. 6.13 ). At least two orthogonal views of a part should be acquired in every radiographic examination. Sometimes even with multiple radiographic views, a more sensitive tomographic y modality, such as computed tomography, will be needed to localize a lesion conclusively. Since patients have thickness, some parts will be closer to the x-ray tube than others when the radiograph is made. The parts closer to the x-ray tube, and further from the plate, will be magni ﬁ ed ( Fig. 6.14 ). As magni ﬁ cation increases, so does image blur ( Fig. 6.15 ). A familiar example of this is the shadow of a hand against a wall cast by a ﬂ ashlight. The closer the hand gets to the ﬂ ashlight, the shadow gets larger but is more blurry. The absolute value of the magni ﬁ cation factor can be calculated by dividing the distance from the x-ray focal spot to the plate by the distance from the x-ray focal spot to the part of interest. No matter how the patient is positioned, there will always be some parts that are closer to the x-ray tube than others. Therefore, it is not possible to eliminate magni ﬁ cation from radiographs. This is one reason that patients are always positioned the same and images are always oriented the same . so that the effects of magni ﬁ cation become part of the normal radiographic anatomy. Many structures in the patient will overlap relative to the path of the x-ray beam. Thus, in the two-dimensional image, this overlapping either creates an opacity that does not exist in the patient ( summation ) or an opacity that is misplaced and misinterpreted as a lesion ( superimposition ). Summation is an area of altered opacity occurring when two overlapping objects are in the path of the x-ray beam but are not in contact with each other ( Fig. 6.18 ). Summation creates an opacity that is not actually in the patient. Summation opacities are usually white (opaque) but can be black (lucent). Consider a block of Swiss cheese. When looking at the cheese visually, the holes on the exterior are caused by a cut made through gas bubbles that formed as the cheese fermented. However, there are other gas bubbles completely encased within the block, some of which overlap when viewed from the perspective of the x-ray beam. If the cheese is radio- graphed, fewer x-rays are absorbed in areas where gas bubbles overlap. The more overlapping bubbles that are present, the greater the number of x-rays that penetrate the cheese and reach the plate ( Figs. 6.19 and 6.20 ). In the Swiss cheese, the summation opacities are radiolucent. In patients, summation usually creates an area of increased opacity. Cohen T o recognize and prevent errors and potential pitfalls in any type of image interpretation, it is important to ﬁ rst understand how our eyes and brains work to view and interpret an image. At the core, interpreting images is composed of physical vision (looking at an image), visual perception (what we see), and cognitive decision making (interpreting what we see). 1 3 Different types of errors or pit- falls can occur in each pathway. HOW WE SEE Light reaching the eye, or luminance, must occur before we can perceive an image. Luminance is regulated by the amount of light incident on surfaces, re ﬂ ected or absorbed by those sur- faces, and whether there are other conditions in the air or media the light is passing through that can further scatter or interfere with the light. 4 Once light reaches the eye, visual perception can occur. This is the ﬁ rst step in image interpre- tation, as no analysis of an image can be made before it is viewed. When light strikes the retina, the response is not ho- mogeneous. At the center of the retina is the fovea which contains the largest concentration of cone cells and the largest number of neurons dedicated to it from the primary visual cortex. As a result, the fovea is the portion of the retina with the highest visual acuity and contrast sensitivity. However, the physical world is more complex than can be resolved by the retina and transmitted to the brain, resulting in a compressed signal which is then augmented by memory. 3 In this way, while light signal may strike the retina and activate neurons, what is actually seen or perceived is in part a construction by the observer ( Fig. 7.1 ). 3 This includes mechanisms such as lateral inhibition of the retina, whereby light not only stimulates light receptors of the retina, but also results in inhibition of neigh- boring light receptors to enhance edge detection. We perceive lateral inhibition as optical illusions known as Mach lines (also called Mach Phenomenon, Mach bands, edge effect), which are bright or dark lines that are not real at the edges of real ob- jects. 5 6 This is just one type of optical illusion, as the light we perceive as a representation of the physical world also relates to the type, number, and depth of surfaces or objects. Our visual system also biases us to perceive the highest luminance in a scene as white, so the background impacts what we focus on ( Fig. 7.2 ). 4 What we see or perceive, therefore, is not an ac- curate representation of the physical world. Understanding these optical illusions that are always at play can help us to recognize and leverage them to avoid misperception. Human vision has a large ﬁ eld of view (over 180 degrees), but foveal vision has a small visual angle (1 2 degrees). When viewing images, we either move our eye or head to place ob- jects of interest into foveal vision. When a visual target is at a visual angle of 2 to 30 degrees from us, the eye will move, and when it is more than 30 degrees the head will move. 7 9 This is why most people do not want to sit in the front row of a movie theater, as you have to constantly turn your head to keep the scene in your foveal vision. This is also why it can be helpful to move away from the screen when viewing radiographs (foveate on the forest instead of just a tree). These physical parameters also come into play when considering the layout of a viewing workstation, as a larger number of monitors require greater movement to foveate across all screens. 10 For our brain to recognize a foveated target, we must ﬁ xate or dwell on that target for at least 100 to 300 ms. Beyond this time the retina loses sensitivity, resulting in blurring of the image. To overcome this, the eye makes rapid involuntary movements called saccades which are so fast the visual infor- mation during the movement cannot be registered by the brain, and effectively refreshes visual targets on the fovea. 7 9 Eye tracking studies have shown that when we ﬁ rst look at an im- age, a gist or global impression is formed, then various search patterns are employed to further assess the image. 1 2 10 11 While we seek to foveate targets, studies show that much of an image is not assessed with foveal vision, and peripheral vision is also employed when assessing or comparing targets. 2 3 11 The radiographic description, or ﬁ ndings, in the radiographic report is the representation of the visual search, or what we saw. HOW W E THINK Once an image or target is seen or perceived, the cognitive task begins to decide what that image or target means (e.g., normal vs. abnormal). Dual process theory and the Bayesian model are useful ways to think about thinking. Dual process theory describes thought in terms of system 1 (or type 1) and system 2 (or type 2). System 1 thinking is characterized by decisions that are fast, unconscious, auto- matic, associative, re ﬂ exive, and implicit. These relate to intu- ition or your gut reaction, and are reliant on reader experience. System 1 is advantageous in that it is a fast process with low effort, does not require working memory, and generates con- ﬁ dence, but is error prone and subject to reader bias. This system relates to how we have evolved to group information into patterns, which become the inherent biases of our minds. System 1 is ef ﬁ ciency at the cost of accuracy and is only ac- curate under predictable or typical circumstances. 12 13 Consider when you walk into any kind of kitchen, whether it is commercial, residential, or rustic, you instantly register the scene as a kitchen. You do not have to take stock of exactly what is in the kitchen. However, if there is something out of place or unexpected for that pattern, you may not recognize it even if it is relevant ( Fig. 7.3 ). Conversely, system 2 thinking is characterized by decisions that are slow, conscious, deliberate, re ﬂ ective, and explicit. System 2 is accuracy at the cost of ef ﬁ ciency. 12 System 2 can challenge the pre- conceptions of system 1, and avoid falling into the trap of pattern recognition. The SOAP (subjective, objective, assess- ment, and plan) method is commonly employed in medical records to switch our brain into system 2. This method to think about a patient and their clinical presentation takes time but allows construction of differential diagnoses to accurately weigh available evidence. In diagnostic imaging, system 2 can be seen in search patterns or methods to view an image, and in reporting. Simply having templated prompts for regions of in- terest (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary, pleural, mediastinal, musculoskeletal, extrathoracic) for a thoracic radiograph en- sures all regions have been assessed. We can experience switching from system 1 to system 2 when learning a new language or encountering a word we are unfamiliar with. When we read familiar words and phrases, we often skip words and can still understand the meaning of the sentence. When we encounter an unfamiliar word or phrase, we will sound out the word, breaking it into its component parts ( Fig. 7.4 ). In imaging, people often employ tricks to switch their brains into system 2. For example, over time, when we interpret thoracic radiographs, each view (lateral, ven- trodorsal) will become a diagnostic pattern in our brains. This allows increased ef ﬁ ciency over time. Some have advocated ﬂ ipping a radiograph or digitally inverting the grayscale, particularly when looking for rib fractures or pulmonary nod- ules. In doing so, they are breaking the image out of the schema of “ ventrodorsal thoracic radiograph ” or “ pulmonary nodules are opaque, ” to force their brain into system 2 ( Fig. 7.5 ). However, while these tricks may work for a time, performed enough times, they will simply create a new schema, and the same type of errors can again occur. Having a reading method and consciously moving between system 1 and system 2 is a more robust long-term strategy to achieve best accuracy and reduce errors. Cognition and decision making can also be framed with the Bayesian model. In this way, an output or decision is generated by inputs coded by probabilities. The probability assigned to an input and the resultant output or decision can be related to three functions, likelihood, prior density, and cost. In the context of assessing the lung for metastatic nodules, the likeli- hood function relates to how likely will the patient have pul- monary nodules. Are they young or old? Do they have a known primary neoplasm? It highlights the importance of patient signalment and pertinent clinical history when our brain cal- culates this probability. The prior density function in this example relates to how often you have seen pulmonary nod- ules, be it in any patient or for this speci ﬁ c indication (e.g., pulmonary nodules with mast cell tumor would be un- common, which could and should affect interpretation). The cost function could relate to the implications of the decision of identifying or missing pulmonary nodules. ERRO RS Franz Kafka said, “ All human errors are impatience, the pre- mature breaking off of what is methodical, and apparent fencing in of the apparent thing. ” A true diagnostic error (or variance from accuracy) is a result or decision that could result in patient harm, with no scienti ﬁ c data to uphold it. Error severity can be termed negligible (no ill effect), minor (minimal ill effect), moderate (cause short-term ill effect), major (cause long-term ill effect), and extreme (cause severe long-term effect or death). 14 In a literature review over 20 years in human radiology, a rate of 2% to 20% was found for clinically signi ﬁ cant or major errors. 15 A diagnostic discrepancy relates to differ- ences in opinions between clinicians, whereby those differing opinions can be justi ﬁ ed with available data. 16 Errors leading to incorrect decisions can be thought of within the following framework: prereporting errors, reporting errors, and post- reporting errors. 1. Prereporting errors encompass technical factors during im- aging acquisition or generation. This could include per- forming the wrong imaging test, imaging the wrong patient, imaging the wrong region of anatomy, or acquiring nondiagnostic images (poorly positioned, poor technique, image artifacts). 16 A B C D Fig. 7.4 When we encounter words or images that we have seen before (or think we have seen before), we canemploy type 1 thinking to ef ﬁ ciently gener ate a pattern of that word or image. 2. Reporting errors encompass errors committed by the reader during assessment, and can be further classi ﬁ ed into the following categories: a. A search error is one in which we simply “ don t see ” the lesion, meaning we never physically foveate on it. It is the inability to discriminate embedded targets or a lesion from normal anatomy. Multiple factors lead to search errors. i. This can include physical/environmental factors including individual eye anatomy and health, work- station setup (proper monitor resolution and lumi- nance, ambient light, veiling glare, uncluttered interfaces which do not distract attention), image quality (resolution, contrast, motion, positioning), and fatigue (time of day, image volume). Simply hav- ing proper/higher luminance monitors results in shorter search time, time to ﬁ xate on targets, and dwell time before reaching a decision. Reading per- formance will also wane later in the day as visual fa- tigue increases. 1 3 10 11 17 ii. Behavioral or systematic factors can also lead to search errors, including inadequate time to search an image, not searching the whole image, and hav- ing inadequate target knowledge. Being rushed when reading an image can decrease performance because it can prevent a systematic search. Target knowledge, or knowing what we are looking for, will physically change how we view an image. This highlights the importance of clinical history when interpreting an image. 1 3 11 It can be useful to inter- pret images without the history ﬁ rst (to limit bias), with a subsequent read after reading the history in order to provide target knowledge. b. A ﬁ xation error is one in which we “ see ” the lesion, meaning our eye physically foveates or ﬁ xates on a target, but we do not perceive or recognize it consciously. This type of error is directly impacted by training and experience. This is evident when you “ see ” a lesion only after someone else points it out even though you may have “ looked ” at it before. You will be better able to recognize that type of lesion on future radiographs. i. Fixation errors can also occur secondary to inade- quate or incorrect target knowledge, as we are more apt to ﬁ nd what we are looking for. This concept is called inattentive blindness. In a prior study, a series of computed tomography (CT) lung images were provided to expert readers (radiolo- gists) and naïve observers with no medical training. The images had lung nodules, but experimenters also inserted an image of a gorilla 48 larger than a typical nodule into the study. Both groups were asked to count nodules, but were not told to look for gorillas. Some 83% (20/24) of the radiologists did not report seeing the gorilla, even though 60% (12/ 20) did foveate on it identi ﬁ ed with eye tracking ( Fig. 7.6 ). None (0/24) of the naïve observers saw the gorilla. The results show that while expert readers may be less affected by inattentive blind- ness, both naïve and expert readers are affected by inadequate target knowledge even when a lesion is physically visible. The study also showed the radiolo- gists outperformed the naïve observers in nodule detection (55% vs. 12%), which is the relevant clin- ical task for a radiologist. 18 c. This is the cessa- tion of thinking once a diagnosis is made. 19 Satisfac- tion of search is making a diagnosis (such as esophageal distention consistent with megaesopha- gus on thoracic radiographs) but discontinuing the search and not identifying that the patient also has pneumonia. 19 This can be thought of as only identi- fying the tip of the iceberg. Intraobserver variability is the variation/accuracy of search, recognition, and decision making by the same person over multiple times points and interobserver variability is the variation/accuracy between separate observers. As humans all the factors mentioned earlier impact accuracy and performance, which is unlikely to be completely consistent and uniform over time (even when evaluating the same images). i. Human studies have shown that intraobserver vari- ability can be as high as 20% and interobserver vari- ability as high as 30% to 50%. 22 23 Reader training, experience, and skill directly affect performance, as do physical and environmental factors. You may be less likely to identify pulmonary nodules at the end of the day when you are fatigued or if there are increasing distractions. Even if a nodule or lesion is identi ﬁ ed, there could be variation in reporting of size over time, which affects treatment decisions (stable disease, remission, progression). ii. In human radiology, studies have shown false- negative rates of 20% to 30%, and false-positive rates of 2% to 15%. 1 3 17 22 More experienced observers will typically have more ef ﬁ cient visual search/ ﬁ xa- tion/dwell patterns, ﬁ nd lesions faster, process more information, and be more accurate than novice observers. 17 24 3. Th es e ca n ra n ge fr om ty po s or mi st ak es in t he i ma gi ng re po rt , pa rt ic ul ar ly if re po rt s g en er at ed us in g vo ic e di ct at i on ar e n ot pr oo fr ea d, fo rm at or re po rt i ng st yl e, la c k of or in ap pr op ri at e re c om me n- da t io ns , de la ye d re po rt in g, or si m pl y m is un de rs ta nd in g be - tw ee n pe op le wh en th e cl in ic al in fo rm at io n i s ex ch an g ed . 16 ERRO R REDU CTION As humans, we are not infallible, and even the most competent and experienced clinician will occasionally commit an error. While no one is accurate 100% of the time, we can employ strategies to reduce errors, and control variables. As has been related in legal writing surrounding medical errors, this in- cludes reaching and maintaining competence, developing habits of practice, and using proper techniques. 25 1. Physical factors and limiting distractors/stressors a. Having a proper workstation, including high-resolution monitors with appropriate luminance. b. Acquiring studies with impeccable technique and posi- tioning whenever possible. c. Limiting ambient noise and light (quiet and dark reading room). d. Managing fatigue i. Taking regular breaks. ii. Allow your eyes to accommodate to different dis- tances during breaks. iii. Maintaining a manageable workload. 2. Accurate and complete clinical history/target knowledge a. Performing a blind read without the clinical history to avoid clinical bias. b. Performing an unblinded read with signalment and clin- ical history for appropriate context and to avoid inat- tentional blindness. c. Availability of prior reports and imaging for comparison when possible. 3. Structured reporting/checklists a. Checklists are a way to build system 2 thinking into your practice, providing prompts to ensure the reader has assessed all parts of the imaging study. Checklists have been shown to reduce error, particularly task- focused checklists. 26 28 4. Double reads/second opinions a. Leverage the visual and cognitive resources of more than one person. b. Independent second reads can reduce false-negatives but may increase false-positives and interobserver vari- ability. One study showed optimal balance between ac- curacy and agreement was four independent readings with a reviewer of composite results. 14 20 22 23 5. Metacognition a. Metacognition is thinking about thinking. b. Being familiar with the types of errors and biases that can occur allows for error reduction (consciously switching from system 1 to system 2 thinking). 16 c. In practice, this could be stopping after interpretation of a set of images, to check that all anatomic regions and parts of the image assessed, the signalment and clinical history considered, and questioning whether the imaging ﬁ ndings ﬁ t with the clinical picture. 6. Follow-up/communication a. There should be open and effective communication with all members of the medical team, and between the medical team and pet owner. 16 b. Clear communication ensures that what was perceived and interpreted is relayed accurately so that treatment steps can re ﬂ ect those diagnoses. c. Communication also allows for feedback and learning from both accurate and inaccurate interpretations. 7. Error assessment a. When errors occur, a root cause analysis should be performed. b. Donald E. Thrall SKULL The skull is anatomically complex, therefore the numerous overlapping soft tissue and bone structures result in many ab- normalities being inconspicuous radiographically. Also, most intracranial lesions are not visible in radiographs. Therefore, skull radiography is rarely done in small animals in specialty practices, having been replaced by computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Skull radiography is more common in small animal general practice and in equine practice but, unfortunately, particularly in dogs and cats, there is a high incidence of technical and positioning errors that negatively affect the diagnostic quality of the study. Positioning: Dog and Cat The anatomic complexity of the skull makes it imperative that radiographic positioning be standardized and repeatable; this removes a source of variation caused by obliquity that can complicate radiographic interpretation. At a minimum, obtain- ing good skull radiographs requires sedation, but general anesthesia is preferable. Making skull radiographs without sedating or anesthesia leads to poor-quality images that cannot be interpreted accurately and is a waste of time, effort, and money. Lateral and dorsoventral (DV) views comprise the minimum radiographic study of the canine and feline skull but these are rarely adequate without additional views. The DV view is preferred over the ventrodorsal (VD) view, because for the DV view slight downward pressure will facilitate more symmetric positioning as the mandibles will provide a ﬂ at, stable surface to support the head ( Fig. 9.1 ). As the dorsal surface of the canine or feline head is rarely ﬂ at, symmetric positioning of a VD view is more dif ﬁ cult. For the lateral view of the skull, the dog or cat cannot be allowed to rest naturally on the x-ray table. The nose will need to be elevated by a positioning sponge in most patients. A sponge may also be needed to elevate the mandibles. The goal is to have left-sided and right-sided structures superimposed perfectly ( Fig. 9.2 ). The positioning devices should be kept free of dirt and debris that can introduce artifacts into the image (see Fig. 9.2 ). The mouth can be closed or held open with a speculum, preferably a nonmetallic speculum so as not to obscure anatomy. If the disease affects the mandible or maxilla, then there is value in having the mouth open to reduce superimposition. Because of the anatomic complexity of the skull, many ancillary projections are available to increase the conspicuity of certain regions. 1 2 Some are listed in Table 9.1 , and a few ex- amples included ( Figs. 9.3 9.9 ). An ancillary view is not used in every patient but should always be considered depending on the purpose of the radiographic examination. The use of an antiscatter grid will improve image quality in larger patients where the thickness of the skull exceeds approximately 10 cm. An external marking system must be used to label oblique radiographs of the skull so that the left side can be distinguished reliably from the right side. Both “ L ” and “ R ” markers are needed to designate which structures are being projected ( Fig. 9.11 ). If only one marker is used, it is not possible to differentiate left-sided from right-sided structures ( Fig. 9.12 ). Positioning: Horse Sedation is not required for equine skull radiography, but it is recommended to facilitate positioning, especially for the DV view, where the dropped position of the head will make it easier to position the x-ray tube dorsally. Skull radiographs of adult horses are typically acquired with the horse standing. For the lateral view, the cassette is positioned against the head of the standing horse and a horizontal x-ray beam directed from the opposite side ( Fig. 9.13A ). The thickness of the equine head leads to radiographic magni ﬁ cation being more pro- nounced than in the dog or cat. Magni ﬁ cation of a lesion on the side of the head closest to the x-ray tube may result in the lesion not being visible because of blurring. Thus, if the laterality of a lesion is known, the plate should be positioned against that side of the head and the x-ray beam directed from the opposite side. If the laterality of the lesion is not known, it is good practice to obtain both left-right and right-left radiographs to make sure that a lesion is not overlooked because of magni ﬁ cation. For the DV view, the plate is ventral to the mandibles and the x-ray beam directed onto the dorsal aspect of the head (see Fig. 9.13B ). It is important to keep the x-ray beam perpendic- ular to the plate. As already noted, sedation is helpful for the DV view because as the horse lowers its head in response to the sedative, dorsal positioning of the x-ray tube is facilitated. Without sedation, one might be able to acquire a DV view of the nasal passage, but a DV view of the calvarium or brain case will usually not be possible. VD views of the skull are not made in the standing horse. Radiation safety becomes paramount when radiographing the equine head. Positioning the plate by placing it in a plate holder with an extension handle is impractical because of the weight of the plate. This commonly results in motion and blurring of the image. In many practices, equine skull radio- graphs are acquired by handholding the plate. If this is done, a lead apron, lead gloves, a lead thyroid shield, and lead- impregnated glasses should be worn. The x-ray beam must also be collimated such that the gloved hands, or any other part of the body, are never in the primary x-ray beam. As in the dog and cat, ancillary oblique views of the equine skull are often needed because of the anatomic complexity. Oblique views are commonly used in the horse to evaluate a nasal passage or a dental arcade ( Fig. 9.14 ). As in the dog and cat, use of properly placed L and R markers is critical to ensure that the structures being projected are identi ﬁ ed accurately ( Fig. 9.15 ). Radiographic Technique The wide exposure latitude of digital imaging systems means that selecting kVp and mAs values for skull radiography is much less critical than when ﬁ lm-screen technology was used. In digital imaging, many more kVp/mAs combinations will result in a diagnostic image than with ﬁ lm. Exposure latitude also results in the ability to evaluate both the thicker and thinner parts of the skull in the same image; for example, proper exposure of a thicker part does not result in overexposure of a thinner part, and vice versa. Despite the exposure latitude of digital systems, an inherent problem associated with equine skull radiography is the ten- dency to overexpose the image ( Fig. 9.16 ). This probably oc- curs because of a concern that the thick bony components require massive exposure factors for proper imaging. Ancillary Factors Although use of an antiscatter grid would be very useful in equine skull radiography, the necessary increase in mAs needed to compensate for the grid may not be possible. Also, a cassette that contains a grid is heavy and dif ﬁ cult to hold steadily by hand, leading to motion and/or grid-line artifacts. A wall- mounted plate holder, discussed subsequently for equine cer- vical radiographs, is one method to incorporate the use of a grid for equine skull radiography without increasing the risk of motion artifact. Interpretation Paradigm The following is a reasonable step-by-step process for inter- preting skull radiographs.  Have adequate radiographic views been obtained accord- ing to the clinical problem being assessed? If not, what additional views would help?  Are there positioning problems that will interfere with interpretation?  Are the images overexposed or underexposed?  Has sedation or anesthesia been used? If not, did this affect the usefulness of the radiographs?  What species or breed characteristics should be considered?  Are external markers adequate to distinguish between left and right sides? After these variables have been considered, the images can be scrutinized for abnormalities. The Roentgen sign and DAMNITV (degenerative, anomalous, metabolic, neoplastic, infectious [in ﬂ ammatory, immune], traumatic, and vascular) methods described in Chapter 6 should be used. In many pa- tients, the cause of the clinical signs will not be found in skull radiographs, or the lesion will be incompletely characterized, and other modalities, such as CT or MRI, will be needed. 3 5 And, even when the lesion is identi ﬁ ed, aspiration or biopsy is commonly necessary to obtain a de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Experienced radiologists may have a random search pattern, but it is recommended that inexperienced interpreters use an organized approach. 6 Having a mental checklist to guide the interpretation of skull radiographs will reduce the number of errors ( Box 9.1 ). SPINE Survey spinal radiographs are acquired commonly in small an- imal practice due to the high incidence of back pain and pelvic limb paresis, and to rule out root signature as a cause of fore- limb lameness. Equine spinal radiographs are obtained less frequently due to the relatively low prevalence of cervical dis- ease and the inability to obtain diagnostic radiographs of the thoracic and lumber spine in adult horses. There are some unique anatomic features of the spine that should be kept in mind. 1  The vertebral formula for the dog and cat is C7 T13 L7 S3 Cd variable.  The vertebral formula for the horse is C7 T18 L6 S5 Cd15- 21.  There is no intervertebral disc between C1 and C2.  C1 has large transverse processes.  C2 has a large spinous process and there is a bony projec- tion from the cranial aspect of the body, the dens.  C6 has proportionally larger transverse processes in the dog and horse that can serve as an anatomic landmark ( Fig. 9.17 ).  Thoracic spinous processes in the horse are longer, on a relative basis, than in the dog or cat.  In the horse, the dorsal aspect of cranial thoracic spinous processes is often highly irregular. This can be confused with an aggressive process or fracture ( Fig. 9.18 ).  In the dog and cat, the thoracic vertebra with a vertically oriented spinous process is called the anticlinal vertebrae ; this can be either T10 or T11 ( Fig. 9.19 ). 7  Cranial to the anticlinal vertebra, the spinous processes angle caudally, whereas caudal to the anticlinal vertebra, the spinous processes angle cranially.  The disc space cranial to the anticlinal vertebra is often narrowed; this should not be confused with intervertebral disc disease.  The ventral cortex of the L3 and/or L4 vertebral bodies in the dog may be indistinct compared with other lumbar vertebrae and this can be confused with effacement from an aggressive process ( Fig. 9.20 ). The initial radiographic examination should also be limited to lateral views in dogs with suspected atlantoaxial instability. If instability at C1 C2 is not con ﬁ rmed in the lateral images, it may be tempting to ﬂ ex the neck and acquire additional views. This should be undertaken with extreme care and performed either under ﬂ uoroscopy or with only minimal ﬂ exion as increasing the malalignment will exacerbate spinal cord compression, especially if a dens is present on C2. Another scenario where lateral views of the spine are often made without additional orthogonal views is in patients being surveyed for discospondylitis. The equine thoracic spine is more dif ﬁ cult to assess radio- graphically than the cervical spine. The thoracic spinous pro- cesses can be imaged satisfactorily, but whether thoracic vertebral bodies can be imaged depends on the size of the horse and which thoracic vertebral bodies are of interest. The cranial thoracic vertebral bodies can often be evaluated, but the caudal thoracic vertebral bodies are more dif ﬁ cult to assess because of superimposed soft tissue. Caudal thoracic spinous processes can usually be imaged adequately ( Fig. 9.28 ). The equine lumbar spine can only be evaluated in very small horses, and usually only in lateral views. The lumbar spine can be assessed in a VD radiograph in small horses, but this requires general anesthesia. Superimposed fecal material will reduce lumbar vertebral detail in VD radiographs, even in small horses. The cranial aspect of the sacrum cannot be assessed in a lateral radiograph, except in very small horses. The sacrocaudal junction can be seen in most horses in a lateral view. The sacrum can be assessed more thoroughly in a VD radiograph, but this requires general anesthesia. As with the lumbar spine, overlying fecal material will reduce sacral detail in VD radiographs. Incidental Factors The most important incidental factors associated with spinal radiography in the dog and cat are breed variation and some congenital anomalies. Congenital transitional vertebral anoma- lies are common and occur at the cervicothoracic, thor- acolumbar, and lumbosacral junctions. In this anomaly, a vertebra at the junction has anatomic characteristics of each adjoining region. The most common cervicothoracic transi- tional anomaly is the presence of vestigial ribs on C7 ( Fig. 9.30 ). Cervical ribs are not clinically signi ﬁ cant in dogs or cats, but in human beings they are sometimes associated with Horner s syndrome. The most common thoracolumbar transitional anomaly in- volves asymmetric development of the 13th ribs. There are multiple variations to this anomaly, 1 but the most clinically signi ﬁ cant is having a unilateral rib on T13. This anomaly is not signi ﬁ cant itself, but can lead to spinal surgery being performed at the wrong location if rib morphology is used to locate the surgical site ( Fig. 9.31 ). Sacralization of L7 is the most common transitional anomaly at the lumbosacral junction. In this anomaly, one side of L7 has the form of a vertebra with a transverse process while the opposite side has the form of a sacrum and articulates with the ilium ( Fig. 9.32 ). The altered biomechanical loading associated with a lumbosacral transitional anomaly predisposes dogs to lumbosacral disk herniation and nerve root compression. 8 9 Interpretation Paradigm As mentioned, there are relatively few things other than breed variation and congenital anomalies that in ﬂ uence the radio- graphic appearance of the spine. But because of the complex morphology of the spine, an organized approach is still needed. Assessing whether there is an abnormality in the spinal radio- graphs of a patient should be the last step in the interpretive process. The following questions should always be considered ﬁ rst:  Is radiographic technique adequate?  Are all needed views present?  Is there a need for additional views?  Has the study been tailored to the results of neuroana- tomic localization?  Is the positioning adequate, or are there positioning prob- lems that will interfere with interpretation? Lenin Arturo Villamizar Martinez D iagnostic imaging of the maxillofacial and dentoal- veolar structures is critical for pre-, intra-, and post- operative assessment of intraoral and extraoral conditions in dogs and cats. 1 2 Several imaging techniques are available for the veterinary practitioner, from conventional intra- or extraoral radiography to more sophisticated tomo- graphic methods such as computed tomography (CT), mag- netic resonance imaging (MRI), and more recently, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) ( Fig. 10.1 ). 3 6 This chapter is an introduction to the anatomy of dentoalveolar structures and changes associated with the most common dental abnormal- ities. It is beyond the scope of this chapter to describe dental radiographic techniques. Dental radiographs can be performed using an x-ray ma- chine that is mounted to the wall, on a set of wheels or held by hand ( Fig. 10.2 ). 7 8 X-ray dental machines operate at lower mAs values than the other types of dental x-ray equipment (high- frequency x-ray, CT, or CBCT units). However, to comply with the ALARA (as low as reasonably achievable) principle, the operator must leave the room if possible, or be at least 6 feet away from the x-ray source during the dental examination. 9 10 On the other hand, when a handheld x-ray unit is in use, the operator should wear a lead apron and thyroid collar to avoid unnecessary radiation exposure. 11 Dental images were originally acquired with analog dental radiographic ﬁ lm that is available in several sizes for obtaining periapical and occlusal views. Periapical radiographs (sizes 0, 1, and 2) allow evaluation of the entire dental structure and the surrounding bone. In contrast, the occlusal ﬁ lm (size 4) cap- tures intraoral radiographic images of more extensive regions of the maxilla and mandible ( Table 10.1 ). 12 13 Occlusal ﬁ lms may also be used to obtain extraoral views of the more caudal portion of the mandibles and the temporomandibular joints in cats and small dogs. 14 16 Analog dental ﬁ lms have been largely replaced by direct and indirect digital radiographic systems (see Chapter 2 ),which improves patient and operator radiation safety since they require shorter exposure times (about 0.1 0.2 seconds) than analog ﬁ lm (0.8 seconds). 7 17 In the direct system, the solid-state intraoral sensor, mainly available in similar sizes to the analog dental counterpart ﬁ lm sizes 0 and 2, captures the attenuated x-rays after passing through oral tissue. The attenuated photons recorded by the sensor are converted into an electrical signal that is transformed later into a digital signal with a digital-analog converter and transmitted to a computer to form an almost instantaneous radiographic image ( Fig. 10.3 ). One disadvantage of this type of sensor is that it can be easily damaged by a bite if the patient is not under deep sedation or general anesthesia. 17 18 Indirect systems use reusable photostimulable plates (PSPs) available in sizes 0, 2, 3, and occlusal size 4 to store the latent images formed by the attenuated x-ray beam after passing through the oral tissues. The PSPs must be processed in a dental scanner, where the laser converts the latent image into a digital signal ( Fig. 10.4 ). 7 One of the main disadvantages of PSP is that they can be scratched or bent by teeth, causing artifacts. Therefore, they must be replaced after a certain number of exposures (approximately up to 200 exposures, depending on the manufacturer) to maintain optimal image quality. 18 19 The radiographic dental examination complements a thor- ough oral cavity examination and is considered the pillar for assessing the dentoalveolar components and the surrounding maxillary and mandibular bone. 2 20 Dental radiography is preferred over conventional skull radiographs due to the ability to project speci ﬁ c anatomic regions of the dental arcades without excessive overlap between maxillary and mandibular structures. Dental radiography is mainly accomplished intra- orally, but the extraoral dental technique may be required when other anatomical structures appear superimposed with the dentoalveolar region ( Fig. 10.5 ). Intraoral dental radiographs are acquired through bisecting and paralleling techniques. The intra- and extraoral structures in dogs and cats may be affected by in ﬂ ammatory, neoplastic, traumatic, developmental, metabolic, congenital, or hereditary disorders. The anatomic complexity of the skull poses a challenge during radiographic interpretation when two-dimensional images of three- dimensional structures are evaluated. 26 27 Knowledge of the dentoalveolar anatomy is critical for understanding alterations of the normal radiographic appearance. The maxillofacial structures, including the dentoalveolar complex, consist of soft and hard tissues. Depending on the structural chemical composition, each tissue type has a different capacity to attenuate the x-ray beam during a radio- graphic exam. In this way, highly mineralized structures, such as the enamel, dentin, and alveolar bone, are the most radi- opaque areas in the radiograph. At the same time, regions like the pulp cavity, the periodontal ligament space, the gums, and the nasal cavities are less radiopaque ( Fig. 10.10 ). 26 28 The radiographic assessment of patients undergoing pro- fessional dental cleaning includes full-mouth intraoral dental radiographs ( Fig. 10.11 ). However, intraoral views of a speci ﬁ c area may be required if the primary concern and the reason for the consultation are a speci ﬁ c dental structure or region of the oral cavity (e.g., dental fracture). Orthogonal views may be necessary when the dental and maxillofacial structures are superimposed, which can make it challenging to identify a radiographic alteration. 26 27 Radiographic interpretation of dental radiographs should be systematic. The anatomical structures may be approached from the most general to the most speci ﬁ c to ensure that all relevant information is evaluated. Thus, a general view of the radio- pacity and integrity of the maxillary or mandibular bone that supports the teeth, areas of bone lysis or proliferation, and bone morphologic alterations that may be associated with current or past pathologic events should be recorded. 7 The initial general evaluation can be followed by a more speci ﬁ c assessment of the periodontal structures. This assess- ment may include 7 12 :  Identi ﬁ cation of alveolar bone loss at the alveolar margin, the periapical and furcation regions  Widening or absence of the periodontal ligament space  Loss of the lamina dura, which is the radiographic term for the cribriform plate of the alveolar socket  Radiopaque or radiolucent areas next to the dental roots The dental element and its endodontic system can ﬁ nally be evaluated. Tooth assessment includes 7 29 31 :  Identi ﬁ cation of morphological alterations of the crown and root, unerupted teeth, external tooth resorption, and excessive or missing number of teeth.  Evaluation of the endodontic system includes comparing the pulp cavity size between permanent teeth in the same patient (e.g., maxillary left vs. right canine), internal tooth resorption, increased radiopacity of the pulp cavity, and periapical lesions associated with tooth fractures or tooth discoloration. These structures are the alveolar bone, the periodontal ligament, the gums, and the cementum. Identifying the radiographic changes in the periodontium associated with periodontal disease is extremely valuable for determining the treatment plan and prognosis. At the initial stage of the disease, the gingival tissue appears edematous due to the presence of bacterial plaque at the gingival sulcus. 34 At this moment, radiographic alterations on the periodontium are not present, as the in ﬂ ammatory process is limited to soft tissue. If dental plaque is not removed, the subsequent in ﬂ amma- tory reaction can cause, depending on the stage of the disease, mild, moderate, or advanced alveolar bone loss with destruc- tion of the lamina dura and the periodontal ligament. The pulp has sensory and nourishment functions that keep the tooth alive, allowing the odontoblasts located at the most outer region of the pulp tissue to build up dentin during the normal development of the tooth. The pulp, and hence the viability of the odontoblast, is supported by arterioles that enter the pulp cavity through the apical delta ( Fig. 10.15 ). 22 The intraoral radiographic approach of the endodontic system in- cludes assessing the size and shape of the pulp cavity and radiographic appearance of the periapical region. Dental radi- ography allows visibility of the pulp cavity as a narrow radio- lucent band in the center of the tooth. In young animals, the pulp cavity is still wide; as the animal ages, this space narrows due to dentin deposition. Asymmetry of the pulp cavity be- tween adjacent or contralateral teeth may indicate pulp ne- crosis and lack of dentin deposition by odontoblasts ( Fig. 10.16 ). 30 42 Dentoalveolar injuries such as tooth concussion, subluxa- tion, luxation, or alveolar fracture along the apical portion of the root may also lead to tooth devitalization due to severe pulpitis or disruption of blood supply. Tooth discoloration is the most frequent clinical ﬁ nding (87% 92%) in teeth suffering from pulp necrosis. 30 42 Periapical in ﬂ ammatory lesions associated with endodontic disease may be acute or chronic depending on the host auto- immune response and virulence of the bacteria in the necrotic pulp. During the early stage of the in ﬂ ammatory lesion, the micro ﬂ ora from the affected pulp triggers an in ﬂ ammatory response at the apical periodontal ligament and surrounding alveolar bone, known as acute apical periodontitis. Depending on the autoimmune response, pus may form at this stage of the in ﬂ ammatory process, leading to an apical abscess. 43 44 Acute apical periodontitis is histologically characterized by the presence of lymphocytes and neutrophils, along with vascular congestion, hyperemia, and edema of the periodontal ligament. Since it is possible that destruction of the mineralized tissues (dentin, cementum, and bone) has not occurred during acute apical periodontitis, the radiographic changes can be limited to widening of the periodontal ligament space only, and radiographic identi ﬁ cation can be challenging or underestimated. 44 46 If the initial in ﬂ ammatory injury is not resolved, a more chronic in ﬂ ammatory response occurs with the formation of a periapical granuloma. Radiographically, a periapical granuloma is characterized by ill or well-de ﬁ ned circumscribed radiolucent or radiopaque areas around the tooth apex. During this stage of the in ﬂ ammatory process, in an attempt to heal, the periapical region is in ﬁ ltrated by granulation tissue and in ﬂ ammatory cells such as plasma cells, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. 46 47 The effect of in ﬂ ammatory byproducts of a nonvital tooth on the epithelial cells of Malassez located in the periodontal liga- ment may result in a radicular or periapical cyst formation. 47 Radiographically, a radicular cyst generally corresponds to a single round radiolucent cavitary lesion with a well-de ﬁ ned cortical wall. During the early stage of the periapical cyst, it is challenging to differentiate it from the periapical abscess or granuloma due to its similar osteolytic appearance on dental radiography. 47 Although the radiographic examination may aid in localizing apical periodontitis, histopathology remains the method of choice to identify the type of in ﬂ ammatory lesion. Histologically, a periapical cyst is associated with an epithelium- lined cavity with an in ﬂ amed ﬁ brovascular connective tissue wall. 48 49 Fig. 10.17 depicts the radiographic features of some in ﬂ ammatory periapical lesions in different patients. Dental radiography can help identify the origin of the end- odontic pathologic condition. In an endo-perio lesion, the endodontic injury from dental trauma leads to the destruction of the periapical periodontal structures. In contrast, in a perio- endo lesion, the endodontic disease results from the invasion of the tooth apex by periodontal micro ﬂ ora from deep peri- odontal pockets in patients suffering from severe periodontitis ( Fig. 10.18 ). 50 51 The chevron sign, a nonpathologic radiolucent area that resembles periapical in ﬂ ammatory lesions, can be observed in * * Fig. 10.14 In traoral radiographs of the right mandi bular molar teethshowing the region s of the pulp cavity: pulp chamber ( asterisk ), root canal( arrows ). Among the most common clinical ﬁ ndings observed during the physical examination in patients suffering from tooth resorption are gingivitis, periodontitis, fracture or loss of dental structure, and, particularly in cats, the presence of granulation tissue at the resorptive lesion location at the cervical region of the tooth. 57 58 Although the physical examination, which in- cludes deep probing of the gingival sulcus and exploring the dental hard tissue under general anesthesia, is mandatory for the initial approach of patients suspected of tooth resorption, intraoral dental radiography is critical to establish the extension of the lesion. 57 Tooth resorption may be asymptomatic, and clinical mani- festations may depend upon the extension and localization of the lesion. Dental destruction associated with tooth resorption can be observed radiographically as a radiolucent region affecting the enamel, cementum, or dentin. However, its radiographic identi ﬁ cation depends on the level of destruction of the dental substance. In an early stage of the disease, an incipient resorptive lesion may be radiographically occult. For example, in human beings, more than 30% of enamel demin- eralization is necessary before it can be detected using con- ventional dental radiography. 59 According to the AVDC, tooth resorption is classi ﬁ ed as stage 1 to 5, depending on the anatomical location and severity of the lesion ( Figs. 10.21 and 10.22 ) and as type 1 to 3 ac- cording to its radiographic appearance ( Fig. 10.23 ). 25 In 2010, the radiographic patterns and types of tooth resorption in dogs were assessed retrospectively, using a classi ﬁ cation previously suggested in human beings. The initial evaluation and follow-up of a patient suffering from dentoalveolar trauma must include intraoral dental radiography. Dental radiography aids in determining the extent of the anatomical damage and the presence of other disorders that may be associated with the current pathology, for example, in a mandibular fracture as a consequence of severe periodontitis or a neoplastic process ( Fig. 10.28 ). 65 Due to the bidimensional nature of intraoral radiography, more than one radiographic view may be necessary to identify a dentoalveolar fracture. Identifying the type of neoplasia utilizing incisional or exci- sional biopsy and cancer staging through diagnostic imaging is important for establishing the possible treatment and prognosis. The most common malignant tumor in the dog is malignant melanoma, with an incidence ranging between 27% and 45%, followed by squamous cell carcinoma and ﬁ brosarcoma. In the cat, the most common malignant neoplasm is squamous cell carcinoma, followed by ﬁ brosarcoma. 68 74 75 Although CT and MRI are the gold-standard diagnostic im- aging techniques for assessing maxillofacial neoplastic condi- tions and cancer staging, veterinary practitioners still widely use intraoral radiography during the initial approach. 76 77 Intraoral radiography may help differentiate between benign and malignant conditions; however, this assumption may be problematic since both tumors may share similar radiographic features. Benign odontogenic tumors are typically slow-growing dis- orders characterized by ( Fig. 10.29 eFigs. 10.12 10.15 ) 78 :  Well-de ﬁ ned smooth borders  Mild periosteal reaction with cortical bone reaction  Homogeneous radiopaque, radiolucent, or mixed intratu- moral composition  Possible mass effect with the displacement of adjacent anatomical structures, including the teeth Odontogenic tumors such as the CAA have also been char- acterized as being locally aggressive, presenting lytic and pro- liferative multilocular radiographic patterns. 79 In contrast, malignant intraoral neoplasms are radiographi- cally characterized by ( Fig. 10.30 ) 80 81  Ill-de ﬁ ned borders  Exuberant proliferative, lytic, or mixed appearance  Geographic, moth-eaten, or permeative radiolucent areas resulting from bone destruction  Destruction of the periodontal structures can lead to tooth loss In addition to diagnostic imaging for evaluation of tumor extension and possible metastasis, incisional biopsy is needed for diagnosing neoplasia since radiographic patterns resembling a neoplastic process may be present in nonneoplastic disorders such as osteonecrosis and osteomyelitis ( Fig. 10.31 eFig. 10.16 ). In cats, about 45% of mandibular lesions resem- bling an aggressive neoplastic condition were con ﬁ rmed as osteomyelitis associated with periodontitis or endodontic disease. DEVELO PMEN TAL ABNORMA LITIES OF THE TE ETH Disturbances associated with the number of teeth and roots, the shape of the crown and the root, and malformation of the dental components such as enamel and dentin can have a po- tential hereditary or congenital origin. Diagnostic imaging of these dental disorders is paramount to determine if surgical intervention is required or, in contrast, monitoring is adequate ( Fig. 10.32 ). Malocclusion, supernumerary teeth, nonerupted or devel- opmental absence of teeth, and persistent deciduous dentition may have a hereditary origin due to their prevalence in speci ﬁ c breeds of dogs. For example, Yorkshire terriers and Maltese are commonly affected by persistent deciduous dentition, leading to dental malocclusion and severe periodontitis in puppies or young adult dogs. 82 Other dental abnormalities over- represented in small-breed dogs are root dilaceration and mal- formation of the mandibular ﬁ rst molar or dens invaginatus. If underestimated or not identi ﬁ ed in dental radiography during the ﬁ rst years of the patient s life, an abnormality such as dens invaginatus can result in severe endodontic and periodontic pathoses ( Fig. 10.33 ). 83 T he ab se nc e of te et h du ri ng ph ys i ca l ex am in at i on in do gs an d ca ts sh ou ld b e el uc i da t ed us i ng de nt al ra di og ra ph y. Lisa J. Forrest NORM AL ANA TOMY General Skull The skull encompasses the brain and houses the sense organs for hearing, equilibrium, sight, smell, and taste. Along with the skull, facial bones provide attachment sites for teeth, tongue, larynx, and muscles. 1 There is pronounced variation in the shape of the skull in the dog. Three terms are used to designate the different shapes. Dolichocephalic breeds, such as collie and Russian wolfhound, have long, narrow heads with an extensive nasal cavity from rostral to caudal. Mesaticephalic breeds, such as German Shepherd and beagle, have heads of medium pro- portion ( Fig. 11.1 ). Brachycephalic breeds, such as Boston terrier and Pekingese, have short, wide heads. Cats are more uniform in their skull conformation. However, Siamese tend to have increased facial length as compared with Himalayan and Persian breeds. Calvaria and Associated Structures The calvaria comprises the bones of the brain case, with the occipital bone forming the base of the skull. The occipital crest is the most dorsocaudal aspect of the skull (see Fig. 11.1 ), and the occipital condyles are caudoventral as seen on lateral ra- diographs. The foramen magnum, centered between the oc- cipital condyles, forms an ori ﬁ ce for passage of the spinal cord. Nasal Passages and Paranasal Sinuses The nasal passage extends caudally from the external nares to the cribriform plate and nasopharynx. The cribriform plate is a sieve-like partition between the olfactory bulb and nasal pas- sage. The nasal passage is divided in half by the nasal septum and is ﬁ lled with thinly scrolled conchae ( Fig. 11.2 ). Caudally, the nasal septum is osseous and fuses with the cribriform plate; it becomes cartilaginous as it extends rostrally. 1 The vomer bone is unpaired and forms the caudoventral bony part of the nasal septum. The cartilaginous nasal septum cannot be seen in radiographs, although it can be distinguished in computed to- mography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) images. Both dogs and cats have frontal sinuses (see Fig. 11.1 ), lateral maxillary recesses, and small sphenoidal sinuses. These are named for the bones in which they are located. Tympanic Bullae and Temporomandibular Joint The tympanic bullae (see Fig. 11.1 ) form the ventral part of the temporal bone. These air- ﬁ lled cavities of the middle ear communicate with the nasopharynx via the auditory tube. The temporal bone consists of the petrosal, tympanic, and squa- mous sections that are fused in the adult. The petrosal portion is medial and dorsal to the tympanic bulla and is composed of dense bone in the mature animal. The squamous portion of the temporal bone extends rostral and lateral to form the zygomatic arch. The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is a condylar joint. The temporal portion consists of the zygomatic process of the squamous temporal bone, which forms the mandibular fossa and the retroarticular process. The retroarticular process is the ventral extension of the squamous temporal bone. The mandibular aspect of the joint includes the condyloid process, which articulates with the mandibular fossa. Cross-Sectional Imaging The cross-sectional imaging techniques of CT and MR imaging are being used more commonly for imaging the head. CT and MR technology provides images without superimposition of structures and better soft tissue delineation compared with radiography ( Fig. 11.4 ). 7 There are several sources describing the normal CT and MR image anatomy of the dog and cat head. 4 6 14 CONG ENITAL ANOM ALIES Hydrocephalus Hydrocephalus is excessive accumulation of cerebrospinal ﬂ uid (CSF) within the ventricular system of the brain. Congenital hydrocephalus occurs secondary to an interruption of CSF ﬂ ow or defective absorption of CSF. 14 16 Canine breeds affected with congenital hydrocephalus include the Maltese, Yorkshire terrier, English bulldog, Chihuahua, Lhasa Apso, Chinese pug, toy poodle, Pomeranian, Pekingese, Cairn terrier, and Boston terrier. 14 15 Hydrocephalus is less common in cats. 14 16 Radiographic signs associated with hydrocephalus include ( Fig. 11.5 ):  Doming of the calvaria and cortical thinning  Persistent fontanelles  Homogeneous appearance to the brain, resulting from the loss of normal convolutional skull markings Radiographs are insensitive for detection and characteriza- tion of hydrocephalus, and that information is now acquired using CT or MRI. 15 17 With persistent fontanelles, ultrasound can also be used to assess ventricular size, 17 19 and normal ventricular appearance and size have been quanti ﬁ ed in the dog. 17 19 20 The advantage of CT and MRI for evaluating ven- tricular size is the ability to assess the entire brain for causes of hydrocephalus ( Fig. 11.6 ) (see Chapter 12 ). Occipital Dysplasia Occipital dysplasia (also called keyhole malformation) is the dorsal enlargement of the foramen magnum, secondary to a developmental defect in the occipital bone. 17 The bone defect, which is better assessed using CT than radiography ( Fig. 11.7 ), may be covered by rigid connective tissue to prevent brain prolapse. Occipital dysplasia has been related to clinical neurologic disease and is usually found in miniature and toy breeds. 18 20 21 There is considerable variation in shape of the foramen magnum and occipital dysplasia may be a normal morphologic variation in brachycephalic dogs without clinical signs. 18 22 Occipital Bone Malformation and Syringomyelia (Chiari-Like Malformation) Occipital bone malformation may result in overcrowding of the caudal fossa, leading to obstruction of CSF ﬂ ow, hydrocephalus, and secondary syringomyelia. This hereditary defect, termed caudal occipital malformation syndrome (COMS) or Chiari- like malformation , is common in the Cavalier King Charles spaniel, 22 25 but is also found in other brachycephalic breeds. 26 De ﬁ nitive diagnosis is made with MRI, 23 whereby the crowding of the cerebellum in the caudal fossa can be detected.
