A positive correlation has been found between foramen magnum size and length of cerebellar herniation. 20 22 Temporomandibular Joint Dysplasia Open-mouth jaw locking can be caused by TMJ dysplasia. This congenital condition is uncommon; it is reported most frequently in the Basset Hound but has also been seen in Irish Setters. 27 The open-mouth jaw locking occurs after hyperex- tension of the jaw, excessive lateral movement of the condyloid process, and subsequent entrapment lateral to the zygomatic arch. Physical entrapment usually occurs on the side opposite from the joint with the most severe dysplastic changes. Yawning often precipitates jaw locking when it results in extreme opening of the mouth. 27 In spaniels, Pekingese, and dachshunds, TMJ dysplasia is an asymptomatic anatomic anomaly. 4 28 Open-mouth jaw locking also occurs in cats, 27 29 30 and CT is routinely used to diagnose TMJ dysplasia, with three- dimensional (3D) reconstructions aiding in surgical planning. 31 Mucopolysaccharidosis Mucopolysaccharidoses are a group of hereditary disorders of lysosomal storage, which occur in humans, dogs, cattle, and cats. Mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS-VI) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease recognized in Siamese cats. 32 34 Radiographic skeletal changes in cats with MPS-VI include epiphyseal dysplasia, generalized osteopenia, pectus excavatum, and vertebral and skull changes. 35 Speci ﬁ c skull changes seen on radiographs include shortened nasal conchae, aplasia and hypoplasia of the frontal and sphenoid sinuses, and shortened dimensions to the incisive and maxillary bones. 35 Another form of MPS, MPS-I, has been documented in the do- mestic short-haired cat, 34 with radiographic skeletal changes that are similar to those in MPS-VI; however, the facial dys- morphia may not be as pronounced as it is in the Siamese. 33 Several different types of MPS have been reported in various dog breeds. MPS in animals has clinical and pathologic mani- festations similar to people and therefore represents an excel- lent model for studying approaches to therapy and care. 32 34 36 METAB OLIC ANOM ALIES Primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism can result in overall decreased bone opacity, sometimes visible on skull radio- graphs. A parathyroid adenoma or carcinoma, or adenomatous hyperplasia of one or both parathyroid glands, causes primary hyperparathyroidism. This results in excessive synthesis and secretion of parathyroid hormone, which leads to hypercalce- mia and subsequent bone resorption. 37 39 Secondary hyper- parathyroidism, which includes renal and nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism, is subsequent to nonendocrine alter- ations in calcium and phosphorus homeostasis and lead to increased levels of parathyroid hormone and ultimate bone resorption. 40 41 An early radiographic sign of hyperparathyroidism (primary and secondary) is loss of the lamina dura ( Fig. 11.8 ). This is followed by overall demineralization of the skull bones as the disease progresses ( Fig. 11.9 eFig. 11.1 ). In fact, it is uncom- mon to see loss of the lamina dura without some concurrent generalized skeletal demineralization. The level of cortical thinning and degree of overall osteolysis and osteomalacia depend on duration and severity of the hyperparathyroidism. Also, because young animals have rapid skeletal turnover, they are affected more severely than older animals. In extreme hy- perparathyroidism, demineralization is followed by ﬁ brous tis- sue hyperplasia, termed ﬁ brous osteodystrophy . This uncommon development leads to skull thickening, and partic- ularly by maxillary enlargement, caused by ﬁ brous tissue proliferation. External beam radiotherapy is the current treatment of choice, 54 60 with most centers using advanced radiotherapy techniques, such as intensity-modulated radiation therapy, im- age guidance, and stereotactic radiation therapy. 55 57 58 61 64 With these advanced techniques, tumor dose delivery is improved, and critical adjacent tissues are avoided resulting in reduced treatment side effects. 61 62 The most useful radiographic views for evaluating nasal disease include the intraoral dorsoventral and/or the open- mouth ventrodorsal view for detailed evaluation of the nasal cavity without superimposition of the mandible ( Fig. 11.10 eFig. 11.2 ). The open-mouth ventrodorsal view is better for cribriform plate assessment, because a radiographic ﬁ lm cassette or digital plate cannot be inserted caudal enough to include the cribriform plate in the intraoral view. The cribri- form plate is represented by a V-shaped to C-shaped bony opacity on radiographs, varying according to skull shape (doli- chocephalic vs. mesaticephalic and brachycephalic). 65 Evalua- tion of the cribriform plate is important because nasal tumors often originate from the ethmoid conchae and cribriform plate, and bone lysis detected on radiographs indicates tumor exten- sion into the cranial cavity (see Fig. 11.10A ). The rostrocaudal frontal sinus projection is necessary for evaluation of individual frontal sinuses ( Fig. 11.11 ) and is useful especially if CT or MRI is not available. 66 General anesthesia is an absolute requirement for achieving accurate radiographic positioning, and it facilitates evaluation and comparison of the complex nasal passages. Techniques for obtaining radiographic views of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses can be found elsewhere, 68 and they were discussed brie ﬂ y in Chapter 9 . Positron emission tomography combined with CT (PET/CT) has been investigated in dogs with spontaneously occurring nasal tumors using 18 F-FDG (2-deoxy-2-[18F] ﬂ uoro-D- glucose), 18 F-FLT (3 0 -deoxy-3 0 ﬂ uorothymidine), and 61 Cu-ATSM (diacetyl-bis [ N 4 -methylthiosemicarbazone]). 69 78 In initial studies in 20 dogs, the relationships of glucose metabolism (FDG), cell proliferation (FLT), and cell hypoxia (Cu-ATSM) were generally heterogeneous across both nasal carcinomas and sarcomas. 78 FDG, FLT, and Cu-ATSM imaging were also evaluated with regard to predicting the locations of residual FDG PET uptake in tumors following radiotherapy. Mandibular and Maxillary Tumors Tumors of the oral cavity account for approximately 6% to 7% of all canine cancers and 3% of feline cancers. 79 80 Squamous cell carcinoma commonly affects the mandible or maxilla in the dog and cat. 79 Fibrosarcoma 81 and malignant melanoma 79 82 are common in the dog but occur rarely in cats. 82 In the dog, the rostral mandible is a common site for oral squamous cell car- cinoma. This tumor has variable bone lysis, and regional or distant metastasis is rare. 79 Oral ﬁ brosarcoma in dogs can affect the maxilla or mandible with a predilection for the palate. 79 In dogs, 82% of squamous cell carcinomas and 78% of ﬁ brosar- comas were characterized radiographically by bone involve- ment. 79 81 Often, oral ﬁ brosarcoma appears benign histologically, but biologic activity is aggressive. These tumors, often found in the maxilla and mandible of large-breed dogs and commonly in Golden Retrievers, are histologically low-grade yet biologically high-grade aggressive tumors and bone lysis is a common feature. 67 Dogs with oral ﬁ brosarcoma have a lower median survival as compared with those with soft-tissue sar- comas at other sites 83 ( Fig. 11.15 ). In contrast, malignant mel- anoma occurs in large- and small-breed dogs, commonly metastasizes to regional lymph nodes and lungs, and has vari- able bone lysis. 82 84 Squamous cell carcinoma in cats affects the mandible or maxilla, causing sclerotic and/or lytic changes to bone 85 ( Fig. 11.16 eFig. 11.4 ). The sino-orbital form is an invasive mycosis and caused by Asper- gillus felis , whereas the sino-nasal form can be invasive or noninvasive and commonly caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and Aspergillus riger 121 122 Cryptococcus neoformans , a fungal infection more commonly seen in cats, can infect the nasal passages, but generally causes a nondestructive hyper- plastic rhinitis ( Fig. 11.21 ). 121 Sinonasal fungal disease reported in cats include aspergillosis, cryptococcosis, and hyalohypho- mycosis, and clinical signs, age, and CT features can overlap with those found with sinonasal neoplasia. 118 121 Destructive rhinitis secondary to fungal disease can be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate radiographically from neoplasia. Both diseases cause loss of conchal detail, but a nasal cavity mass effect and invasion of bones surrounding the nasal cavity are more common features of nasal cavity neoplasia. 65 69 120 CT and MRI have been used for evaluating nasal aspergillosis, with cross-sectional imaging modalities superior to radiography due to greater contrast resolution and their tomographic nature ( Fig. 11.22 ). However, diagnosis of fungal disease requires direct visualization of fungal plaques by endoscopy or fungal elements found by cytology or histopathology. 116 119 Rhinitis Rhinitis secondary to bacterial infection, or corticosteroid- responsive rhinitis with lymphoplasmacytic in ﬁ ltrates, can have a variable radiographic appearance in dogs and cats. Depending on chronicity and severity of rhinitis, destruction of conchae and evidence of bone erosion can occur but it is usually mild and focal. 125 127 Chronic rhinitis and sinusitis in cats are common sequelae to viral upper respiratory tract dis- ease ( Fig. 11.23 ). 126 Radiographic changes are usually bilateral and can range from none in mild infections to an increased opacity of the nasal cavity and frontal sinuses with conchae and vomer bone destruction in severe infections. Nasal Foreign Bodies Intranasal foreign bodies occur in dogs and cats, 128 131 and foreign plant matter is common in certain environments, for example, grass awns in California. Affected dogs have an acute onset of sneezing and pawing at the nose, and they often have unilateral nasal discharge that may be purulent and malodorous. 128 131 Radiographic ﬁ ndings include:  Focal increase in soft-tissue opacity  Focal bone lysis if chronic  Radiopaque foreign bodies may be visible CT is more sensitive for identi ﬁ cation of foreign bodies than radiography as the ﬁ ndings can be very subtle and focal, but not all foreign objects will be hyperattenuating in CT images. Otitis Radiographs are an integral part of the diagnostic workup of a dog or cat presenting with ear disease for evaluation of otitis media. Diagnosis of otitis interna is based on clinical signs and requires CT or MRI for identi ﬁ cation. However, in ventrodorsal radiographs, external ear canal stenosis and/or mineralization can often be identi ﬁ ed. Otitis media is often secondary to chronic otitis externa. Radiographic ﬁ ndings of otitis media include:  Increased opacity of the tympanic cavity  Thickening of the osseous bulla  In advanced disease, exuberant bone proliferation may involve the petrous temporal bone or the TMJ The tympanic bullae are best evaluated in lateral oblique and open-mouth radiographic projections ( Fig. 11.24 ). Otitis media can be unilateral; when this occurs, the diagnosis is simpli ﬁ ed by a comparison between the two tympanic bullae (see Fig. 11.24 ). Positioning is crucial when radiography is per- formed for evaluation of the tympanic bullae; general anes- thesia facilitates proper positioning and allows personnel to vacate the room during radiographic exposure. A review of imaging techniques and anatomy for middle ear disease can be found elsewhere. 132 134 CT is a more sensitive test for evaluation of otitis media, 132 134 but proper technique is necessary to avoid arti- factual wall thickening of the bulla on CT images ( Fig. 11.25 ). CT images need to be viewed in a bone and soft-tissue window for complete evaluation (see Chapter 4 ). 133 Middle ear changes are commonly identi ﬁ ed in MR and CT images of dogs with neurologic disease or with subclinical otitis media, and there was no correlation with the signal intensity of material within the middle ear and ﬁ nal diagnosis. 135 136 Evidence of material within the middle ear in MR images of dogs without clinical signs of otitis media was thought to represent subclinical otitis media or ﬂ uid accumulation without in ﬂ ammation, 135 137 whereas in cats, it is thought that obstruction of the auditory tube by sinonasal disease results in effusive tympanic bulla disease seen on CT images. 138 Often, clinical and subclinical ear disease will be identi ﬁ ed in cats undergoing CT imaging of the skull. In 310 cats undergoing CT imaging of the skull, 103 had middle ear disease and 34% of these had no clinical evidence of ear disease and most had concurrent nasal disease, 136 consis- tent with bullous effusion. Middle ear changes in CT in this evaluation were not speci ﬁ c for clinical or subclinical middle ear disease. Although not common, Aspergillus otitis has been reported in dogs and cats and is typically unilateral. 139 Primary secretory otitis media (PSOM) has been described in Cavalier King Charles spaniels. 140 Clinical signs include pain localized to the head and neck and neurologic signs, which are similar to in ﬂ ammatory central nervous system (CNS) and cer- vical disc disease, making it dif ﬁ cult to separate this disease from the common neurologic diseases seen in this breed. 140 Abnormalities of the external ear canal and bulging of the tympanic membrane may not be seen clinically, and CT or MRI is necessary for diagnosis. Treatment involves myringotomy and ﬂ ushing of mucus and mucus plugs, which may need to be repeated. The cause of PSOM is thought to be from the middle ear or auditory tube and may relate to either increased pro- duction or decreased drainage of middle ear secretions. 140 An association of trigeminal nerve disease with bulla effusion has been recognized in dogs. 141 142 The trigeminal nerve innervates the muscle that controls opening of the pharyngeal ori ﬁ ce to the auditory tube. The increasing use of CT and MR skull im- aging has resulted in documentation of other incidental or subclinical middle ear changes, such as otoliths and hyperos- totic tympanic bone spicules in dogs and cats. 143 144 Feline nasopharyngeal polyps are nonneoplastic growths originating from the mucous membrane of the auditory tube or middle ear. 145 146 Nasopharyngeal polyps generally occur in younger cats and can extend into the external ear canal, the osseous bulla, or the nasopharynx. Although rare, cats can have multiple polyps. 147 Cats may have signs of middle ear disease, rhinitis, or upper airway disease secondary to the space- occupying polyp. Signs of otitis media (increased soft-tissue opacity of the affected bulla) or nasopharyngeal obstruction ( Fig. 11.26 ) may be noted on radiographs. Masticatory Muscle Myositis Masticatory muscle myositis is an immune-mediated in ﬂ amma- tory disease where antibodies are formed against type 2M muscle ﬁ bers that are present in the temporalis, masseter, and pterygoid muscles. Dogs with this condition often present with a history of lethargy, fever, regional lymphadenopathy, reluc- tance to eat, and swelling and/or atrophy of the masticatory muscles. The diagnosis is made by detection of antibodies against type 2M ﬁ bers in the serum or with histopathology. Cross-sectional imaging can be useful in identifying typical changes and guiding further diagnostics. Typical ﬁ ndings include change in size of the masticatory muscles, and hetero- geneous appearance of the musculature with multifocal strong contrast enhancement ( Fig. 11.31 ). The digastric muscle is not affected by the changes. Regional lymphadenopathy is usually present. 154 TRAUMA TIC INJ URIES TMJ luxation can occur in both dogs and cats after external trauma. In the cat, TMJ luxation often occurs after the cat has jumped from a height, and in both dogs and cats, dislocation can occur secondary to vehicular trauma. 155 The TMJ is capable of luxation without fracture because it has considerable lateral sliding movement, and the synchondrosis of the mandibular symphysis allows independent movement of the mandibular rami. 4 Dislocation of the TMJ tends to be in the rostrodorsal direction ( Figs. 11.32 and 11.33 eFig. 11.9 ), because ven- trocaudal luxation is prevented by the retroarticular process of the temporal bone. 4 Dogs and cats with TMJ dislocation are unable to close the mouth completely, have dental malocclu- sion with the mandible displaced to one side, and display excessive salivation. 4 Luxation is most often unilateral; it may A B Fig. 11.31 T1-weighted precont rast (A) and postcontrast (B) transverse MR images of a dog with masticatorymuscle myositis. Seiler T he superior soft tissue contrast of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) makes it the preferred modality for im- aging almost all aspects of intracranial disease, whereas computed tomography (CT) is less sensitive. CT is suitable for brain imaging in trauma cases, as outlined later, and if magnetic resonance (MR) is not available. This chapter is a basic over- view of the MR and CT characteristics of common small animal intracranial disorders. A review of the technical details associ- ated with brain imaging in small animals and a more compre- hensive review of uncommon disorders is available elsewhere. 1 2 BASI C MAGN ETIC RES ONANC E EXAMIN ATION OF THE BRAIN A standard MR examination of the canine or feline brain in- volves the acquisition of multiple pulse sequences in different anatomic planes ( Table 12.1 ). In MR, it is the tissue chemical characteristics that determine the signal intensity in the various sequences. Pulse sequences are selected to assess anatomy and to maximize lesion conspicuity. Images are usually acquired in transverse, sagittal, and dorsal planes ( Fig. 12.1 ). Rationale for Sequence Selection In T2-weighted sequences, free ﬂ uid (e.g., cerebrospinal ﬂ uid [CSF]) is extremely bright/T2 hyperintense. Bright/T2-hyperin- tense tissues have a longer T2 relaxation (see Chapter 4 for a discussion of T1 and T2 relaxation). Most common pathologic processes, whether neoplastic or in ﬂ ammatory, result in increased ﬂ uid within tissues, and this results in an increase in brightness of the abnormal tissue relative to surrounding normal tissue; the term increased T2-signal intensity is commonly used to describe this. Sometimes it is dif ﬁ cult to identify a T2-hyperintense lesion when it is adjacent to a normal region of high signal, such as adjacent to CSF within the ventricles. With respect to T2- weighted sequences, the signal from free ﬂ uid can be elimi- nated using a ﬂ uid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence. In T2-weighted FLAIR images, free ﬂ uid has very low signal, while other hydrated lesions remain bright ( Fig. 12.2 ). 3 Proteinaceous or in ﬂ ammatory ﬂ uid will have less or no signal reduction. The term nulling or null is used to describe the signal change produced when using an inversion recovery sequence like FLAIR (e.g., the T2 hyperintensity nulls in the FLAIR sequence). A FLAIR sequence may also provide addi- tional information about T2-hyperintense lesions that must be distinguished from CSF, such as cystic meningioma, dermoid and epidermoid cysts, and arachnoid cysts. 4 In T1-weighted spin-echo sequences, high signal arises from tissues having rapid T1 relaxation, such as fat and methemo- globin. Conversely, ﬂ uid and hydrated lesions have reduced signal intensity in T1-weighted images, appearing dark or hypointense. A T1-weighted image is excellent for evaluation of extracranial anatomy, but on its own has poor sensitivity for detection of most intracranial lesions because of their hydrated nature, which leads to low T1 signal. However, blood-brain barrier disruption and regions of altered perfusion can be detected in T1-weighted sequences acquired after the admin- istration of MR contrast medium. The most common MR contrast media are chelated forms of gadolinium, a transitional compound with paramagnetic properties that shorten the T1 relaxation time of tissue in which the material accumulates. 5 Therefore, regions of higher gadolinium concentration will have increased signal (bright) in T1-weighted sequences. Many pathologic processes in the brain result in some disruption to the blood-brain barrier, often allowing an accu- mulation of contrast medium after intravenous injection, and thereby increased signal intensity in postcontrast T1-weighted images. Contrast medium should be administered after all other imaging sequences have been acquired, because contrast medium can sometimes affect the appearance of tissues/organs in other sequences. Certain abnormalities are easier to detect in a speci ﬁ c scan plane, and ensuring these scan planes are part of the routine examination is imperative. For example, a T2-weighted sagittal sequence should be performed routinely to allow better eval- uation of the morphology of the midbrain, cerebellum, and caudal brainstem. This is particularly important in the assess- ment of increased intracranial pressure and caudal fossa crowding. 6 C H A P T E R 12 M a g n e t i c R e s o n a n c e I m a g i n g a n d C o m p u t e d T o m o g r a p h i c F e a t u r e s o f B r a i n D i s e a s e i n S m a l l A n i m a l s Table  12.1 Stan dard Seq uences for Brain Ma gnetic Reson ance Imagi ng. As discussed in Chapter 4 , images can be acquired using spin-echo or gradient recall echo (GRE) pulse sequences. GRE images are more susceptible to magnetic ﬁ eld inhomogeneity, and this is exploited when assessing the brain for evidence of chronic hemorrhage (longer than 2 3 days). As hemorrhage is broken down, the magnetic properties of the ferric/ferrous ions in hemoglobin metabolites cause a local ﬁ eld distortion that destroys the MR signal. This appears as a signal void (a black, so- called susceptibility artifact). This is an extremely sensitive in- dicator of chronic hemorrhage as might occur in patients with intracranial trauma, hemorrhagic tumors, hemorrhagic infarcts, coagulopathies, or hemorrhagic metastasis. The image void is typically much larger than the actual lesion because of blooming (see Hemorrhagic Infarct section). Putting It All Together The imaging characteristics of a lesion need to be evaluated in various sequences, so that an accurate assessment of the underlying disease process can be established. For example, a T2-hyperintense region in the brain may represent free ﬂ uid such as CSF or brain edema and the two conditions can be differentiated with a T2 FLAIR sequence (see Fig. 12.2 ). T2 hyperintensity may also represent pathology such as neoplasia which may be contrast enhancing, or necrosis which does not enhance and does not null in a T2-weighted FLAIR sequence ( Fig. 12.3 ). All pulse sequences must be interpreted together to reach the correct conclusion. Secondary Effects of Focal Intracranial Disease In addition to altering local signal intensity, brain masses and swelling can also cause major changes to brain morphology. Many masses and the secondary perilesional edema result in brain compression, with a contralateral midline shift, ventricu- lar compression and obstruction, and ultimately either trans- tentorial and/or cerebellar herniation at the foramen magnum ( Fig. 12.4 ). Images should always be viewed in both a bone and soft- tissue window. Contrast medium administration facilitates detection of extra-axial lesions originating outside the brain tissue (meninges, skull). If associated with a breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, intra-axial lesions originating from brain tissue may also be delineated based on an increase in attenua- tion. Nonenhancing brain lesions, if large enough, can become visible due to an associated mass effect (shift of the falx cerebri, compression of the ventricular system, brain herniation) or presence of hypoattenuating perilesional edema. There are a few indications, namely, trauma with suspected skull fractures and/or intracranial hemorrhage, where contrast medium administration may not be necessary. Imaging the caudal fossa with CT can be particularly challenging due to the artifact of beam hardening from the petrous temporal bone. Know Normal Anatomy A working knowledge of normal MR and CT brain anatomy and neuropathophysiologic correlations are prerequisites to char- acterizing any lesion accurately and correlating it with the clinical signs. Many electronic and hard-copy references for these subjects are available. 7 10 Developmental Conditions of the Brain The array of intracranial developmental malformations is well described. 11 Only the most common of these anomalies are discussed here. Abnormal Fluid Accumulations Hydrocephalus, the most common developmental anomaly, is the excessive accumulation of CSF within the ventricular sys- tem. Hydrocephalus occurs when normal ﬂ ow is obstructed, when there is overproduction compared to absorption, or when there is brain atrophy. The most common form of hy- drocephalus is congenital hydrocephalus, where excessive CSF accumulates before or soon after birth. An inherited malfor- mation of the ﬂ uid pathway may be present, or perinatal infection or injury may lead to scarring that affects CSF reab- sorption. Less commonly, hydrocephalus occurs in adult pa- tients, usually the result of tumor or infection, which obstructs CSF ﬂ ow ( Fig. 12.6 ). The lateral ventricles are usually relatively symmetric, but there is considerable variation in what is considered normal ventricular size, particularly in small-breed dogs. 12 Agenesis of the septum pellucidum, a thin membrane separating the two cerebral hemispheres and the two lateral ventricles, is a common, typically asymptomatic, ﬁ nding most frequently seen in larger brachycephalic breeds. In one study, the septum pellucidum was considered intact in only 25% of dogs 13 ( Fig. 12.7 ). In addition to hydrocephalus, there are other conditions that result in the accumulation of ﬂ uid within the cranial vault, the most common being ﬂ uid accumulation in the supracollicular region. Three different patterns of supracollicular ﬂ uid accu- mulation have been characterized based on establishing the location of the thin membrane separating the third ventricle from the quadrigeminal cistern. 14 This membrane likely repre- sents the third ventricle wall where the pia mater joins the ependymal layer forming the tela choroidea of the third ventricle. 14 In the ﬁ rst pattern, there is enlargement of the caudodorsal recess of the third ventricle ( Fig. 12.8 ) with the thin membrane separating the third ventricle from the quad- rigeminal cistern being displaced caudodorsally. In pattern 2, there is enlargement of both the caudodorsal aspect of the third ventricle and the quadrigeminal cistern and the membrane separating these compartments is visible ( Fig. 12.9 ). In pattern 3, due to enlargement of the quadrigeminal cistern alone, the membrane separating the quadrigeminal cistern and the third ventricle is displaced rostrally. 14 Enlargement of the quad- rigeminal cistern results in varying degrees of ﬂ attening of the rostrodorsal aspect of the cerebellum ( Fig. 12.10 ). Other ﬂ uid accumulations within the developing brain also occur. Focal ﬂ uid accumulations are termed porencephaly whereas extensive ﬂ uid accumulations are termed hydra- nencephaly. Developmental porencephaly is due to a focal neuronal migration disorder and results in a gap in the devel- oping cerebral hemisphere. Encephaloclastic porencephaly is an all-encompassing term describing cortical loss from various causes, including ischemia, infection, or trauma 15 ( Fig. 12.11 ). These accumulations of ﬂ uid usually communicate with the lateral ventricles or the subarachnoid space. Dandy Walker syndrome is a developmental disorder whereby there is failure of development of the caudoventral aspect of the cerebellar vermis. This results in enlargement of the dorsocaudal aspect of the fourth ventricle ( Fig. 12.12 ). The clinical signs associated with this condition depend on the volume of absent cerebellum. There are a number of manifes- tations of this condition and a more correct overarching term is probably Dandy Walker variant. There are a number of uncommon cystic structures that can occur within the cranial vault as a result of incomplete or aberrant separation of the neuroectoderm from the overlying ectodermal tissue. Intracranial epidermoid cysts, intracranial dermoid cysts, Rathke cleft cysts, and craniopharyngiomas originate during gestation from remnants of ectodermal tissue due to defects of neural tube closure. 16 Intracranial epidermoid or dermoid cysts are most commonly located in the fourth ventricle or the cerebellopontine angle ( Fig. 12.13 ). Cystic structures are hypoattenuating in CT images. Signal intensity is variable and dependent on cyst content in MRIs. Cysts with a high lipid content appear hyperintense in T1-weighted and T2- weighed images, whereas cysts with lower lipid content appear T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense. 17 Dermoid cysts con- taining adnexa (e.g., hair) may have suspended low intensity foci in all sequences. 18 Cysts often contain protein and keratin and, therefore, do not null in FLAIR sequences. Typically, these complex cysts do not enhance, although ring enhancement may occasionally be present. Rathke cleft cysts and cranio- pharyngiomas occur in the region of the sella turcica and are typically associated with anomalous development of the pitui- tary gland. Other Developmental Morphologic Anomalies Chiari-like malformation , also called caudal occipital mal- formation syndrome (COMS) , is an all-encompassing term that describes anomalies in the development and morphology of the caudal fossa. This commonly results in crowding of the cere- bellum and varying degrees of protrusion of the cerebellum into and through the foramen magnum ( Fig. 12.14 ). The Cavalier King Charles spaniel is the most affected breed, wherein the condition is inherited and thought to affect as much as 95% of the population. 19 22 However, COMS is observed in many other small breeds. MR is commonly used as a screening tool to assist breeding programs in reducing the incidence and severity of COMS. Crowding of the caudal fossa results in protrusion of the caudal cerebellar vermis against or through the foramen magnum. This can result in disruption to CSF ﬂ ow and an in- crease in pressure within the spinal cord, leading to the development of ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled cavities within the central and dor- socentral aspect of the spinal cord, termed syringohy- dromyelia . In some patients, syringohydromyelia extends to the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord. There is some association between Chiari-like malformation syndrome and the develop- ment of dorsal atlanto-axial bands. 23 While CT is a valuable tool to assess bone pathology, evaluation of the soft tissues of the caudal fossa is limited due to lower contrast resolution and beam hardening artifact. With CT, sagittal reconstructions are most valuable to identify presence of caudal fossa crowding or cerebellar herniation. The accuracy and interobserver agree- ment for identi ﬁ cation of cerebellar herniation and presence of syringomyelia were shown to be higher using high- ﬁ eld MRI compared to multislice CT. 24 Holoprosencephaly is the failure of the forebrain to bifurcate normally into two discrete cerebral hemispheres. Hol- oprosencephaly exists in three forms depending on the severity of the malformation, alobar, semilobar, and lobar. Lobar hol- oprosencephaly has been described in dogs, 25 and dysgenesis/ agenesis of the corpus callosum is a feature of this condition. Dogs with developmental abnormalities of the corpus callosum may have hypodipsic hypernatremia. Miniature schnauzers appear to be overrepresented for both dysgenesis of the corpus callosum and lobar holoprosencephaly ( Fig. 12.15 ). Lissencephaly is an extremely rare condition whereby there is an absence or severe lack of normal gyral formation resulting in a smooth outer surface to the brain ( Fig. 12.16 ). It results from failure of normal neural migration during fetal develop- ment. In dogs, the Lhasa Apso is overrepresented, and there may be a genetic predisposition in this breed. 26 Inherent Disorders in Brain Metabolism There are many developmental, often breed-speci ﬁ c, inborn errors of brain metabolism that result in MR changes. These conditions, collectively known as storage diseases , can result in changes to both brain morphology and signal characteristics due to the abnormal accumulation of one or more products of interrupted metabolic pathways. Mucopolysaccharidosis, neuronal cell lipofuscinosis, cerebellar abiotrophy, and globoid cell leukodystrophy are the most common d albeit rare. Mucopolysaccharidosis and neuronal cell lipofuscinosis typi- cally result in progressive juvenile cortical atrophy and hydro- cephalus and an abnormally small corpus callosum, and in the latter, there is often severe peripheral meningeal thickening and enhancement 27 ( Fig. 12.17 ). Globoid cell leukodystrophy typically results in symmetrical white matter disease, mild hydrocephalus, and symmetrical contrast enhancement of the corpus callosum, internal capsule, and corona radiata. Nutritional, Metabolic, and Toxic Disorders There are a number of nutritional disorders that result in morphological signal change within the brain that are detect- able with MR. Most commonly, nutritional, toxic, and metabolic disturbances are bilaterally symmetrical. There is considerable overlap in the MR features of many nutritional, metabolic, and toxic disorders, and this confounds the MR assessment. Generally, the presence of lesion symmetry should alert the reader to the possibility of such disorders. Subtle changes in attenuation may be visible with CT imaging; however, in a majority of cases, CT imaging is not sensitive enough and the study will be normal. There are a number of metabolic disorders that result in intracranial changes that can be detected with MR. A full description of these is beyond the scope of this chapter. One example is subacute necrotizing encephalopathy, which has been documented in the Alaskan husky. This condition closely resembles Leigh syndrome in people and is an incapacitating, ultimately fatal neurodegenerative disorder. 32 The condition has been reported in the Bull terrier 33 and also the Yorkshire terrier. The disorder is characterized by degeneration and ne- crosis that manifests as bilaterally symmetrical regions of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity within the central aspect of the thalamus. Additionally, focal T2 hyperintensity has been documented within the midbrain and medulla ( Fig. 12.21 ). Severe electrolyte disturbances in otherwise normal patients (unrelated to holoprosencephaly) can result in parenchymal changes that manifest with MR detectable changes. Severe hypernatremia can result in a number of symmetrical signal changes, most commonly a bilaterally symmetrical increase in T2 signal in signal at the junction of the internal capsule and lateral margin of the thalamus ( Fig. 12.22 ). In people, this is an uncommon but important postpartum complication. 34 In ﬂ ammatory Conditions Encephalitis and meningoencephalitis can often be detected using MR, whereas changes may or may not be detectable with CT. Most commonly, cytologic and immunologic analysis of CSF is required to help establish a de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Meningoen- cephalitis is typically either infectious or due to dysregulation of the patient s immune system d so-called immune mediated. The group of idiopathic noninfectious meningoencephalo- myelitides (NIME) includes several subtypes, including steroid responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA), eosinophilic meningo- encephalitis (EME), granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis (GME), necrotizing meningoencephalomyelitis (NME), and necrotizing leucoencephalitis (NLE). As SRMA and EME have fairly distinct diagnostic characteristics, the term meningitis of unknown etiology (MUE) is used to describe the three speci ﬁ c subtypes that can only be con ﬁ rmed based on histopathology. These include GME, NME, and NLE. 35 Generally, immune-mediated brain disease is more common than infectious brain disease. 36 Small breed dogs are more likely to have an immune-mediated etiology and large breed dogs could have either infectious or immune-mediated disease. While there are some breed-speci ﬁ c predispositions and some disorders affect different regions of the brain more commonly, overall, the lesions are patchy or diffuse, T2 and FLAIR hyper- intense, T1 iso or hypointense and have variable enhancement d ranging from no enhancement to intense enhancement ( Fig. 12.23 ). The T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity could re ﬂ ect focal pathology or perilesional edema. In chronic cases, regions of brain necrosis from any etiology may be pre- sent, sometimes manifesting as compensatory hydrocephalus, depending on the maturity of the lesion ( Fig. 12.24 ). Enceph- alitis is often accompanied by meningitis, where there is increased meningeal contrast enhancement. 37 Contrast enhancement is best detected by comparing T1-weighted im- ages acquired before and after contrast medium administration. Not acquiring the precontrast sequence or using different acquisition parameters will invalidate objective assessment of meningeal enhancement. Increased meningeal contrast enhancement and/or multifocal poorly delineated hypoattenu- ation of the brain tissue with no or mild contrast enhancement may be seen in CT imaging ( Fig. 12.25 ). Idiopathic hypertrophic pachymeningitis is an uncommon condition whereby there is marked nonspeci ﬁ c thickening and ﬁ brosis of the pachymeninges without extension into the sulci. The Greyhound breed appears overrepresented, and the con- dition appears to have an immune etiology. The condition should be considered as a possible differential diagnosis for dogs with pachymeningeal thickening and marked enhance- ment with no identi ﬁ ed underlying cause 37 ( Fig. 12.26 ). In 25 patients with CSF alterations consistent with in ﬂ ammatory brain disease, 24% of the MR studies were normal. 37 MISCELL ANEOU S DISOR DERS Reversible seizure-associated brain edema is typically charac- terized by nonenhancing T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity with negligible mass effect in patients with a recent history of extensive seizures. The regions most commonly affected are the piriform and temporal lobes. 40 Typically, the changes are bilateral, but changes can also be unilateral and occur else- where, including the region of the cingulate gyrus ( Fig. 12.30 ). Otitis media and interna are important differentials for nystagmus and head tilt. The assessment of inner ear disease is a practical application of using signal differences between T2 and FLAIR sequences to establish a diagnosis. 41 Normal inner ear ﬂ uid is T2 hyperintense and should null completely in the T2 FLAIR sequence, similar to CSF. Incomplete nulling suggests altered inner ear ﬂ uid content, as occurs with otitis interna ( Fig. 12.31 ). As with all patients with aural disease, close interrogation of the osseous structures and neuroparenchyma is important. Meningiomas are often ﬁ rm and encapsulated, are usually discrete, and may contain mineralization or pockets of ﬂ uid ( Fig. 12.32 ). Basal and plaque-like meningiomas are common in the ﬂ oor of the cranial cavity, especially in the optic chiasm and suprasellar regions. They also occur commonly over the cere- bral hemispheres, less commonly in the cerebello- pontomedullary region, and rarely in the retrobulbar space, arising from the optic nerve. Multiple meningiomas can occur; this is more common in cats than in dogs. Thickening of bone adjacent to meningiomas, termed hyperostosis , may occur, especially in cats ( Fig. 12.33 ). Meningiomas can usually be distinguished from intra-axial tumors because meningiomas are usually peripherally located, or falx-associated broad-based masses that enhance following contrast-medium administra- tion in both CT and MR imaging (see Fig. 12.33 ). Meningiomas are also often associated with linear contrast enhancement of thickened dura mater adjacent to an extra-axial mass, termed a dural tail . In one study, the predictive value of the dural tail sign for meningioma was 94%. 6 It is uncertain whether the dural tail represents neoplastic in ﬁ ltration beyond the margins of the meningioma or a manifestation of associated in ﬂ amma- tion. The amount of disruption to adjacent parenchyma is var- iable, depending on tumor size and location. Some meningiomas have minimal peripheral edema, although others may have extensive peripheral edema that can result in ven- tricular compression and brain herniation. An important dif- ferential for meningeal enhancement/masses is round cell neoplasia (histiocytic sarcoma and lymphoma). Choroid Plexus Tumors and Ependymomas Choroid plexus tumors most commonly occur in the third ventricle and in the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. The choroid plexus epithelium originates from differentiation of the primitive medullary epithelium and is embryologically related to ependymal cells. Choroid plexus tumors have a tendency to bleed, and exfoliation of choroid plexus cells, from both benign and malignant variants, may occur with subsequent tumor seeding to other areas of the brain or spinal cord through the CSF. 42 Because of the intraventricular location of choroid plexus tumors, obstructive hydrocephalus is common and may be life-threatening. A rare neural tumor that does traverse the cribriform plate is an olfactory neuroblastoma (esthesioneuroblastoma). 51 VASCU LAR DISRUP TIONS Occlusive Infarcts Occlusive brain infarcts are being diagnosed with increasing frequency with MRI but are rarely detectable with CT imaging. 30 32 Infarcts occur most commonly in the cerebellum but also occur in the brainstem and forebrain. Patients with brain infarction are typically older and present with acute nonprogressive focal neurologic signs. When the brainstem or cerebellum is involved, an important clinical dif- ferential is idiopathic peripheral vestibular disease, in which no abnormal MR ﬁ ndings are present. The typical MR characteris- tics of an acute cerebellar infarct include a triangular or segmental region of T2 hyperintensity that persists in the FLAIR sequence. The shape of the signal change usually closely re- ﬂ ects the territory of the affected artery ( Fig. 12.46 ). With cerebral infarction, the MR ﬁ ndings may overlap with those of a glioma or focal encephalitis; there is usually ill- de ﬁ ned T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, no mass effect, and little to no initial contrast enhancement ( Fig. 12.47 ). the periphery of the lesion. 33 One differentiating feature be- tween infarction and glioma is the initial lack of a mass effect with an infarct. Later, however, a mass effect may develop 3 to 5 days post infarct due to vasogenic edema. Differentiating a cerebral infarct and glioma may not be possible in some pa- tients, and diffusion-weighted MR or follow-up imaging may be necessary. Diffusion imaging quanti ﬁ es the rate of Brownian motion of water molecules in brain tissue. Brownian motion refers to the random movement of molecules. Water molecules are in constant motion, and the rate of movement or diffusion depends on the kinetic energy of the molecules and tempera- ture. In acute infarction, brain cells become overhydrated from failure of the adenosine triphosphate pump, resulting in restricted movement of water ( Fig. 12.48 ). In tumors, water movement is usually less restricted, and tumors will have less evidence of restricted water diffusion. However, restricted water diffusion in an infarct typically only lasts up to 3 to 5 days post infarct, so after this time the ability of diffusion-weighted imaging to distinguish infarct from glioma is lost. When an occlusive infarct is suspected, the patient should be evaluated for conditions resulting in a hypercoagulable state (e.g., Cushing disease) and loss of antithrombin III. Hemorrhagic Infarcts Hemorrhagic infarcts are most commonly associated with hy- pertension, thrombocytopenia, or other coagulopathies. The MR characteristics may be similar to those for an occlusive infarct ( Fig. 12.49 ). However, the presence of hemorrhage typically results in more signal heterogeneity and larger size of the lesion. The appearance of cerebral hemorrhage changes as the hematoma matures ( Table 12.2 ). The use of standard spin- echo sequences sometimes allows one to estimate the age of a hemorrhagic lesion, based roughly on the signal characteristics. The change in appearance of a hematoma in different sequences over time is related to the magnetic prop- erties of iron within hemoglobin as it transitions through intracellular deoxyhemoglobin to methemoglobin and ﬁ nally extracellular hemosiderin ( Fig. 12.50 ). As discussed previously, in comparison to fast (turbo) spin- echo sequences, GRE sequences are more susceptible to mag- netic ﬁ eld inhomogeneity created by hemoglobin degradation. Chronic hemorrhage acts like ferromagnetic material, causing pronounced local distortion of the local magnetic ﬁ eld resulting in a signal void ( Fig. 12.51 ; see Figs. 12.44 and 12.49 ), and for this reason, a GRE sequence should be acquired routinely, even though hemorrhage may not be suspected. Low signal in T2- weighted spin-echo and GRE images is, however, not speci ﬁ c for hemorrhage and may also be seen with mineralization, gas, ﬁ brous tissue, or iron deposits. 33 Susceptibility artifacts in GRE images must be interpreted in light of information gained from all other sequences in the study and the available clinical information. Trauma Both MRI and CT can be used to assess patients with head trauma; however, CT is often preferred due to faster acquisition time and excellent ability to detect skull fractures and intra- cranial hemorrhage in the acute stage. Acute hemorrhage is hyperattenuating to brain tissue in precontrast CT imaging due to the high hemoglobin content. The average Houns ﬁ eld units (HUs) of hemorrhage is between 60 and 100, whereas those of gray and white matter are in the range of 30 to 40 and 20 to 30, respectively. Edema may be present as a hypoattenuating halo around the hemorrhagic focus. 52 53 Viewing the CT images in a narrow window is essential to detect subtle changes in atten- uation and small foci of hemorrhage ( Fig. 12.52 ). DISE ASES OF THE NASAL CAV ITY/PARAN ASAL SINUSES Radiographic Projections Maxillary/nasal anatomy is complex ( Fig. 13.2 ). To fully char- acterize pathology, a minimum of four standard radiographic projections, centered on the sinuses, should be performed in horses with suspected sinus or nasal disease: lateral projection, DV projection, right 30-degree dorsal to left ventral, and left 30- degree dorsal to right ventral obliques. Sinusitis Sinusitis is the most common disease of the paranasal sinuses, caused by infection (usually bacterial) within the paranasal si- nuses. Affected horses have purulent nasal discharge with a fetid odor and may have facial swelling. In roughly a quarter of horses with sinus disease, there is no history of trauma, dental disease, or other underlying cause for sinusitis, and these are considered cases of primary sinusitis. Secondary sinusitis oc- curs when there is a predisposing factor resulting in bacterial infection. Dental disease is the most common cause of sec- ondary sinusitis, although prior facial fractures, cysts, or other masses affecting the nasal cavity may also result in sinusitis. Radiographs or CT are indicated to con ﬁ rm the presence of sinus ﬂ uid, and screen for possible underlying causes of sec- ondary sinusitis. In some cases, CT can discriminate soft tissue masses that might be obscured by ﬂ uid on radiography. Sinusitis causes distinct ﬂ uid lines on radiography which are horizontal to the ground ( Fig. 13.3 eFig. 13.1 ). There are two bullae within the nasal conchae rostral to the maxillary sinus: the dorsal and ventral nasal conchal bullae. These bullae may become infected in cases of sinusitis. Chronic empyema of these bullae may serve as a source of chronic, recurrent sinusitis if not treated ( Fig. 13.3 ). 1 Cysts Paranasal sinus cysts are the second most common cause of equine secondary sinusitis after dental disease. 2 Their cause is unknown, although there may be an association with ethmoid hematomas given the presence of hemorrhage in cyst walls on histopathologic examination. 3 On radiographs, cysts cause a soft tissue opaque mass within the paranasal sinuses, although it may be gas opaque if internal ﬂ uid drains. Cysts can cause mild pressure resorption of regional bones, but rarely cause severe regional lysis. On CT, cysts often have a discrete hyper- attenuating wall at their periphery which discriminates cysts from other sinus masses ( Fig. 13.4 eFig. 13.2 ). 4 Progressive Ethmoid Hematoma (PEH) PEH is an expansile mass typically arising from the submucosa of the ethmoidal labyrinth, but can occur anywhere within the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses. The cause is unknown but presumably due to repeated hemorrhage into the submucosa. The result is a mass comprised of blood and ﬁ brous tissue, encapsulated by respiratory epithelium. Radiographs reveal a mass in the area of the ethmoid turbinates ( Fig. 13.5 eFig. 13.3 ). Most PEHs have a characteristic appearance on CT with internal hyperattenuating “ swirling ” heterogeneity attrib- utable to the presence of hemorrhage or early mineralization in the mass ( Fig. 13.6 ). Unlike radiographs, CT and MR readily identify cribriform plate lysis caused by the PEH, which may preclude some forms of therapy. 5 Neoplasia Sinonasal neoplasms are an uncommon cause of sinusitis. Various tumor types are reported, including epithelial tumors (carcinomas of various types), sarcomas such as osteosarcoma and hemangiosarcoma, neuroendocrine tumors/neuroblas- toma, hemangiosarcoma, and lymphoid tumors. 6 7 The radio- graphic appearance of sinonasal neoplasia overlaps with other C H A P T E R 13 The Equine Head 217

Polyps Polyps are uncommon, benign soft tissue proliferations that occur within the nasal passage or sinuses and likely represent polyploid epithelial proliferation as a response to regional chronic in ﬂ ammation. 9 On radiographs ( Fig. 13.9 ), polyps are soft tissue masses that have a nonaggressive appearance. They generally do not cause signi ﬁ cant bone lysis or production though may cause bone pressure resorption ( Fig. 13.10 ). DENT AL DISE ASE Normal Dentition Discussions of equine dentition employ the modi ﬁ ed Triadan system, which assigns each tooth a speci ﬁ c number depending on its anatomic quadrant in the mouth ( Fig. 13.11 ). The term “ cheek teeth ” informally refers to the premolar and molar teeth. The hypsodont (continually erupting) nature of equine teeth means younger horses will have a long reserve crown, which extends further into the sinuses and nasal cavity compared to older horses. Horses between 2 and 4 years of age develop “ eruption bumps, ” sometimes incorrectly referred to as “ erup- tion cysts, ” over the premolar teeth of the maxilla and mandible. The periapical area of these teeth appears relatively lucent compared to older horses and should not be confused with periapical abscessation ( Fig. 13.12 ). Young horses will have “ caps ” (retained deciduous teeth) over their mandibular and maxillary teeth when they are between 3 and 5 years of age. The Triadan 05s are small brachydont teeth referred to as “ wolf teeth ” ( Fig. 13.13 ) that may be retained. Wolf teeth typically do not directly cause clinical signs, but can cause discomfort particularly if they interfere with a bit in the mouth. Equine teeth are subjected to high abrasive forces and continual wear, which shapes the occlusal surface of the tooth and ultimately affects the rate of dental attrition. A complete description of equine dental anatomy is beyond the scope of this text. Like brachydont teeth, the equine tooth is constructed of cementum, dentin, and enamel, but unlike the brachydont tooth, the grinding surface is continually worn. The common pulp chamber resides in the apex of the tooth and the pulp horns extend towards the occlusal surface. Deposition of sec- ondary dentin closes these pulp horns as the tooth undergoes normal wear, but there is risk for pulp exposure, infection, and apical abscessation if there is failure of this process. The peri- odontal space surrounding the tooth should be thin and well de ﬁ ned, and can be dif ﬁ cult to see radiographically compared to CT. Dental Radiographic Projections Maxillary cheek teeth: If maxillary premolar/molar dental dis- ease is suspected, the standard projections listed for the maxillary sinuses may be employed, although opening the mouth with a gag during image acquisition facilitates evaluation of the occlusal surfaces. Additional oblique projections are available that better isolate the apices of the maxillary cheek teeth, projecting the palatal root dorsal to the buccal roots: open-mouth right 60-degree ventral to left dorsal oblique and open-mouth left 60-degree ventral to right dorsal oblique ( Fig. 13.14 ). A shallow lateral oblique projection is ideal for evaluation of occlusal abnormalities (wavemouth) (see Fig. 13.14 ). An offset DV projection (when the mandible is distracted to one side relative to the maxilla) prevents super- imposition of the mandibular and maxillary arcades on the DV projection ( Fig. 13.15 ). Mandibular dental disease: Projections to isolate the mandibular dental apices are similar to those for the maxillary arcade, but centered on the mandible and steeper angles may be necessary to prevent superimposition of the contralateral side. Maxillary/mandibular incisor disease: Open mouth, intraoral projections allow evaluation of incisor teeth without superimposition of the opposite dental arcade. The complex nature of dental anatomy and pathology pre- cludes an exhaustive review of equine dental disease in this chapter; however, the most common diseases will be discussed later. Conformational Defects The occlusal surface may wear in an abnormal pattern. In some cases, the harder enamel folds of the teeth will protrude from the occlusal surface due to differential wear between the enamel and the softer cementum and dentin. These “ enamel points ” are the most common equine dental disease and cause discomfort during chewing by impinging on regional soft tis- sues. Enamel points are typically diagnosed on oral examina- tion, but may be apparent on CT imaging or radiographs. This res ults in an occl usal con forma tion referr ed to as “ wavem outh ” ( Fig. 13.17 ). 10 Cheek Teeth Fractures Cheek teeth fractures are common, with the 109/209 most commonly affected (see Fig. 13.15 ). Fractures are most often sagittal in their orientation, and usually extend centrally through the infundibula or more peripherally through the pulp horns. These may lead to pulp exposure and periapical infec- tion if left untreated. Apical Infections of Cheek Teeth Periapical cheek tooth infection is a common disorder. Most are caused by blood or lymphatic borne bacterial infection. Pulp exposure, due to imbalance between cheek tooth wear and the formation of secondary dentin or due to dental trauma/frac- tures, can also lead to infection which ascends to the apical region of the tooth. 10 Regardless of cause, infected teeth are recognized radiographically by surrounding alveolar sclerosis, blunting of tooth roots, and widening of the periodontal space ( Fig. 13.18 eFig. 13.5 ). The interpretation of dental radiographs is challenging; CT greatly improves the speci ﬁ city when determining which teeth have apical or pulpal infection. The caudal maxillary cheek teeth extend into the paranasal sinuses, so periapical infection can lead to sinusitis. The mandibular and rostral maxillary check teeth do not extend into the sinuses; infection of these teeth can eventually cause ﬁ stula formation and a draining tract ( Fig. 13.19 ). Fistulas are more easily iden- ti ﬁ ed on CT compared to radiographs ( Fig. 13.20 ). Odontogenic Tumors Odontogenic tumors are uncommon and arise from embryonic remnants of the dental lamina. 11 Multiple tumor types occur, including ameloblastoma, ameloblastic carcinomas, and odon- tomas. There is overlap in the imaging appearance of different tumor types, but all result in an expansile, aggressive lesion centered on the teeth ( Fig. 13.21 ). 11 Equine Odontoclastic Tooth Resorption and Hypercementosis (EOTRH) EOTRH is a common dental disorder predominantly affecting the incisors and canine teeth. It causes various degrees of progressive internal and external root resorption and excessive cemental deposition ( Fig. 13.22 ). EOTRH is recognized most commonly in middle aged and geriatric ( < 15 years of age) horses, although younger horses can also be affected. 12 13 In one study of horses 10 years and older, 94% of horses had at least minor and 62% had moderate to severe radiographic changes from EOTRH. 14 The etiology is likely multifactorial, and represents a response to periodontal disease or infection, ischemic necrosis, mechanical stress, or genetics. 12 Radio- graphic ﬁ ndings mimic those on histopathology, with some teeth primarily showing resorptive or proliferative change, but most commonly a mix of both. 12 Hypercementosis results in root and reserve crown enlagement. 13 With the advent of high resolution digital images and increased use of standing CT ex- amination of the head, earlier lesions are being recognized. They may be idiopathic or occur secondary to other underlying conditions such as ﬁ brous dysplasia or trauma. 15 Radiographically, cysts appear as lucent, multiloculated structures that cause pressure resorption of regional cortical bone and mimic some types of non- proliferative neoplasms (such as ameloblastoma or carcinoma). They may affect the maxilla or the mandible and, while slowly growing, may become very large. 16 Metabolic diseases such as nutritional hyperparathyroidism may cause similar features, such as reduced trabecular and cortical bone density, but are differentiated by the diffuse nature of radiographic abnormal- ities, compared to bone cysts, which are focal. 17 Nondentigerous Neoplasia of the Mandible/Maxilla Mandibular or maxillary neoplasms share many imaging fea- tures with bone cysts and tumors of dentigerous origin. Soft tissue neoplasms such as squamous cell carcinoma may invade regional bone, and primary osseous tumors such as ﬁ brosar- coma and osteosarcoma are also reported 18 ( Fig. 13.24 ). Fibro-osseous Lesions of the Craniofacial Complex “ Fibro-osseous lesions of the craniofacial complex ” describe a group of related conditions that result in replacement of normal bone with ﬁ brous connective tissue and mineralization. 19 Within this complex, there are three conditions that share similar histologic features: ossifying ﬁ broma, ﬁ brous dysplasia, and osteoma. 19 Ossifying ﬁ broma is a benign, tumor-like lesion in young ( < 1 year old) horses that usually affects the mandible, and may occasionally occur in older horses ( Fig. 13.25 ). 20 Radiographically, ossifying ﬁ bromas appear similar to other types of soft tissue or osseous neoplasms affecting the mandible, but are usually more mineralized than bone cysts. Fibrous dysplasia also typically occurs in young, growing ani- mals. 19 Histologically, ﬁ brous dysplasia appears similar to other ﬁ bro-osseous lesions, but tends to have very little internal mineralization and appears cyst-like. It may also be more diffuse than mass-like. 16 Osteomas most commonly occur on the mandible and rarely in the paranasal sinuses and characterized by benign peripheral cortical proliferation ( Fig. 13.26 ). 19 Suture Exostosis Sutures of the equine skull should completely fuse/ossify be- tween 3 months and 5 years of age. 21 Suture exostosis describes swelling and proliferation at the sutures and has numerous other names including suture periostitis and suture separa- tion. 22 The cause is unknown, but likely results from instability or prior injury/facial trauma. On radiographs, soft tissue swelling precedes bone proliferation surrounding a suture line. Instead, abnormal- ities of the guttural pouch may be seen “ incidentally ” when evaluating skull radiographs or CT for other reasons. Radio- graphs to evaluate the maxilla or mandible typically include only the rostral aspect of the guttural pouch. Complete radio- graphic examination of the guttural pouch consists of DV and lateral projections centered on the area. The cause is unknown, although a congenital defect or in ﬂ ammation may prevent gas from exiting the guttural pouch. Arabian and Paint horse foals have a breed predisposition. 29 Radiographs show a severe distension of the guttural pouch with gas ( Fig. 13.34 ). Trauma The guttural pouch is well protected from direct trauma due to its location ventral to the calvarium and medial to the caudal mandible. The basilar skull is composed of the basisphenoid bone that articulates caudally with the basioccipital bone and is immediately dorsal to the guttural pouch. Multiple ﬂ exors of the head, the largest being the longus capitis muscle, insert on the basilar skull. Basilar skull fractures occur sequential to a horse rearing up and falling backwards, directly striking the poll causing hyperextension of the head. Hyperextension exerts acute traction to the basilar skull musculature, causing frac- turing usually at the junction of basisphenoid and basioccipital bones ( Fig. 13.35 ). These fractures may be minimally displaced, complicating radiographic diagnosis, but the resultant hemor- rhage ﬁ lls the guttural pouch and is readily apparent on lateral radiographs. Fluid within the guttural pouch of a patient with recent head trauma should alert the clinician to the possibility of basilar skull fractures. LARYN X/UPPER AI RWAY Most laryngeal diseases are diagnosed through direct inspection with endoscopy at rest and during exercise on a treadmill or with a portable videoendoscopy system. Radiography, ultra- sound, or CT is performed if imaging of the deeper laryngeal tissues is desired. Laryngeal Mineralization Five cartilages comprise the larynx (the epiglottis, thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, and left/right arytenoid cartilages). 32 Laryngeal cartilages and regional muscles are soft tissue opaque; however, the ventral portion of the thyroid cartilage is reliably mineralized ( Fig. 13.36 ). 33 Variable cricoid and arytenoid cartilage mineralization is also commonly identi ﬁ ed. Despite earlier suggestions that arytenoid mineralization indicates the presence of arytenoid pathology, more recent research suggests arytenoid mineralization is an incidental ﬁ nding and not indic- ative of signi ﬁ cant underlying disease. 34 36 Palatal Dysfunction On the lateral projection in a normal horse, the epiglottis is dorsal to the caudal soft palate, with a small gas- ﬁ lled gap be- tween them (see Fig. 13.36 ). Some horses develop palatal dysfunction, consisting of dorsal displacement of the soft palate (DDSP) and palatal instability (PI). 37 With DDSP, the soft palate shifts dorsal to the epiglottis and is often a dynamic process resulting in upper airway noise and exercise intolerance. 32 PI is a dynamic “ billowing ” of the soft palate during high air ﬂ ow situations and often precedes DDSP, but is rarely recognized radiographically without induction of high-performance/high- air ﬂ ow situations. The etiologies of DDSP and PI are poorly understood but may be related to neuromuscular dysfunction of the intrinsic soft palate muscles or abnormal movement of the laryngohyoid apparatus. 37 Diagnosis of DDSP is usually made during high-speed treadmill endoscopic examination (as displacement may only occur during exercise), but lateral ra- diographs display displacements that persist at rest ( Fig. 13.37 ). Epiglottic Masses The epiglottis can develop different mass-like thickenings, including subepiglottic granulomas, subepiglottic cysts, ab- scesses, and epiglottitis that may be apparent radiographi- cally. 38 39 The distribution of epiglottic thickening depends on the underlying lesion. Subepiglottic cysts and granulomas arise ventral to the epiglottis, and result in an abnormal fullness to the tissues in this area causing loss of the gas that typically separates the palate from epiglottis ( Fig. 13.38 ). Epiglottic Entrapment Epiglottic entrapment is the most common epiglottic abnor- mality in racehorses and mature nonracehorses. 38 40 The normal subepiglottic mucosa extends to the peripheral aspect of the epiglottis, but in some cases becomes positioned above the dorsal epiglottic surface causing a continuous surface with the adjacent aryepiglottic folds. 41 Entrapment is typically diag- nosed on endoscopy, but may be identi ﬁ ed on lateral laryngeal radiographs as a blunted/shortened appearance to the epiglottis ( Fig. 13.39 eFig. 13.6 ). On radiographs and CT, THO is de ﬁ ned by bone prolifera- tion which ranges between subtle and exuberant ( Fig. 13.41 ). The associated stylohyoid bone will become diffusely, pro- gressively thickened as a response to increased stresses from restricted mobility of the temporohyoid joint. Early/mild degenerative changes are much more readily identi ﬁ ed with CT compared to radiography. If severe, ankylosis forms between the stylohyoid and temporal bones, increasing the risk of frac- ture of one or both of these bones during normal tongue movement ( Fig. 13.42 eFig. 13.7 ). 44 Dentigerous Cysts Dentigerous cysts (also referred to as heterotopic polyodontia) are congenital defects during prenatal development that result in ectopic dental tissue. 45 This results in tooth-like material that develops in an abnormal location, often near the base of the ear (hence the colloquial name “ ear tooth ” ) but can occur else- where in the sinuses or cranium. Their lining produces mucoid discharge, which can lead to a chronic draining tract. Imaging demonstrates dental-like tissue in an abnormal location. This abnormal tissue may resemble teeth, with opaque areas con- taining enamel-like material, although sometimes the minerali- zation is amorphous and less well formed ( Fig. 13.43 ). CT is better suited for surgical planning, particularly when the cyst is in an atypical location other than the base of the ear. BRAIN CT or MRI of the brain is less commonly performed in horses compared to small animals, although is an important part of the diagnostic approach to neurologic equine patients in some cases. 46 When a brain disorder is suspected, the decision to proceed with MRI or CT depends on a combination of factors. MRI is the best modality to demonstrate brain pathology, but anesthesia is necessary. For that reason, MRI may be reserved as a “ last test ” in horses after collection/analysis of cerebrospinal ﬂ uid and other imaging tests (such as standing CT or radiog- raphy) have been performed, even though those are low yield in comparison. In ﬂ ammatory Brain Disease A variety of infectious in ﬂ ammatory conditions may affect the brain, including equine protozoal myeloencephalopathy and viral encephalitides. They cause an in ﬂ ammatory pattern, including multifocal T2 hyperintensity in the brain parenchyma and various degrees of contrast enhancement ( Fig. 13.44 ). Ab- scesses are focal masses that contain central ﬂ uid, some degree of regional hemorrhage, and strong contrast enhancement. They may be associated with traumatic injury to the head, and their presence more easily identi ﬁ ed on CT compared to other in ﬂ ammatory brain conditions ( Fig. 13.45 ). 47 Neoplastic Brain Disease Primary brain parenchymal neoplasms are rare in the horse. Given the paucity of tumors, the prevalence of different tumor types is unknown, and generally limited to intermittent case reports, although ependymomas tend to be the most commonly reported. 48 In comparison, benign adenomas or hyperplasia of the pituitary pars intermedia are common tumors in horses and result in pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (PPID). 49 These benign, functional tumors cause hyperadrenocorticism and secondary clinical signs such as hirsutism and secondary dia- betes mellitus. The normal pituitary gland can be seen in horses on postcontrast CT and on MRI, with normal size ranges typi- cally less than approximately 10 to 12 mm in height. 50 51 In horses with PPID, the pituitary gland will appear both increased in height and width than nonaffected horses, and on MRI may have heterogeneous signal characteristics ( Fig. 13.46 ). 52 Cholesterol Granulomas Cholesterol granulomas (also called cholesterolinic granulomas) are benign, non-neoplastic masses that arise from the choroid A B C Fig. 13.22 Intraoral radiograph s of the maxillary incisors in two horses with equine odontocl astic toothresorption and hypercementosis (EOTRH). plexus, most commonly in the lateral ventricles, though the fourth ventricles may also be involved. Their exact etiology is unknown, but likely result from chronic/intermittent vascular congestion and secondary hemorrhage. This releases choles- terol from erythrocytes which acts as a foreign body inciting a granulomatous, mineralizing response. 53 They are very com- mon, being present in up to 20% of older horses, and rarely cause clinical signs, although can cause ataxia, blindness, depression, and somnolence when large. 53 54 They have a characteristic appearance on CT, being relatively hyper- attenuating to adjacent parenchyma with Houns ﬁ eld units (HU) values that indicate the presence of mineralization ( Fig. 13.47 ). Traumatic Brain Injury Traumatic brain injury (TBI) in horses is usually due to blunt force trauma or occasionally penetrating injuries. 55 Blunt force trauma from rearing and falling over backwards is the most common cause of injury (especially common in younger hors- es) but TBI also occurs from struggling after being cast, kick injuries, and injuries during anesthetic recovery. 55 56 The choice of imaging modality in cases of head trauma depends on cost and availability, as well as the capability of the patient to stand or recover from anesthesia. Radiographs are less sensitive for skull fractures compared to MRI/CT, and do not directly image the brain. CT is particularly useful in detecting hematoma formation, as the high proteinaceous and hemoglobin content of acute hemorrhage renders it hyperattenuating on pre- contrast images ( Fig. 13.48 ). OTHE R COND ITIONS OF THE HEAD Other Fractures Due to the uncertain nature of head trauma, fractures may occur anywhere in the head, beyond those previously discussed in this chapter. Horses have a complete bony orbit, comprised of the frontal, lacrimal, zygomatic, and temporal bones. 57 Ra- diographs or CTs are indicated in horses with orbital fractures to determine whether there is sinus or nasal involvement, with most fractures in this area requiring a combination of medical and surgical therapy. 57 Multiple oblique radiographs at varied, steep angles may be necessary to better characterize fractures in this location ( Fig. 13.49 ). The paracond ylar processe s are bilateral, long osseous struc- tures caudal to the bulla extending ventrally from the occipital region. There may be neurolog ical signs (such as facial nerve paralysis given the prox- imity to the paracondyla r process of the facial canal and stylo- mastoid foramen where the facial nerve emerges), but these fractures may also be seen incidentally in clinic ally normal horses, presumabl y from prior healed or unrecognize d trauma. Para- condylar process fractures may be dif ﬁ cult to recognize as they superimpose with the complex anatomy of the skull base, and often easiest seen on the DV projection by comparing the frac- tured process to the contralat eral side. CT provides more sensi- tive detection of small or nondispl aced fractures ( Fig. 13.50 ). Melanomas Melanomas are common neoplasms in horses (representing up to 15% of equine neoplasms) with a known genetic predispo- sition to the gray horse. 30 While they occur in multiple loca- tions, including the perineal/tail base region, they are also frequently seen on the head. They may be super ﬁ cial in nature, and affect the eyelids and ears, but also occur deeper within the head and can affect lymph nodes, sinuses, guttural pouch, and salivary tissue. Most melanomas are pigmented due to a high concentration of melanin. William R. Widmer S pinal pain and spinal neuropathy are common problems in small animal practice. This leads to the vertebral col- umn being one of the more frequently imaged anatomic regions. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are the modalities of choice for full character- ization of abnormalities of the vertebrae and spinal cord in small animals. Many conditions including intervertebral disc disease; various myelopathies; and tumors of the spinal cord, meninges, and vertebral column cannot be completely characterized with a conventional survey radiographic examination. However, judicious use of conventional radiography can provide valuable, cost-effective information regarding numerous conditions of the vertebral column, and survey radiographs should always be made before pursuing advanced imaging. Survey radiographs may or may not lead to identi ﬁ cation of the cause of the pain or neuropathy; but, especially in older patients, they are rarely normal. Therefore, it is important to have not only an appre- ciation for the types of spinal abnormalities that can be diag- nosed radiographically but also to understand the signi ﬁ cance of commonly encountered changes that may not be related directly to the clinical signs. The focus of this chapter is on vertebral diseases that can be imaged effectively with conven- tional radiography and myelography (including CT myelog- raphy), and the signi ﬁ cance of commonly encountered incidental ﬁ ndings. Radiographic abnormalities will be supple- mented with CT and/or magnetic resonance (MR) images where appropriate. Advanced imaging related speci ﬁ cally to the spinal cord is covered in Chapter 15 Radiographic technique plays a vital role in radiography of the vertebral column. 1 Suboptimal information occurs when positioning is inaccurate, multiple centered images are not made, and images do not have adequate spatial resolution. Chemical restraint is absolutely necessary for accurate posi- tioning and should be used unless prohibited by the patient s condition. Technical information relating to spinal radiography is discussed in detail in Chapter 9 ANAT OMIC CONSI DERATION S A vertebra consists of the body, also referred to as a centrum and the vertebral arch ( Fig. 14.1 ). 1 2 The vertebral arch is composed of paired right and left pedicles and laminae and the unpaired spinous process. The vertebral arch bounds the vertebral canal, which houses the spinal cord. The articular processes of the lamina form the synovial joints along the dorsum of the vertebral column ( Fig. 14.2 ). The articular pro- cess joints are diarthrodial (synovial) joints, being composed of articular processes covered with articular cartilage, a synovial membrane and capsule, and contain synovial ﬂ uid. They pro- vide dorsal mechanical stabilization of the vertebral column. The anatomic structure of C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) is complex and differs widely from the remainder of the vertebrae ( Fig. 14.3 ). 1 5 C1 has a well-developed vertebral arch, but the body is rudimen- tary with no distinct vertebral body, endplates, or spinous process, and the cranial and caudal articular processes are convex. C1 articulates cranially with the occipital condyles, forming the atlantooccipital joint, and caudally with C2, form- ing the atlantoaxial joint. The wings of C1 are extensive trans- verse processes that project laterally and serve as attachments for numerous cervical muscles. The lateral and transverse foramina contain the paired vertebral arteries. C2 has an elon- gated vertebral body and a massive spinous process. The dens is a ﬁ nger-like projection extending cranially from the vertebral body of C2 into the cranioventral aspect of the vertebral canal. The dens originates from the intercentrum of C1, but during development, it attaches to C2 and lies within the vertebral canal of C1. C2 has a small transverse process, two cranial articular processes that articulate with the fovea of the atlas, and a caudal endplate. The sacrum is also much different morphologically than a prototypical vertebra. It is broad in the transverse plane, con- sists of three fused vertebrae, and articulates cranially with the seventh lumbar vertebra, caudally with the ﬁ rst caudal vertebra, and laterally with the ilium on each side, forming the sacroiliac joints. 1 2 The spinous processes of the sacrum are fused, making up the median sacral crest, and the sacral wing has a large facet for the sacroiliac articulation. The sacroiliac joint is a combined synovial and cartilaginous joint capable of only limited motion due to thick ventral and dorsal ligaments. Multiple foramina are present dorsally and along the pelvic surface of the sacrum, allowing for passage of spinal nerves and blood vessels. There are 6 to 23 caudal vertebrae in most dogs and cats typically have 20 to 24 caudal vertebrae. 6 Cranially, the caudal vertebrae are similar to the lumbar elements; caudal to Cd6, they become elongated and lack a vertebral arch. Y-shaped hemal arches are present ventrally on Cd4-Cd6 and protect the median coccygeal artery, which lies ventral to the vertebral centra.
