Epidermoid and Dermoid Cysts or Sinuses Epidermoid and dermoid cysts and sinuses are caused by failure of separation of the surface ectoderm (forming the epidermis) and neuroectoderm (forming the nervous system) during embryogenesis. They have a complex wall and contain both epidermoid tissue and adnexa. They can be associated with the dermal, ocular, and central nervous system (CNS), and the most common CNS manifestation is of a sinus connection with the skin surface that may extend into the vertebral canal to affect the spinal cord ( “ dermoid sinus ” ). 141 As opposed to sinuses, epidermoid and dermoid cysts do not have an opening onto the midline surface of the skin. 142 With epidermoid cysts or si- nuses, the wall of the lesion consists of strati ﬁ ed squamous epithelium, supported by connective tissue stroma. Keratin squames are found within the lesion along with a few in ﬂ am- matory cells. Dermoid cysts and sinuses differ from epidermoid cysts because the dermoid cyst contains other features of skin, such as sweat glands, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands. Epidermoid and dermoid cysts con ﬁ ned strictly to the CNS without a cutaneous or subcutaneous tract develop from skin- determining ectoderm, which remains attached to mesoderm and as the neural tube closes becomes surrounded by the meninges. 143 In such instances, no tract or sinus is present in the dorsal paraspinal soft tissue or skin. 143 Spinal dermoid sinuses fall into one of six categories, depending on how deep the connecting tract penetrates 144 :  Type I: Tubular sac extending from the skin to the supra- spinous or nuchal ligament  Type II: More super ﬁ cial tract, with a deep ﬁ brous strand connecting to the supraspinous or nuchal ligament  Type III: Super ﬁ cial tract with no connection to the supra- spinous or nuchal ligament  Type IV: Deep tract that communicates with the vertebral canal and is attached to the dura mater  Type V: True dermoid “ cyst, ” with a closed capsule and no deeper connection or opening to the skin  Type VI: Deep tract that extends to the supraspinous or nuchal ligament and continues deeper as a ﬁ brous strand that connects to the dura mater Only types IV and VI may be associated with neurologic signs, due to their relationship with the dura mater; in these cases, neurologic signs can be the result of infection (absces- sation, meningitis, meningomyelitis, and so on), compression of the spinal cord due to progressive enlargement of the deeper portion of the tract with accumulated debris (hair follicles, sebum, keratin, desquamated epithelial cells), tethering of the spinal cord, 144 and syringomyelia. 144 There are only a few reports on the use of CT and MRI in the diagnosis and presurgical assessment of epidermoid and der- moid cysts in dogs. CT imaging can allow detection of a communication with the vertebral canal through a defect in the vertebral arch, with subsequent spinal cord compression and displacement. 145 146 The MRI abnormalities reported with spinal dermoid sinus include a focal invagination of the cutaneous tissues toward the spinous processes corresponding to the clinically palpable lesion ( Fig. 15.30 ). Deep to that area, there may be a focal rounded or lenticular subcutaneous lesion, corresponding to the main cavity of the sinus, followed by a tubular tract extending ventrally to a variable depth, depending on the type of dermoid sinus. The lumen of the sinus and its tract is often ﬁ lled with sebum, keratin debris, and hair, resulting in a vari- able and unpredictable MR signal. Compared to muscles, the lesions tend to be T2-hyperintense to muscles, whereas T1W signal is more variable (hypo-, iso-, hyperintense). 147 149 Areas that are hyperintense on both T1W and T2W images may correspond to lipid lining. 147 In a report where gadolinium contrast medium was administered intravenously, only minimal enhancement was seen. 147 In a patient where the sinus was abscessed, the lesion was markedly T2-hyperintense and T1- hypointense with a hypointense wall on both T1W and T2W images, suggestive of a thick capsule. 142 In types IV and VI, which have a dural connection, additional signs may include a linear, somewhat tortuous tract of variable signal intensity, extending deep to the skin toward the spine and entering the vertebral canal, connecting with the dura mater, usually through an interarcuate space, and in some instances through a defect of the dorsal arch (schisis). 147 149 151 Concurrent verte- bral malformations may be present, such as spina bi ﬁ da vertebral blocks, partial fusion of adjacent spinous processes, and incomplete dorsal lamina. 144 147 149 151 Such anomalies seem to be more commonly associated with dermoid sinuses that have connection with the dura mater, and therefore their identi ﬁ cation should trigger a careful examination of the meninges, subarachnoid space, and spinal cord in that general area. That lesion was heterogeneous but pre- dominantly hyperintense on both T1W and T2W images with no contrast enhancement. 141 Articular Process Cysts Cysts associated with the articular process are extradural ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled round or oval well-de ﬁ ned structures that develop as a result of degeneration of the articular process joint. 115 152 155 They are divided histologically into (1) synovial cysts lined by synovium-like epithelial cells resulting from outpouching of synovial membrane through weakened capsular tissue and (2) ganglion cysts, which are the result of mucinous degeneration of periarticular connective tissue and which do not have a sy- novial lining. From clinical and imaging perspectives, the two entities are indistinguishable and can therefore be grouped under the terminology articular process cyst 154 Clinical signs associated with articular process cysts vary from pain to ataxia and tetra- or paraparesis, although in a number of instances, the clinical signs are not attributable to the cyst, but to other causes of spinal cord compression, such as disc herniation, articular process hypertrophy, and vertebral instability. These articular process cysts appear to be more common in large- to giant-breed dogs. 115 152 155 In giant-breed dogs, the cysts tend to be multiple and located in the cervical spine and more common in young dogs. 153 In large-breed dogs, cysts are more commonly found in the thoracolumbar or lumbosacral area in young adults and older dogs. 115 152 155 The cysts can be single or multiple and present at one or several locations. Extradural Tumors The most common extradural spinal cord tumors in dogs include osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma. 157 In cats, extra- dural lymphosarcoma is also frequent. 158 159 Solitary or disseminated histiocytic sarcoma can also affect the vertebrae and cause spinal cord compression. 160 Other disseminated canine tumors with possible vertebral involvement include lymphosarcoma and multiple myeloma. 157 Metastatic vertebral tumors are also common, in particular prostatic carcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder and urethra in dogs. 157 Tumors of the paravertebral soft tissues or extradural soft tissue components of the vertebral canal are also possible, and local invasion can cause spinal cord compression. Exam- ples include soft tissue sarcoma, in ﬁ ltrative lipoma, 161 165 extradural lymphosarcoma, mast cell tumor (primary or meta- static), and hemangiosarcoma. 166 171 Both MRI and CT are more sensitive than radiography in detecting vertebral lesions and in particular bone lysis that is not apparent radiographically can be demonstrated readily us- ing CT. Vertebral canal tumors can be dif ﬁ cult to localize to the intradural, extradural, or intramedullary compartments on noncontrast CT images. 172 Injection of intravenous contrast medium and, more important, CT myelography are more pre- cise for determining the location of masses in the vertebral canal with respect to the dura. MRI is also good for localizing these lesions; however, with MRI, it is more dif ﬁ cult to localize vertebral canal masses with respect to the dura because of lower spatial resolution. 173 There are no speci ﬁ c CT or MRI features that are associated with a speci ﬁ c tumor type. 172 173 Vertebral tumors produce variable degrees of bone lysis or proliferation, which is detected easily on CT images ( Fig. 15.32 eFig. 15.7 ). In MR im- ages, periosteal reaction appears as hypointense material sur- rounding the lesion in the affected vertebra. The signal intensity of the lesion itself varies between patients and depends on tu- mor type. Detection of peripheral nerve sheath tumors with CT can be dif ﬁ cult and depends on detecting soft tissue asymmetry, because they often have attenuating properties similar to muscle. Small or diffuse peripheral nerve sheath tumors may be subtle and hard to detect, and it can also be dif ﬁ cult to assess nerve structures that are oriented obliquely to the transverse CT imaging plane. CT changes associated with peripheral nerve sheath tumors include unilateral muscle at- rophy, presence of a soft tissue mass that is isoattenuating to surrounding muscles, and contrast enhancement that is either uniform, patchy, or rim-like. 190 The mass occasionally tracks in a linear fashion into a neighboring intervertebral foramen and can invade the vertebral canal ( Fig. 15.36 ). Invasion into the thoracic cavity can also be seen. Masses as small as 1 cm can be identi ﬁ ed on CT. 190 With MRI, multiple sequences in various planes are neces- sary to identify and stage peripheral nerve sheath tumors and depict their relationship to the surrounding structures, espe- cially the intervertebral foramen and spinal cord. 187 Imaging should be performed with perfect positioning of the patient usually in dorsal recumbency with symmetric positioning of the limbs. 187 Peripheral nerve sheath tumors can be focal masses or diffuse thickening of affected nerves ( Figs. 15.37 and 15.38 eFig. 15.9 ). 187 189 Whether the tumor is mass-like or diffuse, proximal extension of the lesion into the intervertebral foramen and vertebral canal is possible, and this feature is important to detect because it affects whether the tumor can be excised completely. Compared to surrounding skeletal muscles, the tumor is usually T2-hyperintense, although mixed signal in- tensity is possible (see Fig. 15.37 ). 42 187 189 Short tau inversion recovery (STIR) pulse sequences, which reduce the signal from fat, are useful in increasing the conspicuity of the tumor. 176 187 Fat saturation on postcontrast images helps identify the tumor by increasing the contrast of enhancing tumor against the background (see Fig. 15.37 ). The tumor is most commonly T1 isointense on precontrast images but can be hyperintense or of mixed signal intensity. Most tumors have mild to strong contrast enhancement. 176 187 Additional changes seen include ipsilateral muscle atrophy. The atrophic muscles often have abnormal signal, including T2 and T1 hyperintensity, and possible mild contrast enhancement; these changes are consistent with neurogenic atrophy, edema, fat in ﬁ ltration, and ﬁ brosis. 187 Meningioma Meningiomas are slowly growing tumors of the meninges that cause neurologic de ﬁ cits primarily by compression of the spinal cord. A golf-tee sign, similar to the one observed on conventional myelography, appears when the contrast medium diverges to encompass the mass in the subarachnoid space. Widening of the subarachnoid space cranial or caudal to the mass (golf-tee sign) can be present and help determine its intradural location. However, this sign is not present consis- tently, and, as with CT, it can be dif ﬁ cult to determine the intradural/extramedullary origin of the mass, especially when the tumor invades the spinal cord ( Fig. 15.40 ). 185 Intramedullary Tumors Intramedullary tumors are rare in dogs and cats, and they can be primary or metastatic. 156 In a retrospective study, the most common canine primary intramedullary tumor was ependy- moma, followed by astrocytoma, and less commonly nephro- blastoma, chordoma, oligodendroglioma, and teratoma. 196 The most common metastatic lesions were transitional cell carci- noma and hemangiosarcoma, with less common metastatic le- sions including pheochromocytoma, mammary/pancreatic/ prostatic carcinoma, and sarcoma of unknown etiology. 196 Intramedullary neoplasia is even less common in cats, and most are glial cell tumors (most commonly astrocytomas, but also ependymomas and oligodendrogliomas). 158 197 198 They seem to be more common in the cervical spinal cord. 158 197 198 CT is poorly sensitive for diagnosis of intramedullary tumors; focal cord swelling may be seen, with variable degrees of parenchymal enhancement on postcontrast series. Reports of the MRI appearance of intramedullary neoplasms are scarce in the veterinary literature. Astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas form ovoid to elliptical mass lesions that are well marginated, located eccentrically in the spinal cord causing variable degrees of spinal cord swelling; the lesions are T1 iso- to hypointense, T2 and STIR hyperintense, and moderately contrast enhancing. 196 Ependymomas appear as elongated fusiform to ellipsoid lesions with a central location in the spinal cord, and sometimes a multifocal distribution along the neuraxis; they are T1 isointense, T2 hyperintense and strongly contrast enhancing; on sagittal T2W or T2*W images, a hypointense curved area may be seen along the cranial and caudal margins of the lesion due to chronic hemorrhage, and has been referred to as a “ cap sign. ” 196 199 Tumors With Variable Spinal Distribution Some types of spinal tumors may have variable distributions and can involve several compartments simultaneously (extradural, intradural/extramedullary, and intramedullary). The most com- mon tumors with this behavior are histiocytic sarcoma, lym- phoma, and hemangiosarcoma. Histiocytic Sarcoma Histiocytes are a category of leukocytes that occur in many tissues throughout the body. They are derived from stem cell precursors and differentiate into cells of the monocyte/macro- phage lineage or dendritic cell lineage. 200 Histiocytic sarcoma is due to neoplastic transformation of interstitial dendritic cells, with the exception of a hematophagocytic variant, which oc- curs within the splenic red pulp and arises from macro- phages. 201 Histiocytic sarcoma can be localized (most commonly as a soft tissue mass along the limbs), or dissemi- nated, affecting multiple organ systems, including the spleen, liver, lungs, lymph nodes, bone marrow, and CNS. 201 The spinal cord can be secondarily affected in histiocytic sarcoma arising from a vertebra. This has been reported more commonly in the disseminated form than the localized form. 160 Such lesions can cause extradural spinal cord compression when they invade into the vertebral canal. They may arise from the soft tissues around the bone and invade bone secondarily, or they may grow initially within the bone marrow and extend to the cortex and adjacent soft tissues. The appearance is similar to that of other aggressive vertebral neoplasm, with bone lysis and soft tissue proliferation. Direct involvement of the CNS can occur both in the disseminated form of histiocytic sarcoma and as an entity iso- lated to the CNS ( “ primary CNS histiocytic sarcoma ” ). In both cases, all parts of the neuraxis can be affected. 200 203 Retrievers and Pembroke Welsh corgis may be predisposed to CNS involvement with histiocytic sarcoma, with corgis possibly predisposed to the primary CNS form. 201 Histopathologically, neoplastic in ﬁ ltration in the subarachnoid space and lep- tomeninges with in ﬁ ltration into the white matter of the spinal cord and nerve roots is commonly found. Ill-de ﬁ ned diffuse intramedullary T2 hyperintensity with loss of the epidural fat and gray/white matter de ﬁ nition may also be seen, with mod- erate parenchymal contrast enhancement after gadolinium in- jection and mild diffuse meningeal enhancement. Meningeal enhancement in the vicinity of focal mass lesions, sometimes with a dural tail sign, may also be seen; this meningeal enhancement often extends over long distances from the mass lesion, and isolated areas of meningeal enhancement away and separate from the mass lesion is also possible, suggestive met- astatic spread of the condition through the subarachnoid space. In some cases, the only abnormality can be meningeal enhancement without a mass lesion (leptomeningeal histiocytic sarcoma). MRI features of spinal histiocytic sarcoma, such as focal mass lesions, meningeal thickening, and enhancement, can also be seen with other neoplasms (such as, lymphoma) or rare tumors (such as, meningeal oligodendrogliomatosis) and are therefore nonspeci ﬁ c. Intradural/extramedullary masses with dural tail can also be seen with meningioma. Lymphoma In both dogs and cats, lymphoma may involve many tissues outside of the lymphatic system, including the CNS. Spinal lymphoma can be secondary or primary, based on whether neoplastic lymphocytes are or not identi ﬁ ed in other organ systems, respectively. Clinical signs depend on the distribution of the lesions in the CNS and on the presence and extent of other organ systems involvement. In cats, lymphoma is the most common tumor affecting the spinal cord. 158 159 Affected cats are typically young, with short duration of clinical signs. 158 204 205 In that species, the most common location of spinal lymphoma is extradural, or mixed extra- and intradural (affecting the leptomeninges and/or the spinal cord). 158 205 Exclusive intradural location is rare. 158 Extramedullary hematopoietic tissue has been cited as the possible anlage for the development of primary lymphoma of the spine. 205 Involvement of other organ systems is common in cats with spinal lymphoma, with bone marrow and kidneys being more commonly affected. 158 204 205 In some case series, affected cats had lesions in multiple regions of the CNS, including the brain, 158 whereas in other series, single epidural lesions were more common. 205 At MRI, feline spinal lymphoma manifests as both intradural and extradural lesions, often affecting multiple compartments including the paraspinal tis- sues; the lumbar and lumbosacral regions are more commonly affected. 167 168 206 Lesions are ill-de ﬁ ned, hypointense on T1W images, hyperintense on T2W images, with homogeneous, often strong enhancement on postcontrast T1W im- ages. 167 168 206 Another study where MRI was used reports intramedullary location of lymphoma in less than half the cases of spinal lymphoma, although it does not describe details on their MRI appearance. 207 Pathologic studies are in agreement with these imaging reports, reporting involvement of both ex- tra- and intradural structures, including the spinal cord paren- chyma and nerve roots. 159 There are also reports on speci ﬁ c in ﬁ ltration of the nerves of the brachial plexus, forming mass- like lesions of the affected plexus, resembling a peripheral nerve sheath tumor, and extending into the subarachnoid space and spinal cord parenchyma proximally. 188 205 The MRI appearance of these lesions has not been reported, but one should keep this in mind when identifying mass-like lesions in ﬁ ltrating the brachial plexus and extending into the vertebral canal in cats. In dogs, lymphoma is one of the most common neoplasms, and the multicentric form accounts for about 80% of cases. In this species, lymphoma can affect the epidural tissues of the vertebral canal, vertebrae, nerve roots, paraspinal soft tissues, and less commonly the spinal cord (although the spinal cord is commonly affected secondary to compression by extradural neoplastic in ﬁ ltrates). 173 206 208 214 At MRI, canine spinal lym- phoma causes multifocal disease more commonly than focal disease. 208 There is common simultaneous regional involve- ment of multiple spinal compartments (vertebrae, paraspinal soft tissues, epidural space). 208 210 213 214 The paraspinal lesions A C B Fig. 15.40 Sagit tal T2- weighted (A) , T1-weighted with ﬂ uid-att enuatedinversion recovery (FLAIR) (B) , and postcontrast T1-weighted FLAIR (C)images of a young dog with a nephroblas toma. There are variable degrees of spinal cord compression by the epidural component of the neoplasm. 208 213 214 Signal characteristics are similar for the le- sions in the paraspinal and vertebral canal areas, being T1 iso- to hypointense, T2 and STIR hyperintense, moderately to strongly contrast enhancing. 208 In some cases, the lesions can be hyperintense on T1W precontrast images. 173 214 Heterogeneous signal on T2W images, with hypo- and hyperintense areas, is also reported, 213 as well as isointensity to surrounding mus- cles. 173 Visible vertebral lesions may involve none, one, several, or all vertebrae, and consist of patchy hyperintense areas on T2W images, which unlike fat, remain hyperintense on STIR images. In one case series, vertebral cortical involvement was not observed, even when paravertebral and epidural in ﬁ ltration around the affected vertebrae was present 208 ; however, other reports have described changes in shape of the affected vertebra with cortical involvement, seen as T2W and STIR hyperintense signal with enhancement on T1W postcontrast images, disrupting the normal hypointense signal of the cor- tex. 210 Cortical involvement has also been reported in patho- logic studies. 211 Visible vertebral bone marrow involvement on MRI is not necessarily present, even in cases of simultaneous paravertebral and epidural in ﬁ ltration. 213 214 Depending on the cellularity of the in ﬁ ltrate, vertebral bone marrow involvement with lymphoma may be present even in the absence of changes in MRI signal, including on fat-suppressed images. 215 Lep- tomeningeal involvement with enhancement on postcontrast images is also reported, 206 as well as involvement of the nerve roots and spinal cord parenchyma. 212 Due to the multicentric nature of this tumor, additional lesions may be seen in the ﬁ eld of view, including lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, spleno- megaly, and splenic nodules. Hemangiosarcoma Hemangiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm of vascular endo- thelial origin and can arise from any vascular tissue. Spinal hemangiosarcoma has been reported in dogs, either in the intramedullary location, 173 196 216 or extradural location. The extradural form can arise from the vertebrae, 217 218 accounting for about 2% to 3% of primary bone tumors of the vertebral column in dogs. Rarely, hemangiosarcoma can affect the epidural space. 171 219 Intramedullary hemangiosarcoma is usu- ally metastatic, 196 216 while the vertebral and the rare epidural forms are typically primary tumors. 166 169 220 Intradural/extra- medullary hemangiosarcoma has only been reported once. 221 MRI features of primary vertebral hemangiosarcoma include monostotic or segmental polyostotic lesions affecting several consecutive vertebrae. Signal intensity is variable and hetero- geneous and signal voids due to susceptibility artifacts may be seen on T2*W images. Signal enhancement is usually strong and heterogeneous, and cortical lysis with extension into the vertebral canal and paraspinal tissues is common. 166 169 220 At MRI, epidural or intramedullary hemangiosarcoma typi- cally shows a focal mass lesion, usually well de ﬁ ned, that is either in the epidural location causing spinal cord compression, or intramedullary. 171 173 196 216 219 Epidural lesions are isolated (primary tumor), 169 171 whereas intramedullary lesions, being metastatic, can be multifocal. 196 The signal of the mass is typically hyperintense to normal spinal cord parenchyma on T2W images (homogeneous or heterogeneous), hyperintense on STIR images, isointense to hyperintense on T1W precontrast images, and moderately to strongly contrast enhancing (some- times rim-like). 169 171 Signal voids associated with hemorrhage can be seen within the lesion on T2*W gradient echo images or susceptibility weighted imaging. 216 The spontaneous hyperintensity on T1W images may also re ﬂ ect the presence of blood degradation products. MYELOM ALACIA Myelomalacia corresponds to gross softening of the spinal cord resulting from hemorrhagic necrosis. 222 223 It can occur following acute spinal cord injury and is caused by extensive damage to intramedullary vasculature. A core of necrosis may extend cranially and caudally from the level of the spinal cord injury, typically in the base of the dorsal funiculi. A small pro- portion of dogs with acute disc extrusion will have diffuse myelomalacia, often called ascending or descending myelo- malacia. 223 Myelomalacia can affect up to 10% of dogs with acute disc extrusion that exhibit paraplegia and loss of deep pain perception. 223 The prognosis for patients with myeloma- lacia is usually poor, but improvement is possible in focal dis- ease. Therefore, MRI is useful in determining prognosis by providing information about the extent of involvement. On MRI, myelomalacia is characterized by diffuse swelling of the spinal cord that is recognized by loss of visualization of the hyperintense signal from CSF and fat around the spinal cord on T2W images. There is diffuse patchy T2 hyperintensity of the spinal cord ( Fig. 15.41 ) that extends over the length of several vertebral bodies. The affected spinal cord parenchyma is iso- intense to normal spinal cord on T1W images. 222 Areas of hypointensity associated with spinal cord hemorrhage may be visible in T2*W gradient recalled echo images. 223 In addition to the areas of T2 hyperintensity, areas of T2 hypointensity may be detected at high ﬁ eld strengths because of deoxyhemoglobin in hemorrhagic spinal cord foci. 222 223 Studies have suggested that in dogs with thoracolumbar disc herniation, a longitudinal extent of spinal cord parenchyma T2W hyperintensity higher than 4.5 to 6 times the length of L2 vertebral body could be a predictor of developing ascending/descending myelomala- cia. 222 224 A length of CSF signal attenuation on HASTE/SSFSE pulse sequences ( “ T2-myelogram ” ) > 7.4 times the length of L2 vertebral body has also been reported as a predictive MRI criterion, 225 and some studies have found this criterion as more reliable than the length of parenchymal T2W hyperintensity. 226 Another recent study found that the length of parenchymal T2 hyperintensity was not a useful predictor for future develop- ment of myelomalacia in dogs with severe neurologic de ﬁ cits who are not exhibiting clinical signs of myelomalacia. 227 Absence of T2W spinal cord hyperintensity, however, does not rule out future development of myelomalacia particularly if imaging occurs less than 24 hours after onset of paraplegia. 224 226 228 229 Fig. 15.41 Sagittal T2-weighted image of the lumbar spine in a dog withacute disc herniation at L5 L6 and secon dary ascending myelomalacia .There is an ill-de ﬁ ned patchy intram edullary T2 hyperintensity in visiblesegments of the lumbar spinal cord. Traditionally, dis- cospondylitis was diagnosed based on characteristic radio- graphic changes together with laboratory ﬁ ndings. A limitation of radiography is the delay of up to a few weeks between the onset of clinical signs and detection of radiographic changes. Paravertebral in ﬂ ammation with similar signal characteristics is also frequently seen. 259 Spinal Epidural Empyema Spinal epidural empyema is presence of a suppurative lesion in the epidural space. 255 260 263 The clinical signs include fever, pain, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Spinal empyema is relatively rare in dogs. Causes include extension of adjacent osteomyelitis or discospondylitis or hematogenous spread. On noncontrast CT, an epidural mass is suspected based on lack of visualization of hypoattenuating epidural fat around the spinal cord, but the epidural mass is best identi ﬁ ed with CT myelography. 261 262 Intrathecal contrast medium injection can facilitate spread of the infection in the subarachnoid space because of iatrogenic contamination. MRI is better for diagnosing spinal empyema, because it does not require subarachnoid injection of contrast me- dium. 255 260 263 Spinal empyema appears as a well-de ﬁ ned epidural mass in the dorsal or ventral aspect of the vertebral canal. The lesion forms a high or mixed signal mass on T2W images but is usually T1-hypointense. Hyperintense le- sions in the gray matter of the spinal cord adjacent to the epidural mass can be seen, which may be caused by compression of the spinal cord by the mass or by vascular compromise. 260 Meningomyelitis Meningitis and myelitis can have an infectious or noninfectious origin. 264 272 Infectious agents in dogs include viruses (e.g., canine distemper), bacteria (e.g., Staphylococcus Pas- teurella Actinomyces , and Nocardia spp.), fungi (e.g., Cryptococcus Blastomyces Histoplasma , and Cocci- dioides spp.), Rickettsiae (e.g., Ehrlichia spp., Rickettsia rick- ettsii ), protozoa (e.g., Toxoplasma gondii Neospora caninum ), parasites (e.g., Diro ﬁ laria immitis Angios- trongylus spp.), and rarely algae (e.g., Prototheca wick- erhamii Prototheca zop ﬁ i ). 267 In cats, feline infectious peritonitis and toxoplasmosis have been reported. 207 Noninfectious causes of canine meningomyelitis include granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis, pyogranulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis, and steroid-responsive meningitis arteritis. 265 267 270 272 CT changes in dogs with meningomyelitis include spinal cord swelling, spinal cord hypoattenuation, and occasionally intramedullary or meningeal contrast enhancement. 266 General MRI ﬁ ndings in dogs and cats with meningomyelitis include irregular areas of intramedullary T2 hyperintensity ( Fig. 15.47 ), which are isointense or hypointense on precon- trast T1W images and have various degrees of contrast enhancement. 264 265 267 Meningeal enhancement may or may not be present. The use of fat suppression on postcontrast spinal images is important in animals with a clinical suspicion of in ﬂ ammatory pathology, as it may facilitate the recognition of subtle meningeal enhancement. 176 273 Cervical MRI abnormalities are quite common in dogs with steroid-responsive meningitis arteritis, and include T1W post- contrast enhancement of the meninges, synovium of the artic- ular process joints, and paravertebral muscles with less commonly spinal cord parenchymal enhancement. 273 Intradural hemorrhage causing cord compression has also been reported (see “ Spinal Hemorrhage ” section). 242 In general, MRI changes of meningomyelitis are nonspeci ﬁ c, and other conditions (such as myelomalacia, ischemic myelopathy, or some neoplastic conditions such as histiocytic sarcoma 202 or lymphosarcoma 207 264 ) can produce similar changes. Therefore, correlation with clinical signs and labora- tory test results is necessary. VERTEBR AL ANOM ALIES Congenital anomalies of the spine that can be assessed with CT or MRI include atlantoaxial malformation, hemivertebrae, block vertebrae, butter ﬂ y vertebrae, transitional vertebrae, and spina bi ﬁ da (see Fig. 15.30 ). Most of these anomalies can be diag- nosed radiographically (see Chapter 14 ); however, CT and MRI can provide important additional information. CT provides a better understanding of the bony abnormality and spatial rela- tionship between the abnormal and adjacent vertebrae and ef- fect of the anomaly on the vertebral canal and intervertebral foramina ( Fig. 15.48 ). MRI is indicated when assessment of the spinal cord and associated nerve roots is desired, especially when the consequences of the vertebral anomalies need to be assessed. It can be caused by various primary problems, including abnormalities of the caudal fossa (Chiari-like malfor- mations), but also other conditions, such as a quadrigeminal cistern cyst, tethered spinal cord, trauma, arachnoiditis, and neoplasia. Any condition that results in altered CSF ﬂ ow in the caudal fossa of the skull or in the vertebral column can result in the development of a syrinx. 130 281 309 Chiari-like malformation is common in the Cavalier King Charles spaniel but is reported in other breeds as well. 310 The A B C Fig. 15.47 Sagittal T2-weight ed (A) , transverse precontrast T1-weighted (B) , and transverse postcontrast T1-weighted (C) images at the level of C2 in a dog with meningomy elitis caused by Cryptococcus infection. basioccipital bone is presumed to be short, resulting in a reduced caudal fossa volume. This causes the caudal aspect of the cerebellar vermis and medulla to extend into or through the foramen magnum causing obstruction of CSF ﬂ ow. CSF dis- placed by each systolic cycle through the compressed sub- arachnoid space results in a high-velocity jet, and this causes an abnormal pressure differential between the spinal cord and subarachnoid space in the cervical area. 289 290 293 303 There is a relative increase in intramedullary pressure and decrease in subarachnoid pressure, the consequence of which is repeated mechanical distention of the spinal cord. This in turn results in ﬂ uid accumulation in the spinal cord, with cavitation and accumulation of extracellular ﬂ uid that coalesces eventually into elongated cavities and syrinx formation; these cavities are commonly separate from the central canal. 289 303 MRI is a good modality to assess the presence and extent of the syrinx. 284 The syrinx may take the form of a cavity or be complex with septations. A portion of the central canal is usually involved at some level. The longitudinal extent of the syrinx can be evaluated on sagittal images, appearing T2- hyperintense and T1-hypointense ( Fig. 15.50 ). In Chiari-like malformation, the cerebellar vermis and medulla extend into or through the foramen magnum, which is occluded with little or no CSF around neural structures. The magnitude of cerebellar herniation is not correlated with severity. There is typically ventricular dilatation. The cranial cervical and cranial thoracic segments of the spinal cord are typically the most severely affected by the syrinx. Maximum syrinx width is the strongest predictor of pain, scratching behavior, and scoliosis; 95% of Cavalier King Charles spaniels with a maximum syrinx width of 0.64 cm or more will have associated clinical signs, 302 although myelopathic signs develop as soon as the syrinx reaches 4 mm width. 311 Larger syringes with involvement of the dorsal horns of the gray matter of the spinal cord and asymmetrical appearance on transverse images may be associated with persistent neuropathic pain, although the relative contribution of the asymmetry and syrinx size is controversial. 302 312 R E F E R E N C E S 1. There are a few highly speci ﬁ c ancillary projections in dogs that allow evaluation of the edge of surfaces that cannot be assessed in the conventional views. Examples include a cra- nioproximal/craniodistal view of the bicipital groove for changes associated with bicipital tenosynovitis ( Fig. 17.1A ) and a ﬂ exed dorsoplantar view of the canine tarsus for evaluation of the trochlea of talus without superimposition of calcaneus, for changes associated with osteochondrosis of the talus (see Fig. 17.1B ). These speci ﬁ c views are provided only as examples of how changing the orientation of the x-ray beam can lead to projection of clinically important surfaces that cannot be assessed adequately in more standard views. These ancillary views, and others, are discussed throughout the textbook where appropriate. 1 POSITIO NING: HORSE One aspect of equine radiography that deserves special mention is the common practice of holding the plate by hand. Equine extremity radiographs are almost always acquired with the horse in a standing position, and holding the plate by hand is convenient. However, handholding the plate increases the chance that radiation safety practices will be compromised. Individuals holding a plate by hand should wear protective lead aprons and lead gloves, as well as a thyroid shield and protec- tive lead glasses. And the positioning must be such that no part of the holder is in the primary x-ray beam. The use of a plate holder for equine extremity radiography is encouraged because it will minimize occupational radiation exposure. A plate holder secures the plate and has an extension handle so that the hands are distant from the primary x-ray beam. A potential disadvantage of a plate holder is the strength needed to position the plate properly. There are very few instances in the horse where two orthogonal views of a limb will suf ﬁ ce. Two orthogonal views might be adequate for examining the radius or tibia, but even in those sites, oblique views are often needed for completeness. Oblique views are intended to project edges of a joint or region that cannot be evaluated in standard orthogonal views. More than the edge of a structure can be assessed in any radiograph, but important edge lesions can be overlooked unless they are projected at the periphery of the part. Oblique views maximize the chances of detecting an edge lesion in a complex joint. In oblique views, the point of entrance of the primary x-ray beam is typically moved 30 to 45 degrees medial or 30 to 45 degrees lateral to the point of entrance used for a conventional view. The geometry of oblique projections can be confusing, and this will be explained using the equine carpus as a model ( Table 17.1 Figs. 17.2 17.5 ). y In a dorsopalmar view of the carpus, the x-ray beam strikes the dorsal surface and the medial and lateral edges are pro- jected in an unobstructed fashion (see Fig. 17.2 ). A palmar- odorsal view would be similar. In a lateromedial view of the carpus, the x-ray beam strikes the lateral surface, and the dorsal and palmar edges are pro- jected in an unobstructed fashion (see Fig. 17.3 ). A mediolateral view would be similar. In a dorsolateral-palmaromedial view of the carpus, the x-ray beam strikes the dorsolateral surface (between the true dorsal and lateral surfaces) with the dorsomedial and palmarolateral edges projected in an unobstructed fashion (see Fig. 17.4 ). A palmaromedial-dorsolateral view would be similar. In a dorsomedial-palmarolateral view of the carpus, the x-ray beam strikes the dorsomedial surface with the dorsolateral and palmaromedial edges projected in an unobstructed fashion (see Fig. 17.5 ). A palmarolateral-dorsomedial view would be similar. Destruction of the Cortex For cortex destruction, also referred to as cortex effacement , to be apparent radiographically, the region of destruction must be hit tangentially by the primary x-ray beam. In other words, the edge of the cortex destruction must be visible radiographically, and this depends on the orientation of the cortical destruction with the primary x-ray beam ( Figs. 17.6 17.8 ). If the cortex destruction is not projected tangentially, the affected region of bone will appear more radiolucent, but a discrete area of cortex destruction will not be identi ﬁ ed. Not all bone destruction involves the cortex. Bone loss can be totally within the medullary cavity with preservation of the cortex. Purely medullary bone loss does not mean that the lesion is not aggressive; it means only that one feature of lesion aggressiveness (i.e., cortical destruction) is not present. Periosteal Reaction Periosteal bone proliferation is most commonly caused by elevation of the periosteum or regional hyperemia causing activation of bone-forming mesenchymal cells ( Fig. 17.13 ). An active periosteal reaction is a feature of an aggressive bone lesion and is one where the margin of the periosteal reaction is irregular , not smooth. There are various degrees of periosteal reactivity and almost innumerable speci ﬁ c appearances of an active periosteal reaction. The presence of an irregular margin is the clue that the periosteal reaction is active. Any evidence of periosteal irregularity is consistent with an aggressive bone lesion ( Figs. 17.14 17.16 ). In comparison, a nonaggressive periosteal reaction is characterized by a smooth edge to the periosteal new bone growth ( Figs. 17.17 and 17.18 ) due to remodeling of the periosteal surface after a previous insult or a very slowly proceeding disease process. A smooth periosteal reaction does not mean that the lesion is not aggressive as there may be another ﬁ nding that characterizes the lesion as aggres- sive. In aggressive bone lesions, the host bone is unable to contain the lesion as the ongoing disease process does not allow for mineral deposition to contain the lesion, and there is no demarcation between the lesion and the host bone ( Fig. 17.20 , see Fig. 17.17 ). As already noted, it is not necessary for a lesion to have all three radiographic features of aggressiveness (cortical destruc- tion, active periosteal reaction, and an indistinct transition zone) to be characterized as aggressive. Any single criterion is suf ﬁ cient. Moreover, the combined radiographic features of the aggressiveness of a bone lesion are a continuum from a minor alteration in cortex integrity, periosteal response, or transition zone, to major alterations in all three parameters. Importantly, there is not a clinically signi ﬁ cant correlation between the number of aggressive features of a lesion, or the extent of their aggressiveness, and the biologic behavior of the lesion. In other words, low radiographic aggressiveness does not mean low biologic aggressiveness. But, importantly, the absence of radiographic evidence of aggressiveness usually means no bio- logic aggressiveness. Finally, as already mentioned, the catego- rization of aggressiveness does not take into account whether the lesion is primarily productive or primarily destructive. Causes of an Aggressive Lesion If an aggressive bone lesion is identi ﬁ ed, the DAMNITV (degenerative, anomalous, metabolic, neoplastic, infectious [in ﬂ ammatory, immune], traumatic, and vascular) approach should be used to formulate the list of possible causes. Of most concern is whether the lesion is neoplastic or infectious. A de ﬁ nitive distinction between neoplastic and infectious bone lesions is impossible by radiographic means. However, the radiographic features of the bone lesion, such as the number of bones involved and the location of the lesions within the bones, along with the signalment, history, and physical and laboratory ﬁ ndings can be used to prioritize the possible causes ( Table 17.3 ). Nevertheless, a biopsy or ﬁ ne-needle aspirate with histopathologic or cytologic evaluation and possibly microbio- logic culture is almost always needed for the de ﬁ nitive diag- nosis of any aggressive bone lesion where a diagnosis cannot be assumed from the clinical scenario. Primary Bone Tumors There are many types of primary bone tumors in the dog, but osteosarcoma is the most common. Canine osteosarcoma is usually characterized by a single (monostotic) aggressive bone lesion originating in the metaphysis. 3 The age distribution of canine osteosarcoma is bimodal with a small peak in incidence at approximately 2 years of age and then a larger peak in inci- dence later in adult life. 3 Age distribution in cats is not bimodal and osteosarcoma typically occurs in older cats. 4 Most primary bone tumors enlarge from the metaphysis into the epiphysis or diaphysis, or both. Common osteosarcoma sites in the forelimb are the proximal humerus and the distal radius (away from the elbow), and in the hindlimb the distal femur and proximal tibia (toward the sti ﬂ e). Tumors in the distal tibia are also relatively common. However, a primary bone tumor can arise at any location in either the axial or appendicular skeleton. The most common canine subungual tumors are squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma ( Fig. 17.25 ), commonly occurring in large-breed dogs with black hair coats. 10 In ﬂ ammatory condi- tions of the digit are also common. The development of an aggressive digital lesion is equally frequent with neoplastic and in ﬂ ammatory conditions. Bacterial Bone Infections Bacterial osteomyelitis is more common than fungal osteomy- elitis, and in dogs and cats is usually acquired by direct inocu- lation as from an open fracture, a bite wound, or surgery. 13 Hematogenous bacterial osteomyelitis is relatively uncommon in dogs and cats, but can occur, particularly in skeletally immature, potentially immune-compromised, dogs. Bacterial osteomyelitis resulting from direct inoculation obviously has no predilection for skeletal localization and lesions develop at the site of injury. Therefore, bacterial osteomyelitis in dogs and cats usually involves one limb, but more than one bone may be involved. Bacterial osteomyelitis rarely causes a monostotic aggressive bone lesion. Bacterial osteomyelitis is covered in Chapter 19 Protozoal Bone Infections Hepatozoonosis is a rare protozoal infection that may cause polyostotic aggressive lesions. 14 Hepatozoon infections have been diagnosed in dogs throughout the world. Most infections occur in the southern portion of the United States. Radio- graphically, lesions are mainly periosteal and range from irreg- ular periosteal proliferation to smooth laminar thickening of the periosteum. Lesions can occur in the axial or appendicular skeleton. 15 The smooth periosteal reaction form can be misleading because one does not typically associate smooth periosteal reaction with disseminated bone infection. Although neoplasia and infection are the two most impor- tant considerations for an aggressive bone lesion, there are many other clinical entities that result in an aggressive bone lesion. In these instances, the diagnosis is usually made radio- graphically, in combination with the clinical scenario, rather than with an aspirate or biopsy. Some examples are canine panosteitis and metaphyseal osteopathy (hypertrophic osteo- dystrophy). However, the appearance of this lesion in the medullary cavity of a long bone in a 7-month-old German shepherd is so characteristic of canine panosteitis that other possibilities are not considered, and a biopsy or thoracic radiographs are not indicated. Interpretation Paradigm Like in all body systems, an organized approach to radiographic interpretation of the appendicular skeleton is needed. This begins with an overview of technique, according the following questions, followed by evaluation for abnormalities. Are the radiographic views adequate, and are all of the views that are needed present? Are oblique or other ancillary views needed? Do the views correspond to the clinical localization of the lesion? Are the radiographic technique and positioning adequate? Has a grid been used? Did this affect the quality of the image? Has sedation or anesthesia been used? If not, how will this affect the utility of the radiographs? What is the species and breed of the patient? Was a horizontally directed x-ray beam used with handhold- ing of the cassette or a wall-mounted cassette holder? Was the cassette held by hand? Is there motion artifact? Has the joint above and below the location of a suspected bone lesion been included in the imaging study? Will radiographs of the contralateral limb be helpful? What congenital anomalies are present that alter the normal appearance of the bone but may not be clinicall y signi ﬁ cant? After these variables have been considered, the images can be scrutinized for abnormalities. The roentgen sign and DAM- NITV methods described in Chapter 6 should be used, along with an assessment of lesion aggressiveness. Unfortunately, bone is very limited in its response to injury. There will be either more or less bone than normal, a periosteal response will be either present or not, and the soft tissues will be either involved or not. Thus, the distribution within the skeleton and the assessment of the patient signalment become extremely important factors in formulating a reasonable differential diag- nosis and for formulating a plan ( Table 17.4 ). Regardless, especially for aggressive bone lesions, cytologic and/or micro- biologic testing of a tissue sample, from bone or other involved tissue, will be needed for de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Experienced radiologists may have a random search pattern, but it is recommended that inexperienced interpreters use an organized approach. 7 Having a mental checklist to guide the order of interpretation will reduce the number of errors ( Box 17.1 ). In addition to a general examination of the images, it is also helpful to scrutinize appendicular radiographs with a precon- ception of what disease might be found in a particular region in a particular patient. This is particularly true in young canine and feline patients, where developmental and juvenile bone dis- eases are often characterized by very speci ﬁ c ﬁ ndings. This is de ﬁ ned as targeted viewing and was introduced earlier (see Chapter 6 ). Examples of targeted viewing are close examination of the (1) proximal margin of the anconeal process in dogs at risk of having elbow dysplasia, (2) proximal margin of the medial ridge of the talus in dogs at risk for tarsal osteochond- rosis, and (3) distal radial and ulnar metaphysis in young dogs at risk for hypertrophic osteodystrophy. It is critical that targeted viewing be used as an ancillary method. It is a way of double checking that all possibilities have been addressed. Assessing radiographs with only a preconceived idea of what will be present will invariably lead to overlooked lesions and missed diagnoses. Kathryn L. Phillips D evelopmental orthopedic disease is a grouping of variable diseases tied together by the population that they affect. This chapter reviews the basic patho- physiology and radiographic appearance of the more common developmental orthopedic diseases in dogs and cats. There are a few trends across this diverse grouping. The lesions are often generalized or at least bilaterally symmetric, for example, affecting all the epiphyses as with congenital hypothyroidism, or all the physes as with rickets, or mirroring lesions on both thoracic or both pelvic limbs as with hypertrophic osteodys- trophy (HOD) and osteochondrosis (OC). Because these dis- eases have known predilection sites, the anatomic distribution of the lesions can be used to make the diagnosis or at least limit the differential list. In this chapter the diseases are grouped based on their anatomic distribution ( Table 18.1 ). Degenerative joint disease is a common sequela to devel- opmental disorders of the immature skeleton, particularly when the primary lesion involves joints or produces limb deformity. Adult patients will frequently present with lameness attribut- able to the secondary degenerative joint disease. Advanced degenerative changes can mask the original developmental lesion on radiographs. DISOR DERS PRIMA RILY AFF ECTING JOINTS Osteochondrosis and Osteochondrosis Dissecans Osteochondrosis (OC) is a common cause of lameness in young, rapidly growing, large-breed dogs. Clinical signs usually develop between 6 and 9 months of age. OC occurs from epiphyseal cartilage necrosis, resulting in a failure of normal endochondral ossi ﬁ cation. If the vascular bed of the adjacent subchondral bone can envelop and bypass the region of carti- lage necrosis, endochondral ossi ﬁ cation may resume without development of a clinical lesion. Otherwise, focal failure of endochondral ossi ﬁ cation leads to divots within the sub- chondral bone and progressive chondromalacia may lead to development of clefts or ﬁ ssures extending from the surface of the cartilage to the subchondral bone. The terms osteochond- rosis and osteochondritis have both been historically used in the literature. Osteochondritis implies in ﬂ ammation, and in ﬂ ammation is not a component of the primary developmental disease and the term is therefore not used in this chapter. 1 Osteochondrosis (OC) is further characterized into osteo- chondrosis dissecans (OCD) when there is a complete ﬁ ssure through the cartilage creating a ﬂ ap. As chondral ﬂ aps and fragments are of soft tissue opacity, they cannot be radio- graphically identi ﬁ ed. However, when they become ossi ﬁ ed and an osteochondral fragment is radiographically apparent, the term osteochondrosis dissecans is more speci ﬁ c. OC occurs at speci ﬁ c anatomic locations and is frequently bilaterally symmetric; thus, if an OC lesion is identi ﬁ ed, radio- graphs of the contralateral limb should be performed. It is rare for a lesion to occur outside of the predilection sites. In dogs the predilection sites are caudal aspect of the humeral head, distomedial humeral trochlea, lateral and medial femoral con- dyles, and the medial and lateral trochlear ridges of the talus. Radiographic Signs Radiographic ﬁ ndings of OC include ﬂ attening or concavity of the affected subchondral bone surface with or without sub- chondral bone sclerosis. This may result in nonuniformity and apparent widening of the joint space. When mineralized, a cartilage ﬂ ap is sometimes seen within the subchondral defect, and separate osteochondral fragments (joint mice) may migrate within the joint space. Fragments that have migrated often adhere to the synovial lining and may become vascularized and continue to mineralize and enlarge over time. Joint effusion or joint capsule thickening may present as a localized region of soft tissue thickening centered on the affected joint. A sub- chondral bone defect is occasionally seen involving the artic- ular surface opposite the primary lesion. These defects are called kissing lesions . Degenerative joint disease is a common sequel to OC. Detection of lesions on the caudal humeral head can be dif ﬁ cult as this surface is spherical in shape and the beam must be tangential to the subchondral bone divot to be detected. If a lesion is not identi ﬁ ed but clinically suspected, obtaining addi- tional lateral views in varying degrees of supination can aid in detection of focal subchondral bone ﬂ attening. OC of the lateral trochlea of the talus can be obscured by superimposition of the calcaneus in the dorsoplantar view. In this instance, a dorsolateral-plantaromedial oblique 2 or a ﬂ exed dorsoplantar view can be acquired to provide an unobstructed view of the lesion. In the sti ﬂ e, the fossa for the origin of the long digital extensor muscle is sometimes mistaken for a lateral femoral condyle OC lesion because it is superimposed on the dorso- lateral aspect of the condyle on both the lateromedial and the caudocranial views ( Figs. 18.1 18.3 eFig. 18.1 ). Ununited Anconeal Process Ununited anconeal processes are a disease of large-breed dogs. A number of large-breed dogs have a normal separate center of ossi ﬁ cation at the anconeal process during development. 4 5 Small, separate centers of ossi ﬁ cation can be seen radiograph- ically in puppies starting at 13 weeks of age. The anconeal process should be fused normally to the olecranon of the ulna by 150 days (5 months) of age. Radiographic Signs The primary radiographic ﬁ nding is best seen on the ﬂ exed lateral view and consists of a radiolucent line separating the anconeal process from the olecranon in dogs older than 150 days ( Fig. 18.4 eFig. 18.2 ). This lucent line is at the base of the anconeal process and can be sharply de ﬁ ned or it may appear irregular and of variable width. Degenerative joint dis- ease of the elbow is a common sequel, and periarticular new bone production from osteoarthrosis may partially obscure the lucency between the ulna and the anconeal process. Medial Coronoid Process Disease Medial coronoid process disease is the most common devel- opmental disorder involving the elbow joint and one of the most common causes for thoracic limb lameness in dogs. Medial coronoid process disease includes fragmentation as well as sclerosis and remodeling of the medial coronoid process. It affects medium- and large-breed dogs primarily and has a signi ﬁ cantly higher incidence in males. Clinical signs may be apparent as early as 4 to 6 months of age. Radiographic visibility of the medial coronoid is hampered by superimposition of the radius ( Fig. 18.5 eFig. 18.3 ). In most instances, the radio- graphic diagnosis of fragmented medial coronoid process is made indirectly through recognition of degenerative changes that accompany the primary lesion. Radiographic Signs Primary radiographic signs include an abnormal contour or poor de ﬁ nition of the cranial margin of the medial coronoid process on the lateral view. Often the margin, which is radio- graphically distinct in normal dogs, cannot be followed proxi- mally to the articular surface in affected animals. On the craniocaudal view, the medial margin of the medial coronoid process may appear blunted, rounded, or tipped distally. A separate osseous body, representing the fragmented coronoid process, is seen rarely. Joint incongruity or subluxation may also be present and appears as a stair-step lesion between the ulna and the radial head on the lateral view. However, caution should be used to prevent overinterpretation of this ﬁ nding. On the lateral view, the normal overlapping lucent lines repre- senting the complex elbow joint margins can be confused with joint incongruity if there is any proximal to distal or vice versa obliquity present. 6 7 Secondary degenerative joint disease is frequent even in young patients. Osteophyte formation on the proximal margin of the anconeal process is one of the earliest signs of degenerative joint disease. Subchondral bone sclerosis also develops along the distal border of the trochlear notch in the region of the lateral coronoid process. 7 10 These secondary ﬁ ndings are best appreciated on the lateral view. A large osteophyte may arise from the medial coronoid margin on the craniocaudal view in addition to the more generalized osteo- phyte production. Congenital Radial Head Luxation Congenital caudolateral radial head luxation has been reported in a variety of dog breeds including bull-dogs, Bouvier de Flandres, Shih Tzu, and Afghan hounds. 11 Affected puppies present with mild forelimb lameness ﬁ rst noticed at 3 to 4 months of age with physical examination ﬁ ndings of pain and reduced range of motion in the affected elbow. Radiographic Signs Caudal and lateral luxation of the radius relative to the distal humerus is the primary radiographic ﬁ nding ( Fig. 18.6 ). The radial epiphysis may appear convex because articulation with the humeral condyle has not resulted in normal development. The articulation of the humerus with the ulna is typically normal and there is no evidence of trauma. Hip Dysplasia Hip dysplasia is an extremely common disease caused by abnormal development of the coxofemoral joints. It is a disease that ranges from mild alterations in gait and mobility to debili- tating lameness. The majority of the clinical signs are caused by secondary osteoarthritis. Hip dysplasia mainly occurs in large- breed dogs, but it can also affect small dogs and cats. Canine hip dysplasia is a polygenic inherited disease that is in ﬂ uenced by environmental factors. It is a disease that is not detectable at birth but during growth laxity of the joint de- velops. As the animal moves, the joints subluxate resulting in altered biomechanical forces on the articular surfaces. Without normal forces applied, the acetabulum does not develop a normal cup-like shape and the femoral head is ﬂ attened. The osteophytes have predilection site for the cranial border of the acetabulum, and unlike dogs, cats have little remodeling around the femoral neck. 17 Distraction techniques are used to measure hip laxity. Several ways of performing distraction views have been re- ported, but the most common method is the PennHIP method. The patient is in dorsal recumbency, and a specially shaped distraction device is placed between the femurs which are in a neutral position relative to the acetabulum and pointing up- wards at a right angle to simulate the dog standing. The device is used as a fulcrum to distract the femoral heads from the ac- etabulum as the femurs are pressed against the bars of the distraction device. The DI is calculated by drawing a circle of best ﬁ t around the femoral head and a second circle of best ﬁ t of the acetabulum, then measuring the distance from the center of both of these circles divided by the radius of the circle of the femoral head ( Fig. 18.9 ). The smaller the DI, the less laxity is present. The DIs vary for different breeds of dogs. The PennHIP group has collected data on thousands of dogs and is commercially available. The PennHIP method has inherent ad- vantages over the extended hip method of evaluating the cox- ofemoral joints. First, it quanti ﬁ es joint laxity, which is generally accepted as the beginning of a chain of events that culminates in coxofemoral degenerative joint disease. Second, the exami- nation can be performed on young dogs. The predictive value of the DI is constant after 6 months of age, thereby providing valuable information to breeders at an early age when selecting their stock. Third, the technique predicts a DI below which degenerative changes are unlikely to occur. Conversely, the DI and the subsequent development of degenerative joint disease appear to have a direct relation when the DI is greater than 0.3 (for German shepherd dogs) or 0.4 (for Labrador Retrievers and Rottweilers). Aseptic Necrosis of the Femoral Head (Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease) Aseptic necrosis of the femoral head occurs in adolescent toy and small-breed dogs ( Fig. 18.10 eFig. 18.5 ). Compromised blood supply to the femoral capital epiphysis causes necrosis of subchondral bone while overlying articular cartilage continues to grow. Revascularization occurs in an attempt to repair the defect, and removal of necrotic bone causes decreased opacity in the affected femoral head. Incomplete removal of necrotic bone and invasion of granulation tissue interferes with healing, resulting in a misshapen femoral head of nonuniform opacity. 18 Radiographic Signs As with many of the other developmental skeletal disorders, the radiographic ﬁ ndings of aseptic necrosis of the femoral head vary with the duration of the lesion. Radiographs of the hip joints may appear normal early in the course of the disease. As the disease progresses, lucencies can be detected within the subchondral bone within the femoral head. Areas of decreased opacity may also appear in both the femoral epiphysis and the metaphysis. Flattening and irregularity of the femoral head and neck become apparent as the affected bone remodels and col- lapses on itself. Remodeling of the femoral head may cause coxofemoral joint space widening and subluxation. Fragmen- tation of the femoral head may eventually occur from patho- logic fracture. Muscle atrophy and radiographic ﬁ ndings associated with degenerative joint disease usually develop. Radiographic evaluation of both hips is indicated because this disease may be bilateral. After identifying an epiphyseal dysplasia radiographically, the diagnosis can be con ﬁ rmed by measuring thyroid and thyroid stimulating hormone concentrations. Radiographic Signs Radiographic ﬁ ndings consist of epiphyseal dysplasia that ap- pears as reduced or delayed ossi ﬁ cation of the epiphyseal cartilage model. This is seen most easily in the proximal tibia and the humeral and femoral condyles. Cuboid bone ossi ﬁ ca- tion in the carpus and tarsus is also delayed. Vertebral bodies are shorter than normal as a result of endplate dysplasia. The skull may appear shorter and broader than normal. Degenera- tive joint disease may be seen as a sequel. More than 10 forms are recognized in people, each produced by a different enzyme defect. Many of these have also been identi ﬁ ed in dogs and cats. 22 24 The best-studied animal form is the feline form of mucopolysaccharidosis VI (MPS-VI). It causes polyarthropathies because of faulty cartilage formation. The morphologic appearance of affected cats ranges from normal to short-legged dwarfs with facial dysmorphism. Feline MPS-VI has two genotypes. The least affected phenotype ranges from being physically and clinically normal to having degenerative joint disease of the shoulder and sti ﬂ e joints. The classic form produces phenotypic features of dwar ﬁ sm and facial dysmorphia. These cats tend to have lameness and develop hind limb paresis. The diagnosis is con ﬁ rmed by an MPS urine spot test that looks for the presence of undegraded glycosaminoglycans in the urine. Radiographic Signs Radiographic changes of mucopolysaccharidosis involve both the axial and the appendicular skeleton. Generalized epiphyseal dysplasia is present, involving long bones and vertebral end- plates. Severely affected animals are osteopenic. Findings include delayed and incomplete mineralization of the epiphy- seal cartilage model. Ossi ﬁ ed regions of the epiphyses are smaller than normal and have a nonuniform opacity with a granular appearance. Vertebral bodies appear cuboid and shorter than normal ( Fig. 18.12 eFig. 18.8 ). The maxilla is short and ﬂ attened; the frontal sinuses may be small or absent. Pro- gressive degenerative joint disease occurs as a result of the epiphyseal malformations. Coxofemoral subluxation or luxation may result from femoral head epiphysis remodeling. Ventral bridging spondylosis is seen in older animals. Multiple Epiphyseal Dysplasia Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is described in people where at least ﬁ ve different familial mutations have been identi ﬁ ed and result in variation of inappropriately mineralized epiphyses. Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is very rare, with only sporadic reports in veterinary medicine including a cohort of Beagles reported in the 1970s and a retrospective evaluation that yiel- ded 19 cases from 10 different litters of Hygenhund, Dunker, Golden Retriever, and English pointers. The breeding of two affected Beagle dogs yielded an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. 25 27 The dogs are normal at birth and by 5 to 8 months of age the puppies are chronically lame. Some have angular limb deformities. The disease is characterized by failure of ossi ﬁ cation of the epiphyses, apophyses, cuboidal bones, and sesamoids. Affected individuals have delayed growth and never reach normal size. This is a diagnosis of exclusion as speci ﬁ c genetic mutations are not known in dogs. Epiphyseal dysplasia is diagnosed radiographically and the more common causes including congenital hypothyroidism and mucopolysacchar- idosis are excluded by measuring serum thyroid concentrations and evaluating for glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in the urine. Radiographic Signs These include stippling of the epiphyses and irregular epiphy- seal margins. Affected epiphyses eventually mineralize but are moderately deformed. Aberrant separate centers of ossi ﬁ cation that eventually fuse with the normal ossi ﬁ cation centers have also been described. Accelerated degenerative joint disease occurs. Sporadic reports have been made of other medium- and large-breed dogs affected by this disor- der. 30 31 Two separate centers of ossi ﬁ cation in the humeral condyle appear typically by approximately 22 days after birth. The medial and lateral centers of the condyle should fuse by approximately 84 days after birth. Incomplete ossi ﬁ cation leads to the presence of a thin ﬁ ssure separating the medial and lateral halves of the humeral condyle in skeletally mature dogs. The ﬁ ssure line can be subtle and dif ﬁ cult to detect radio- graphically, whereas CT is more sensitive. An increased incidence of frag- mented coronoid processes appears to be associated with this disorder. Rickets Rickets is a rare disease of dogs and cats and is de ﬁ ned as osteomalacia of the physes in juvenile patients due to inade- quate vitamin D or heritable disorders affecting vitamin D metabolism or utilization. The decreased vitamin D results in insuf ﬁ cient absorption of calcium and phosphorus from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Affected juvenile patients present with hypocalcemia, alopecia, thickening at level of metaphyses, bowing or angular deformities, and lameness. Rickets can be concomitant with secondary hyperparathyroidism as the lack of vitamin D will inhibit GI absorption of calcium. Vitamin D can be manufactured in the skin with ultraviolet light in reptiles, amphibians, birds, and herbivores whereas carnivore dogs and cats obtain vitamin D from dietary sources. 32 Fortunately, rickets from dietary de ﬁ ciencies is rarely seen in dogs and cats. Hereditary disorders of vitamin D metabolism are sporadically reported in both dogs and cats and are categorized as vitamin D dependent rickets type I, where there is a de ﬁ ciency in the enzyme that converts vitamin D to its active form. Type II is also known as hereditary vitamin D resistant rickets where there is an anomaly of the vitamin D receptor on the target organs. 33 Radiographic Findings Radiographic ﬁ ndings of rickets include marked widening of the physes creating large, nonmineralized gaps with ﬂ aring and cupping of the adjacent epiphyses and metaphyses ( Fig. 18.15 eFig. 18.10 ). Flared osteochondral junctions along the ribs are called “ rachitic rosary ” and are usually easily palpated. Diffuse osteopenia with thin cortices may be appreciated and can progress to folding fractures. Chondrodysplasia and Osteochondral Dysplasia Chondrodysplasia and osteochondral dysplasia result in short limb disproportionate dwar ﬁ sm. There are multiple dog breeds (and other species) where short, curved limbs are the breed standard. In fact, the 19 different American Kennel Club chondrodysplastic dog breeds all share a common retrogene that encodes ﬁ broblast growth factor 4 (fgf4). 34 Distinguishing between chondrodystrophic breeds that have been bred for many generations to establish a defect as a breed characteristic and chondrodysplastic dwarves that arise sporadically from normal parents is important. Chondrodysplasia and osteo- chondrodysplasias as undesirable genetic mutations have been reported in a number of breeds ( Table 18.2 ). 35 41 This category of diseases includes a conglomerate of different genetic muta- tions. These different causes for chondrodysplasia can appear clinically and radiographically similar with widened physes, ﬂ ared metaphyses, and angular limb deformities. Further char- acterization is hampered because speci ﬁ c genetic mutations are not described for many of these examples, and the sporadic nature of both the occurrence and the literature reporting them. Osteochondrodysplasia of Scottish Fold Cats A single gene variant in the TRPV 4 that is autosomal dominant results in the folded ear appearance of the breed and osteo- chondrodysplasia. The degree of limb deformity and degener- ative change is variable and appears worst in individuals that are homozygous dominant for this trait. Heterozygous in- dividuals still have folded ears. Similar but less pronounced abnor- malities are seen involving the phalanges. The metacarpi, met- atarsi, and phalanges are shorter than normal resulting in decreased limb length. Caudal vertebrae are reduced in length and have widened endplates. There is accelerated degenerative joint disease. An anky- losing arthropathy frequently results in fusion of the carpi and tarsi and their articulations with the metacarpi and metatarsi (see Fig. 18.16 ). 40 43 DISE ASES OF THE METAP HYSIS Hypertrophic Osteodystrophy Hypertrophic osteodystrophy (HOD), also called metaphyseal osteopathy, is a systemic illness that usually affects large- and giant-breed dogs between the ages of 2 and 7 months. The cause is unknown. 44 47 Clinical signs, including marked py- rexia, diarrhea, footpad hyperkeratosis, leukocytosis, anemia, and pneumonia, are occasionally seen with HOD, lending credibility to the possibility of a systemic infection as a cause for this disease. Resulting bone lesions are generally bilaterally symmetric and involve the metaphyses of long bones, particularly the distal radius, ulna, and tibia. The costochondral junctions, metacarpal and metatarsal bones, and proximal humerus may also be involved. Although HOD is self-limiting and resolves after a few weeks, more severe involvement can ultimately result in abnormal/ premature physeal closure and subsequent skeletal deformity. Histologically, lesions in the metaphyses consist of a neutro- philic in ﬂ ammatory response associated with necrosis, hemor- rhage, and increased osteoclast numbers. Collapse of necrotic metaphyseal trabecular bone and subperiosteal hemorrhage are also seen. Radiographic Signs Early radiographic signs include transversely oriented lucent zones within the metaphysis that are parallel and adjacent to the physes ( Fig. 18.17 eFig. 18.11 ) These are usually best seen in the distal radius and ulna and this appearance is sometimes referred to as the double physis sign , although the second radiolucent zone is not actually a physis. A thin margin of subchondral bone sclerosis may parallel the lucent zone and is caused by the collapse of necrotic trabecular bone. Irregular periosteal new bone forms around the metaphysis and is usually distinct and separate from the underlying cortex in the earlier stages of the disease. The extent of new metaphyseal bone formation depends on the severity and duration of the disorder, and such formation may extend to the diaphysis in severely affected dogs (see Fig. 18.17C ). Diffuse soft tissue swelling can be seen centered on the metaphyseal regions. Widening, con- cavity, and increased opacity of the distal rib ends may be present in some dogs. GENER ALIZE D BONE DISO RDERS Nutritional Secondary Hyperparathyroidism Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism is caused by a diet that is either calcium de ﬁ cient or calcium and phosphorus imbalanced. Inadequate dietary calcium intake causes an in- crease in parathyroid hormone. This, in turn, results in bone calcium resorption and generalized osteomalacia. The skeletal changes are diffuse and generalized. 40 42 Radiographic Signs Bone opacity is decreased, and cortices may appear abnormally thin. In severely affected animals, bone opacity may be similar to that of soft tissue. A loss of de ﬁ nition of the normally dense dental lamina that surrounds the teeth may also occur. Spinal deformity and pathologic folding fractures of the appendicular and the axial skeleton are common ( Fig. 18.21 ). Osteogenesis Imperfecta Osteogenesis imperfecta is a rare, brittle bone heritable disease caused by a structural defect in type 1 collagen, which consti- tutes the majority of the nonmineral bone matrix. 43 44 It has been reported in Dachshunds and Finnish Laphunds. Affected puppies may or may not have stunted growth, multiple reoc- curring fractures, and laxity of joints, and the teeth may appear pink. The cortices are thin and contain woven bone with no Haversian canals. Radiographic Signs A generalized decrease in bone opacity is present and long bone cortices are thin. Pathologic fractures are common and may be associated with excessively opaque callus formation and medullary sclerosis. The dentin of the teeth is thin. Findings are similar to and can be confused with generalized bone mineral loss from secondary hyperparathyroidism. Osteopetrosis Osteopetrosis is a rare, inherited metabolic bone disease that is presumed to be caused by abnormal osteoclast function ( Fig. 18.22 eFig. 18.13 ). 47 Affected animals have a generalized increase in bone opacity speci ﬁ cally affecting medullary cav- ities. A resulting decrease in the number of normal hemato- poietic cells subsequently occurs, leading to myelophthisic anemia. In cats, varying degrees of osteosclerosis with non- regenerative anemia induced by FeLV have also been reported and the radiographic appearance is identical to that described for osteopetrosis. 46 Until more information is obtained, the ﬁ nding of generalized osteosclerosis in cats should be consid- ered nonspeci ﬁ c, but viral testing for FeLV should be considered. Radiographic Signs Bone opacity is generally increased, particularly in medullary cavities. The normal trabecular pattern is diminished as a result of the uniform increase in bone opacity and the internal cortical margins become indistinct. Age of onset of the ﬁ rst fracture ranges from 4 months to 8 years with a mean age of the ﬁ rst patellar fractures at 28 months. Some 78% of these cats develop contralateral patellar fracture.
