DEVELO PMEN TAL OSSEOUS COND ITIONS Osteochondrosis and Osteochondritis Dissecans Osteochondrosis (OC) is a common juvenile bone disorder. OC is caused by focal endochondral vascular failures often of un- known etiology, 7 and current investigations of heritable/ge- netic causes or acquired causes such as sepsis, physiologic or traumatic vascular insult, or metabolic/nutritional imbalances are ongoing. 7 8 Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) is a condition in which OC leads to the separation of bone and cartilage fragments into the joint resulting in joint in ﬂ ammation. Sepa- rated osteochondral fragments may remain attached or become loose within the joint and may never ossify requiring ultrasound or arthroscopy for identi ﬁ cation. OC can occur in any breed, although is most common in Standardbreds (10.5% 35%), Warmbloods (20%), and Thoroughbreds (20%) and uncommon in ponies. 9 Affected yearlings or juvenile horses early in training generally present with variable tibiotarsal joint effusion (bog spavin) and/or variable degrees of lameness. Severity of joint effusion does not always correlate with the degree of lameness. Clinical signs are occasionally absent. Because OC is found in multiple joints in 50% of cases 7 and commonly bilateral, screening radiographs or systematic ultrasound 10 of the contralateral joint and other joints with OC predilection is often performed in racing and performance stock. The four major tarsal OC predilection sites are within the tibiotarsal joint and include the intermediate cochlear ridge of the tibia (ICRT, also known as DIRT for distal intermediate ridge of the tibia), lateral talar trochlear ridge, medial talar trochlear ridge, and tibial medial malleolus articular margin 11 13 ( Figs. 22.2 and 22.3 eFigs. 22.1 and 22.2 ). DMPLO and D20PLMO are the most helpful projections; thus, acquiring a D20PLMO for evaluation of the medial malleolus articular margin is crucial when evaluating horses for tarsal OC lesions. Other less common OC locations include the proximal weight- bearing portion of the medial trochlear ridge of the talus 14 and medial margin of the intermediate cochlear ridge of the talus 15 (see Fig. 22.2 ). These unique OC locations often require addi- tional oblique and/or ﬂ exed projections for detection. OC of the lateral tibial malleolus and medial proximal tubercle of the talus has been reported although soft tissue avulsion fragments, particularly of the deep collateral ligaments, may mimic OC at these locations. 16 Tarsal osteochondral lesions identi ﬁ ed in young foals with no clinical signs may be monitored for progressive ossi ﬁ cation with maturation however bone abnormalities are likely per- manent after 5 months of age. 9 17 OC associated with joint effusion or lameness of any aged animal should prompt surgical consultation. Radiographic features of OC include: 1. Intracapsular swelling of the tibiotarsal joint. 2. Subchondral bone margin ﬂ attening, irregularity or concave defect of parent bone generally accompanied by peripheral sclerosis. 3. Faint to well-mineralized rounded osseous fragments, although fragmentation may remain as unossi ﬁ ed cartilage requiring ultrasound or arthroscopy for identi ﬁ cation. 4. Eventual osteoarthritis (OA). Fragmentation of the Proximal Talar Tubercle Osseous fragments originating from the proximomedial tuber- cle of the talus ( Fig. 22.4 ) are more common in Warmbloods and are occasionally bilateral. They may represent an additional site of OC, although trauma to the medial short deep collateral ligament, medial talocalcaneal or tarsal plantar ligament has also been proposed. Medial fragmentation of this tubercle may be more clinically signi ﬁ cant compared to plantar fragmentation, as the medial aspect serves as the insertion site of the medial short deep collateral ligament. A calcaneal dorsoplantar skyline projection can improve localization. However, tubercle frag- mentation is often incidental in sound horses without tibiotarsal effusion, so its clinical signi ﬁ cance should be carefully weighed against other plausible causes. Subchondral Osseous Cyst-Like Lesions Tarsal subchondral osseous cyst-like lesions (SOCLs) are rare and sparsely reported. They occur in both older and younger horses and may be either developmental or acquired. Possible causes include joint sepsis, trauma to the articular cartilage or underlying bone, or OC. The central and third tarsal bones, talus, and distal tibia are most affected, and horses may be lame or sound, with or without joint effusion. Classically, SOCLs are centrally radiolucent or hyperintense on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with intense surrounding regional sclerosis ( Fig. 22.5 ). A ﬂ exed lateral projection to remove calcaneal summation may assist in identifying talar 18 ( Fig. 22.6 eFig. 22.3 ) or distal tibial SOCLs since standard radiographs occasionally appear normal. As many SOCLs cause intense sclerosis addi- tional evaluation with computed tomography (CT) or MRI is helpful in differentiating a cyst-like lesion from other causes of sclerosis. 19 20 Incomplete Cuboidal Bone Ossi ﬁ cation (Also Termed Aseptic Necrosis ) If cuboidal bone ossi ﬁ cation is incomplete, typical of premature or dysmature foals, and the foal is allowed to exercise normally, the underdeveloped bones are prone to collapse and crush injury ( Fig. 22.7 eFig. 22.4 ). In ﬂ ammatory forms of physitis are generally attributed to rapid growth phase, high nutritional plan, excessive work, trauma, and/or nutritional imbalances. Radiographic features include irregular physeal margins with widening and ﬂ aring of the growth plate often with mild soft tissue swelling. The in ﬂ ammatory form has more uniformly distributed physeal margin irregularity and widening, has less associated soft tissue swelling, and no osteolysis compared to septic physitis. 23 Development of angular limb deformity is less common given more even distribution of in ﬂ ammation, although development should still be monitored. DEGENE RATIVE AN D ACQ UIRED OSSEOUS COND ITIONS Osteoarthritis (Degenerative Joint Disease, Bone Spavin) Osteoarthritis (OA) is common in all horse breeds and can occur at any age, with older horses and Icelandic horses more often affected resulting from repetitive, low-grade bone trauma. 24 25 Other inciting causes include ligamentous injury, sepsis, hemarthrosis, conformational faults such as tarsal valgus or increased or decreased tarsal angulation, or underlying bone malformation as with wedge-shaped cuboidal bones. 24 The centrodistal and tarsometatarsal joints are most often affected ( Fig. 22.8 eFigs. 22.5 and 22.6 ), usually dorsomedially although can be dorsolateral in distribution, as commonly seen in Ice- landic horses, highlighting the importance of acquiring both DMPLO and DLPMO projections. Lameness severity, duration, and response to ﬂ exion examination does not correlate well with the severity of distal tarsal joint radiographic change, 25 emphasizing the importance of diagnostic anesthesia. Well- de ﬁ ned dorsal third metatarsal bone proliferation without other bone changes is generally regarded as incidental enthes- opathy 26 (see Fig. 22.1 ). Tibiotarsal OA is less common 27 and generally secondary to chronic OC, sepsis, or injury to the collateral ligaments, synovium, cartilage, or subchondral bone. It often requires evaluation with ultrasound, 28 cross-sectional imaging, 29 or exploratory arthroscopy 30 if the inciting cause is not radiographically apparent. OA of the tibiotarsal joints ( Fig. 22.9 ) or talocalcaneal joints is generally associated with signi ﬁ cant lameness and less responsiveness to medical therapy. 27 Radiographic features of OA include: 1. Intracapsular soft tissue swelling if tibiotarsal joint affected 2. Periarticular bone proliferation (osteophytes) 3. Subchondral bone resorption/lysis in later stages 4. Possible development of osseous cyst-like lesions 5. Eventual joint space collapse due to cartilage degradation ( Fig. 22.10 eFig. 22.7 )Unique to distal tarsal OA, the normal, more radiolucent trabeculation of the central and third tarsal bones is often effaced by radiopaque sclerosis. Cata- strophic displaced and/or comminuted fractures of the talus and calcaneus ( Fig. 22.12 ) are most common and carry a grave prognosis. Smaller displaced or minimally displaced fractures or avulsions of the tarsus have better outcomes for survival and possibly athletic career if diagnosed and managed properly and are discussed below. Tibial Malleolar Fractures The lateral ( Fig. 22.13 ) and less commonly medial tibial malleoli are the most common tarsal fractures, almost always articular, and occur after kick or fall trauma and/or severe rotational stress when the hoof is ﬁ xed to the ground. The long and short medial and lateral collateral ligaments of the tibiotarsal joint originate from the malleoli, and thus, malleolar fractures war- rant sonographic assessment of the collateral ligaments. Smaller collateral avulsions tend to respond favorably to surgical removal of the bone fragment. 34 Fractures that are comminuted and involve a signi ﬁ cant portion of the collateral ligament sur- face area, but are too small for ﬁ xation, carry an elevated risk of tibiotarsal luxation during the recovery process ( Fig. 22.14 ). Trochlear Ridge Fractures These articular fractures are uncommon but generally related to external trauma as with a kick by another horse (see Fig. 22.12 ). They can be associated with favorable outcomes with expe- dited surgical intervention. 35 Incomplete or Minimally Displaced Fractures These fractures are overall uncommon and can be challenging to detect both clinically and radiographically due to inherent summation of bone and lack of fracture displacement. Incom- plete talar, central, and third tarsal bone slab fractures are most common. Cross-sectional imaging with CT or high- ﬁ eld MRI can also con ﬁ rm fractures although is generally reserved for animals undergoing surgical ﬁ xation to avoid catastrophic displacement during anesthetic recovery. Central Tarsal Bone Sagittal Slab or Comminuted Fracture. Slab fractures are bicortical fractures that are also biarticular. Sagittal slab fractures are uncommon and most prevalent in nonracing breeds. Repetitive dorsomedial loading forces inherent of the equine pelvic limb result in predictable fracture orientation in a dorsomedial to plantarolateral plane, often requiring several DM30-55 PlLO obliques at 5- to 10-degree increments to best align the x-ray beam tangential to the fracture plane 37 ( Fig. 22.15 eFig. 22.8 ). Third and Central Tarsal Bone Dorsal Slab Fractures. These rare articular fractures occur in racing Thoroughbreds and Standardbreds or rarely during other high-speed work and are attributed to repetitive dorsal bone stress. Wedge-shaped conformation of the cuboidal bones is a suggested risk factor 21 ( Fig. 22.16 eFig. 22.9 ), although fractures at this location occur in horses with and without wedge-shaped conformation. 38 Third tarsal dorsal slab fractures are more common than similar fractures of the central tarsal bone and occur along the dorsolateral aspect of the T3 dorsal facet. 38 Occasionally, dorsal slab fractures are bilateral in distribution. Incomplete Sagittal Fracture of the Talus. This rare fracture occurs at the proximal aspect of the trochlear groove in racing breeds or, rarely, other breeds competing in speed work often with history of chronic lameness with acute exacerbation shortly after strenuous work. Neonatal Infectious Polyarthritis and Septic Physitis Certain factors, such as immaturity, dysmaturity, failure of passive transfer, urachal patency, omphalitis, respiratory or gastrointestinal disease, wounds, or malnutrition may increase the risk of bacteremia and joint or growth plate infection in neonates and weanlings. Sepsis is con ﬁ rmed via joint cytology and culture. CT or MRI, when available, can detect the devel- opment of osteomyelitis earlier, 43 as 30% to 50% bone loss is needed before lysis is visible radiographically. Sedated CT ( Fig. 22.18 ), where available, is a growing modality for quickly assessing multiple joints and concomitant infections within the thorax or abdomen in septic foals. 42 43 MRI can reveal charac- teristic osteomyelitis changes 44 but requires general anesthesia and a longer scan time compared to CT. Serial radiographs 1 to 3 days apart can also be helpful in monitoring for development of osteomyelitis. Septic physitis is usually seen in foals less than 6 months of age, with risk factors similar to infectious arthritis. As with sy- novial sepsis, clinical signs and radiographic changes offer a presumptive diagnosis although sampling of the joint ﬂ uid or physeal bone abnormality is required for de ﬁ nitive diagnosis and therapeutic guidance. Septic physitis most often affects the distal tibia and is asymmetric compared to aseptic forms 23 generally affecting one side of the growth plate with accom- panying discrete regions of radiolysis (see Fig. 22.18 ). Despite aggressive and early treatment, asymmetric physeal growth may lead to eventual angular limb deformity and maturation should be monitored closely. Calcaneal Tuber Osteitis/Osteomyelitis and Septic Calcaneal Bursitis Osteolytic lesions associated with the calcaneal tuber are more often septic than aseptic and often involve the calcaneal bursae as the result of blunt trauma and/or wound, although they can also be hematogenous, especially in foals. Standard tarsal ra- diographs including a ﬂ exed calcaneal skyline projection and ultrasonography of the plantar tarsus aid in complete evaluation of the osseous and soft tissue structures involved. Positive contrast ﬁ stulography is recommended if a draining tract is present to better understand the soft tissues involved ( Fig. 22.19 eFig. 22.10 ). Bone lysis and/or sequestra may take one to several weeks to declare themselves radiographically; thus, serial imaging is important. Medial and Lateral Soft Tissue InjuriesCollateral Ligament Enthesopathy, Desmopathy, and Avulsions The medial ( Fig. 22.21 ) and lateral ( Fig. 22.22 ) tibiotarsal collateral ligament anatomy is complex, with each composed of one long and three short components (super ﬁ cial, middle, and deep) with the short ligaments running oblique to nearly perpendicular to the long ligaments. 49 50 Collectively, the collateral ligaments have variable insertions onto the talus, calcaneus, cuboidal, and metatarsal bones to provide robust joint stability. 49 50 In general, when the limb is extended, the long components of the collateral ligaments are under tension while the short components are relaxed and vice versa when the limb is in ﬂ exion. 50 Injury of the tibiotarsal collateral liga- ments is relatively common 49 51 52 and most often related to supraphysiologic rotational forces during sharp turns or a fall/ kick injury, although repetitive cyclic loading may be related to lateral collateral ligament injuries in Standardbred racehorses. 49 Acute injury typically results in severe lameness and extensive joint effusion. Radiographs are often normal aside from intra- capsular swelling unless bone avulsion or other fractures occurred. Acute sonographic ﬁ ndings often show characteristic swirling echogenic effusion, supportive of hemarthrosis due to capsular tearing, which often is a concurrent injury with collateral ligament tears. 49 In the chronic phase, synovial distension often progresses to proliferative synovitis with thick multiloculated septae and reduced ﬂ uid component. Com- plete ﬁ ber disruption or core lesions are rarely seen. 52 Depending on lesion severity and management osteoarthritis may eventually develop due to joint instability and/or chronic synovitis. Prognosis for return to prior athletic use in horses with tibiotarsal osteoarthritis is generally guarded. 52 As collat- eral ligament ultrasound is complex and often challenged by severity of effusion or pain response with examination diag- nosis of collateral ligament injuries can also be con ﬁ rmed by high- ﬁ eld MRI ( Fig. 22.23 ), CT arthrography 53 and/or explor- atory arthroscopy. 50 54 Plantar Soft Tissue InjuriesCurb Prior to routine use of ultrasonography, “ curb ” was a colloquial term indicative of long plantar ligament (LPL) injury, but today “ curb ” is used to describe nonspeci ﬁ c soft tissue swelling of the plantar tarsus ( Fig. 22.24 ) with the primary injury requiring sonography or less commonly MRI or CT to fully characterize. Types of Curb: Long Plantar Desmitis/Des mopathy. The LPL originates along the plantarolateral calcaneus with a broad insertion onto the fourth metatarsal and fourth tarsal bones. Common in racing and Western performance breeds, long plantar injury is more often acute in onset and sonographically associated with focal or diffuse ligament enlargement with ﬁ ber disruption or large core lesions. 55 57 Types of Curb: Plantar Fasciitis (Peritend inous-Periliga mentous In ﬂ ammation). The plantar fascia is a thin, ﬁ brous fascial layer deep to the skin and super ﬁ cial to the LPL and super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon (SDFT). Plantar fasciitis is in ﬂ ammation and thickening of this fascia uncomplicat ed by other tendon or ligament injury. Sonograp hically, the plantar fascia is thickened with echogenic to heterogeneou s soft tissue prolifera tion with or without ﬂ uid accumulation . The cause may be related to fatigue injury from athletic overload and/or exercise in deep footing in endurance and racing breeds, though trauma is more commonly reported in sport horses. Prognosis for plantar fas- ciitis uncomplicat ed by tendon or ligament injury is favorabl e with appropriat e rest and rehabilitation. 56 Conversely, fasciitis is generally a component of proximal SDFT or LPL lesions and may be an early indicat or of impending tendinous or ligamen- tous injury. 57 Types of Curb: Proximal Super ﬁ cial Digital Flexor Tendonitis/ Tendinopathy. The super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor originates from the femoral supracondylar fossa as the caudal arm of the reciprocal apparatus. It wraps around the gastrocnemius muscle dorso- medially and forms a ﬁ brocartilaginous cap on the plantar lobe of the tuber calcaneus. 58 Injury to the proximal SDFT along the plantar tarsus results in generalized enlargement with loss of the normal elliptical shape becoming rounder and generally enlarged (see Fig. 22.23 ). Injury that extends distal to the tarsus is associated with more severe lameness and worsened prognosis. 55 Super ﬁ cial Digital Flexor Subluxation/Luxations Talocalcaneal ligaments secure the ﬁ brocartilaginous cap medially and laterally to the calcaneal tuber, and tears of these ligaments can result in calcaneal bursitis as these structures communicate. Partial tears ( Fig. 22.25 ) cause subluxation without dynamic instability, while full tears result in dynamic luxation of the ﬁ brocartilage. Lateral luxations resulting from a medial tear are more common and offer better outcomes compared to medial luxations. Longitudinal tears through the ﬁ brocartilage can lead to the tuber calcaneus pro- truding through the cap. 59 Conservative and surgical therapies are both viable options for treatment, with surgery providing improved tendon stability but risks other complications including implant infection. 60 Thoroughpin: Tarsal Sheath Tenosynovitis/ Tenovaginitis The tarsal sheath is a synovial lining covering the lateral digital ﬂ exor (LDF) tendon from the distal tibia to the proximal metatarsus. The tarsal sheath is bounded dorsolaterally by an osseous tarsal groove created by the calcaneal shaft and sus- tentaculum tali, which is covered by thick ﬁ brocartilage for enhanced tendon gliding. The deep plantar ligament and thick plantar retinaculum (also called the metatarsocalcaneal liga- ment), 61 respectively, form the dorsodistal and plantaromedial tarsal sheath boundaries. These boundaries prevent distension of the tarsal sheath at the tarsal bone level, but proximal re- cesses at the level of the common calcaneal tendon can enlarge and cause visible distension ( Fig. 22.26 eFig. 22.11 ), colloqui- ally termed thoroughpin . Recurrent tarsal sheath effusion or effusion accompanied by lameness should be taken seriously due to the poorer outcomes associated with both septic or chronic sterile tenosynovitis of the tarsal sheath. 47 48 62 Chronic tarsal sheath effusions in horses are usually a result of tendo- vaginitis, which affects both the sheath and LDF tendon. Ra- diographs may reveal soft tissue swelling in the region of the proximal tarsal sheath recesses, mineralization of the tendon or tarsal sheath, and/or sustentacular osseous changes like exos- tosis, fragmentation, or lysis. Ultrasound can con ﬁ rm radio- graphic pathology and provide additional insight into the severity of synovial thickening, the presence of synovial masses or fronds that may form adhesions with the LDF, as well as al- terations in the size, shape, or ﬁ ber pattern of the LDF ( Fig. 22.27 ). 48 Importantly, some horses with lateral digital ﬂ exor tendinopathies do not present with signi ﬁ cant effusion or radiographic or ultrasound abnormalities and require intra- thecal diagnostic anesthesia and MRI for diagnosis. 62 False thoroughpin is described as unilocular or multilocular perisynovial ﬂ uid distention near but not communicating with the tarsal sheath, tibiotarsal joint, or calcaneal bursae, occurring more commonly along the lateral aspect. 63 Differentiation of a true and false thoroughpin requires contrast radiography or endoscopy to evaluate communication with synovial structures. 64 65 Gastrocnemius Tendinitis/Tendinopathy The GT, along with the SDFT, originates from the femoral supercondylar fossa and together they make up the largest fascicles of the common calcaneal tendon. The FT then bifurcates into smaller dorsal and lateral branches which insert on the dorsal metatarsus and dorsal and lateral distal tarsal bones. 71 72 FT complete or partial rupture d or tendinitis are caused by hyperextension injury or trauma and will present with varying degrees of dorsal tarsal or crus swelling and lameness depending on the severity and location of the injury. While radiographs are indicated to rule out concurrent osseous trauma, ultrasound is paramount and may show tendon enlargement, margin irregularity, and vari- able degrees of ﬁ ber disruption (see Fig. 22.27 ). 73 Complete rupture results in inappropriate extension of the tarsus when the sti ﬂ e is ﬂ exed. 72 Generally, rupture occurs within the mid- or distal portion, although can occur at the origin resulting in femoropatellar effusion and possibly osseous avulsion. 71 74 Dystrophic mineralization or insertional enthesopathy of the FT is occasionally identi ﬁ ed radiographically and generally well tolerated when not associated with other changes. Long Digital Extensor Tenosynovitis A synovial sheath envelops the long digital extensor tendon (LoDET) as it traverses the dorsal tarsus and is a palpable structure just lateral to the medial trochlear ridge. The prox- imal, middle, and distal dorsal tarsal retinaculae are situated between the LoDET and skin and generally prevent visualiza- tion of LoDET sheath effusion. Distal to the tarsus, the lateral digital extensor tendon, which also has its own sheath, fuses with the LoDET and travels dorsally along the metatarsus to insert on the distal phalanx. Severing of these tendons once conjoined below the metatarsus has a poorer prognosis than more proximal at the tarsus/metatarsus, where they are sepa- rated and the retinacular attachments afford collateral stabilization. 75 Focal Peritarsal Cellulitis This is a rare, acute, and painful cellulitis localized to the dorsal tarsus and results in severe, sudden-onset lameness. It is char- acterized by expansion and increased echogenicity of the sub- cutaneous and peritendinous structures, with diffuse hypoechoic ﬂ uid locules, 76 and may be associated with septic tenosynovitis of the LoDET. 77 Early and aggressive diagnosis and treatment without complications of osteomyelitis or lami- nitis are associated with favorable outcomes. Gilmour T he equine carpus is a complex anatomical region comprised of seven cuboidal bones that are arranged in two rows to create three main joints: antebrachiocarpal (radiocarpal), middle carpal (intercarpal), and carpometacarpal. The proximal row of cuboidal bones contains the radial, inter- mediate, and ulnar carpal bones. The accessory carpal bone is situated palmar to and articulates with the radius and ulnar carpal bone. The distal row of cuboidal bones contains the second, third, and fourth carpal bones with inconsistent appearance of ﬁ rst and ﬁ fth carpal bones. The bulk of the horse s weight-bearing load falls upon the radial, intermediate, and third carpal bones. 1 Small intercarpal joints between articulating cuboidal bones are stabilized by numerous extrac- apsular and intracapsular ligaments. Range of motion within the carpus is largely limited to ﬂ exion and extension of the ante- brachiocarpal and middle carpal joints while the carpometa- carpal joint is relatively immobile. 2 Indications for carpal imaging are similar to those in other areas of the equine limb and include a history of regional trauma, external wounds, soft tissue swelling or palpable thickening, pain or lameness that is relieved with regional or intra-articular diagnostic analgesia, and prepurchase examina- tions plus screening for incomplete ossi ﬁ cation of cuboidal bones in foals with suspected prematurity or dysmaturity. 3 Radiographic ﬁ ndings should always be correlated with a complete patient history, physical and lameness exam ﬁ ndings, and the results of diagnostic analgesia, if performed. The focus of this chapter will be radiography of the equine carpus, which is a practical ﬁ rst step for diagnostic imaging of this region. RADIOG RAPH IC STUDY ACQUIS ITION Soft tissues surrounding the carpal region in a full-sized, adult horse are thin enough that the area can be successfully imaged using a standard portable x-ray machine and image receptor. At minimum, a standard radiographic study of the carpus will include four projections made with the x-ray beam centered on the middle carpal joint in a standing and evenly weight-bearing patient. Projections include dorsopalmar, lateromedial, and paired dorsolateral-palmaromedial (DLPMO) and dorsomedial- palmarolateral oblique (DMPLO) views. 3 In many patients, the addition of one or more special views to the standard carpal study will further aid in radiographic interpretation. A ﬂ exed lateromedial projection is obtained to aid in differentiation of the cuboidal bones as the intermediate and fourth carpal bones will move proximally relative to the radial and third carpal bones, respectively. This view allows supplementary evaluation of articular surfaces and joint spaces. Its high clinical utility leads some clinicians to consider this view part of a standard carpal study. 1 Three additional ﬂ exed dorsoproximal-dorsodistal oblique projections, also called tangential or “ skyline ” views, can be made at increasing angles from the horizontal plane ( Fig. 23.1 ). One or more skyline views can be added to a study for the purpose of enhanced evaluation of the dorsal aspects of the distal row of carpal bones, proximal row of carpal bones, and the distal radius. Radiographic projections made while stress is manually applied to the carpal joints can be used to diagnose and/or characterize joint subluxation that is otherwise suspected based on clinical examination of a patient. The typical ﬂ exed lateral radiographic projection can be considered a stress projection, while others include a lateral view with the carpus held in extension and dorsopalmar views made while lateral or medial bending pressure is applied to the carpus. Stress projections are employed in an attempt to demonstrate abnormal dorsopalmar or mediolateral movements within the carpus that result in joint space widening and asymmetry secondary to partial or com- plete rupture of the supporting soft tissue structures. Manipu- lation of unstable joints in this manner is expected to be very painful for the patient. Adequate sedation and analgesia are critical to perform stress radiographs humanely in these cases. Radiation safety should not be compromised, and the diagnos- tician must ensure that patient and equipment handlers are wearing protective equipment with their hands always posi- tioned outside of the primary x-ray beam. 4 Carpal lesions are bilateral in many instances. Radiographic examination of both carpi can be especially valuable when investigating an equine patient for stress-related pathology, fractures and osteochondral fragments, and developmental disorders. It is also important to note that normal radiographs do not necessarily indicate lack of osseous or soft tissue pa- thology. There are many reports where radiographic ﬁ ndings (or lack thereof) con ﬂ ict with ﬁ ndings of other imaging mo- dalities such as ultrasound, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and arthroscopy. 1 NORM AL ANA TOMICAL VARIA NTS AN D INCIDEN TAL FINDIN GS Medial and Lateral Protrusions on the Caudal Aspect of Distal Radial Physis The caudomedial and caudolateral aspects of the distal radius have normal osseous projections at the level of the physis that are highlighted on lateral, DLPMO, and DMPLO projections ( Fig. 23.2A ). A smooth indentation in the caudal aspect of the distal radial epiphysis known as the radial fossa is also apparent on dorsopalmar projections of the carpus ( Fig. 23.2B ). These normal features should be recognized to avoid a misdiagnosis. Vestigial Ulna In some horses, a vestigial ulna is visible as a thin, mineral opacity separated from the caudolateral aspect of the radius. This structure should not be misinterpreted as periosteal pro- liferation or other disease 5 ( Fig. 23.2C ). C H A P T E R 23 Equine Carpus 470

Incomplete Fusion of the Lateral Styloid Process Developmentally, the distal aspect of the ulna becomes the lateral styloid process via a separate center of ossi ﬁ cation that fuses with the radial epiphysis by 9 months of age. 1 The lateral styloid process is usually completely fused with the radius in skeletally mature horses. Occasionally, horses may have incomplete fusion that is incidental but results in radiographi- cally visible retention of a small radiolucent zone in the distal radial epiphysis without surrounding sclerosis or bone irregu- larity. This should not be mistaken for an osseous cyst-like lesion or fracture 6 ( Fig. 23.2C ). Variable Appearance of Ulnar Carpal Bone Lucent regions, irregularities, and variable shapes of the axial, non weight-bearing surface of the ulnar carpal bone and, sometimes, the adjacent fourth metacarpal bone can be seen on the DLPMO images 5 ( Fig. 23.3 ). These lesions are very rarely associated with lameness or joint effusion and are commonly considered as having low clinical signi ﬁ cance despite the like- lihood of an early traumatic avulsion of the lateral palmar intercarpal ligament. Radiolucencies on the subchondral, weight-bearing surface of the ulnar carpal bone are sometimes associated with lameness but may also heal before 12 months of age and/or respond to conservative management. 7 First and Fifth Carpal Bones Vestigial ﬁ rst and ﬁ fth carpal bones are inconsistently present in adult horses and should not be mistaken for osteochondral fragments. In a study of radiologic anatomic variation of the carpus, ﬁ rst carpal bones were found in 29% of horses and ﬁ fth carpal bones in 1.4% of horses. 5 The ﬁ fth carpal bone is usually smaller than the ﬁ rst carpal bone, although their size is highly variable and either bone may be present in one or both limbs. Occasionally, the ﬁ rst carpal bone is incompletely separated from the second carpal bone. Vestigial ﬁ rst and ﬁ fth carpal bones can also be associated with incidental, focal concavities or lucent defects in the adjacent cuboidal and metatarsal bones as a result of variable articulation 5 ( Fig. 23.4 ). Physitis/Epiphysitis Physitis can manifest in the distal radius of young horses up to 2 years old. Physitis may be septic or aseptic in nature, and radiographic features of these two different pathogeneses can overlap. Knowledge of the normal, evolving physeal appear- ance in growing horses is crucial for radiographic interpretation ( Fig. 23.6A ). Acquisition of complementary radiographic views of the contralateral limb can be valuable for comparison and diagnosis of physitis. Radiographs have been shown to under- estimate the presence and severity of physitis compared to computed tomography. 9 Sometimes referred to as physeal dysplasia, aseptic physitis is an in ﬂ ammatory but noninfectious process identi ﬁ ed in young horses. It is correlated with nutritional factors and rapid bone growth. Radiographs may be normal in the early stages of physitis, and in more chronic stages may show:  metaphyseal ﬂ aring  irregularity and widening of the physis  asymmetry and sclerosis of the metaphysis  wedge-shaped epiphysis 10 ( Fig. 23.6B ) Septic physitis is caused by hematogenous bacterial spread that is most common in younger foals between 1 week and 4 months of age. 10 This process rarely occurs in isolation and is usually associated with septicemia and respiratory, gastroin- testinal, or umbilical disease. Foals with failure of passive transfer are at greatest risk for development of septic arthritis and septic physitis. The distinguishing radiographic feature of septic physitis in foals is aggressive osteolysis presenting as a focal irregularity of the physis with irregular radiolucency extending into the adjacent epiphysis and/or metaphysis ( Fig. 23.6C ). Detection of radiolucency and physeal irregularity is more challenging if the osteolysis extends along the entire length of the physis. The bone adjacent to the physis may be sclerotic and it may have an altered trabecular pattern, ﬂ ared abaxial contour, and/or periosteal proliferation. Concurrent soft tissue swelling surrounding the affected physis and septic arthritis of the antebrachiocarpal joint or any other synovial joint are other radiographic ﬁ ndings that may be present in foals with septic physitis. 11 Differentiation of aseptic versus septic physitis will be further guided by patient clinical data such as the presence or absence of a fever and other systemic comorbidities. Iatrogenic infection secondary to joint injections or arthroscopic procedures is also possible. 21 In addi- tion to these causes, foals can also acquire septic arthritis secondary to hematogenous inoculation of the joint resulting from bacteremia. Foals with failure of passive transfer, multi- systemic disease, and/or septicemia are at high risk for develop- ment of septic arthritis as well as osteomyelitis and physitis. 22 23 Horses with septic arthritis of the carpus usually present with acute, severe, and rapidly progressive lameness with concurrent heat, pain, and soft tissue swelling over the affected region. The earliest radiographic sign of septic arthritis is often joint effusion with distention of the synovial capsule and/or extracapsular soft tissue swelling, although this can vary depending on the underlying cause of the septic process. Joint effusion can result in widening of the joint space in early stages, while articular cartilage loss leads to joint space narrowing in more advanced stages of disease. Other radiographic features of septic arthritis and osteomyelitis include:  subchondral radiolucency caused by osteolysis  increased subchondral bone opacity caused by sclerosis  extracapsular soft tissue swelling  progressive bone proliferation with aggressive morphology-like amorphous, palisading, or spiculated pat- terns ( Fig. 23.14 ). If there is a suspicion of sepsis, it is essential to evaluate radiographs for osteomyelitis both at the time of initial assess- ment as well as at follow-up intervals throughout the course of treatment. The presence of carpal osteomyelitis will worsen the prognosis for return to athletic function and therapy may be altered if osteomyelitis is identi ﬁ ed. Approximately 30% to 50% reduction in bone opacity is required before osteolysis becomes radiographically visible, making radiographs a relatively insen- sitive measure for bone loss. 24 Traumatic Orthopedic DiseaseIntra-Articular Fractures Racehorses are most likely to be affected by traumatic osteo- chondral injury compared to non-racehorses. Osteochondral Fragmentation The pathogenesis of osteochondral fragmentation is generally accepted to involve microdamage of subchondral bone that ultimately leads to separation of necrotic tissue from the orig- inal bone margin or separation through the base of new bone growth (osteophytosis). These intracapsular bits of separated bone are often referred to as fragments rather than fractures due to this pathogenesis. Osteochondral fragmentation is a common underlying cause of carpal osteoarthritis and it is also suggested that subchondral bone brittleness associated with osteoarthritis can lead to osteochondral fragmentation. 18 Osteochondral fragmentation in the carpus typically arises from a single articular surface along the dorsal periphery of a carpal bone. Some of the most commonly reported sites are the dorsoproximal aspects of the intermediate, radial, and third carpal bones and the disto- lateral aspect of the radius ( Fig. 23.11 ). Fragments originating within the dorsal aspect of the carpus are commonly seen bilaterally, and fragmentation is frequently identi ﬁ ed in conjunction with joint effusion and variable lameness. Frag- ments within the palmar aspects of the carpal joints may be associated with trauma to the palmar surface of any carpal bone including avulsion of palmar intercarpal ligaments, palmar migration of fragments that originated along the dorsal surface of a carpal bone, or comminuted fractures of any carpal bone. Treatments including arthroscopic fragment removal are routinely recommended because fragments can cause pain, induce synovial in ﬂ ammation, and hasten the progression of osteoarthritis. The poorest prognosis for return to athletic function is reserved for fragmentation and secondary damage within the middle carpal joint. 2 Slab Fractures Slab fractures are generally described as being biarticular with fracture lines extending to the proximal and distal articular surfaces of a carpal bone, although incomplete fracture is possible with involvement of only one articular surface. Slab fractures can be simple or comminuted, displaced, or non- displaced. They can be oriented in a dorsal or, less commonly, a sagittal plane ( Fig. 23.16 eFig. 23.5 ). Dorsal plane fracture fragments are very commonly dorsally displaced to some de- gree, and this displacement can be reduced when the limb is positioned for ﬂ exed lateral radiographs. Axial instability con- current with displacement can result in “ collapse ” of a frac- tured cuboidal bone such that a proximally positioned bone can sink distally into the fracture gap ( Fig. 23.17 ). Sagittal plane slab fractures are inherently more stable and displacement is less common. Slab fractures tend to propagate deeper within the bone compared to the more peripheral location of many osteochondral fragments. Both dorsal and sagittal plane slab fractures are most common in the radial facet of the third carpal bone. 2 Slab fractures are most easily identi ﬁ ed on radiographic studies in which the x-ray beam is parallel with the fracture gap. Radiographic identi ﬁ cation can be particularly challenging for dorsal plane fractures involving both the radial and intermedi- ate facets of the third carpal bone and incomplete sagittal plane fractures through the radial facet ( Fig. 23.18 eFig. 23.6 ). Some sagittal slab fractures are oriented in a proximolateral- distomedial oblique plane and may be dif ﬁ cult or impossible to detect on standard images and appropriate skyline views. The addition of a special dorsoproximal lateral-palmarodistal medial oblique skyline projection has been shown to increase sensitivity of radiographic detection of these fractures in race- horses with consistent clinical signs. 25 Horses with carpal slab fractures can present with a range of clinical severity from mild lameness to severe, non weight-bearing lameness. Intra- capsular soft tissue opacity may be an effect of hemarthrosis, joint effusion, or synovitis. Conservative management of non- displaced carpal slab fractures has been reported, although surgical stabilization is more often recommended to restore joint congruity, minimize secondary joint damage, and slow the progression of osteoarthritis. Return to athletic function in racehorses may be possible following surgical ﬁ xation of third carpal bone slab fractures. Not surprisingly, the best outcomes are seen in horses lacking severe concurrent or pre-existing joint pathology. Thoroughbreds and Standardbreds with sig- ni ﬁ cant fracture displacement, large fragment size associated with a fracture originating deep within the bone, osteolysis of the third carpal bone, and articular cartilage damage at the time of injury have a more guarded prognosis in terms of racing performance following surgical fracture stabilization. 26 Accessory Carpal Bone Fracture A cc es so ry c ar pa l b on e fr ac tu re s ar e re la ti ve ly un co mm on co m pa re d to th e va ri ou s fr ac tu re /f ra gm e nt ty pe s di sc us se d ea rl i er . Although relatively uncommon, luxation and subluxation are usually a result of collateral ligament injury affecting any of the three main carpal joints. 29 More than one joint can be affected concurrently. Luxation and subluxation are diagnosed radiographically as malalignment of the bone column through the carpal region. Malalignment may be identi ﬁ ed on standard radiographic pro- jections or may require additional stressed projections where pressure is manually applied to the joints via ﬂ exion, extension, and medial or lateral angulation. Radiographs may also reveal intracapsular and/or extracapsular soft tissue swelling, features of osteoarthritis, carpal bone fractures, or osteochondral frag- mentation ( Fig. 23.20 ). In some cases, angular limb deformity (varus or valgus) is also present. Lameness associated with carpal subluxation is often severe. Treatment is often initiated with goals of palliative pain management and breeding sound- ness rather than return to full athletic capability. Radiographic healing of carpal subluxation is centered on the subluxated joint and demonstrated by stabilizing external bone callus for- mation, enthesopathy at collateral ligament attachment sites, subchondral sclerosis, variable bone erosion or osteopenia, and progressive osteoarthritis. Periarticular ﬁ brous tissue commonly contributes to reduced range of motion in the joint(s) over time. 30 Sclerosis and New Bone FormationCarpal Bone Sclerosis Sclerosis of the carpal bones is generally understood to be an effect of repetitive trauma resulting from abnormal compres- sion of the carpal bones that leads to microdamage of the subchondral bone (i.e., “ exercise/stress adaptation mismatch ” ). Carpal hyperextension, exercise at extreme speeds or on poor quality footing, inferior conformation, and improper hoof care can all lead to abnormal stresses on the carpal bones. Carpal bone overload results in adaptive increases in bone density and stiffness that is frequently followed by osteochondral fragmen- tation and/or fractures. 2 Sclerosis itself is radiographically characterized by loss of distinction between the cortex and medullary cavity. Although sclerosis can be identi ﬁ ed on standard radiographic views, assessment of the skyline projections of the proximal and distal row of carpal bones can be particularly helpful. The radial facet of the third carpal bone is the most common carpal site affected by sclerosis. Mild sclerosis of the third carpal bone is relatively common in young racing and sport horses and is sometimes considered an incidental ﬁ nding because sclerosis does not al- ways correlate with development of pathology, pain, or lame- ness. 1 Pronounced radiopacity of the medullary cavity with loss of corticomedullary distinction, however, is a sign of maladap- tive, stress-related bone remodeling that could predispose the bone to fracture and is therefore considered abnormal. Com- parison of the medullary opacity of the third and fourth carpal bones on a dorsal 35-degree proximal-dorsodistal oblique radiograph is a useful technique to determine the extent and severity of carpal bone sclerosis ( Fig. 23.21 ). This view is also used to assess for fractures of the third carpal bone ( Figs. 23.16C and 23.18 ). 3 Further comparison between right and left thoracic limbs is also recommended, as bilateral disease is possible. Osteochondroma and Other Exostoses (Distal Radius) An exostosis is de ﬁ ned as a benign bony outgrowth from an existing bone. An osteochondroma is a benign exostosis with a cartilage cap that is most typically found near a physis. The caudodistal surface of the radial metaphysis is the most com- mon site for solitary osteochondroma in the horse, although they have also been described in other locations including the craniodistal radius and caudodistal tibia ( Fig. 23.22 ). 31 Caudally oriented exostoses that are histopathologically different from osteochondromas have also been reported at the level of the caudal distal radial physis ( Fig. 23.23A ). Both osteochondromas and other exostoses in this area can result in similar clinical syndromes as they protrude caudally to impinge upon or penetrate the carpal sheath. This results in tenosynovitis and effusion, with or without concurrent deep digital ﬂ exor injury, secondary to super ﬁ cial abrasion of the collagen ﬁ bers by the bone proliferation ( Fig. 23.23B,C ). Associated clinical signs of carpal sheath effusion and/or lameness may be constant or intermittent, and arthroscopic removal of the impinging exos- toses is reported to result in a good prognosis for the patient s return to athletic activity. 32 33 Lateral and ﬂ exed lateral pro- jections are usually most helpful for radiographic diagnosis of exostoses affecting the carpal sheath. Soft Tissue Abnormalities Ultrasonography is often more useful in the assessment of soft tissue injury; however, radiographs are used to identify under- lying bone trauma and/or signs of chronic enthesopathy at tendon and ligament attachment sites. Extracapsular/extra- synovial swelling tends to be regional and diffuse, extending beyond the expected geographic con ﬁ nes of the joint capsules and tendon sheaths. It is important to recognize that intra- capsular (synovial) distension and extracapsular soft tissue swelling can occur concurrently, and radiographic differentia- tion between intra- or extrasynovial location of soft tissue swelling can be dif ﬁ cult or impossible due to border effacement among these tissues. Collateral Ligament Injury Collateral ligament injury often results in soft tissue swelling overlying the affected ligament. 34 Radiographic features of moderate to severe and/or chronic carpal collateral ligament injury that affect the underlying bone or limb alignment might be detectable. Horses with collateral ligament injury may present concurrently with avulsion fractures or enthesopathy at the ligament origin and/or insertion sites and osteoarthritis of the carpal joints ( Fig. 23.24 ). Medial collateral ligament injury is reportedly more common than lateral collateral ligament injury in the carpus and may result in development of carpal varus deformity. 35 Radiography is an insensitive diagnostic test for many soft tissue lesions that do not affect the underlying bone, and ultrasound may be bene ﬁ cial as a complementary imaging modality for collateral ligament injury. Intercarpal Ligament Desmopathy Primary injury to the intercarpal ligaments is an uncommon cause of joint effusion and lameness in horses. Carpal luxation or other trauma can also result in secondary injury to these ligaments ( Fig. 23.20 ). Radiographically, intercarpal ligament desmopathy can be associated with intracapsular effusion and enthesopathy along the dorsal aspect of the cuboidal bones. 1 The lateral palmar intercarpal ligament is also sometimes asso- ciated with avulsion fragments from its attachment on the ulnar carpal bone as seen on the DLPMO projection. 36 However, fragmentation and lucency in this area have also been described as an incidental ﬁ nding in horses without lameness or other clinical signs. 7 Joint Effusion and Synovitis Radiolucent, perisynovial fat pads are normally visible along the dorsal surface of the antebrachiocarpal and middle carpal joints on lateral projections of the carpus ( Fig. 23.12 ). These fat pads can be obscured in cases of intracapsular effusion or synovitis. Carpal Sheath Effusion The carpal sheath extends from the distal radial metaphysis to the mid-metacarpus, and the concave medial surface of the accessory carpal bone serves as the lateral boundary of the carpal canal. 2 Through this region, the sheath contains the su- per ﬁ cial and deep digital ﬂ exor tendons. may be smooth or palisading, and concurrent enthesopathy on the dorsal aspect of the radial, intermediate, and third carpal bone is also possible. 37 Carpal Hygroma, Synovial Hernia, and Synovial Fistula A carpal hygroma is a nonpainful soft tissue swelling on the dorsal aspect of the carpus that is acquired following trauma or repetitive injury ( Fig. 23.27 ). 38 Hygromata are not connected to synovial structures, although they are sometimes called “ false bursae ” because it is common to identify subcutaneous ﬂ uid accumulation deep to the soft tissue swelling. Synovial hernias result from a defect in the joint capsule through which a portion of the synovial membrane (and sy- novial ﬂ uid) protrudes. This term is sometimes used synony- mously with “ synovial cyst ” or ” synovial ganglia, ” although the three terms are distinct entities as cysts do not necessarily have a patent communication with the joint cavity and ganglia do not have a synovial lining. 39 Synovial hernias are also typically nonpainful and identi ﬁ ed as an incidental ﬁ nding with contrast radiographs, ultrasound, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Synovial ﬁ stulae are communications between two synovial structures (e.g., joints and tendon sheaths) that are often pre- sumed to be secondary to previous, concurrent trauma to the communicating structures. Fistulous communication between a carpal hygroma, the antebrachiocarpal joint, and the extensor carpi radialis tendon sheath has also been reported. 40 Soft Tissue Trauma, Draining Tracts, Foreign Bodies Following acute carpal trauma, radiographs are indicated to identify osseous lesions such as fractures, luxations, and avul- sions as well as to assess the region for radiopaque foreign bodies. Hematomas and hemarthrosis can result in extra- and intracapsular soft tissue swelling, respectively. In the chronic stages of healing, soft tissue wounds sometimes develop sup- purative draining/ ﬁ stulous tracts secondary to bone sequestra or foreign material that remains embedded within the soft tissues. Following survey radiographs, contrast medium can be aseptically injected into hygromas, synovial cavities, and draining tracts to better characterize and aid in differentiation of these various soft tissue lesions of the carpus 41 ( Table 23.2 ). Calcinosis Circumscripta Calcinosis circumscripta is a collection of calcium salt deposits in the subcutaneous tissue that manifests radiographically as a granular, mineral opaque mass. This is a variation of dystrophic mineralization that is uncommonly identi ﬁ ed at sites of previ- ous soft tissue trauma or chronic irritation, over bony promi- nences and pressure points, or near joint spaces. Calcinosis circumscripta may be intra- or extracapsular. 42 Hypertrophic Osteopathy Hypertrophic osteopathy is characterized most commonly by painful lower limb swelling, stiffness and/or lameness, joint effusion, and/or restricted ﬂ exibility of affected joints. Radio- graphically, the metacarpal and metatarsal bones are affected most commonly with symmetrical, palisading periosteal prolif- eration along the diaphyses and metaphyses without involve- ment of the subchondral bone or articular surfaces. This bone proliferation can be seen in other bones including the radius and carpal bones. Similar to what is seen in small animal pa- tients, equine hypertrophic osteopathy occurs in tandem with a variety of intrathoracic and, rarely, intra-abdominal pathology including granulomatous disease, pulmonary abscess, pneu- monia, pleural space disease, and neoplasia. The osseous le- sions of hypertrophic osteopathy may regress or resolve following treatment of the primary disease process. 43 Acknowledgment With special thanks to prior authors of this chapter for their contribu tions. Porter T hroughout this chapter, we will refer to the metacarpus and metatarsus collectively as the metacarpus; howev- er, discussion also applies to the metatarsus unless otherwise speci ﬁ ed. Relevant anatomical and pathological dif- ferences between the metacarpus and metatarsus will be dis- cussed. In order to obtain high quality radiographs of the metacarpus, appropriate patient positioning and restraint is imperative. The patient should stand with all four limbs squarely positioned and equally weight bearing, and light sedation may be necessary. Comprehensive radiographic eval- uation of the metacarpus includes the carpometacarpal joint in collimation proximally, and the metacarpophalangeal joint, distally. Depending on the size of the x-ray detector available, this may require a proximally and distally collimated view of each projection. A standard radiographic series includes dor- sopalmar (DP), lateromedial, dorsomedial-palmarolateral obli- que (DMPLO), and dorsolateral-palmaromedial oblique (DLPMO) projections. In the pelvic limb, the term palmar should be replaced by plantar . Additional projections may be indicated based on the history, clinical exam, and available imaging ﬁ ndings and these projections will be further discussed where indicated. RADIOG RAPH IC ANATOM Y AND CO MMON VARIAN TS The Third Metacarpal Bone (The Cannon Bone) The third metacarpal bone lies between the second and fourth metacarpal bones and is the largest of the three bones. When there is partial superimposition of two bones, as is seen in radiography of the metacarpus, a linear lucent line can be seen paralleling the region of superimposition. This phenomenon, known at Mach bands or Mach lines, is due to an optical illusion of edge enhancement created by the observer s retina, and should not be mistaken for a fracture line ( Fig. 24.1 ). 1 While all three metacarpal bones articulate with the distal row of carpal bones to form the carpometacarpal joint, it is only the third metacarpal bone that contributes to the articulation of the metacarpophalangeal joint. The third metatarsal bone is slightly longer than the third metacarpal bone and has a more convex dorsal margin and more palmar angulation of the condyle. The principal nutrient foramen is present in the proximal to middle third of the third metacarpal bone. On the dorsopalmar pro- jection, it is easily identi ﬁ ed as a well-de ﬁ ned, oval lucency, but on lateral and oblique projections, it is obliquely oriented in the palmar cortex of the third metacarpal bone, and should not be mistaken for a fracture ( Fig. 24.2 ). On the dorsopalmar pro- jection, a variable number of pinpoint nutrient foramina may be seen in the proximal subchondral bone of the third metacarpal bone, just distal to the carpometacarpal joint (see Fig. 24.2 ). The palmaroproximal cortex of the third metacarpal bone normally has a coarser trabecular pattern than the remainder of the cortex (see Fig. 24.2 ). The dorsal cortex of the third metacarpal bone is normally thicker than the palmar cortex, as seen on the lateral projection, which should not be mistaken for pathology. A well-de ﬁ ned exostosis or “ bone spur, ” which may be bilateral, may be present at the dorsoproximal aspect of the third metatarsal bone in up to 25% of horses, and although it is not correlated with lameness, it is more frequently seen concurrent with radiologic abnormalities of the distal tarsal joints ( Fig. 24.3 ). 2 The condyle of the third metacarpal bone consists of medial and lateral parts separated by a sagittal ridge, which is the most distal extension of the condyle and articulates with the sagittal groove of the proximal phalanx. The medial portion of the condyle is mildly larger than the lateral portion, which can be helpful for determining laterality on the dorso- palmar projection if necessary. At birth, the proximal physis of the third metacarpal bone should be completely closed and the distal physis closes at 3 to 6 months of age. Metacarpal Soft Tissues Multiple tendons, ligaments, and soft tissue structures provide support for the metacarpus and allow for extension and ﬂ exion of the digit. The extensor tendons, which lie along the dorsal and lateral aspect of the third metacarpal bone contribute little to the radiographic appearance of the metacarpus and are rarely of clinical relevance. The ﬂ exor tendons of the meta- carpus include the super ﬁ cial and deep digital ﬂ exor tendons, which run palmar to the third metacarpal bone. At the mid- metacarpus, the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon is joined dorsally by an accessory (check) ligament which originates from the palmar carpal ligament and palmar aspect of the third and fourth carpal bones in the forelimb. 5 In the pelvic limb, the accessory ligament of the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon originates from the plantar aspect of the ligament between the calcaneus and central and third tarsal bones. It is usually smaller, report- edly absent in 6% of hindlimbs, and has more variable morphology than in the thoracic limb. 6 In the distal third of the metacarpus, between the splint bones and the proximal sesa- moid bones, is the manica ﬂ exoria, a sleeve that wraps dorsally from the super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon and encircles the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon to maintain both tendons in a central po- sition within the digital sheath. The third interosseous muscle (suspensory ligament) origi- nates primarily from the palmar or plantar aspect of the third metacarpal or metatarsal bone. It has smaller attachments on the third carpal and metacarpal bone or fourth tarsal bone, calcaneus, and fourth metatarsal bones, and it is bordered by the splint bones. 5 7 9 The proximal portion of the suspensory ligament is bilobed in the forelimb and somewhat triangular in the hindlimb, and it fuses distally to form a ﬂ at, oval body before dividing into branches. Up to 29.5% of the length of the suspensory ligament branches is subsynovial to the metacarpophalangeal and metatarsophalangeal joints. 11 The suspensory ligament contains variable amounts of fat and muscle, which are typically located in two medial and lateral bundles proximally and become more randomly positioned in a zig-zag pattern within the body of the ligament. 10 Synovial structures of the metacarpus and metatarsus include the carpal and tarsal sheath, respectively, and the digital ﬂ exor tendon sheath. The carpal sheath encircles the super ﬁ cial and deep digital ﬂ exor tendon and accessory ligament of the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon and extends to the proximal third of the metacarpus. The tarsal sheath encircles the lateral digital ﬂ exor tendon and accessory ligament of the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon and extends to the proximal third of the metatarsus. The digital ﬂ exor tendon sheath extends from the distal third of the metacarpus to the mid to distal pastern and surrounds the super ﬁ cial and deep digital ﬂ exor tendons. COMM ON RADIOG RAPHIC ABN ORMALIT IES OF THE METAC ARPUS Soft Tissue Structures When evaluating the metacarpus for soft tissue pathology, it is important to have a thorough understanding of relevant soft tissue anatomy. Due to the limited amount of fat in the meta- carpus, soft tissue swelling due to enlargement of the super ﬁ cial soft tissue structures such as the suspensory ligament branches or super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon may be radio- graphically apparent. Moderate to marked effusion and/or sy- novitis of the digital ﬂ exor tendon sheath may result in the appearance of soft tissue enlargement of the medial and lateral aspect of the distal third of the metacarpus on the DP projec- tion or increased soft tissue opacity between the suspensory ligament branches and digital ﬂ exor tendons on the lateral projection ( Fig. 24.8 ). Dystrophic mineralization of soft tissues structures such as the ﬂ exor tendons or suspensory ligament branches may be radiographically apparent (see Fig. 24.8 ). Soft tissue thickening of the metacarpus may be focal or diffuse. Differentials for focal soft tissue thickening depend on the anatomic location, how extensive the lesion is, and if there is concurrent osseous pathology. Differential diagnoses may include focal edema, hematoma, granuloma formation as sec- ondary to trauma or infectious etiologies such as habronemiasis, ﬁ brosis from prior/chronic soft tissue injury or soft tissue neoplasia ( Fig. 24.9 ). Subcutaneous emphysema may also be seen due to a wound, abscess, or iatrogenic introduction. Thorough evaluation of the osseous structures in the region of the soft tissue pathology is pertinent, and acquiring multiple oblique radiographic projections may be helpful to rule out associated pathology such as sequestrum formation, periosteal proliferation, or osteomyelitis. Differential diagnoses for diffuse soft tissue thickening surrounding the metacarpus may include subcutaneous edema, cellulitis, lymphangitis, and vasculitis and should be prioritized in light of the clinical exam and other imaging ﬁ ndings (see Fig. 24.9 ). Periostitis Periostitis is in ﬂ ammation of the periosteum which may result in osseous proliferation and can occur due to trauma, infection, or less commonly, neoplasia. The equine metacarpus is a common location for focal periosteal proliferation due to trauma, as there is a limited amount of fat and soft tissue overlying the bone to provide protection. Radiographic evalu- ation should be performed when ﬁ rm, osseous thickening is noted in order to rule out fractures and attempt to differentiate between benign and malignant processes. Although these periosteal reactions are not frequently associated with lame- ness, they will often have persistently increased radiopharma- ceutical uptake when evaluated with nuclear scintigraphy. 12 Focal regions of osseous proliferation may also be seen at the interosseous space between the metacarpal bones, commonly referred to as “ splints. ” 13 These occur due to trauma to the interosseous ligament or syndesmosis between the metacarpal bones, and are very common, especially in young horses as they are started into work. Splints most commonly develop between the second and third metacarpal bones in the forelimb, and between the third and fourth metatarsal bones in the hindlimb. Splints can be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from periostitis radiographically and may have a similar clinical pre- sentation. In the initial, active phases, these lesions are often warm and painful upon palpation and may have associated soft tissue swelling. After the in ﬂ ammation resolves, nonpainful osseous proliferation will persist for an extended period of time. The proliferation may have irregular margins with multiple linear lucent regions, which, when superimposed on the underlying bone, can be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from fracture formation ( Fig. 24.10 ). Radiographic evaluation should include oblique projections at various angles of obliquity of the metacarpal region as needed to evaluate the interosseous spaces between the metacarpal bones. Dorsal metacarpal disease, also known as “ bucked shins, ” is a common cause of periostitis, most often seen in 2-year-old Thoroughbred racehorses. It is caused by cyclic fatigue due to excessive compression of the dorsal and dorsomedial aspects of the third metacarpal bone, often bilaterally, and can lead to incomplete (saucer) fractures of the dorsal cortex of the third metacarpal bone. With this disease, the bone undergoes re- petitive stress without the necessary amount of time needed to adequately remodel. New, weaker bone is produced at the points of stress on the bone, and the rapid bone formation causes the periosteum to be elevated from the underlying cortex and become in ﬂ amed. Diagnosis is often made by the physical exam and history of pain on palpation over the dorsal aspect of the third metacarpal bone and/or soreness after strenuous athletic activity. Radiographic ﬁ ndings may include smooth periosteal proliferation over the dorsal and dorsal medial aspect of the third metacarpal bone and incomplete, dorsal cortical fractures. This region should be carefully evalu- ated for incomplete fractures ( Fig. 24.11 ). Hypertrophic osteopathy is a rare condition in horses resulting in symmetrical periosteal proliferation along the diaphysis and metaphysis of long bones, most often affecting the metacarpal and metatarsal bones. This disease process typically occurs in association with other pathology, most commonly intrathoracic disease. 15 Osteomyelitis and Sequestra Due to limited fat and soft tissue surrounding the metacarpal bones, this region is especially predisposed to bone trauma, which in some cases, may result in infectious osteitis or oste- omyelitis. Radiographically, aggressive processes in bone, such as infection and neoplasia are more likely to result in irregularly margined, ill-de ﬁ ned proliferation and/or lysis with indistinct margins or a long zone of transition between normal and abnormal bone. Sequestrum formation is a common sequela to trauma and infection in the metacarpal region, often affecting the thick dorsal cortex of the third metacarpal bone. 16 Sequestra consist of a central piece of devitalized, sclerotic bone (the sequestrum) which has become separated from the adjacent, healthy bone and surrounded by a radiolucent region consisting of purulent material and granulation tissue encircled by a zone of dense bone (the involucrum). A draining tract (cloaca) may also be present, extending from the sequestrum through the surrounding tissues. The radiographic appearance of sequestra depends on the angle at which it is struck by the x- ray beam ( Fig. 24.12 eFig. 24.1 ). As the sequestrum serves as a nidus for infection, surgical debridement is often necessary to facilitate healing. Sclerosis of the proximal third metacarpal bone at the attachment of the suspensory ligament may be multifocal or localized to the lateral or medial aspect and can range from mild to severely increased mineral opacity resulting in loss of the normal trabecular bone pattern ( Fig. 24.14 eFig. 24.2 ). Osteolysis may be seen as focal or multifocal regions of decreased mineral opacity at the palmar- oproximal cortex of the third metacarpal bone. These radio- graphic ﬁ ndings may be subtle and more thorough evaluation of the proximal suspensory ligament attachment site may be achieved with collimated projections centered on the proximal one-third of the metacarpus. Abnormal mineral opacity or changes in the trabecular bone pattern will be best seen on the dorsopalmar projection, while endosteal sclerosis and osseous proliferation will be better evaluated on the lateromedial pro- jection. Osseous proliferation or sclerosis at the proximal sus- pensory ligament attachment site is likely chronic in nature and does not always indicate a source of lameness. When evaluated in Quarter horses, radiographically identi ﬁ ed osseous changes on the third metatarsal bone were not predictive of either the presence or severity of proximal suspensory desmopathy, but there was a positive correlation between the severity of radio- graphic and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) ﬁ ndings for osseous proliferation and resorption at the ligament attachment site. 19 Avulsion fractures at the attachment site of the suspen- sory ligament can also occur. 20 21 In these cases, additional projections including collimated dorsopalmar and lateral pro- jections of the proximal aspect of the third metacarpal region can be helpful to better elucidate the fracture line ( Fig. 24.15 ). Splint Bone Fractures The second and fourth metacarpal and metatarsal bones will be referred to as the splint bones in this section unless otherwise speci ﬁ ed. Similar to the third metacarpal bone, the splint bones are particularly prone to external trauma due to their super ﬁ cial location and limited soft tissue coverage to offer protection. Trauma such as kicks can result in open fractures of the prox- imal and mid portions of the splint bones, which can lead to osteomyelitis and sequestration. The distal aspect of the splint bones may be abaxially displaced and even fractured in asso- ciation with desmopathy of the suspensory ligament branches ( Fig. 24.16 eFig. 24.3 ). 22 Nonunion fractures or unfused sepa- rate centers of ossi ﬁ cations may be seen in the distal aspects of the splint bones, without clinical relevance. Management of splint fractures depends on the location of the fracture and the weight-bearing status of the bone. 21 23 When a splint bone fracture is clinically suspected, it may be helpful to obtain ra- diographs at multiple angles of obliquity between lateromedial and dorsopalmar in order to obtain an image with the primary x-ray beam tangential to the fracture margin. Repeated radio- graphs over time should be evaluated for fracture healing as well as callus development. The position of any excessive callus formation should be taken into consideration as axial protru- sion of the callus can impinge upon the suspensory ligament and result in desmopathy and adhesion formation ( Fig. 24.17 ). 14 Third Metacarpal/Metatarsal Fractures The third metacarpal bone is a common location for stress fractures in racehorses and sport horses. Stress fractures occur at speci ﬁ c predilection sites along the bone when damage due to repetitive loading accumulates more quickly than can be repaired by the remodeling process. Evidence of osseous remodeling may precede fracture formation and includes endosteal or trabecular bone sclerosis, osseous proliferation and/or lysis, and concurrent soft tissue thickening or joint effusion. Recognizing incomplete fractures as early as possible is imperative because they may progress to complete cata- strophic fractures. Radiographic projections in which the pri- mary x-ray beam is tangential to the fracture line will be most diagnostic; thus, special radiographic projections may be helpful in addition to the standard series. When evaluating for incomplete condylar fractures, more thorough evaluation in- cludes a dorsopalmar projection of the joint in ﬂ exion or a dorsodistal-palmaroproximal oblique projection. 29 30 Even with ideal positioning, however, fractures may not be radiographi- cally apparent for 10 to 14 days and, even then, may be subtle. For thorough evaluation of cases in which stress fractures are clinically suspected, but not identi ﬁ ed radiographically, alter- native imaging such as nuclear scintigraphy or positron emis- sion tomography (PET) should be considered. Ultrasonography Ultrasound is commonly performed of the palmar metacarpus and provides a widely accessible, portable, and practical approach for more thorough evaluation of soft tissues. The super ﬁ cial nature of the palmar soft tissues of the metacarpus makes ultrasound ideal for evaluation of this region when per- formed by experienced ultrasonographers. When preparing for transcutaneous ultrasonography, adequate preparation of the site is imperative and should include clipping the hair, thoroughly cleaning the skin, and applying acoustic coupling agents such as alcohol and/or ul- trasound gel. Structures should be evaluated in both transverse (short axis) and longitudinal (long axis) planes, with consistent transducer orientation and comparison to the contralateral limb. For evaluation of the palmar metacarpus, a linear transducer with a frequency range of 8 to 15 megahertz is an ideal starting point; however, it is recommended to use the highest frequency possible while still achieving the depth penetration needed to image the entire area of interest. Use of an acoustic standoff pad is necessary to eliminate the effect of near- ﬁ eld artifact when evaluating more super ﬁ cial structures. Frequency, focal zones, gain, and depth should be routinely adjusted as needed to maximize image quality. Recognizing ultrasound artifacts including, but not limited to, edge shad- owing, distal acoustic enhancement, and distal acoustic shad- owing is essential for accurate image interpretation. Anisotropism is a particularly important principle to understand with regard to musculoskeletal imaging. It explains the effect that the incident angle of the ultrasound beam has on the appearance of ﬁ brillar structures such as tendons or liga- ments. 31 When the ultrasound beam is perpendicular to such structures, the majority of sound is re ﬂ ected and echogenicity is maximized, and when the angle of insonation is decreased, the echogenicity of that structure is decreased, and the tendon or ligament will appear hypoechoic ( Fig. 24.19 ). 32 This artifact can be helpful in differentiating tissue types such as fat or fascia surrounding a tendon or ligament. Without a thorough under- standing of this phenomenon, areas of hypoechogenicity due to decreased angles of insonation can be falsely interpreted as pathology. Abnormal sonographic ﬁ ndings in the equine metacarpus may include focal or diffuse ligament or tendon enlargement, margin irregularity/tearing, or changes in echogenicity. Cross- sectional area measurements can be obtained to objectively measure size and to compare these measurements over time, and normal measurements have been reported in the meta- carpus/metatarsus. 37 39 Tendon or ligament hypoechogenicity, termed core lesions when they occur centrally, may result from areas of ﬁ ber pattern irregularity, edema, or hematoma forma- tion and can be focal or diffuse. Focal regions of increased tendon or ligament echogenicity may result from scar tissue/ ﬁ brin formation or mineralization. The use of color and power Doppler interrogation has been described as a complement to B-mode ultrasound evaluation of tendons and ligaments in the metacarpus and may be helpful for assessment of healing 40 42 ( Fig. 24.21 ). Super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendinopathy is the most common tendon injury in athletic horses and frequently involves tendon enlargement and palpable heat, pain, and swelling in the mid metacarpus. Sonographic ﬁ ndings often include focal areas of hypoechogenicity centrally or peripherally within the tendon; however, diffuse hypoechogenicity throughout a region of the tendon may also occur ( Fig. 24.22 ). Although the mid meta- carpal region is most commonly affected, super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendinopathy can occur at the most proximal aspect of the tendon, 43 as well as in the carpal canal of middle-aged to older horses, where it is often characterized by focal, palmar hypoechogenicity. 44 Less commonly, lesions of the super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon may be seen at the level of the digital sheath. 45 Deep digital ﬂ exor tendinopathy is often located at the level of the digital sheath, and may have concurrent digital sheath effusion and/or tenosynovitis. 46 Most commonly, lesions consist of marginal tears. Hypoechoic lesions, which may extend to the tendon periphery, tendon enlargement, and perilesional tissue proliferation, may be seen ( Fig. 24.23 ). 47 The pathology of the manica ﬂ exoria may also be seen in the digital sheath and in- cludes asymmetry, heterogeneous echogenicity, lack of margin de ﬁ nition, partial or complete tears, abnormal sliding of the deep and super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendons, and displacement of the super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon on dynamic exam. 45 48 Complete evaluation of the tendons in the digital sheath is challenging. It is important to note that sonographic abnormalities of the suspensory branches can be seen in nonlame horses. 17 Due to the subsynovial location of a portion of the suspensory ligament branches, concurrent pathology of the metacarpophalangeal joint should be evaluated. 11 Computed Tomography and Magnetic Resonance Imaging Cross-sectional imaging, such as CT and MRI, often provide a valuable complement to radiography of the metacarpus. With increasing availability of these modalities, and ability to image the equine limb without general anesthesia, the utility of these modalities is becoming more apparent. MRI is generally considered the gold standard for soft tissue evaluation due to its superior contrast resolution, and allows for evaluation of increased osseous ﬂ uid content such as secondary to contusion, edema, or necrosis. 9 54 55 CT allows for rapid cross-sectional image acquisition and provides excellent contrast and spatial resolution. Because it eliminates the challenges of radiographic superimposition, CT allows for more complete evaluation of complex anatomical structures, and may be more sensitive for identi ﬁ cation of subtle osseous pathology that may not be radiographically apparent ( Fig. 24.28 ). Both CT and low- ﬁ eld- strength MRI can be performed in the standing horse; however, more complete MRI evaluation of the metacarpus and meta- tarsus requires general anesthesia to limit the motion artifact inherent in the standing horse.
