Bills ANAT OMY The equin e fetl ock, or met aca rpoph alang eal (MCP ) and meta- tarso phala ngea l (MT P) arti cula tions are hig h mot ion hinge joint s, for med by the dista l end of the met acarp al (or metat arsa l) bone and the prox imal end of the prox ima l phala nx. It is not poss ibl e to relia bly diff erent iate the righ t fro m the left or the for elimb from the hind limb on unla beled rad iogra phs. The arti cula r surf ace of the prox imal phalan x is conca ve and has a sagi ttal groo ve oppo sing the sagi ttal ridg e at the dist al end of the thir d metac arp al (MC III ) or the thir d met atars al (MT III) bone. This ridge and groo ve divi de the wei ght-be arin g surf ace into two uneq ual parts , the thir d metac arp al/m etac arpal cond yles and the prox imal phala nx med ial and late ral fove a. The larg est surf ace is on the medi al (or axia l) side , whe re loadi ng is grea t- est. The sagi ttal ridge of MC III or MT III is recei ved into a depr essio n at the palm ar * surf ace tha t is crea ted by the prox imal sesa moi d bones and the inte rses amoid ean liga ment . The joint has two rad ii of arti cula tion. The dorsal rad ius serves the weigh t- bear ing port ion, and the palm ar radi us con forms to the arti cu- latio n wit h the prox ima l sesa moid bon es. 1 The junc tion of these rad ii of arti cula tion ofte n appea rs ﬂ at in late ral radi ograph s and may be conf use d wi th a lesi on of the arti cula r surf ace and subc hondr al bon e, whi ch is com plica ted by the fact tha t pa- tho logy occurs in the same loca tion . The joint capsule attachments at the proximal end of the proximal phalanx are immediately periarticular, with a pal- marodistal recess between the proximal phalanx and the distal sesamoidean ligaments. The capsule attaches to the distal end of MC III or MT III at the periarticular margins. Dorsally, a large recess extends proximally and forms a pouch. The palmar joint capsule extends proximal to the sesamoid bones between the suspensory ligament and MC III or MT III. 1 Ligaments associated with the MCP and MTP articulations are described elsewhere. 2 RADIOG RAPH IC EXAMIN ATION The examination of the fetlock joint should include the prox- imal interphalangeal joint and the distal third of the metacarpal or metatarsal bones. Identi ﬁ cation markers are essential in radiographic examination of the MCP or MTP articulation; right versus left and front versus hind should be designated clearly. If oblique views are obtained, the direction of the x-ray beam designates the name of the projection from point-of-entrance to point-of-exit. Markers should be placed at the lateral aspect of the anatomic part of interest on all views, except for the lat- eromedial view for which markers should be placed dorsally. 3 Survey radiographic examination of the joint should include a lateromedial, a dorsopalmar, and two oblique projections (dorsal 15-degree proximal 45-degree lateral- palmarodistomedial and dorsal 15-degree proximal 45-degree medial-palmarodistolateral), with the limb bearing weight if possible. In the author s opinion, using a horizontal oblique projection has less utility than the incorporation of 15-degree proximal to distal angle as palmar fragments are easily missed on the horizontal oblique projections. The survey examination should precede any special radiographic projections or contrast studies of the joint. The lateromedial projection should be made with the primary beam centered at the artic- ulation and directed parallel to an imaginary line connecting the condylar fossae at the distal end of MC III or MT III. A true lateromedial projection is essential to properly assess the sagittal ridge of distal MC III or MT III. 4 For the dorsopalmar projection, because the plane of the joint is at an angle to the solar surface of the hoof, the primary beam is directed from dorsoproximal to palmarodistal at least 10 to 15 degrees (forelimb 10, hindlimb 15). This should result in the projection of the proximal sesamoid bones over the distal aspect of MC III or MT III and the joint space projected with maximal width. 5 The dorsal 15-degree proximal 45-degree lateral/palmar- odistomedial and dorsal 15-degree proximal 45-degree medial/ palmarodistolateral projections should be a routine part of the survey examination. These oblique views are necessary to view the abaxial aspects of the articular surfaces, the periarticular margins, and the proximal sesamoid bones. Oblique views made in a dorsal 60-degree lateral/palmaromedial or dorsal 60- degree medial/palmarolateral direction allow the best visibility of the dorsal eminence of the proximal phalanx, which is located near midline, and the axial aspect of the proximal sesamoid bones as well as the joint space between the dorsal margin of the proximal sesamoid bone and the palmar condyle. Some prefer using the 60-degree oblique view as the routine oblique view rather than the oblique views made at 45 degrees because of improved delineation of the axial margin of the proximal sesamoid bones ( Fig. 25.1 ). 6 Additional projections of the joint may be indicated ac- cording to the information gained from the routine survey ra- diographs or based on discipline-speci ﬁ c indications, such as the ﬂ exed dorsopalmar projection for the Thoroughbred race- horse. 4 7 The lateromedial projection during ﬂ exion is per- formed while the foot is held off the ground as if the sole of the hoof were being inspected visually. Alternate positions include variations in the degree of ﬂ exion and ﬂ exed oblique views. These projections may provide better visibility of subarticular surfaces at the dorsal aspect of distal MC III or MT III, the proximal part of the proximal phalanx, and the articular mar- gins of the proximal sesamoid bones. 5 A dorsal 30-degree proximal 70-degree lateral- palmarodistomedial oblique projection, or “ elevated angle oblique, ” can be used to assist in the evaluation of the palmar C H A P T E R 25 Equine Fetloc k Joint * “ Palmar(o) ” is used throughout this chapter with the understandin gthat “ plantar(o) ” should be substitute d if reference is being made to thehindlimb. 511

In this projection, a tangential view of the articular margin of the distal aspect of MC III or MT III is created. The foot is elevated on a block, and the limb is extended. The primary beam direction is approximately 125 degrees to the axis of the metacarpal or metatarsal bone. 8 The angle of the primary beam determines the tangent of the joint surface that is visible. In an ideally positioned radiograph, the distal third of the proximal sesamoid bones will be super- imposed with the articular margin. This projection is particu- larly helpful for identifying incomplete condylar fractures and characterizing palmar comminution. The palmaroproximal-palmarodistal projection is used to see the palmar articular surface of MC III or MT III and the proximal sesamoid bones. Positioning of the patient requires that the x- ray tube be placed close to the horse s body. The limb should be positioned as far caudal as possible, and the foot is placed on a supporting tunnel containing a cassette. 5 Inherent magni ﬁ cation results from the use of this projection because of the distance between the proximal sesamoid bones and the detector. The abaxial surfaces of the proximal sesamoids may be examined further by placing the detector medial or lateral to the joint on the affected side. The x-ray beam is then directed in a dorsal 50-degree proximal, 45-degree lateral/dis- topalmaromedial or dorsal 50-degree proximal, 45-degree medial/distopalmarolateral direction, respectively, to create a tangential view of the proximal sesamoid bones. 9 This posi- tioning results in the x-ray beam being directed downward at the sesamoid bones at an angle of 50 degrees from horizontal. This tangential projection is bene ﬁ cial in assessing whether articular involvement is present with sesamoid lesions and to better characterize occult suspensory ligament avulsions or basilar sesamoid fractures. A ﬂ exed dorsopalmar projection is acquired by positioning the foot in a block (e.g., Hickman navicular block) to provide a more predictable degree of fetlock ﬂ exion. The primary beam is angled between 0 and 35 degrees depending on the tangential surface of the condyle attempting to be imaged. 10 The projec- tion is particularly useful for identifying unicortical condylar fractures, palmar comminution of said condylar fractures, and axial sesamoid lesions ( Fig. 25.3 ). 11 The dorsoproximal-dorsodistal projection is used to improve visualization of the dorsal margin of the metacarpal/metatarsal condyles. With the metacarpus aligned perpendicular to the ground, the fetlock is held in a ﬂ exed position with the detector held horizontal to the ground under the joint. The beam is variably angled, between 45 and 70 degrees, to create a tangential image of the dorsodistal metacarpal condyle and helps to characterize the dorsal articular margin ( Fig. 25.4 ). The ideal projection angle will depend upon where a particular lesion is located along the curvature of the condyle, most commonly in the dorsal to mid-thirds of the medial aspect. 12 Contrast arthrography of the MCP or MTP joint and intra- thecal injection of the digital ﬂ exor tendon sheath is sometimes useful but has largely been replaced by ultrasonographic assessment. For contrast arthrography, 5 to 10 mL of water- soluble contrast medium containing 300 mg/mL of iodine is injected using aseptic technique. Injection of contrast medium should follow arthrocentesis and withdrawal of an equal vol- ume of synovial ﬂ uid. Injection is made into the lateral pouch of the joint, proximal to the lateral sesamoid bones and dorsal to the suspensory ligament or into the dorsal synovial recess. The joint should be ﬂ exed, extended, and massaged vigorously before radiography to distribute the contrast medium throughout the joint. ALTE RNATIV E IMAGING MODA LITIES Ultrasound offers detailed evaluation of soft tissues surrounding the MCP or MTP joint and is used frequently to complement the radiographic examination. Portable ultrasound machines can be used to image the extensor and ﬂ exor tendons, manica ﬂ exoria, the suspensory and distal sesamoidean ligaments, the inter- sesamoidean ligament, the synovial lining and joint recesses, collateral ligaments, cortical margins, and portions of the articular cartilage of standing horses at rest. 13 More recently, non weight-bearing and dynamic ultrasound of the suspensory branches and digital ﬂ exor tendon sheath has been per- formed. 14 15 The normal sonographic features of the MCP and MTP joints have been described. 16 Nuclear scintigraphy for evaluation of bone utilizing 99m Tc- methylene diphosphonate (MDP) or 99m Tc-hydroxymethylene disphosphonate (HDP) has been performed for decades. It is highly sensitive for detecting osseous fetlock pathology in many disciplines. 17 18 Pathologic changes and nonpathologic mani- festations of adaptive remodeling of bone can be identi ﬁ ed, so knowledge of discipline-speci ﬁ c patterns of uptake is impera- tive for correct interpretation. 19 In addition to conventional radiography, computed tomog- raphy (CT) may be useful in selected patients to image the MCP or MTP joint. 20 CT excels in the evaluation of bone and is useful in imaging condylar and complex fractures, developmental or- thopedic disease, and manifestations of early joint disease, such as small osteophytes, subchondral and trabecular sclerosis, osseous cyst-like lesions (OCLLs), subchondral bone injury secondary to repetitive trauma, and ill-de ﬁ ned lysis as found in joint sepsis and septic osteomyelitis 21 22 ( Fig. 25.5 ). There is wider availability of standing fan- and cone-beam CT systems with similar performance in identi ﬁ cation of osseous fetlock pathology in various disciplines. 23 25 The speed of image acquisition is also a bene ﬁ t compared to other standing cross- sectional imaging modalities, such as low- ﬁ eld magnetic reso- nance imaging (MRI). Finally, similar to certain MRI sequences, CT volume data acquisition allows for multiplanar reconstruc- tion and reformatting of images such that an in ﬁ nite number of planes can be evaluated with a single scan of the region of interest. MRI is commonly used to evaluate the equine distal limb, including the MCP or MTP joints. 21 26 31 A distinct advantage of MRI is the exceptional soft tissue contrast resolution and ability to evaluate articular cartilage ( Figs. 25.6 25.8 ). Magnetic resonance (MR) examinations usually include several types of acquisition sequences to allow evaluation of different anatomic and pathologic features, based on the composition of each tis- sue. MR systems employing high- ﬁ eld magnets require that horses be under general anesthesia for imaging. Cortisone Arthropathy Cortisone arthropathy may involve articular and periarticular structures and may lead to variable degrees of degeneration and proliferation. Repeated steroid injections result in localized demineralization of bone and decreased trabecular detail. Long- term changes include mineralization in the periarticular soft tissues associated with deposition of steroid within those structures. A differential diagnosis of steroid-induced arthritis should be considered in the presence of degenerative change or collapse of subchondral bone with mineralization in peri- articular soft tissue ( Fig. 25.14 ). Osteochondrosis and Osteochondritis Dissecans Osteochondral fragments of the dorsoproximal aspect of the proximal phalanx are common in young, untrained horses of all breeds but particularly in Warmblood populations. There is a similar distribution between the fore and hindlimbs; however, the medial aspect of the proximal phalanx is highly over- represented. The fragments are typically smooth and histolog- ically are not representative of any particular disease process, but given they are surrounded by smooth hyaline cartilage, a developmental orthopedic condition though juvenile trauma has also been suggested. Fragments are not typically associated with lameness in this population. 38 Osteochondral fragments of the palmar aspect of the joint have been given three classi ﬁ cations. 39 Type I fragments occur at the proximal end of the proximal phalanx, just medial or lateral to the sagittal groove in the region of attachment of the short distal sesamoidean ligaments; type II fragments have an origin from the wing of the proximal phalanx ( Figs. 25.15 and 25.16 ). Type III fragments originate from the basilar margin of the sesamoid bones and are discussed under the section on sesamoid basilar fractures ( Fig. 25.17 ). Type I or II fragments have the highest incidence in Standardbreds and were origi- nally reported as avulsion fractures. 40 Because of the anatomic origin, symmetry, and breed predilection, these fragments have been suggested by some to be the result of osteochondrosis. These fragments are the subject of much controversy. Osteochondrosis of the sagittal ridge of MC III or MT III is usually diagnosed in young horses and occurs with variable radiographic expression ( Fig. 25.18 eFig. 25.2 ). Radiographic signs may vary from small areas of ﬂ attening to large excava- tions of subchondral bone of the sagittal ridge and free osseous fragmentation. Lesions are best seen on ﬂ exed lateral pro- jections of the MCP or MTP joint and can also be seen on dorsopalmar projections. Detached osteochondral fragments may be found in close association to the bone defect or may be nestled in distant recesses of the joint. 50 Osseous Cyst-Like Lesions Ovoid lucent regions with thin rims of surrounding sclerosis can be found in the distal metacarpal condyle and proximal aspect of the proximal phalanx and variably can be a cause of lameness ( Fig. 25.19 eFig. 25.3 ). The etiology is uncertain with both developmental and juvenile trauma etiologies proposed. Subchondral OCLLs can also occur at the proximal end of the proximal phalanx and are often dif ﬁ cult to see radiographically. Septic Arthritis Septic arthritis may be associated with hematogenous spread of microorganisms, such as occurs with omphalophlebitis, or by direct contamination because of trauma or nonsterile invasive techniques. Radiographic signs of early septic arthritis are periarticular soft tissue swelling and distention of the joint. Progression of the disease results in malalignment, subluxation, or collapse of the joint ( Fig. 25.20 ) and subchondral bone lysis and periosteal proliferation at the joint margins ( Fig. 25.21 ). The cartilage space may appear increased at areas of sub- chondral bone lysis. Diminished joint space is evidence of the loss of articular cartilage that typically precedes subchondral bone change. The radiographic signs of increased apparent joint space must be analyzed critically. Incomplete ossi ﬁ cation of the cartilage model is normally present in young, developing ani- mals. The large soft tissue space at articular margins diminishes progressively with skeletal maturity. Furthermore, radiographs made in non weight-bearing horses will cause joint spaces to be widened compared with weight-bearing projections. Whenever possible, the horse should bear normal weight on the joint at the time of radiography. Increased thickness of the articular cartilage has not been documented in animals. Exces- sive ﬂ uid or soft tissue in the joint space, as occurs with immune-mediated arthritis, results in a wider joint space. However, such diseases have not been documented in the horse. Nonseptic in ﬂ ammatory joint diseases have varied causes and may be dif ﬁ cult to classify. Radiographic signs are disten- sion of the joint and displacement of periarticular soft tissues. If the condition is chronic, periarticular osteoproliferation may develop. There is increasing recognition that nonracing sport horses are af ﬂ icted by subchondral bone disease in discipline-speci ﬁ c patterns, but the imaging manifestation of regions of sclerosis with central demineralization is conserved across breeds and disciplines. The sagittal groove, medial fovea of the proximal phalanx, and the dorsomedial MC III/MT III condyles are overrepresented in nonracing sport horses 17 52 ( Fig. 25.22 ). Variable angle dorsopalmar projections can improve the conspicuity of sagittal groove lesions, while the dorsoproximal to dorsodistal oblique projection is best to characterize medial condylar injury (see Fig. 25.4 ). The forelimbs are more affected than the hind. The palmar aspect of the lateral parasagittal groove is the most commonly affected site and lesions can be dif ﬁ cult to identify radiographically until more advanced disease is present. Lateral condylar fractures most commonly propagate proximally and laterally toward the lateral cortex while medial fractures are more likely to spiral proximally; thus, radiographic evaluation of the latter requires radiograph acquisition of the entire metacarpus/metatarsus. With the exception of Standardbred racehorses, distal MC III or MT III condyle fractures in other breeds are typically the result of a single traumatic event. Radiographic signs include uneven joint surface, interruption of the metaphyseal cortex, and the presence of a radiolucent fracture line extending from the joint surface to the cortex. The fractures in Thoroughbred racehorses ( Fig. 25.23 ) may be dis- placed, complete but nondisplaced, or incomplete and in a lower percentage of horses, associated with axial fracture of the ipsilateral sesamoid bone. 54 55 Prognosis after surgical treat- ment varies but is best for fractures without concurrent sesa- moid fracture, palmar comminution, or intra-articular fragmentation. 55 57 A dorsal 20-degree medial-palmarolateral projection can improve the sensitivity of detection for this lesion. 58 Sagittal or parasagittal fractures of the proximal phalanx in racehorses often result from prodromal accumulated micro- trauma. 59 If there is distal extension of the fracture, this may extend to the proximal interphalangeal joint or obliquely through the lateral cortex of the proximal phalanx. 60 Highly comminuted proximal phalanx fractures resulting from rota- tional or torsional forces are not uncommon in nonracing sport and pleasure horses. Fracture location and severity must be considered relative to surgical repair and prognosis. 61 Traumatic Osteochondral Fragmentation, Chip Fractures Traumatic osteochondral fragmentation is most common in racehorses, with the forelimbs and the medial periarticular eminence of the proximal phalanx highly overrepresented. This is the result of repetitive impact of the proximal phalanx with the dorsodistal metacarpus/tarsus in extension. 62 64 Acute chip fractures may have sharp borders and angular con ﬁ gurations. Chronic chip fractures undergo remodeling and have smooth, rounded borders. The latter are usually attached to the joint capsule or to the joint margin as an exostosis ( Fig. 25.24 eFig. 25.4 ). Free joint bodies may displace or move about within the joint.Osteochondral fragments arising from the palmarolateral/ plantarolateral or palmaromedial/plantaromedial eminences of the proximal phalanx ( Fig. 25.25 eFig. 25.5 ) have been re- ported as chronic or juvenile avulsion fractures 34 40 45 65 but are considered by some to be manifestations of osteochondrosis as described earlier. 41 49 66 67 Fractures of the Proximal Sesamoids Proximal sesamoid fractures are consistently of three types: apical, midbody, or basilar. Recently, dorsal subchondral bone injury of the proximal sesamoid bones has been implicated as the underlying cause of midbody sesamoid fractures in racehorses. 68 However, these lesions are essentially impossible to detect radiographically and require cross-sectional imaging for diagnosis (i.e., CT, MRI, PET). The prognosis of sesamoid fractures is correlated to the type of fracture and damage to the associated structures. Reviews of the clinical aspects of apical 69 and basilar 70 sesamoid fractures are available. Sesamoiditis, Suspensory Enthesopathy Sesamoiditis is characterized radiographically by bone prolif- eration on nonarticular surfaces of the proximal sesamoid bones. 71 Sesamoiditis is usually associated with degenerative change in the suspensory ligament and degenerative remodel- ing or fracture at the distal ends of MC II or MT IV. Linear or ovoid lysis may appear to penetrate the sesamoid from the abaxial surface. The linear lesions typically represent widened vascular channels while ovoid or cyst-like lesions represent suspensory branch enthesis resorption ( Fig. 25.28 eFig. 25.7 ). Axial sesamoiditis is somewhat rare with numerous speculative etiologies, including infarction, infection, and trauma. 72 Axial and intersesamoidean sesamoid pathology is notoriously painful typically with a poor prognosis for athletic soundness regard- less of the underlying etiology. Disuse Atrophy of Bone The earliest manifestation of disuse atrophy is typically in the proximal sesamoid bones but may also be recognized in the long bones as a reduction in medullary opacity and cortical thinning. Trabeculae within the bone become large and coarse. This change occurs because of altered stress or axial weight bearing and may not signify primary pathologic change in the joint ( Fig. 25.29 ). The ergot can be visible as a round soft tissue to mineral opacity superimposed with the proximal phalanx on the dor- sopalmar view (see Fig. 26.2 ). On the corresponding later- omedial view, the ergot will be located along the palmar aspect of the skin. A small palmar concavity is present between the medial and lateral condyles of the distal aspect of the proximal phalanx. This concavity may create another round radiolucent region near midline on dorsopalmar radiographs and should not be mistaken for a cyst in the distal aspect of the bone (see Fig. 26.2 ). A nutrient foramen may be identi ﬁ ed radiographically in the proximal phalanx but can be variable in position. The position of the nutrient foramen of the proximal phalanx on forelimb radiographs has been characterized in two studies. 8 9 A nutrient foramen was identi ﬁ ed radiographically in the majority of forelimbs reviewed (77% of Thoroughbreds and 69.5% of Standardbreds) and was present either within the dorsal or palmar cortex. The appearance of the nutrient foramen can be bilaterally symmetrical in some horses but asymmetrical in others. A nutrient foramen was not found in both the dorsal and palmar cortex of the same limb; however, both were occa- sionally present in the proximal phalanx of foals ( Fig. 26.3 ). In another review of dorsal foramina in the proximal phalanx, the nutrient foramen was found in the dorsal cortex of 27.5% of the forelimbs and hindlimbs evaluated. 10 In this study, three breeds of horses (Standardbreds, Warmbloods, and Friesians) were included, and in most of the horses the dorsal foramen was identi ﬁ ed unilaterally. The nutrient foramen in the dorsal aspect of the proximal phalanx is best seen on the lateromedial view and most commonly courses obliquely from proximal to distal at the level of the mid diaphysis (see Fig. 26.3 , also see Fig. 26.6B ). Osteochondral fragments, secondary to osteochondrosis, are occasionally found in the proximal interphalangeal joint. In one study assessing presale radiographs of Warmbloods, an osteochondral fragment was present in the proximal interphalangeal joint in 0.9% of horses. 11 Osteo- chondral fragments have been described along the dorsal/dor- somedial and palmar/plantar aspects of the proximal interphalangeal joint, originating from the distal aspect of the proximal phalanx (most common) or proximal aspect of the middle phalanx. 12 17 Dorsal fragments have been suggested to be developmental in origin, whereas palmar fragments have been proposed to be due to partial avulsion fractures of the soft tissue attachments along the proximal interphalangeal joint during hyperextension of the joint. 3 12 13 17 Osteochondral fragments in the proximal interphalangeal joint may be inci- dental ﬁ ndings but have also been associated with lameness. In these horses, removal of the fragments is often recommended and return to previous levels of athletic performance has been reported. 12 17 18 Osseous Cyst-Like Lesions Osteochondrosis can also manifest as subchondral cystic lesions along the proximal interphalangeal joint, especially in a juvenile patient with no history of trauma. 19 20 Osseous cyst-like lesions (also known as subchondral cystic lesions or cysts, osseous cysts, or subchondral cyst-like osteochondrosis) can occur in the pastern region and are typically found in the subchondral bone near, and often communicating with, the proximal interphalangeal joint 21 ( Fig. 26.4 eFig. 26.1 ). These cysts are most commonly identi ﬁ ed unilaterally in the distal condyle of the proximal phalanx, although bilateral lesions are possible. These lesions are more common in the hindlimb. 15 19 22 23 Radiographically, these lesions may initially appear as a small depression, ﬂ attening or concavity in the articular margin but can later progress to a round, ovoid, conical-shaped or multi- chambered radiolucency in the subchondral bone. 3 21 Single cysts or multiple cysts may be present, with varying degrees of surrounding sclerosis. Two variations of this fracture occur: (1) biarticular fracture involving the fetlock and proximal inter- phalangeal joints and (2) monoarticular fracture, often exiting through the lateral distal palmar/plantar cortex. Comminuted fractures of the proximal phalanx are also relatively common. These fractures typically involve the fetlock and proximal interphalangeal joints (biarticular) and more frequently exit the lateral cortex. These fractures may involve the entire length of the proximal phalanx or only be found in the proximal or distal portion. Not surprisingly, these fractures have the most guarded prognosis for survival and poor prog- nosis for return to performance. 30 35 39 Dorsal plane fractures of the proximal phalanx are less common and are best seen on lateromedial views. There are three different con ﬁ gurations for dorsal plane fractures: (1) incomplete proximal dorsal articular fractures, (2) complete proximal dorsal articular fractures, and (3) fractures that extend from the midportion of the proximal articulation into the proximal phalanx, toward the proximal interphalangeal joint. 15 40 Proximal dorsal fractures occur most commonly in the hindlimb of Standardbred and Thoroughbred racehorses. 15 26 41 Other infrequently reported fractures of the proximal pha- lanx include physeal fractures (typically Salter-Harris type II) in foals and weanlings and incomplete distal articular fractures. 15 Avulsion fractures of the proximal annular ligament in the hindlimb have also been described. 42 These fractures are identi ﬁ ed along the proximal plantar aspect of the proximal phalanx, at the proximal site of attachment of the proximal digital annular ligament, and are associated with variable de- grees of lameness. Fractures of the middle phalanx more commonly affect the hindlimbs; however, forelimb fractures are more frequently comminuted. 15 17 43 45 Fractures of the middle phalanx can be: (1) comminuted (most common), (2) involving the palmar/plantar eminences (uni- or biaxial), and, less frequently, (3) osteochondral (chip) fractures. Physeal fractures have been reported in young horses but are rare. Fractures of the palmar (plantar) eminences more commonly involve both eminences (biaxial). 17 When the distal palmar (plantar) eminences are fractured, without comminu- tion, the fragments are displaced in a palmar or plantar direc- tion ( Fig. 26.8 ). This is most often identi ﬁ ed in the hindlimb. Biaxial eminence fractures typically result in instability of the joint and, in severe cases, the proximal interphalangeal joint is luxated with proximal displacement and overriding of the middle phalanx relative to the proximal phalanx ( Fig. 26.9 eFig. 26.2 ).The comminuted fractures are typically biarticular, involving both the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints ( Fig. 26.10 eFig. 26.3 ). Additionally, comminution of the fracture may only be present in the proximal aspect of the bone with one or more fracture lines extending distally to the distal interphalangeal joint. 17 43 Involvement of the distal interphalangeal joint signi ﬁ cantly affects the prognosis, and treatment of this type of fracture and multiple radiographic views or advanced imaging may be needed to identify involvement of this joint. Additional imaging (i.e., CT) may be needed to better determine the de- gree of comminution and joint involvement or to assist with surgical planning. 46 Osteomyelitis Infection of the pastern region is most common secondary to trauma, a complication of surgery, or less commonly, due to hematogenous dissemination. Penetrating trauma and lacera- tions can result in a secondary infection of the soft tissue and/or bone. Additionally, sequestrum formation can occur in the pastern region, often associated with a history of a draining wound. There is one report of osteomyelitis developing after proximal interphalangeal arthrodesis due to a fracture where osteolysis and osteoproliferation of the proximal and middle phalanges occurred with sequestrum formation. 47 Increased rates of infection have also been reported after surgical repair of highly comminuted fractures of the proximal phalanx. 35 He- matogenous osteomyelitis and septic physitis are much more common in foals ( Fig. 26.11 eFig. 26.4 ). In a study of foals, hematogenous osteomyelitis was frequently identi ﬁ ed in the distal limb but more commonly in the distal phalanx than the more proximal phalanges. 48 One case of fungal osteomyelitis caused by Cryptococcus gattii has been reported in the prox- imal phalanx of an adult horse. 49 New Bone Formation Enthesophyte formation can occur at the sites of ligament at- tachments along the pastern region. Bone proliferation is often identi ﬁ ed along the palmar aspect of the mid to distal aspect of the proximal phalanx associated with the distal sesamoidean ligaments. These changes may be associated with desmopathy and should prompt further assessment of the soft tissue struc- tures in this region. Focal periosteal new bone formation/periostitis and regional soft tissue swelling in the diaphyseal region of the proximal or middle phalanges not corresponding to ligament or capsular attachments are most likely secondary to trauma. Bone Marrow Lesions Horses with an acute onset of severe lameness localized to the pastern region may not have radiographic evidence of disease. In these horses, advanced imaging (i.e., MRI) is often pursued for further assessment. MRI is helpful to better exclude the possibility of a fracture and to look for evidence of a bone marrow lesion, which is a lesion characterized by increased ﬂ uid signal (high signal on fat- suppressed or inversion recovery sequences) and reduced T1 signal within the bone ( Fig. 26.12 ). Bone marrow lesions, also known as bone edema or edema-like change, can be secondary to an osseous contusion (bone bruise), bone edema, ﬁ brosis, or osteonecrosis, and often, these lesions are clinically signi ﬁ cant. Many of these lesions will resolve with rest and time; however, some will be persistently lame due to development of osteonecrosis, subchondral and trabecular bone loss, and progressive joint pathology. 50 52 J o i n t P a t h o l o g yOst eo ar thr it is Osteoarthritis a chronic degenerative disorder of synovial joints that occurs when articular cartilage deteriorates, over time resulting in radiographically detectable changes including per- iarticular new bone formation, subchondral sclerosis and/or lucency, and changes in the width of the joint space. Regional soft tissue swelling may also be seen, associated with the adjacent ligaments/tendons, joint effusion, capsular and syno- vial thickening, or periarticular ﬁ brosis. Periarticular new bone can present as osteophytes (new bone arising along the artic- ular margins) and enthesophytes (new bone at the attachments of periarticular soft tissues, including ligaments, tendons, and the joint capsule). Causes of osteoarthritis include chronic age- related degeneration, acute or chronic repetitive trauma, infection/septic arthritis, abnormal limb conformation, or developmental joint disease. The inciting underlying cause of proximal interphalangeal osteoarthritis may not be evident radiographically, with limb deformity a notable exception. The proximal interphalangeal joint is commonly affected by osteoarthritis. It is a low-motion joint which bears a high load, particularly in Western performance horses. 24 Since the prox- imal interphalangeal joint does not have a high range of motion during athletic activity, a smaller region of the joint surface has higher weight-bearing load for a longer time period. This results in articular cartilage and subchondral bone damage, and initi- ates the cascade of in ﬂ ammation leading to osteoarthritis. 15 24 Small periarticular osteophytes along the dorsoproximal aspect of the middle phalanx are often the initial radiographic indi- cator of proximal interphalangeal degenerative joint disease ( Fig. 26.13A ). As disease progresses, subchondral bone modeling, sclerosis, and demineralization may become evident (see Fig. 26.13B ). Late-stage changes include joint space nar- rowing, progressive lysis of the subchondral bone, advancing sclerosis, and more extensive periarticular osteophytosis (see Fig. 26.13C ). Over time, ankylosis or partial ankylosis of the joint can develop (see Fig. 26.13D eFig. 26.5 ). The early radiographic changes indicative of proximal interphalangeal osteoarthritis (small periarticular osteophytes and enthesophytes at ligamentous or capsular attachments) can be incidental in some cases, however these lesions could pre- dict future or developing problems and should be considered in light of the clinical exam and response to regional anesthesia, as well as the onset of lameness (acute versus chronic). Subchondral Bone Trauma Severe acute-onset lameness can be seen with trauma and sec- ondary articular cartilage and subchondral bone injury in the proximal interphalangeal joint. The radiographic manifestations can be subtle, and MRI is more sensitive in identifying and characterizing these injuries, particularly in the acute phase ( Fig. 26.14A ). These lesions also demonstrate marked focal radiopharmaceutical uptake on bone scintigraphy (see Fig. 26.14B ). If visible radiographically, lesions can be seen as elongated horizontal or focal circular regions of subchondral lucency in the proximal aspect of the middle phalanx (see Fig. 26.14C eFig. 26.6 ), which may become more evident over time and can extend into the trabecular bone. 3 Periosteal pro- liferation and periarticular osteophyte formation can be seen secondary to this articular cartilage and subchondral bone damage, representing developing degenerative joint disease. The prognosis is guarded in these cases.Subchondral bone trauma also occurs focally in the distal dorsal aspect of the middle phalanx, either medially or laterally, and is only diagnosed with MRI as increased ﬂ uid signal (hyperintensity on fat-suppressed images and hypointensity on T1-weighted images). No radiographic abnormalities are iden- ti ﬁ ed in association with this syndrome. Septic Arthritis Joint infection arises from penetrating wounds, iatrogenic in- jections, or hematogenous spread (most commonly in foals). The proximal interphalangeal joint is uncommonly involved in septic polyarthritis in foals. 53 55 Sepsis of the proximal inter- phalangeal joint should be considered with any lacerations near the joint in conjunction with persistent substantial lameness. Initially, no radiographic changes may be evident with septic arthritis. Synovial proliferation and effusion may cause intra- capsular soft tissue swelling although this is dif ﬁ cult to detect radiographically as the proximal interphalangeal joint pouch is relatively small. Positive contrast arthrography and/or contrast ﬁ stulography can be helpful to con ﬁ rm communication be- tween the joint and a wound/wound tract. Early osseous changes include proliferative bone at the joint capsular at- tachments and/or along the chondro-osseous junctions at the joint periphery. With progressive cartilage deterioration, joint space narrowing can be seen, although care should be taken to ensure even weight bearing when assessing joint space width radiographically. 7 Subchondral irregularity, lysis, and sclerosis can be identi ﬁ ed as intra-articular infection progresses ( Fig. 26.15A,B ). Periosteal new bone also develops along the artic- ular margins. The prognosis is always guarded. Subluxation/Luxation Dorsal displacement of the distal aspect of the proximal pha- lanx with increased ﬂ exion of the proximal interphalangeal joint is generally referred to as subluxation. This is most commonly seen in younger horses although it can occur in older horses, is more common in the hindlimbs, and may be unilateral or bilateral. 3 Potential causes include ﬂ exor de- formities caused by contracture of the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon and straight distal sesamoidean ligament, injuries to the suspensory ligament and extensor branches, or injuries to the palmar/plantar ligaments of the proximal interphalangeal joint. Dorsal subluxation may be appreciated on physical examina- tion as abnormal dorsal movement of the distal end of the proximal phalanx at a walk and can occasionally be appreciated at rest. An audible click is sometimes heard when the sublux- ation is reduced upon full weight bearing. In lateral radio- graphic projections there is mild dorsal displacement of the distal aspect of the proximal phalanx and increased ﬂ exion of the proximal interphalangeal joint. No additional radiographic changes are generally apparent. Palmar/plantar subluxation is typically associated with acute trauma and rupture of the distal sesamoidean ligaments or injury to the super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon branches or middle scutum, and there may be associ- ated avulsion fragments or enthesophytes at ligament in- sertions. 15 Ultrasound examination of the soft tissues of the pastern is indicated in such horses for further evaluation. Luxation of the proximal interphalangeal joint is typically evident clinically and can be seen with signi ﬁ cant trauma to the limb, such as large fractures of the proximal and middle pha- langes and/or with avulsion fractures at supporting ligament attachments (see Fig. 26.9 ). H y pe r e x t e n s i o n o f T h e Pr o x i m a l I n t e r ph a l a n g ea l J oi n t Hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal joint is un- common although can be seen with rupture of both the straight distal sesamoidean ligament and the super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon. Hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal joint can also be seen with concomitant hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal and distal interphalangeal joints, either in foals as a congenital deformity or secondary to weak ﬂ exor tendons (resulting from poor nutrition, systemic disease, or after prolonged splinting or casting of the limb) or as an ac- quired deformity secondary to rupture or avulsion of the deep digital ﬂ exor tendon. Soft Tissue Lesions Soft tissue changes detectable radiographically can include thickening, altered shape/contour, or abnormal opacity. Increased soft tissue can be seen surrounding joints, either con ﬁ ned to the region of the joint capsule (intracapsular ﬂ uid and/or synovial thickening) or external to the joint capsule (extracapsular in ﬂ ammation, ﬂ uid, ﬁ brosis, or cellular in- ﬁ ltrates). Increased extracapsular soft tissue can obscure intra- capsular soft tissue changes. Soft tissue thickening or abnormal contour away from the joint may indicate trauma, infection, tendon/ligament injury, acute or chronic wound, granulation tissue, or a soft tissue mass/neoplasm. Injuries to the tendons and ligaments of the pastern region are common but cannot be accurately diagnosed radiographi- cally. Ultrasound, MRI, and to some degree CT (particularly contrast-enhanced) are superior to radiographs for detecting soft tissue injuries. Regions of osseous proliferation can be seen in association with ligament injury, typically present at the attachment sites as enthesophytes. A thorough knowledge of the soft tissue attachments in the region is necessary for accu- rate radiographic interpretation; several detailed references for soft tissue attachments are available. 3 4 56 The most common sites for enthetic new bone in the pastern region include the attachments of the oblique distal sesamoidean ligaments ( Fig. 26.16 ), the collateral ligaments of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints, the proximal and distal digital annular ligaments, the ligaments between the proximal phalanx and the ungular cartilages, and the palmar/plantar ligaments of the proximal interphalangeal joint ( Fig. 26.17 ). Enthesophytes may be of variable to no clinical signi ﬁ cance, although indicate an area of potential active or historical injury. Enthetic bone pro- duction does not typically resolve following resolution of associated soft tissue injury. Occasionally, avulsion fragmenta- tion can occur at tendinous/ligamentous insertions. Dystrophic mineralization can develop within tendons or ligaments secondary to chronic injury or may be seen in peri- capsular soft tissues associated with previous corticosteroid injections or focal necrosis associated with prior neurectomy. Intraligamentous mineralization is most commonly seen in the distal sesamoidean ligaments (see Fig. 26.16 ). This is of vari- able/equivocal signi ﬁ cance and should be correlated with ul- trasound and clinical examination. Gas opacity in the regional soft tissues is also sometimes identi ﬁ ed, most commonly secondary to regional anesthesia or open skin wounds ( Fig. 26.18 ). Infection with gas-producing organisms is rare. Osseous neoplasia is uncommon in the distal limb of horses but can include benign (i.e., osteoma, ossifying ﬁ broma) and malignant (i.e., osteosarcoma) etiologies. An osteosarcoma has been reported in the middle phalanx of a horse. 67 In this horse, an aggressive bone lesion was identi ﬁ ed radiographically throughout the middle phalanx, with a pathologic fracture. An ossifying ﬁ broma has been described in the proximal phalanx of a horse. 68 Radiographically, multifocal areas of osteolysis with surrounding sclerosis were identi ﬁ ed in the distomedial aspect of the proximal phalanx, involving the distal articular margin and subchondral bone. A traumatic osseous cyst-like lesion was the primary differential as many of these areas were well de ﬁ ned; however, an ossifying ﬁ broma was diag- nosed histopathologically. Benign mineralization, such as dystrophic mineralization or osseous metaplasia, have also been described in the distal limb and typically occur secondary to previous trauma or soft tissue injury. One report of focal osseous metaplasia described a focal, well-circumscribed extraskeletal mineralized mass in the plantar pastern of the right hindlimb causing a chronic lame- ness. 69 This mass was suspected to be causing lameness due to compression on the adjacent plantar digital nerve. Barrett  Elizabeth Acutt  Federica Morandi OVER VIEW The equine digit is comprised of the three phalanges and associated proximal and distal interphalangeal joints; the podotrochlear (navicular) apparatus, including the navicular bone and navicular bursa; the distal termination of the ﬂ exor and extensor tendons; other supporting soft tissues; and the hoof capsule. 1 3 This chapter focuses speci ﬁ cally on the structures of the foot. INDICA TION S FOR RADIOG RAPHY Radiography is the primary imaging modality for evaluation of the foot. Indications for radiographs of the digit include pre- purchase examinations; lameness localized to the foot with regional analgesia (palmar digital and/or abaxial or basi- sesamoid nerve block) or intra-articular analgesia of the distal interphalangeal joint; assessment of osseous and/or synovial involvement in foot wounds or abscesses; suspected trauma; and monitoring the progression or resolution of known abnormalities. TECHN ICAL F ACTORS Patient Preparation Pertinent information obtained from the patient s history and physical examination is crucial to determine the signi ﬁ cance of many radiographic abnormalities of the equine foot. The results of diagnostic nerve blocks should also be considered, whilst noting the growing body of literature suggesting that these blocks may diffuse beyond previously described boundaries. 4 5 Dirt, skin lesions, specialized shoes, pads, and foot packing material can all produce artifactual opacities that complicate radiographic interpretation. All external material should be removed from the haircoat and hoof wall. Whenever possible, shoes and pads should be removed. The sole and sulci of the frog should be cleaned thoroughly. NORM AL RAD IOGRAPH IC ANAT OMY (INCL UDING VARIA TIONS) Osseous Structures The appearance of the dorsal margin of the distal interpha- langeal joint can vary in several ways, and this is a common area of radiographic misinterpretation. The shape of the extensor process of the distal phalanx (P3) and the dorsodistal margin of the middle phalanx (P2) may vary among individual animals from rounded to pointed ( Fig. 27.3 ). 8 Pointed margins may be mistaken for periarticular osteophytes. Closely exam- ining the joint for other signs of degenerative changes and comparing with the contralateral limb to assess for symmetry can help to distinguish between osteoarthritis changes and normal variation. The dorsal cortex of P2 should be smooth on a straight lateral view. If the lateromedial view is slightly oblique, the eminences for attachment of the collateral liga- ments of the distal interphalangeal joint become more con- spicuous and can be misinterpreted as abnormal ( Fig. 27.4 ). The radiographic appearance of the normal P3 in the D65Pr- PaDiO view varies in several respects. 7 9 The most obvious is the number and distribution of vascular channels ( Fig. 27.5 ). The number of vascular channels is typically greater in rear P3 than in front P3. 8 All vascular channels radiate from the solar canal to the solar border. A smoothly rounded concavity in the toe of the distal pha- lanx may be present in the normal horse (see Fig. 27.5 ). This notch is referred to as the crena marginalis solaris or, more commonly, the crena . In a radiographic study of the foredigit of the developing Quarter horse, a crena was identi ﬁ ed in foals between 4 and 22 weeks of age in 83% of the distal phalanges evaluated. 10 The depth of this notch usually does not exceed 1.5 cm. 2 The crena is more conspicuous in front than in hind feet. 9 Ninety percent of sound racing Thoroughbreds have bilateral symmetry in the presence of the crena in the front feet, Fig. 27.2 Positioning of the foot for acquisition of dorsal 60 65-degreeproximal to palm arodistal oblique radiograph using a Redden navicularblock, NANRIC, Lawrencebu rg KY. Joints The distal interphalangeal joint should have smooth margins and be symmetrical in width on the medial and lateral aspect of the joint. If the joint is narrower on one side, then the radio- graph must be assessed for patient positioning, sole confor- mation, or articular cartilage damage. The distal interphalangeal joint should be wider than the proximal interphalangeal joint and this can be used as an internal reference when assessing the joint space. Similarly, the articulation of the navicular bone with the middle phalanx should be smooth and well de ﬁ ned. Pathologic changes of this articulation are less common than palmar navicular bone damage and are part of distal interphalangeal joint degenerative changes. Soft Tissue Structures The equine digit is anatomically complex. The origins and in- sertions of the soft tissues in this region are well described and illustrated in other texts. 7 9 The ﬂ exor tendons run on the palmar aspect of the phalanges. The super ﬁ cial digital ﬂ exor tendon (SDFT) terminates at the proximal aspect of the middle phalanx. The deep digital ﬂ exor tendon (DDFT) runs farther distally, passing over the ﬂ exor cortex of the navicular bone and inserting onto the ﬂ exor surface of the distal phalanx. The distal digital annular ligament originates on the proximal pha- lanx and forms a sheet palmar to the DDFT, extending to the level of the navicular bone. RADIOG RAPH IC CHANG ES SECON DARY TO DISE ASE WITH IN THE FOOT Osseous Pathology Osteochondrosis Osteochondrosis lesions are not common in the distal inter- phalangeal joint. Fragmentation of the P3 extensor process is occasionally seen and may be considered developmental or traumatic dependent on clinical history and presentation, although often the etiology may not be de ﬁ nitively determined. Fragments are usually well identi ﬁ ed radiographically on a lat- eromedial projection ( Fig. 27.9 ). Arthroscopic removal is generally associated with a favorable prognosis, although development of distal interphalangeal joint osteoarthritis is a known sequela, particularly if there is extensive involvement of the articular surface. 12 Fragmentation of the palmar articular surface of the distal phalanx has also been reported. 13 Histological evaluation sug- gested a traumatic origin in some horses but was consistent with a diagnosis of osteochondritis dissecans in one case. These fragments are best seen on the D65Pr-PaDiO and associated 65- degree medial and lateral oblique views ( Fig. 27.10 ). MRI and CT revealed associated articular pathology that was under- estimated on radiography. This report found that all of these fragments were associated with lameness and the majority had a poor prognosis despite conservative and/or surgical therapy. Osseous Cyst-Like Lesions Round to conical, variably sized, radiolucent lesions surrounded by a sclerotic rim occur in the phalanges. The phalanges are the second most common locations for such lesions, the sti ﬂ e being the most common. 14 These have been called subchondral cysts osseous cysts , or subchondral cyst-like osteochondrosis with the current preferred term osseous cyst-like lesions (OCLLs). Because these lesions lack an epithelial lining and frequently communicate with the joint cavity, they are not true bone cysts. The etiology of these lesions is debated. In the young horse with no trauma history, the lesion is likely devel- opmental. Subchondral bone ischemia and necrosis secondary to trauma, infection, and osteoarthritis have also been corre- lated with the presence of these OCLLs. 15 Clinical expression of B C D A Fig. 27.8 Normal variatio ns in the appearance of the navicular ﬂ exor cortex. Others have a thin neck or a broader base of connection to the articular margin. OCLLs of the distal interphalangeal joint have a reported prevalence of 1.9%. 16 The majority of these are located in the central aspect of the distal phalanx, although OCLLs of distal P2 are also observed. In the distal phalanx, the lesion may be in the extensor process or, more likely, at the weight-bearing sur- face. 17 Indentations of the articular surface of the distal phalanx have been identi ﬁ ed uncommonly ( < 3% prevalence) in horses of multiple breeds and disciplines, with a possible predilection in Friesian horses. 18 These may be, but are not always, associ- ated with an underlying OCLL. These lesions are generally evident radiographically. Those of small diameter or shallow depth can be subtle. MRI (region of intermediate to high signal intensity on all sequences), scintigraphic (region of increased radionuclide uptake), and CT (low attenuating center sur- rounded by hyperattenuating rim) imaging can also be used to identify these lesions. MRI can be used to better characterize these lesions and identify associated articular cartilage defects. In one study, MRI was able to identify associated OCLLs not appreciated radiographically in 50% of cases. Some of these defects were identi ﬁ ed on prepurchase radiographs of clinically sound horses. Many occurred in conjunction with additional pathology of the distal interphalangeal joint, including synovitis, osteophytosis, extensor process fragmentation, and distal pha- lanx fracture, which may have contributed to lameness in affected horses. 18 In another study, OCLLs were seen in contralateral limb in horses with bilateral defects but unilateral lameness. 16 The clinical signi ﬁ cance of such lesions therefore remains uncertain. Successful outcomes have been reported following both surgical debridement and conservative treat- ment. 14 19 20 Pathological fracture secondary to a large osseous cyst of the distal phalanx has also been reported. 21 OCLLs in the distal phalanx can be differentiated from other lesions producing an ovoid lucency within the bone by their proximity to, and frequent communication with, the articular surface. The most common of these other lesions is keratoma. Keratoma is an abnormal mass of hyperplastic squamous epithelial cells with abundant keratin and granulation tissue. These develop within the hoof wall arising from the stratum germinativum of the coronary band, from the inner dorsal wall, or in the sole. In most instances, they manifest as an aberrant, tubular proliferation of keratin that progress distally from the coronary band with normal hoof growth. Less commonly, a more spherical solitary growth of keratin is present within the hoof capsule. Keratomas are considered to be caused by trau- matic or infectious insult to the hoof. 22 Lameness ranges from weeks to months and may be associated with unsuccessful resolution of presumed simple solar abscesses. Visible defor- mity at the coronary band, of the hoof wall, or sole is often clinically evident. The mass effect can cause localized resorp- tion of an adjacent area of the distal phalanx, most commonly appearing as a semicircular defect along the solar margin. Navicular bone fractures generally form a ﬁ brous union resulting in radio- graphically persistent fracture lines, even in chronic cases. 43 Complete fractures are more commonly seen in the forelimb. 42 In the authors experience, the athletic outcome from navicular bone fractures is variable and likely depends on other comor- bidities sustained at the time of trauma or as a sequela to the fracture. An incidence of 1.5% was reported for “ clinically si- lent ” navicular fractures during radiographic screening of 200 Warmblood yearlings. 42 Fragments of the distal border of the navicular bone are seen with relative frequency but are more likely to represent a developmental anomaly or feature of navicular syndrome (dis- cussed later) than traumatic fractures ( Fig. 27.14 ). They are commonly seen alongside other degenerative navicular changes and have been identi ﬁ ed more commonly in lame than sound horses in some population studies. 42 However, their frequent presence in nonlame horses makes their clinical signi ﬁ cance questionable in the absence of additional navicular changes. 44 These have been postulated to represent dystrophic minerali- zation or osseous metaplasia within the distal sesamoidean impar ligament, or separate centers of ossi ﬁ cation. The accompanying concave defect in the distal border of the navicular bone suggests they may be avulsed fragments. Larger fragments are relatively well identi ﬁ ed on radiographs, although the sensitivity of this modality for their identi ﬁ cation is lower than cross-sectional modalities. Two large retrospective studies have reported the preva- lence of distal phalanx fracture types. In a predominantly Warmblood population, type I fractures were most often seen, followed by type II. In contrast, in a population in which Quarter horses were the most common breed, type VI fractures predominated. In Thoroughbred racehorses, type II fractures appear to be the most frequently reported con ﬁ guration. 41 45 47 Type II fractures are often distributed in accordance with the direction of racing; the forelimb that bears the most weight in turns is at greatest risk. The type VI fracture is often found in association with radiographic signs of laminitis (32% of type VI fractures in one study) (see Fig. 27.40B,C ). 45 The progression of healing of a distal phalanx fracture is dif ﬁ cult to determine radiographically because of the minimal amount of external (periosteal) osseous callus produced by this bone. The periosteum of the distal phalanx is poorly developed and does not respond with abundant proliferation to the stim- ulation of direct trauma. From a multicenter study of 285 horses with distal phalanx fractures, those that had radiographic follow-up assessment showed evidence of healing of types I to III on average by 16 weeks with a range of 2 to 87 weeks from the start of their treatment. 50 Mean time of bone union was signi ﬁ cantly shorter for horses 3 years old or younger. Bone union began at the solar margin and progressed to the articular surface in these horses; this is speculated to be due to improved blood supply in the periphery of the bone. 51 Because of the ﬁ brous component of healing, radiographic bone union and clinical soundness do not correlate accurately. 50 Nonarticular type I fractures had the best prognosis for return to original or expected level of work or performance than type III followed by type II fractures. Surgical ﬁ xation has been advocated in articular fractures to maximize congruity of the joint surface and mitigate against the development of secondary osteoar- thritic changes. 41 Fractures of the extensor process generally produce more proliferative bone than other types of distal phalangeal fractures (see Fig. 27.18B ). However, large extensor process fragments may not heal by bone union but by ﬁ brous union, making them predisposed to loosening with additional trauma. The normal appearance of the solar surface of the distal phalanx varies considerably, and a mild degree of incidental irregularity may be misinterpreted as disease. Whilst typically a diffuse change, pedal osteitis can be a localized change due to chronic medial-lateral imbalance or secondary to another lesion within the hoof capsule, such as a subsolar abscess. It is dif ﬁ cult to determine radiographically if such focal pedal osteitis is associated with localized infection. In these cases, MRI can provide additional information for differentiating disease processes and thereby help determine the appropriate management plan. InfectionOsteomyelitis and Septic Osteitis Septic pedal osteitis refers to infection of the distal phalanx. The most common cause is penetrating foreign objects through the sole. Common radiographic changes are discrete areas of lysis, irregular margin, and decreased opacity of the distal phalanx, typical of chronic in ﬂ ammation ( Fig. 27.23 eFig. 27.2 ). Gas may be present in the soft tissue adjacent to the surface of the distal phalanx. Separation of a piece of the distal phalanx may represent a pathologic fracture or sequestrum (see Fig. 27.23 ). Clinically, a draining tract at the sole or coronary band may be found. Contrast ﬁ stulography or images made with a radiopaque stylet in the tract can be helpful to assess if the tract includes involvement of bone, tendons, ligaments, or regional synovial structures (distal interphalangeal joint and/or navicular bursa), which necessitates aggressive treatment. If a metallic foreign body is evident at physical examination, ra- diographs should be made before removal to determine the depth of its penetration and its relation to the regional bone ( Fig. 27.24 ). In one study of penetrating injuries to the frog, septic osteitis of the distal phalanx was cited as a reason for euthanasia. 55 These injuries are discussed in more detail at the end of this chapter.Another possible cause of septic pedal osteitis is hematog- enous spread. Of 108 Thoroughbred foals with 141 sites of hematogenous osteomyelitis, there were a signi ﬁ cant number with phalangeal involvement. 56 This included 25 distal phalanx lesions in 21 foals. None of the foals with a solar margin lesion had visible evidence of sole bruising or a penetrating wound. Radiographic lysis was present in four foals with a sequestrum. The hindlimb was affected more commonly (62% of lesions). Three of four foals with extensor process lesions had concur- rent septic arthritis. Although the proximal physis and epiph- ysis of the proximal and middle phalanges are common potential locations for hematogenous osteomyelitis, the distal phalanx has not typically been evaluated. Eighty-six percent of the foals with distal phalanx lesions were discharged from the hospital, and 50% of those that trained for racing had of ﬁ cial race starts. In addition, if such a lesion is identi- ﬁ ed in a nonlame leg, such horses may subsequently develop lameness and progressive arthrosis in the proceeding months. 58 Although some BMLs can resolve quickly (within 3 4 months), with an accompanying rapid improvement in lameness, severe injury can result in the development of osteonecrosis of the trabecular and subchondral bone and progressive articular pa- thology. These horses remain lame during the rehabilitation period and have a poorer prognosis for return to athletic ac- tivity. 58 BM edema-type pattern seen at the entheses of the distal interphalangeal joint (DIPJ) collateral ligament without associated ligament desmopathy has a reportedly good to excellent prognosis for return to activity. 59 It is worth noting that diffuse increased signal throughout the distal phalanx on ﬂ uid-sensitive sequences, particularly within the ﬂ exor surface, can also be seen with demineraliza- tion associated with disuse osteopenia. This is frequently found in horses with chronic lameness or those that have undergone extensive layup. Palmar endosteal ﬂ uid signal is a common ﬁ nding within the navicular bone on MRI. This ﬂ uid signal may indicate edema, in ﬂ ammatory in ﬁ ltrate, trabecular remodeling, ﬁ brosis, hemor- rhage, or necrosis. These various etiologies cannot technically be differentiated based upon the MRI appearance; however, these differential diagnoses can be ranked based upon severity and extent of ﬂ uid signal and when interpreted in light of clinical history (including lameness severity and chronicity), other changes of the navicular bone, and additional regional pathology (e.g., navicular bursitis, deep digital ﬂ exor tendin- opathy etc.) Navicular Syndrome Navicular syndrome, also known as navicular disease, is a chronic, often progressive condition characterized by a spec- trum of changes within the navicular bone and surrounding podotrochlear apparatus. Osseous navicular changes are described here, while the pathology of the soft tissues of the podotrochlear apparatus is discussed in more detail later in the chapter. Navicular syndrome primarily occurs in forelimbs and changes are frequently bilateral, even in cases presenting for unilateral lameness. 60 Breed predispositions are observed, although it is unknown whether a true genetic component of disease exists, or rather if it is a feature of the differences in foot conformation between breeds. The syndrome is seen most commonly in Quarter horses, which often have small, upright feet. 61 Early or mild navicular bone changes that may be detected radiographically include characteristic dilation of the synovial invaginations present along the distal border ( eFig. 27.3 ). These invaginations can vary in size, shape, and number. In a normal horse, these structures appear as a low number (in the region of 3 7) of small (less than a couple of millimeters), concave in- dentations of uniform or tapering width with a broad base. In navicular syndrome, several larger invaginations with a narrow base and bulbous proximal portion, a so-called “ lollipop ” shape, may be seen. It is important to note that there is a variation in size and number across different breeds. This can be dif ﬁ cult to identify radiographically unless more advanced, but is easily appreciated with MRI. Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is a chronic disorder of synovial joints charac- terized by progressive deterioration of articular cartilage and reactive changes in the joint margin, joint capsule, and syno- vium. Primary osteoarthritis is an age-related disease of slow onset, resulting in gradual degradation of normal joint structure and function as a result of the chronic repetitive trauma asso- ciated with intensive athletic activity. Secondary osteoarthritis may occur as a result of acute trauma, infection, poor limb conformation, and developmental orthopedic disease. The distal interphalangeal joints can be affected by any of these causes. Radiographic ﬁ ndings characteristic of osteoarthritis are bone formation (osteophytes) at the periarticular margins, enthesophytes at the sites of supporting ligaments and joint capsule, sclerosis and lucencies in the subchondral bone, and changes in the joint space width. These features are demon- strated in Fig. 27.27 and Fig. 27.28 , which utilizes the proximal interphalangeal joint to illustrate the various osteoarthritic changes. Focally increased soft tissue proximodorsal to the coronary band suggests intra-articular effusion and/or synovitis of the distal interphalangeal joint, which may accompany osteoarthritis of this joint. Degenerative changes within the articular cartilage are an important component of osteoarthritis but cannot be visualized on radiographs unless damage is extensive enough to cause joint space collapse. It is important to rule out uneven weight bearing as a cause of artifactual narrowing. 68 Abduction of the leg by 5 to 10 degrees results in signi ﬁ cant narrowing of the medial aspect of the proximal and distal interphalangeal joint spaces compared to the lateral joint spaces. The effect is more evident in the distal interphalangeal joint space and with the larger degree of abduction. Conversely, a unipedal stance can result in compression of the lateral aspects and widening of the medial aspects of the joint. 67 A wide spectrum of combination and degree of the previ- ously mentioned changes is seen. Synovitis is an early sign of joint disease. Effusion, synovial proliferation, and joint capsule thickening can be best characterized on MRI. CT can also demonstrate these changes, particularly if positive contrast medium is used, either intravascularly or intra-articularly. Septic Arthritis Infective agents are most commonly introduced into the distal interphalangeal joint by penetrating wounds or iatrogenic in- jections. Any laceration near a joint that is associated with sig- ni ﬁ cant and persistent lameness warrants concern for extension to the joint and infection. The joint pouches of the distal interphalangeal joint are large, extending proximal to the midplane of the middle phalanx. 3 One large retrospective study of heel bulb lacerations found that the distal interphalangeal joint was involved in 13% of these injuries. 74 During the initial stage of infection, no radiographic changes may be present. In ﬂ ammation of the synovium and effusion may create a focal enlargement at or just proximal to the coronary band ( Fig. 27.29 ). Options for assessing the likelihood of joint involvement secondary to an acute penetrating wound or laceration on ra- diographs include ﬁ rstly assessing for soft tissue swelling and radiolucent gas foci within the region of the joint recesses. If none is identi ﬁ ed or if the gas cannot be de ﬁ nitively localized to the joint, placement of a sterile metallic probe within the wound/tract and repeating radiographs may be valuable to assess the trajectory and depth of injury. Additionally, use of positive contrast techniques may assist in demonstrating or ruling out joint communication. A ﬁ stulogram may be per- formed in which contrast medium is instilled directly into the wound prior to radiographic assessment. Documenting the subsequent dispersal of contrast medium may demonstrate extension into the region of the joint. However, it can be dif ﬁ cult to generate suf ﬁ cient pressure to distend the tract with contrast medium, particularly if the wound is not fresh. An alternative is positive-contrast arthrography. This was success- ful at identifying communication of the contrast medium from the joint to the external wound in one study of horses sus- pected to have joint infection but no bone changes. 64 This is the authors preferred contrast technique in cases such as these. In the nonacute stage, one of the earliest radiographic signs of septic arthritis is irregularity at the joint capsule insertion or chondro-osseous junction on the perimeter of the joint sur- faces. As cartilage begins to deteriorate, thinning of the joint space is seen. As the infection invades the deeper regions of the cartilage and reaches the subchondral bone, the subchondral bone margin becomes irregular because of lysis (see Fig. 27.28 ). Lysis of the subchondral bone causes the joint to be widened unevenly. At this stage, periosteal new bone should be evident at the joint margins ( Fig. 27.30 ). Septic arthritis always has a guarded prognosis. Ultrasound evaluation of the dorsal joint pouch can be used to identify severe septic distal interphalan- geal synovitis and may also be used for ultrasound guided collection of ﬂ uid, which can be dif ﬁ cult in proliferative joints. Typically, septic effusion will be slightly more echogenic than the ﬂ uid seen with nonseptic in ﬂ ammation and is often asso- ciated with a greater degree of synovial proliferation. MRI provides the ability to detect septic osteoarthritis at an early stage via the identi ﬁ cation of features such as diffuse hyper- intensity within the adjacent tissues, severe, contrast-enhancing synovial proliferation 75 and is also valuable for more rapid identi ﬁ cation of secondary osteomyelitis via the detection of intraosseous ﬂ uid. Deformity of the Distal Interphalangeal Joint The clinical appearance of DIPJ ﬂ exural deformity varies with the degree of hyper ﬂ exion from mild to an almost vertical orientation of the hoof wall to the ground ( Fig. 27.31 ). Flexural deformity may be either congenital or acquired in the foal. Older horses may develop a ﬂ exural deformity secondary to lesions of the accessory ligament of the DDFT or chronic damage resulting in contracture of the DDFT. 76 Radiography is used to assess changes in the distal phalanx and screen for possible concurrent bone or joint lesions. Changes in the distal phalanx range from none to widened vascular channels and bone resorption at the solar margin. If the deformity is cor- rected early, the bone changes can resolve. Hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal joint may occur in newborn foals as a congenital abnormality affecting all three joints of the foot. Weakened ﬂ exor tendons may also be a result of poor nutrition, slow or incomplete recovery from a systemic disease, or after prolonged periods of external support (splint- ing or casting) of the leg. SOFT TISSU E PATHOLO GY Soft Tissue Structures Although the soft tissues of the equine foot are generally poorly visualized radiographically, indirect evidence of soft tissue injury can be gained by associated osseous changes. Therefore, knowledge of the attachment sites of the joint capsules, ten- dons, and ligaments is imperative. The DDFT can often be seen in the lateromedial view as a slightly more opaque soft tissue band as it passes between the level of the proximal aspect of the middle phalanx and the proximal margin of the navicular bone. The most common radiographic ﬁ nding to provide direct evidence of damage to the DDFT in the foot is the presence of mineral within the tendon. To adequately assess the soft tissues of the distal limb, im- aging modalities other than radiography must be employed. Ultrasound and MRI are well recognized for their value in assessing soft tissue injuries, although the use of ultrasound for assessing injuries of the foot is limited by the hoof capsule. CT, particularly with the use of contrast medium, is also valuable for assessing soft tissue damage in the foot. Comparing the results of advanced imaging to radiographs improves the interpretation of radiographs. The radiographic signs of abnormal soft tissue include alteration of thickness, contour, or opacity. A diffuse increase in soft tissue thickness in the region of the foot and pastern may indicate edema and/or cellulitis, whilst more focal, localized swelling may indicate trauma or, depending on proximity to a synovial structures, intracapsular effusion or sy- novial proliferation. An irregular surface contour suggests acute laceration or chronic granulation tissue. Increased opacity within soft tissue is usually caused by dystrophic mineralization ( Fig. 27.33 ). Decreased opacity within the soft tissues is caused by gas, which may be secondary to recent diagnostic nerve block, open skin wounds or abscessation due to a gas- producing organism ( Fig. 27.34 ). Injuries to speci ﬁ c soft tissues of the foot are discussed in more detail below. Injuries to the DDFT are common within the foot and are categorized in four forms: (1) dorsal border tears; (2) core le- sions; (3) sagittal or parasagittal splits; or (4) tendinosis. 64 92 The distribution of these lesions varies by location ( Fig. 27.37 ). Dorsal border ﬁ brillations are most common at the level of the proximal recess of the navicular bursa (also referred to as suprasesamoidean location ) and navicular bone. Insertional tendinopathies occurring immediately proximal to the insertion of the tendon on P3 can have a variety of con- ﬁ gurations. 93 94 DDF tendinopathy in the pastern is readily identi ﬁ ed on ultrasound; more distal tendinopathy is limited by the hoof capsule. Navicular bursitis can be generally categorized into two main types: proliferative bursitis, in which synovial prolifera- tion predominates, and effusive bursitis, characterized primarily by an abundance of synovial ﬂ uid. Proliferative synovium can develop into intrabursal adhesions, most frequently in associa- tion with tearing of the dorsal border of the DDFT. The ligaments of the podotrochlear apparatus are suscepti- ble to the desmopathy changes previously described. One unique feature of the impar ligament is its fenestrated appear- ance in the absence of pathology. In horses with navicular syndrome, this ligament may lose these fenestrations and become thickened, and may contact the dorsal border of the DDFT at its insertion. This feature, along with the other described changes of the podotrochlear apparatus, is best identi ﬁ ed on MRI. 80 99 101 Ultrasound performed between the heel bulbs with a microconvex probe can be used to visualize the suprasesamoidean DDFT, proximal recess of the navicular bursa, collateral sesamoidean ligament, and distal digital annular ligament. 98 However, because the ultrasound beam is not tangential to the structures of interest, assessment of echoge- nicity is limited.
