THE HOOF The hoof wall consists of the epidermis and the dermis (or corium), the latter bound to the parietal surface of the distal phalanx. The epidermal layers are the stratum externum (tec- torium), the stratum medium, and the stratum internum (lamellatum and white line at the ground surface). The lamellae of the stratum internum interdigitate with the dermal lamellae. Between the dermal lamellae and the parietal surface of P3 is a dense network of ﬁ bers that includes vessels and nerves (stra- tum reticulare). Because of the composition of these layers, there is a distinct radiographic opacity difference visible at the junction of the stratum medium and stratum internum and the super ﬁ cial more radiopaque layer and less radiopaque deep layer are readily differentiated ( Fig. 27.38 ) and correlate with MRI depiction of the layers. 104 The complex anatomic connection between the stratum internum, the corium, and the ridges of the parietal surface of the distal phalanx forms a functional suspensory apparatus of the distal phalanx. 105 The junction of the coronary band and the most proximal extent of the hoof wall is not always clearly distinct in lateromedial and dorsopalmar views. Hoof Balance Unbalanced trimming and improper shoeing of the foot can result in lameness. Lateromedial and dorsopalmar radiographic views of the foot can be used to assess foot balance. 106 107 When radiographic views are used in this manner, particular attention must be paid to positioning of the foot, the center of the x-ray beam, and degree of weight bearing on the limb being assessed. The measurements used to assess foot balance radio- graphically are shown in Fig. 27.39 . In the lateromedial view, the dorsal hoof wall should be parallel to the wall at the heel. The pastern axis, as seen in the lateromedial view, is a line that divides the middle phalanx into equal dorsal and palmar halves. Ideally, this line similarly bisects the proximal phalanx and is parallel to the dorsal cortex of the distal phalanx. When this line is carried through to intercept with a line on the bearing sur- face of the hoof wall, it should create an angle of 45 to 55 de- grees (front foot) or 50 to 55 degrees (hind foot) with the bony solar margin. 106 Signi ﬁ cant differences were induced in the angles of the interphalangeal joints when the hoof angle was altered. 106 The greatest difference in angle occurred in the distal interphalangeal joint. Clinically, such a change in the angle of the distal interphalangeal joint may in ﬂ uence the strain on the DDFT. 106 The angle of intercept of a line parallel to the solar margin of the distal phalanx and the line of the weight- bearing surface of the hoof wall should be 5 to 10 degrees. 7 The length of the toe region compared with the heel region of the bearing surface of the hoof wall is judged by comparison with the distal interphalangeal joint. A line from the center of the best- ﬁ t circle of curvature of the joint space, when drawn perpendicular to the weight-bearing surface, should be at the middle of the weight-bearing surface. 7 106 The lateral and medial portions of the hoof wall should be of equal length. elaborate set of measurements has been made on the dorso- palmar view to assess the effects of uneven mediolateral hoof wall trimming. 106 107 This method was used to assess the effects of using the corrective full rolling shoe in horses that were lame because of interphalangeal degenerative joint disease. 108 The distal border of the distal phalanx should be at an angle of 3 to 10 degrees relative to the sole of the hoof. A neutral or negative so-called “ palmar angle ” puts strain on the soft tissues supporting the palmar/plantar soft tissues on the limb and has been associated with scintigraphic evidence of subchondral bone injury in the palmar/plantar third metacarpal/tarsal con- dyles, in addition to hindlimb lameness originating from both the tarsi and sti ﬂ es. 109 110 Laminitis The normal orientation of the distal phalanx to the hoof is maintained by the complex structure of the interplay between the epidermal, dermal, and parietal surface of P3 forming the suspensory apparatus of the distal phalanx as noted in the description of the normal soft tissues of the foot. 105 Insult to this unique anatomic structure can result in the loss of me- chanical support of the distal phalanx within the hoof capsule. Laminitis is the general clinical term used to refer to the complex of signs expressed by the horse and its effects on the structural relations of the hoof wall, the distal phalanx, and sole from a variety of insults. Most horses that develop clinical laminitis do so because of a systemic illness, typically equine metabolic syndrome. 111 Horses with protracted, severe, uni- lateral limb lameness are at risk for developing supporting limb laminitis in the contralateral limb, particularly those in full limb or trans ﬁ xation casts for a long duration. 112 113 The develop- ment of supporting limb laminitis often occurs as rapid, severe failure of the suspensory apparatus of the distal phalanx mani- festing as full sinking of the distal phalanx within the hoof capsule and has associated high mortality. 114 Although differences of opinion exist regarding the termi- nology and categorization of this complex condition, several clinical phases or stages of laminitis are recognized: develop- mental, acute, and chronic. 115 Developmental laminitis is de ﬁ ned as the period between the initial insult to the ﬁ rst expression of lameness. It may be as short as 24 hours or as long as 60 hours. 115 This is likely an imperceptible stage to the owner unless access to excessive grain or grass is known to have occurred or a systemic disease or other condition is pre- sent that warrants concern for initiation of laminitis. This period is a prevention phase for mechanical failure of the foot complex. 115 Acute laminitis represents the phase from the ﬁ rst expression of lameness through 72 hours without evidence of mechanical collapse or at any time that signs of mechanical collapse occur. 115 Radiographs in either the developmental or the acute phase will rarely show signs of laminar in ﬂ ammation and instead serve as a baseline for future comparison. Horses may recover fully from either developmental or acute laminitis with no loss of mechanical support. If, however, radiographic or clinical signs of distal phalanx displacement are seen, the phase of chronic laminitis has begun. 115 Radiographic Evaluation of Laminitis Radiographic evaluation of any horse with a clinical impression of pain and lameness caused by laminitis is justi ﬁ ed. The goals of radiography are to detect changes indicative of mechanical failure and observe changes that contribute to formulation of prognosis and therapy. Front feet are affected most commonly. Placement of radiopaque markers on the foot has been advo- cated, but variation in normal measurements across patient types, in addition to variability in marker positioning may decrease their utility. 116 117 The earliest radiographically detectable signs of laminitis involve the dorsal laminae. Thickening of the more radiolucent, sensitive laminae such that this layer represents more than one- third to one-half of the width of the whole dorsal wall and loss of distinction between this layer and the overlying radiopaque, keratinized hoof wall are both early radiographic signs of laminar in ﬂ ammation. Crucially, these changes are often irre- versible, thus their presence on radiographs is merely evidence of a laminitic episode, which may be the cause of the current lameness, or a residual change from a prior insult. In the normal foot, the dorsal cortex of the distal phalanx should be parallel to the dorsal margin of the hoof wall in the lateromedial view. Divergence of these surfaces, with the toe region of the distal phalanx deviating or rotating in a palmar direction, is an indication of mechanical separation of the dermal and epidermal laminae ( Figs. 27.40 and 27.41 ). This is the easiest of the distal phalanx displacements to detect radio- graphically. The angle at the point of convergence can be measured and is referred to as the degree of rotation (see Fig. 27.41C ). Phalangeal malalignment (broken forward hoof pastern axis) due to rotation of the distal phalanx may be exacerbated by contraction of the DDFT, or if the more rapid growth of the hoof wall at the heel is managed improperly. Vertical displacement or “ sinking ” of the distal phalanx can be dif ﬁ cult to detect, especially earlier in the progression of dis- ease. In the normal foot, the proximal edge of the extensor process of the distal phalanx is positioned roughly at the same plane or just proximal to the junction of the hoof wall and coronary band. Subjective distal displacement of the extensor process in combination with a concave defect and/or radiolu- cent “ halo ” in the soft tissues at the level of the coronary band can be radiographic indicators of sinking. Uniaxial distal displacement of the distal phalanx can occur and is most frequently seen medially. 118 Serial radiographs are often used to monitor laminitic changes and comparison between time points can help to better identify vertical displacement. Other radiographic changes that can be seen with chronic and progressive laminitis include a very thin sole. The change in the position of the toe of the distal phalanx may cause a convex bulge in the sole contour, or the toe may penetrate through the sole. Lateral foot radiographs that are centered at the sole rather than at the coronary band are better for assessing these changes. Separation of the dorsal laminae can be seen as a single lucent line between the layers of the hoof wall on the lateral view (see Fig. 27.40D ) and as a series of vertically ori- ented, thin, parallel lucent lines in the D65Pr-PaDiO view. This may progress to laminar necrosis, with eventual dissection of gas between the laminae once necrosis erodes through to the coronary band or white zone of the sole. Larger regions of radiolucency are more likely to be associated with secondary soft tissue infection. In addition to the laminar changes, the distal phalanx un- dergoes characteristic changes associated with laminitis. These changes include bone production along the dorsal cortex of the distal phalanx dome-shaped contour, lipping or ski-slope-sha- ped bone formation at the toe, enlargement of the vascular channels, solar margin lysis, resorption of the palmar cortex, and/or angular orientation of a solar margin fracture (type VI) (see Fig. 27.40 ). Because of the severe morbidity and protracted treatment required for chronic laminitis, indicators of prognosis for suc- cess or failure of treatment are desired. Various radiographic measurements have been assessed retrospectively to de ﬁ ne reliable predictors of outcome for horses with chronic lami- nitis. Fig. 27.41 and eFig. 27.6 illustrate several of these mea- surements. Sole thickness (sole depth), not included in these illustrations, is measured from the toe of the distal phalanx to the ground surface, or top of the shoe, or to the distal soft tissue border of the sole if the horse has a prominent cup-shaped bottom of the foot (see Fig. 27.40A ). In general, the more deviant from normal, the more guarded the prognosis. The vertical distance between the proximal limit of the dorsal hoof wall and the proximal limit of the extensor process of the distal phalanx has been measured to generate a founder distance ( Fig. 27.41B ). 116 When cor- rected for magni ﬁ cation, this distance in 25 normal horses was an average of 4 mm (range, 2 to 11 mm) in the front feet and an average of 4.6 mm (range, 2 to 9 mm) in the hind feet. 116 The wide variation in these measurements re ﬂ ects the spec- trum of equine foot conformation and a single measurement alone is of limited value. Serial measurements in repeated radiographic studies may give more meaningful information about progression of laminitis in that individual patient. Evalu- ating a large number of horses for prognostic indicators of poor outcome, distal displacement of the distal phalanx was the only radiographic variable associated with an increased probability of death. 120 However, the severity of the lameness was the single best predictor of outcome. Others concur that radio- graphic assessment is important in establishing and monitoring bone stability within the hoof but should not be used as an isolated indicator of outcome. 121 Digital venography can be used to evaluate several foot problems, most notably laminitis. This procedure is described in detail within the literature and involves the administration of positive contrast medium via a palmar digital vein followed by rapid acquisition of lateromedial and dorsopalmar radiographs of the foot. 7 122 In a normal horse, the contrast medium is maintained within the vasculature and the tip of the distal phalanx is located proximal to the circum ﬂ ex vein. In horses with laminitis, there may be compression of vasculature, failure of adequate ﬁ lling, rapid extravascular diffusion of contrast medium, and/or an altered (more distal) position of the tip of the distal phalanx relative to the circum ﬂ ex vein. 7 123 This technique has been used to guide treatment recommendations and inform prognostication; however, imaging ﬁ ndings should be considered in the context of the clinical appearance when making decisions. 124 MRI can be used to detect laminitis, even in the acute stages. A study of active phase laminitis was performed using a 4.7 T magnet, and it was possible to detect changes in laminar and corium structure and signal intensity that correlated strongly with the histologic diagnosis of acute laminitis. 124 In this study the sensitivity of MRI for detecting these changes was 95% to 100%, compared with just 48% to 58% for radiography. Ungual (Collateral) Cartilages The ungual cartilages extend in a proximopalmar direction from the palmar processes of the distal phalanx. There are multiple ligaments associated with these cartilages which an- chor them to adjacent osseous structures. These include the chondropedal (attach to the proximal phalanx), chon- drocoronal (attach to the middle phalanx), chondrotendinous (attach to the extensor process of the distal phalanx), chon- droungular (attach to the palmar processes of the distal pha- lanx), and chondrosesamoidean ligaments (attach to the navicular bone). In addition, ﬁ bers of the distal interphalangeal collateral ligaments connect to the dorsal aspect of these cartilages. 3 125 Tears of the Ungual Cartilages Tears of the unossi ﬁ ed ungual cartilages can occur and are frequently associated with severe injury of the adjacent soft tissues, particularly the collateral ligaments of the distal inter- phalangeal joint. This diagnosis can only be made de ﬁ nitively on MRI or high-quality contrast-enhanced CT. Ossi ﬁ cation/Calci ﬁ cation (Sidebones) This is a common ﬁ nding in radiographs of the distal part of the digit, especially in draft-breed horses. The radiolucent line that separates the center of ossi ﬁ cation generally has smooth, rounded margins and should not be misinterpreted as a fracture. Moderate to extensive grades of ossi ﬁ cation have been suggested to have an associa- tion with foot lameness, including injuries of the collateral lig- aments of the distal interphalangeal joint and the distal phalanx. Fracture of the ossi ﬁ ed cartilage occurs most commonly at the base attachment to the palmar process. Fractures typically occur in an axial proximal to abaxial distal and palmar to dorsal direction. Fracture borders are sharp and irregular compared to the borders of the gap between a separate center of ossi ﬁ cation that has not fused to the base region. These fractures may be visible radiographically, particularly when a comprehensive series of foot radiographs is acquired. In some instances, the fracture line itself may be indistinguishable radiographically; however, the osteosclerosis at the base of the cartilage and proximal aspect of the associated palmar process that often precedes such fractures may be visible. Detection of this change should prompt more careful interrogation of this region for evidence of fracture, possibly to include additional imaging modalities such as MRI and/or nuclear scintigraphy. 127 MRI may also reveal intraosseous ﬂ uid within the surrounding bone. Fractures frequently extend through the ipsilateral distal inter- phalangeal collateral ligament fossa and the majority are asso- ciated with enlargement and signal change within the collateral ligament itself. 128 In addition, the ligaments of the ungual car- tilages are often injured in conjunction with the fracture. These associated soft tissue injuries likely contribute towards lame- ness in these patients. Infection (Quittor) Penetrating wounds or lacerations in the coronary band region can introduce infection into the ungual cartilages. Necrosis associated with infection of this cartilage is called quittor . In acute infections, radiography should be considered to assess for the presence of radiopaque foreign material or a deeper lesion in the adjacent bones. In chronic infections, a draining tract is typical. Fistulography may be used to determine the depth and direction of such tracts. 129 Extension to the distal interphalan- geal joint is uncommon unless it occurs iatrogenically during aggressive establishment of drainage or debridement of the necrotic cartilage. Ultrasound may be used to evaluate the proximal extent of the cartilages that project above the coro- nary band. With infection, they may demonstrate increased echogenicity and irregular margins. It may also be possible to trace draining tracts to the margins of the cartilages. Preoper- ative MRI was used to evaluate ﬁ ve suspected cases of quittor that had been unresponsive to conservative management or had lameness greater than expected. 130 The low- ﬁ eld (0.27 T) standing MR studies showed abnormal signal in the cartilage and abnormalities in the chondrocoronal and chon- drosesamoidean ligaments. Additional extension of involve- ment in three of the horses to either the distal or middle phalanges and involvement of the collateral ligament of the distal interphalangeal joint was identi ﬁ ed and aided in the management of the patients. Penetrating Solar Injuries Radiographic investigation of horses with solar penetration was brie ﬂ y discussed in the previous section on septic arthritis. A key point worthy of mention is, where possible, to obtain ra- diographs with the penetrating object in situ so as to document its precise trajectory. However, radiography is often not able to detect the extent of soft tissue injury or early bone changes in these injuries and CT or MRI can yield important information. CT has improved accuracy for detecting foreign bodies compared to radiography or MRI, so it could be considered when there is suspicion of indwelling foreign material. 131 132 MRI may demonstrate the penetrating tract as a region of signal void with or without signal changes consistent with recent hemorrhage. 131 133 Determination of the structures involved, region of sole penetration, as well as time from sole penetration had a signi ﬁ cant association with outcome ( Fig. 27.44 ). 134 In one study in 55 horses with solar penetration injuries evaluated by low- ﬁ eld (0.3 T) MRI, synovial involvement had a guarded prognosis for survival to discharge and a poor prognosis for return to preinjury athletic performance. 133 Penetration of the central sulcus and involvement of P3, and delayed intensive treatment were associated with euthanasia. In this study, le- sions of the DDFT were most commonly seen at the insertion on the distal phalanx, were often severe, and were the most common reason for euthanasia. Donald E. Thrall A cquisition of thoracic radiographs is a common radio- graphic examination in small animal practice. Radio- graphs of at least part of the thorax can also be obtained in foals and in most adult horses. NOMEN CLATU RE In daily practice, the naming of conventional lateral thoracic radiographs made with the patient lying on their side and a vertically directed x-ray beam violates the point-of-entrance to point-of-exit nomenclature system described in Chapter 6 . If the patient was on the left side, for example, the correct name for this view would be a right-left lateral because the x-ray beam enters on the right side and exits on the left. But in daily practice, the naming of such a view is abbreviated to designate the side the patient is lying on; in this case a left lateral . Simi- larly, a thoracic radiograph made with the patient lying on the right side would be a right lateral view. In the adult horse, lateral thoracic radiographs are made with the patient standing and a horizontally directed x-ray beam. Therefore, the point-to-entrance to point-of-exit system should still be used, and lateral radiographs should be desig- nated as either left-right or right-left laterals. In all species, ventrodorsal (VD) and dorsoventral (DV) ra- diographs of the thorax are named according to the point-of- entrance to point-of-exit of the x-ray beam. RADIOG RAPH IC TECHN IQUE: DOG AND CAT A relatively low contrast image of the thorax is preferred. The air in the lung will provide the necessary level of contrast and there is not a need to enhance contrast using technical factors. With analog technology, a low-contrast image is obtained by using a high kilovoltage peak (kVp) low milliampere-seconds (mAs), combination, and this approach can also be used with digital systems. However, in digital imaging the contrast of the image is controlled primarily by the processing algorithm that is applied to the raw image data. Therefore, it is important that the correct processing parameters are assigned to thorax studies when the digital image system is compiled. For patients thicker than 10 cm, a grid should be used to remove scattered x-rays from the beam. Exposure time is critical when radiographing the thorax. Motion is the biggest enemy of image detail in veterinary radi- ology. Respiratory motion can induce blurring and lead to reduced detail. This reduces the ability to interpret the radio- graph accurately. To minimize the effects of motion, the shortest exposure time and highest milliamperes (mA) setting possible should be used to produce the needed mAs. POSITIO NING: DOG AND CAT The routine thoracic radiographic examination in the dog and cat should consist of left lateral, right lateral, and either VD or DV projections. The entire thoracic cavity should be included in the image. This seems obvious, but omitting the cranial or caudal part of the thorax from the ﬁ eld of view is a common error, which increases the chance of missing a lesion. The ﬁ eld of view should extend from just cranial to the thoracic inlet, to a few centimeters caudal to the last rib. The dorsocaudal tips of the caudal lobes extend further caudally than anticipated. Even in the largest dogs, including the entire thoracic cavity in one 14-inch by 17-inch image is usually possible. For the occasional huge dog where this is not possible, then each projection (left lateral, right lateral, VD or DV) should be divided into cranial and caudal portions. SPEC IFIC FEATURES OF CAN INE AND FELIN E THORA CIC RAD IOGRAPH S Pulmonary Vessels The pulmonary artery and vein in the right cranial lobe are used commonly as a basis for assessing the pulmonary circulation. 4 This is done by comparing the respective size of these vessels, which requires that other structures are not superimposed. These speci ﬁ c pulmonary vessels are isolated, and more con- spicuous, in a left lateral than in a right lateral radiograph ( Fig. 28.11 ). In right recumbency the right cranial lobe vessels are displaced dorsally and become superimposed on the left- sided vessels, whereas in left recumbency the left- and right- sided vessels are not superimposed. The left cranial lobe pulmonary vessels cannot usually be assessed or compared accurately in either the left or right lateral view, because they are located more dorsally in the thorax and usually superimposed on other vessels or the thicker dorsal portion of the mediastinum. Pulmonary arteries and veins can also be compared in the caudal lung lobes. This is best accomplished in a DV view. The caudal lobe pulmonary vessels are more conspicuous in DV compared to VD radiographs for two main reasons: (1) a perpendicular orientation with the primary x-ray beam and (2) less adjacent pulmonary atelectasis ( Figs. 28.12 and 28.13 ). Diaphragm The diaphragm consists of a left crus and a right crus (collec- tively the crura) dorsally and a dome ventrally. The diaphrag- matic hiatus for the caudal vena cava is located slightly to the right of midline and passes through the right diaphragmatic crus. In the left lateral view, the two dorsal crura of the dia- phragm diverge from each other, whereas in the right lateral view they are more parallel ( Fig. 28.14 ). In the right lateral view, the dependent right crus will be cranial to the left crus because of pressure from abdominal contents, and therefore the caudal vena cava will silhouette, or merge, with the more cranial right crus. In the left lateral view, the left crus will be cranial to the right crus, and the caudal vena cava will be superimposed on the left crus before silhouetting, or merging, with the more caudally located right crus that contains the caval hiatus (see Fig. 28.14 ). Therefore, the appearance of the junction of the caudal vena cava with the diaphragm can be used as a way to distinguish a left lateral from a right lateral radiograph if an external marking system has not been used. However, this principle is not 100% accurate, because occa- sionally, the left crus will be cranial to the right crus in the right lateral view, and vice versa. Cardiac Silhouette There is only a minor difference in the appearance of the car- diac silhouette in left vs. right lateral views. In general, the cardiac silhouette will appear slightly rounder and the apex may be slightly elevated from the sternum in the left lateral view compared with the right lateral view ( Fig. 28.15 ). Comparatively, there is a major difference in the appearance of the cardiac silhouette in VD versus DV radiographs. In sternal recumbency for the DV radiograph, the ventral aspect of the diaphragm is displaced cranially where it contacts the heart and displaces it, typically to the left. The heart is also more upright in the thoracic cavity when the patient is in sternal re- cumbency, making it appear rounder ( Fig. 28.16 ). The rounder appearance and displacement to the left that occur normally in DV radiographs are commonly misinterpreted as cardiomegaly. The extent of leftward cardiac displacement in DV radiographs is more pronounced in large dogs and will not be as obvious in small dogs or cats. 5 7 Accessory Lung Lobe The cranial excursion of the diaphragm that occurs in sternal recumbency also impinges on the territory of the accessory lung lobe. This diminishes the ability to evaluate the accessory lobe and caudal mediastinum, and signi ﬁ cant disease in this area can be missed in DV radiographs because of this impingement (see Fig. 28.16 ). As with cardiac displacement, the amount of impingement on the accessory lobe and caudal mediastinal regions in DV radiographs caused by cranial excursion of the diaphragm is more noticeable in large dogs and is not as signi ﬁ cant in small dogs or cats. Randi Drees ANAT OMIC CONSI DERATION S: NORM AL ANAT OMY The upper respiratory system comprises the air- ﬁ lled pharynx, the larynx, and trachea. Typically, the pharynx has the widest lumen, followed by the larynx and the trachea, which is slightly smaller in diameter. Pharynx: The soft palate divides the pharynx into the dorsally located nasopharynx and ventrally located oropharynx. The caudally adjacent larger laryngopharynx is divided from the nasopharynx by the palatopharyngeal arches, which form the soft tissue line extending caudodorsally from the soft palate, and from the oropharynx by the epiglottis ( Fig. 29.1 ). 1 The piriform recesses are caudodorsally oriented extensions of the laryngopharynx. Larynx: The epiglottis is usually surrounded by gas and ex- tends to just overlap the tip of the soft palate dorsally or ventrally. 2 In larger dogs, the cuneiform process, which is the rostral portion of the arytenoid cartilage, is occasionally visible. The other laryngeal cartilages are represented by an indistinct soft tissue opacity superimposed on the laryngeal lumen. Gas- ﬁ lled ventricular saccules are seen occasionally. In older dogs, and even younger large-breed dogs, laryngeal cartilages may become mineralized, the cricoid cartilage often being the most evident ( Fig. 29.2 ). 3 In brachycephalic dog breeds, the larynx can be positioned slightly more caudally compared to mesaticephalic dogs. 4 Anatomic structures of interest surrounding the phar- yngolarynx with potential secondary effects on the upper res- piratory tract are:  Rostrally: base of the tongue and mandibular lymph nodes  Laterally: hyoid bones, mandibular and parotid salivary glands  Caudodorsally: medial retropharyngeal lymph nodes and esophagus  Caudoventrally: thyroid glands The hyoid apparatus is paired, except for the basihyoid bone, which facilitates identi ﬁ cation of unilateral abnormalities. The normal cricopharyngeus muscle representing the cranial esophageal sphincter sometimes appears as a distinct soft tissue structure dorsal to the larynx and can be misinterpreted as a soft tissue mass. Trachea: The tracheal lumen is normally gas ﬁ lled and the luminal diameter is similar between the cervical and thoracic regions. In large-breed dogs, it sometimes widens in the caudal cervical region. The diameter of the normal trachea can also vary mildly between inspiration and expiration. The ratio be- tween tracheal diameter and thoracic inlet height is propor- tionally larger in dogs with greater body weight and smaller in brachycephalic breeds. 5 The cranial thoracic trachea is approximately parallel to the vertebral column and slightly closer to the vertebral column at the level of the thoracic inlet. In the mid-thorax, the trachea deviates ventrally relative to the vertebral column in most patients ( Fig. 29.3 ). Tracheal rings may mineralize with age and become visible. Ventrodorsal (VD) and oblique views are complementary to establish lesion laterality yet are limited by superimposition of the skull and cervical spine. Technique parameters offering high-contrast images (rela- tively low kilovoltage peak [kVp] and high milliampere second [mAs] if using an analog system) selected according to the thickness of the ventral cervical soft tissues are recommended. Differentiation of the various structures is more dif ﬁ cult in obese patients because of narrowing of the air- ﬁ lled compartments. Trachea The lateral view with the head mildly extended is most useful for evaluation of the trachea (see Fig. 29.3 ). The position of the thoracic portion of the trachea can vary with patient posi- tioning: when the patient s head is ventro ﬂ exed, focal dorsal displacement of the trachea can mimic a cranial mediastinal mass ( Fig. 29.4 ). Conversely, extreme extension of the neck can cause tracheal narrowing. On a dorsoventral radiograph, the thoracic portion of the trachea is located on or curves mildly to the right of midline. 7 In brachycephalic breeds and obese dogs with mediastinal widening, the trachea curves more markedly to the right due to the larger amount of mediastinal fat, and this should not be confused with displacement from a mass, such as from a heart base tumor ( Fig. 29.5 ). Trauma and Foreign Body Pharyngolaryngeal trauma occurs most often because of a penetrating wound originating either internally from the upper respiratory tract or esophagus, due to a stick injury, or exter- nally, such as a bite or gunshot wound, less commonly from blunt trauma. Soft tissue thickening representing swelling and/ or a mass may be found with hematoma, cellulitis, granuloma, myositis, and/or abscess. Gas opacities in the subcutaneous tissues and between muscle and tissue planes represent emphysema if linear. Focal rounded gas accumulation may represent an abscess ( Fig. 29.11 ). The sublingual area is re- ported as the most common entry site for stick injuries in dogs. 18 Emphysema has been reported in 83% of dogs with acute oropharyngeal stick injury and can extend to pneumo- mediastinum, pneumothorax, mediastinitis, and pleural effu- sion. 19 Pharyngeal diverticulum, 20 stenosis, cervical swelling, and draining sinus tracts 18 can be complications of trauma. In addition to other surrounding bone structures, hyoid bone fracture and laryngeal cartilage fracture can occur, particularly when the region has been crushed. 21 These struc- tures should be examined for symmetry and normal contour. Oblique projections may help evaluation of the hyoid appa- ratus. Hyoid bone fractures may be open to the upper respira- tory tract and therefore contaminated. Foreign bodies are visible when they are mineral or metallic, such as gunshot particles, needles, ﬁ shhooks, and bones. Plant material is usually only visible radiographically when large, containing (dry wood) or surrounded by gas ( Fig. 29.12 ). CT 22 or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 23 can aid the localization of smaller plant material foreign bodies. In patients with a draining tract, ﬁ stulography with iodinated contrast medium can aid in foreign body detection. Diagnosis is typically made by clinical, radiographic, and laryngoscopic examination. 24 Radiographically, soft palate hyperplasia appears as elongation and thickening of the soft palate beyond the tip of the epiglottis, and subsequent narrowing of the nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal diameters ( Fig. 29.13 ). Aberrant nasopharyngeal turbinates are typically diagnosed using CT examinations ( Fig. 29.14 ). 27 Glottis and cricoid cartilage narrowing as well as dynamic laryngeal collapse occur in a laterolateral direction, and are typically diagnosed with a combination of laryngoscopy and CT examination; radiographic diagnosis using a VD view remains dif ﬁ cult unless severe ( Fig. 29.15 ). It can be identi ﬁ ed on radiographs in some patients, but ﬂ uoroscopy is particularly helpful as the condition is commonly dynamic. It is usually associated with tracheal/bronchial collapse and/or brachyce- phalic syndrome. 33 34 Dynamic upper airway collapse (laryngeal or pharyngeal) has been reported in cats secondary to respiratory distress caused by asthma or presumed in ﬂ ammatory/infectious disor- ders, high-grade lymphoma in ﬁ ltrates in the pharyngeal region, or possibly related to vigorous exercise. 35 37 Nasopharyngeal Stenosis Nasopharyngeal stenosis is a relatively rare pathological nar- rowing of the nasopharyngeal lumen and can present as a congenital abnormality with a septal structure in the lumen or acquired, secondary to an in ﬂ ammatory/infectious condition, surgical manipulation, trauma, tumor, or polyp. In dogs, aspi- ration rhinitis related to an anesthetic event, and in cats, in- ﬂ ammatory or infectious causes are the most common causes of acquired stenoses. 38 40 Radiographically, a narrow band of soft tissue superimposed on the nasopharyngeal lumen and slight focal dorsal deviation of the soft palate may be seen. 41 Cross- sectional imaging (CT or MRI), including sagittal and dorsal reformatted images, provides enhanced identi ﬁ cation of the disease features ( Fig. 29.18 eFig. 29.6 ). A congenital form of nasopharyngeal stenosis has been proposed in Dachshunds, thought to be caused by a primary palatopharyngeal dysgenesis. Thickening of the palatopharyngeal muscles leads to a hori- zontal band of soft tissue that separates or even obliterates the nasopharynx from the rest of the pharynx and larynx. 42 Pharyngitis and Laryngitis Generalize d swelling of the upper airway can be caused by edema due to respiratory distress, as seen in brachycepha lic breeds, and/ or in ﬂ ammatory conditions. Hypoplasia Tracheal hypoplasia is characte rized by generalize d reduction in tracheal diameter ( Fig. 29.24 ) due to apposed or overlap ping tracheal cartilages and a shortened or absent dorsal tracheal membrane. Approxima tely 39% of brachycephalic dogs with signs of brachyceph alic airway obstructio n syndrome have tracheal hypopla sia, 65 and in 10% of dogs, the diagnosis of tracheal hypopla sia is incidental . 66 The diagnosis is made more dif ﬁ cult by the fact that non-bulldo g brachycep halic breeds, both with and without respirator y signs, have a smaller average tracheal- diameter-to-t horacic-inl et-height ratio (16% 3%) than nonbrachyce phalic dogs (20% 3%). English bulldogs have an even smaller ratio (13% 4%). 5 The smallest ratio in asymptom- atic bulldogs was 9%. More recently, tracheal-diame ter to thoracic-in let height ratio was measured in 32 asymptomati c/ grade 1 English bulldogs and found to be 17% 3% on radio- graphs and 26% 3% on CT, which is greater than previous measuremen ts. 67 The ratio between tracheal diameter and cricoid cartilage height is also smaller for brachyceph alic breeds. 5 Normal tracheal diameter:thoracic inlet height in cats is 18% in domestic short-haired cats and 20% in Persians. 68 Tracheal hypoplasia has been reported in a kitten with mucopoly- saccharidosis VII. 69 Tracheitis Generalized tracheal narrowing may be caused by severe tracheitis that leads to thickening of the tracheal mucosa. Tracheitis can be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from tracheal hypo- plasia, and the conditions can occur concurrently. Common causes of tracheitis are inhalation of toxic or chemical irritants, trauma, and upper respiratory infection ( Fig. 29.25 ). Redundant Tracheal Membrane The presence of a dorsal tracheal luminal soft tissue opacity in dogs between the midcervical and midthoracic portions of the trachea can be caused by the dorsal tracheal membrane, rep- resenting the trachealis muscle and connective tissue bridging the gap between the aspect of the tracheal cartilages. 70 The dorsal tracheal membrane can usually be differentiated from the slightly opaquer dorsal tracheal wall. Visibility of the tracheal membrane dorsally does not necessarily indicate abnormal redundancy, but it can be caused by contraction, or invagina- tion, of the membrane. 70 The opacity caused by a visible dorsal tracheal membrane can be dynamic, depending on phase of respiration ( Fig. 29.26 , Video 29.1). Bronchial collapse is dif ﬁ cult to diagnose accurately, with discrepancies between radiographs, ﬂ uoroscopy, and bron- choscopy, probably due to dynamic differences during the respiratory cycle and cough, patient positioning, and poor im- age resolution. It is seen most frequently during ﬂ uoroscopy with induction of cough. 78 Right middle and left cranial lobar bronchi are most commonly collapsed on bronchoscopy. 74 In very small patients, or to better evaluate the mainstem bronchi, additional image detail can be obtained by making a rapid series of radiographic images (dynamic digital radiog- raphy) over a respiratory cycle as opposed to using ﬂ uoros- copy, while recognizing that this results in greater x-ray exposure. Performing ﬂ uoroscopy in both right and left lateral recumbency may improve detection of bronchial collapse and placing the patient in sternal recumbency may additionally help. 78 Complete radiographic evaluation of the thorax should be made in dogs suspected of tracheal collapse to evaluate for related conditions, such as bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and car- diac disease. 71 79 Location and extent of maximal collapse are often evaluated using the following scale: 25%, 50%, 75%, and 90% to 100% reduction of tracheal diameter. 75 This scale is similar to the grading system used to evaluate tracheal collapse at bronchos- copy. A reduction in tracheal diameter of 25% or less is prob- ably within normal limits of variation of the respiratory cycle. 75 Using CT, up to 24% change in cervical tracheal cross-sectional area and 19% variation in thoracic tracheal height are seen in healthy dogs under forced inspiration. 80 Endotracheal stenting through ﬂ uoroscopic guidance has become commonplace for the treatment of tracheal collapse. Prior to placing a stent, complete ﬂ uoroscopic evaluation should be made to characterize the extent of collapse fully and determine the presence of mainstem bronchi involvement. Survival time of dogs with and without bronchial collapse is similar after tracheal stenting. 73 Also, images made during positive-pressure maximal tracheal dilation with a radio-opaque measurement device are required to determine appropriate stent size. 81 During follow-up radiographic evaluation, the stent should be evaluated for correct placement, fraying or fracture, and migration, and the trachea evaluated for in ﬂ ammatory tis- sue ingrowth and progressive tracheal collapse ( Fig. 29.30 ). 72 81 82 Subsequent tracheal collapse can develop in the unstented portion of the trachea. Tracheal collapse in the cat is rare. Although usually sec- ondary to an extratracheal mass effect or intratracheal pressure changes caused by upper airway obstruction, 83 84 primary collapse has been reported. 85 Cranial Lung Lobe Herniation Cranial lung lobe herniation is protrusion of the lung cranial to the cranial skeletal margin of the thoracic cavity and is best seen with ﬂ uoroscopy or occasionally on expiratory radio- graphs ( Fig. 29.31 ). 86 Chronic or acute airway obstruction due to obstructive airway disease including tracheal and bronchial collapse during expiration creates increased intrathoracic pressure and can result in dynamic herniation of the cranial lung lobes through the thoracic inlet (see Fig. 29.31 see Video 29.3). 70 87 88 Associated radiographic ﬁ ndings can include kinking of the extrathoracic trachea (39%), collapse of the intrathoracic trachea, as well as bronchial collapse. 86 Upper Airway Obstruction Radiographic examination of animals with signs of upper res- piratory obstruction should be performed with care and mini- mal restraint. Radiographs should be withheld until the animal is stable enough to undergo complete examination. Several in- direct radiographic ﬁ ndings can be seen secondary to upper airway obstruction in both dogs and cats and can be useful if the primary cause of obstruction is not identi ﬁ ed readily, such as with laryngeal paralysis. These ﬁ ndings are often more marked in cats, possibly because of the pliability of their tissues. With faster multi- detector units, many CT examinations can be done under sedation, thereby avoiding the need for anesthesia and inter- ference with lesion detection through endotracheal intuba- tion. 96 Examination with the mouth opened to approximately 30 to 45 degrees improves visualization of the pharyngeal structures and is particularly important when evaluating pa- tients for nasopharyngeal stenosis. 97 Three-dimensional virtual endoscopic reformatting can be useful and is essential for CT evaluation of laryngeal collapse/paralysis. 29 Images should be acquired suf ﬁ ciently caudally to include the medial retro- pharyngeal lymph nodes. Intraluminal air as well as typically the need for general intubation with placement of an endotracheal tube can limit the usefulness of MRI. 98 Pharyngolaryngeal Masses CT examination is well suited to evaluate extramural, mural, and intraluminal abnormalities. Lymph node involvement and osteolysis associated with aggressive pharyngolaryngeal neoplastic or infectious processes, such as squamous cell car- cinoma and tonsillar neoplasia, can also be identi ﬁ ed using CT. 12 13 99 The tonsillar fossa of the oropharynx is the most common location of pharyngeal neoplasia, speci ﬁ cally squa- mous cell carcinoma, which can also be bilateral. Tumor mineralization is reported in squamous cell carcinoma and pharyngeal osteosarcoma and can occur in both the mass and regional lymph nodes. Hyoid bone lysis can be a feature of tonsillar squamous cell carcinoma 12 and also as a result of ectopic basihyoid thyroid carcinoma, as described earlier. 17 Marked medial retropharyngeal lymph node enlargement, rounded shape, and heterogeneous enhancement have been reported in most cases of pharyngeal neoplasia, and isolated medial retropharyngeal lymphadenomegaly can be seen in tonsillar neoplasia without tonsillar enlargement. 12 13 Trauma and Foreign Body The layered linear appearance of oropharyngeal stick foreign bodies and their contrast-enhancing surrounding in ﬂ ammatory reaction are well seen on CT. 100 Similarly, MRI readily identi ﬁ es the in ﬂ ammatory reaction and regional lymph node enlarge- ment in addition to well-de ﬁ ned linear areas of low-signal in- tensity representing wooden foreign bodies. 101 102 Spatial understanding of the location of the foreign body is more intuitive using cross-sectional imaging in comparison to ultra- sound, thereby helping subsequent surgical planning. 100 102 CT sinography can also be helpful. 103 CT is also described for hyoid bone fractures and malfor- mation, laryngeal cartilage fracture, 21 and tracheal rupture. 104 In tracheal and left mainstem bronchial avulsion, airway discontinuity and pseudoairway formation can be seen, and CT is useful for measuring the extent of the lesion for planning endotracheal intubation and surgical repair. 84 Upper Airway Collapse and Tracheal Hypoplasia CT ha s be en re po rt e d i n do gs wi th re sp i ra to ry di st re ss du e to la ry ng ea l pa ra ly si s, br ac hy c ep ha li c sy nd ro m e, i nc lu di n g tr ac he al hy po pl as ia , la ry n ge al co ll ap se an d sa c cu le ev er si on , tr ac he al / b ro n ch i al co ll ap se , an d tr ac he al st en os is . Acute respiratory signs may develop secondary to compression of the trachea by an esophageal foreign body or as a result of aspiration of regurgitant material. A strong link be- tween a variety of respiratory diseases and digestive disorders has recently been established. 2 4 ANAT OMIC AND PHY SIOLOGI C FEA TURES Swallowing is an essential and complex process that results in bolus delivery from the oral cavity to the stomach. The actions involving lapping of liquid and prehension and chewing of food are voluntary and require coordinated movements of the tongue and jaws. In the cervical region, the esophagus is located slightly to the left of the trachea, gradually becoming completely left sided at the thoracic inlet ( Fig. 30.3A ). 7 The left common carotid artery, vagosympathetic trunk, internal jugular vein, and tracheal duct course through the angle between the esophagus and the longus capitis muscle. The right common carotid ar- tery, vagosympathetic trunk, internal jugular vein, and tracheal duct are lateral to the trachea on the right side. The thoracic portion of the esophagus is in close proximity to the trachea. The esophagus is to the left of the trachea at the thoracic inlet (see Fig. 30.3B ), but gradually courses dorsally over the point of bifurcation of the trachea at the level of the ﬁ fth and sixth thoracic vertebrae (see Fig. 30.3C ). At its dorsal location, it lies to the right of the aortic arch and ventral to the longus colli muscles. Between the tracheal bifurcation and caudal esopha- geal sphincter, the esophagus lies in the median plane (see Fig. 30.3D ). The vagal nerves run dorsocaudally across the sides of the esophagus and unite at the dorsal aspect of the esoph- agus a few centimeters cranial to the esophageal hiatus to form the vagal trunk, which passes through the hiatus with the esophagus. The LES is a focal narrowing of the esophagus at the junction with the stomach that is toned at rest to prevent retrograde movement of gastric contents. When a bolus is transported caudad by the esophagus, the LES relaxes to allow passage into the stomach. Vascular supply to the esophagus is complicated and begins in the cervical region with branches of the thyroid arteries. The bronchoesophageal artery is the main source to the cranial two- thirds of the thoracic portion. Esophageal branches of the aorta and/or intercostal arteries supply the remainder of the esoph- agus, and the terminal portion is supplied by the left gastric artery. The azygous vein and left gastric vein drain the thoracic portion. Lymphatic drainage is through the medial retro- pharyngeal, deep cervical, cranial mediastinal, bronchial, por- tal, splenic, and gastric lymph nodes. Innervation of the esophagus is complex and involves 25 paired spinal ganglia from C2 to L5. Neurologic control of swallowing is coordinated by cranial nerves V (trigeminal), VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), and XII (hypoglossal), and their nuclei in the brainstem that, in turn, are controlled by areas of the reticular formation referred to as the swallowing center. 8 RADIOG RAPH Y Survey radiography of the thorax and neck is often the ﬁ rst imaging step for the evaluation of an animal with suspected pharyngeal, UES, or esophageal disease. This should include three projections of the thorax (dorsoventral or ventrodorsal [VD], right, and left lateral) and at least one lateral projection of the neck. Care should be taken to ensure that the radiograph of the neck is adequately positioned. More speci ﬁ cally, the lateral cervical study must not be rotated and the head should be extended as poor positioning can distort anatomy and seriously compromise interpretation. The pharynx, larynx, and UES should be included. The normal esophagus is usually empty and rarely visible on thoracic radiographs in cats and dogs because of its location within the mediastinum and silhouetting with adjacent muscles and mediastinal structures. On left lateral thoracic radiographs, the normal caudal thoracic esophagus sometimes contains a small amount of ﬂ uid and can be seen as a faint tubular soft tissue opacity between the descending aorta and caudal vena cava ( Fig. 30.4A ); this appearance is rare in right lateral radio- graphs. Gas can accumulate focally in the esophagus in animals that are excited, sedated or anesthetized, and dyspneic; this gas accumulation is usually minimal, and the most commonly located just cranial to the tracheal bifurcation (see Fig. 30.4B ). The tissue band between the trachea and esophagus ( white arrows ) is termed the tracheal stripe sign , also called the tra- cheoesophageal stripe sign and esophageal stripe sign. This is created by summation of the ventral aspect of the esophageal wall with the dorsal aspect of the tracheal wall, each outlined by gas in their respective lumen. General anesthesia or aerophagia may lead to severe dilation of the esophagus, which can appear identical to pathologic meg- aesophagus (see Fig. 30.4C ). Anesthesia-related megaesophagus will resolve spontaneously when the patient is awake again. Survey radiographs will help de ﬁ ne if aspiration pneumonia is present. Aspiration pneumonia is common in animals with swallowing disorders and typically involves the dependent aspect of the right and left cranial and right middle lung lobes. Since the right middle lung lobe is a common site for aspiration, the left lateral thoracic view is essential for complete assess- ment of the lung. 9 When megaesophagus is identi ﬁ ed, the presence of aspiration pneumonia has a negative association with survival time. 10 The absence of abnormal ﬁ ndings on survey radiographs of the esophagus does not eliminate the possibility of esophageal disease. In animals with appropriate clinical signs of esophageal disease, contrast studies of the esophagus should be consid- ered. However, in cases where severe aspiration pneumonia is present, contrast studies should be delayed until such time as pneumonia is resolved as aspiration of barium during the im- aging procedure will further compromise lung function. CONTR AST RAD IOGRAPH Y Survey radiographs of the thorax and cervical region are ideally performed immediately before a contrast esophagram. Box 30.1 contains a list of contrast study techniques used for examina- tion of the esophagus. The type of contrast medium selected to perform contrast radiography depends on several factors. 11 Barium paste or cream is viscous and may adhere best to mucosal irregularities. However, due to the viscosity of these agents, barium paste and cream may not ﬂ ow well around intraluminal lesions and are contraindicated in animals at increased risk for aspiration, because aspirated paste can cause airway obstruction. 6 Liquid barium (60% weight-volume) is the most common medium used for contrast radiography of the pharynx and esophagus. 12 Dosage is related to size so that cats should receive 5 to 7 mL boluses, small- to medium-sized dogs should receive 15 mL boluses, while larger dogs should receive 20 to 30 mL boluses of liquid barium orally. 12 When endoscopy is likely to follow or if perforation of the pharynx, cricopharynx, or esophagus is suspected, nonionic iodinated contrast agents are preferable to barium so as to avoid the granulomatous reaction associated with leakage into the cervical soft tissues or mediastinum. 13 Ionic, iodinated contrast agents are speci ﬁ cally contraindicated due to the potential for life-threatening pulmonary edema that can result from aspira- tion into the lungs. Esophageal perforation should be suspected when survey radiographs identify gas in the cervical soft tissues or mediastinum but no external wounds are present. Soft tissue swelling in the cervical region with regional emphysema is suggestive of perforation. Opaci ﬁ cation and widening of the mediastinum may accompany pneumomediastinum when perforation of the thoracic esophagus has resulted in media- stinitis. 14 In these instances, nonionic, iodinated contrast me- dium should be diluted 50:50 with sterile water and 10 to 15 mL boluses are administered orally. 15 Sedation should generally be avoided unless absolutely necessary since tranquilizers result in signi ﬁ cant alterations in swallowing function. 15 However, should sedation be required, acepromazine may be adminis- tered but may increase esophageal transit times, particularly at higher doses. 16 Regardless of the type of contrast medium used, the animal is restrained in right lateral recumbency and liquid contrast medium is administered orally using a catheter-tipped syringe. Lateral and dorsoventral radiographs of the neck and thorax should be obtained during swallowing or as soon after swal- lowing as possible. It is wise to obtain images of multiple swallows and to con ﬁ rm the presence of a suspected lesion on multiple projections. When perforation is unlikely, kibble is then soaked in barium and administered orally. 12 Additional lateral and VD radiographs of the neck and thorax should be obtained. Barium-soaked kibble is particularly helpful when trying to identify esophageal strictures through which liquid barium may pass unimpeded. Mixing iodinated contrast agents with kibble is not advised since iodinated agents are typically used when perforation is suspected and esophageal leakage of kibble is undesirable. 15 Barium or iodine aspiration is a potential complication of performing esophageal contrast studies. Aspiration of a small amount of liquid barium is usually insigni ﬁ cant. Pneumonia and lung granuloma formation are rare complications of barium aspiration. Aspirated barium is cleared from the airways by ciliary action, as well as coughing. If barium enters the alveolar space, it may remain there permanently ( Fig. 30.5 ). Lymphatic uptake of aspirated barium will also be evident as amorphous mottled opacities in the region of the mediastinal and tracheobronchial lymph nodes, which may also be a permanent ﬁ nding ( Fig. 30.6 ). CONTR AST VIDEO FLUO ROSCOPIC SWALLOW ING STUD IES When a functional or transient disorder of swallowing is sus- pected and cannot be de ﬁ ned by survey or contrast radiog- raphy, contrast video ﬂ uoroscopic assessment of swallowing is indicated. When performing dynamic ﬂ uoroscopic swallowing studies, it is essential to protect personnel involved in the study from scattered radiation by establishing barriers of lead- impregnated rubber or other shielding between the primary beam and the attending personnel. 8 In preparation for a video ﬂ uoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS), the animal is ideally fasted for 12 hours prior to the procedure. Liquid barium (60% weight-volume) is the most common contrast medium used but, similar to contrast radi- ography, nonionic iodinated medium diluted 50:50 with sterile water can be used in cases where perforation of the pharynx or esophagus is suspected. The animal is then positioned on the ﬂ uoroscopy table. The animal can either be restrained in lateral recumbency on the ﬂ uoroscopy table or imaged in sternal or standing position using a cross-table imaging orientation. The differences between sternal and lateral body positioning during VFSS have been reported in the dog and cervical esophageal transit times are signi ﬁ cantly delayed in laterally recumbent dogs. 17 However, a speci ﬁ c positioning device is ideal to minimize patient motion during sternally positioned or standing studies ( Fig. 30.7 ) and, in the authors experience, head motion remains problematic during these examinations, particularly in dogs with dysphagia. As with contrast radiography, sedation should be avoided when performing contrast-enhanced video- ﬂ uoroscopy due to the inherent alteration in swallowing func- tion that results from tranquilization. Recording the study and performing frame-by-frame analysis can provide quantitative measures of swallowing function. Many quantitative parameters have been reported as valu- able assessments of pharyngeal and cricopharyngeal function. 17 21 These include the interswallow interval ([ISI]; time in seconds between two successive, uninterrupted swal- lows from the onset frame of swallow 1 to the onset frame of the subsequent swallow), swallow rate (the number of swal- lows per 3-second interval of uninterrupted prehension), jaw cycles per swallow ratio (the number of licks from maximum jaw excursion to the following maximum jaw excursion), time from swallow onset ( Fig. 30.8A ) to proximal esophageal sphincter/UES opening ( Fig. 30.8B ), time to maximum laryngeal excursion ( Fig. 30.8C ), time to maximum pharyngeal contrac- tion ( Fig. 30.8D ), time to air column reopening/epiglottis reopening ( Fig. 30.8E ), and time to proximal esophageal sphincter/UES closure ( Fig. 30.8F ). When making quantitative measures, videos are viewed frame by frame where each frame represents 1/30th of a second. The frame in which the epiglottis is observed to close over the larynx is considered as the starting point for all time measurements. The swallow is considered completed when the epiglottis is observed to reopen. Once the number of frames to each point in the swallow is calculated, that number can be divided by 30 to obtain the number of seconds from the initiation of the swallow to each particular event within that swallow. The contraction of the pharynx can also be assessed using frame-by-frame analysis to facilitate calculation of the PCR. 19 From the digitized video- ﬂ uoroscopic studies, a hold frame and a maximum contraction frame are selected. The hold frame is identi ﬁ ed as a frame in which the larynx appeared at rest without rostral or caudal motion. For the hold frame, a region of interest (ROI) is drawn around the airspace beginning dorsal to the soft palate then rostrally to the hyoid apparatus and tym- panic bulla, dorsally to the dorsal aspect of the pharyngeal wall, caudally along the dorsal aspect of the pharyngeal wall to the UES, and ventrally around the corniculate process of the arytenoid cartilage to include the vallecula, ﬁ nally connecting the epiglottis to the starting point ( Fig. 30.9A ). The UES is speci ﬁ cally de ﬁ ned as the region in the cranial esophagus that remained the narrowest through the study. 22 For the maximum contraction frame, an ROI is drawn around any residual barium or airspace identi ﬁ ed within the pharyngeal area (see Fig. 30.9B ). ROIs are expressed in pixel numbers and the PCR is calculated by dividing the number of pixels in the maximum contraction frame by the number of pixels in the hold frame. Normal reference ranges for quantitative measures are outlined in Table 30.1 , including measurements made with animals in different body positions, consuming different bolus sizes and of various ages. Techniques for VFSS in dogs with megaesophagus have been reported with the intent of de ﬁ ning LES function, assess for any evidence of peristalsis, and to determine the optimal dietary consistency for expedition of esophageal clearance. 23 24 Dogs are fasted for 12 hours prior to imaging and positioned in a size appropriate Bailey chair with the photon beam directed horizontally to yield a lateral projection of the cervical and thoracic esophagus to the level of the LES ( Fig. 30.10A,B ). Bolus consistencies are similar to above and include liquid barium, barium-soaked soft food/slurry and barium-soaked kibble. VFSS is performed along the entire length of the esophagus at base- line, for the ﬁ rst 20 seconds or until complete esophageal clearance, and then every 5 minutes for up to 15 minutes following liquid administration and 30 minutes after each food type. Fluoroscopic evaluation is discontinued if all material clears from the esophagus or after 15 minutes for liquid and 30 minutes for slurry and kibble, whichever comes ﬁ rst. Regardless of the VFSS study performed, in normal animals, there should be no retention of barium in the oral or pharyngeal cavity during swallowing. Some coating of the mucosa is normal. No contrast medium should be present in the pharynx, larynx, or trachea after swallowing. Small volumes of contrast medium may accumulate in the proximal esophagus if bolus size is inadequate for stimulation of a primary peristaltic wave. However, larger boluses should trigger primary peristalsis, or secondary peristalsis should initiate once boluses accumulate to an adequate size. PHAR YNGEAL AND CRICO PHARY NGEAL DYSPH AGIA Dysphagia can be morphologic or functional in origin. Morphologic causes include trauma, foreign body, an oral or pharyngeal mass, and regional lymphadenopathy. Lateral and VD survey radiographs of the pharyngeal and cervical region and thorax are indicated to screen for radiopaque foreign bodies, such as bones, needles, and ﬁ sh hooks ( Fig. 30.11 ). Soft tissue swelling and gas pockets can be seen with perforating pharyngeal trauma, abscesses, or nonradiopaque foreign bodies, such as wooden sticks. Ultrasonography can be useful to determine the source of nonspeci ﬁ c pharyngeal swelling and to identify nonradiopaque foreign bodies ( Fig. 30.12 ). When a morphologic cause for dysphagia cannot be found, VFSS is indicated to assess function ( Table 30.2 ). Dogs with oral phase dysphagia have dif ﬁ culty with prehension and bolus formation and with transport to the pharynx. Oral dysphagia is usually characterized by the animal dropping food or liquid from its mouth and drooling. 19 The oral phase of swallowing is the only voluntary portion of the swallowing process. In oral dysphagia, there is failure of aboral transport of liquid or food and lack of bolus formation to induce the swallowing re ﬂ ex. These disorders are typically diagnosed by watching the animal eat and rarely require imaging. The onset of the pharyngeal phase of swallowing may also be delayed. If a swallow is achieved, the pharyngeal and esophageal phases of swallowing are usually normal. Pharyngeal dysphagia is often characterized by nonspeci ﬁ c signs, such as gagging, retching, and the necessity for multiple swallowing attempts before movement of a bolus into the esophagus. 20 Pharyngeal dysphagia is diagnosed when the contraction of the dorsal pharyngeal wall against the tongue base is weak so that presentation of the bolus to the UES lacks vigorous momentum. The cricopharyngeal phase may or may not be normal. Pharyngeal dysphagia is often the result of neuromuscular disorders that result in weakness or as a result of pharyngeal in ﬂ ammation. Video ﬂ uoroscopic abnormalities include (1) slow contraction of the pharynx, (2) incomplete enclosure of the bolus, (3) incomplete rostral and dorsal movement of the larynx, and (4) absence of forceful contrac- tion of the pharynx to propel the bolus through the crico- pharyngeal sphincter. The UES may not open or open to a reduced diameter because of the weakness of the pharyngeal contraction, and this could be misinterpreted as a cricophar- yngeal disorder. The PCR was developed to identify dogs with weak pharyngeal contraction that would make them poor candidates for myotomy when cricopharyngeal dysphagia is diagnosed and to better differentiate them from those with cricopharyngeal dysphagia. 19 Dogs with decreased pharyngeal contraction have a signi ﬁ cantly higher PCR compared with healthy dogs, but this can also be present in dogs with crico- pharyngeal dysphagias. The discerning factor between pharyngeal dysphagia and cricopharyngeal dysphagia is the time to opening of the cricopharyngeal sphincter, which is signi ﬁ cantly shorter in pharyngeal dysphagia. 19 Cricopharyngeal dysphagia is a functional abnormality involving failure of the cricopharyngeal sphincter to open fully (cricopharyngeal achalasia) or at the appropriate time (crico- pharyngeal dyssynchrony). The clinical signs of cricophar- yngeal dysphagia are similar to those of pharyngeal dysphagia ( Fig. 30.13 ). 19 Although speci ﬁ c breed predilections have not been reported, cricopharyngeal achalasia is often associated with toy breeds. 25 The exact etiology has not been determined, but most affected patients develop clinical signs soon after weaning, suggesting that cricopharyngeal achalasia is a congenital disorder. 26 Critical to the diagnosis is the docu- mentation of delayed or nonopening of the UES and a lack of coordination between pharyngeal contraction and opening of the UES, which requires ﬂ uoroscopy ( Fig. 30.14 ). Dysphagia in cats is less commonly reported than in dogs. Esophageal phase dysphagia is the most common type occur- ring in cats, with hiatal hernia, dysmotility, and stricture being the most common causes. 27 Quantitative evaluation of the PCR, time to maximal pharyngeal contraction, time to opening of the epiglottis, as well as proximal esophageal sphincter opening and closing times in cats with esophageal dysphagia are similar to that reported in healthy dogs. 27 However, studies in a healthy cat cohort are lacking. ESOPH AGEAL DISO RDERS Esophageal motility disorders may result in abnormal peristalsis, transport, and motor function, and clinical signs of regurgita- tion are common. Survey radiographs can help detect structural abnormalities, such as segmental or generalized dilation of the esophagus, abnormal esophageal content because of lack of normal peristalsis, and the presence of aspiration pneumonia. If survey radiographs are negative in animals with regurgitation, contrast studies are necessary to rule out esophageal disease. Peristaltic abnormalities, hypomotility, strictures, or radiolucent foreign bodies causing obstruction can go undetected on sur- vey radiographs. Mechanical obstruction because of foreign body or stricture can be diagnosed with a static barium esophagram, but accurate assessment of motility requires ﬂ uo- roscopy. Following passage of a bolus through the UES, a pri- mary peristaltic wave should propel the bolus to the stomach. If this process is interrupted, a secondary peristaltic wave may propel the bolus to the LES in normal animals. It is important to note that, when assessed with VFSS, cervical esophageal transit time is signi ﬁ cantly shorter for dogs in sternal recumbency compared to lateral. 17 The percentage of primary waves is signi ﬁ cantly greater in liquid and kibble studies when done in sternal recumbency compared with lateral recumbency. Also, the percentage of swallows that have no associated primary peristaltic waves is higher in lateral recumbency. The per- centage of secondary waves, however, does not differ between the two positions. 17 Primary peristalsis can be disrupted by hypomotile seg- ments, and secondary peristalsis may be absent in disease. Dogs with laryngeal paralysis may also have esophageal dysfunc- tion. 28 Esophageal dysmotility in young dogs in the absence of megaesophagus is characterized by abnormal primary waves that move the bolus less than 5 cm aborally, and abnormal secondary waves that allow bolus retention in the esophagus after two subsequent swallows. 29 Retrograde ﬂ ow of more than 10 cm is another ﬁ nding associated with hypomotility, as is prolonged esophageal transit time ( > 5 seconds). 29 Esophageal dysmotility can be caused by delayed maturation, and sponta- neous improvement after 1 year of age can occur because of maturation of the neuromuscular system. 30 Esophagitis is Fig. 30.13 Lateral digi tal ﬂ uoroscopic image of bar ium swallow in a 2-year-old Border collie with cricopharyngeal dysphagia. Gastroesopha- geal re ﬂ ux occurs when gastric and duodenal contents enter aborally into the esophagus, and this can lead to dysmotility secondary to resultant esophagitis. 30 Esophageal Dilation Esophageal dilatation can be segmental or generalized depending on the cause and location of disease, and the dila- tation can be either functional or mechanical. Generalized dilatation is typically caused by functional disease, whereas segmental dilatation is usually caused by foreign body, in ﬁ ltra- tive disease such as neoplasia or in ﬂ ammation, hiatal diseases, segmental motor disease, stricture, vascular ring anomaly, or redundant esophagus ( Fig. 30.16 ). Megaesophagus The term megaesophagus describes a dilated and hypomotile esophagus resulting from neuromuscular dysfunction; this type of esophageal dilation is often idiopathic in dogs. 31 Megaesophagus in dogs can also result from LES achalasia-like syndrome (LES-AS). 32 Megaesophagus is the most common cause of regurgitation in dogs and the most frequently reported motility disorder affecting the canine esophagus. 33 Mega- esophagus is not common in cats but has been described in instances of pylorospasm. Predominant clinical signs in esoph- ageal neuromuscular dysfunction are effortless regurgitation of tubular-formed, undigested food. Megaesophagus can be segmental (cervical or thoracic) or generalized and occurs secondary to diseases of the neuromuscular junction (myas- thenia gravis), striated muscle (myositis), peripheral nerves (polyneuropathy), or central nervous system (in ﬂ ammatory, toxic, and neoplastic). 31 Radiographic signs of megaesophagus include dilatation of the esophagus with gas, retention of food or ﬂ uid, tracheal stripe sign, visibility of the longus colli muscle, ventral displacement of the intrathoracic trachea, ventral displacement of the heart, and aspiration pneumonia ( Fig. 30.17 ; see Figs. 30.4C and 30.5 ). A cranial mediastinal mass may be pre- sent in dogs with thymoma and paraneoplastic myasthenia gravis ( eFig. 30.1 ). When generalized megaesophagus is pre- sent, the thoracic segment of the esophagus is usually more severely dilatated than the cervical portion because of sur- rounding negative intrathoracic pressure. When gas ﬁ lled, the esophagus can be dif ﬁ cult to discern because of the lucency of the surrounding lung. On lateral thoracic radiographs, two thin soft tissue opaque, parallel bands coursing from cranial to caudal in the dorsal aspect of the thorax represent the wall of the gas- ﬁ lled esophagus. A focal indentation of the dorsal esophageal wall is caused by the azygous vein crossing over on the right. In the VD radiograph, the wall of the gas- ﬁ lled esophagus is most often identi ﬁ ed as a thin, soft tissue band to the left of the vertebral column. If the dilation is severe enough, a second band can also be seen on the right, converging with the left one at the caudal esophageal sphincter (see Fig. 30.17 ). When imaged with VFSS in a Bailey chair, dogs with LES-AS can be distinguished from dogs with idiopathic megaesophagus due to the presence of a “ bird-beak ” appear- ance to the LES. 32 Fig. 30.16 Bari um swallow in an 8-year-old Shar-Pei. Hiatal Diseases Esophageal hiatal diseases include dynamic esophageal and paraesophageal hernias, gastroesophageal intussusception, and gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux. Clinical signs may be absent, or dogs may have recurrent gastrointestinal signs, such as regurgitation, retching, and possibly vomiting. Esophageal hernias can be congenital or acquired. The congenital form has been reported in shar-pei dogs. 34 In the acquired form, weakness of the dia- phragm, elevated abdominal pressure, and upper airway obstruction are predisposing factors. In dynamic hiatal hernias, the caudal esophageal sphincter and part of the gastric fundus move in and out of the caudal mediastinum through a weakened esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm. In most dogs and cats, this may happen intermit- tently and randomly making radiographic identi ﬁ cation chal- lenging. Brachycephalic breeds are prone to hiatal hernias in af ﬁ liation with brachycephalic upper airway obstruction due to excess negative thoracic pressure needed to respire against the obstructed upper airway. 35 36 In these breeds, hiatal herniation often accompanies inspiration and is more frequent, thereby making radiographic identi ﬁ cation more likely. If captured radiographically, there is a soft tissue, or mixed soft tissue and gas opacity between the aorta and caudal vena cava on lateral radiographs that silhouettes with the cranial diaphragmatic contour ( Fig. 30.18 eFig. 30.2 and 30.3 ). If persistent on the VD view, the opacity has a midline location and is slightly on the left of the vertebral column. Dynamic esophageal hernia may be con ﬁ rmed with static barium esophagraphy; however, VFSS is often necessary. If the fundus is herniated along with the esophagus, rugal folds outlined by barium may be visible. The caudal esophageal sphincter will also be located cranial to the diaphragm, and barium can be seen to re ﬂ ux from the stomach into the caudal esophagus with VFSS. Paraesophageal hernias are caused by the fundus being herniated into the mediastinum alongside of the esophagus with the caudal esophageal sphincter remaining in the abdomen ( Fig. 30.19A ). On VD radiographs, the herniated fundus is to the left of the esophagus, and hernia contents may move in and out with respiration (see Fig. 30.19B,C ). Gastroesophageal intussusception occurs when part of the stomach and possibly other abdominal organs, such as the spleen, evert into the esophageal lumen. The intussusceptum may be of homogeneous soft tissue opacity or may be a mixed soft tissue and gas opacity if there is gas trapped in the herni- ated portion of the stomach ( Fig. 30.20 ). A feature that distin- guishes gastroesophageal intussusception from a sliding or paraesophageal hernia is the sharply marginated cranial edge of the intussusceptum contrasted against a gas- ﬁ lled esophageal lumen. Gastroesophageal intussusception is often acquired and secondary to esophageal dilatation or previous surgery at the caudal esophageal sphincter resulting in chalasia. Gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux occurs when gastric acid enters the esophagus; this usually results in esophagitis. Survey radio- graphs are usually normal, or there may be increased soft tissue opacity between the aorta and vena cava on both lateral pro- jections. With increasing severity, the caudal esophagus may become enlarged and contain either air or ﬂ uid. Contrast esophagram studies are usually negative unless severe ulcera- tion is present that leads to adherence of the contrast medium to the mucosa. Focal dilatation of the esophagus with contrast medium and/or obliteration of the linear folds normally out- lined with barium can occur if the esophagitis is severe. Scar- ring and stricture can develop. Redundant Esophagus Redundant esophagus is often an incidental ﬁ nding in brachy- cephalic breeds, such as bulldogs and Shar-Peis (see Fig. 30.16 ). Survey radiographs may be normal, or focal dilatation of the esophagus with gas can be seen at the thoracic inlet. In static barium esophagrams, the esophagus has a tortuous course at the thoracic inlet that appears as a diverticulum ventral to the trachea. The accumulation of contrast medium in a redundant esophagus is usually only temporary, and the esophagus will appear normal on subsequent radiographs. With VFSS, the redundant segment typically has normal motility. Occasionally, there will be a clinically signi ﬁ cant motility disorder associated with the redundant region of the esophagus. Foreign bodies are most often located at the thoracic inlet, base of the heart, or just cranial to the diaphragm, sites where the esophagus is limited in its ability to distend. Common radiographic features are visibility of the distinct foreign material, gas in the esophagus contrasting with the foreign body, esophageal dilation orad to the obstruction, and signs of perforation (pleural or mediastinal effusion or pneumomediastinum). 38 Nonobstructive foreign bodies, such as ﬁ shhooks and other sharp objects, tend to lodge in the pharyngeal region ( Fig. 30.21 ; see Fig. 30.11 ). A soft tissue opaque esophageal foreign body may appear similar to an esophageal neoplasm, an esophageal abscess, mediastinal mass, paraesophageal hernia, or lung mass (see Fig. 30.22 ). A static contrast esophagram can help to differentiate these conditions.
