VASCU LAR RI NG ANOM ALIES Regurgitation due to vascular ring anomalies presents at an early age in most instances; however, it can have late-onset occurrence in both cats and dogs. 39 41 Under normal condi- tions, the aorta is derived from the left fourth aortic arch while the right fourth aortic arch typically regresses. Anomalous development of the aortic arches can lead to secondary extrinsic esophageal compression. Esophageal compression secondary to a vascular malformation is termed vascular ring anomaly . Of the seven types of vascular ring anomalies that are described, types I through III have a persistent right aortic arch, type IV has a double aortic arch, and types V through VII have a left aortic arch with combinations of persistent right liga- mentum arteriosum and right subclavian arteries, all of which cause entrapment of the esophagus. 42 44 Development of the aortic arch from the right fourth aortic arch with regression of the left fourth aortic arch, termed persistent right fourth aortic arch , is the most common vascular ring anomaly that leads to entrapment of the esoph- agus. In the normal situation where the aorta is derived from the left fourth arch, the aorta, main pulmonary artery, and interconnecting ligamentum arteriosum are all on the left side of the trachea and esophagus. 42 When the aorta is derived from the right fourth aortic arch rather than the left, the aorta is on the right side of the trachea and esophagus, whereas the main pulmonary artery is on the left side. In this con ﬁ guration, the ligamentum arteriosum compresses the esophagus against the trachea and base of the heart as it passes from right (aorta) to left (pulmonary artery) ( Fig. 30.24 ). The compression results in esophageal dilation cranial to the base of the heart. Survey ra- diographs may be normal if the esophagus is not dilated, but this is unusual. The dilated portion of the esophagus cranial to the heart base creates a mass effect that contains air and/or ingesta and usually displaces the trachea ventrally ( Figs. 30.25 and 30.26 ), although occasionally the enlarged esophagus will slide laterally and become positioned ventral to the trachea ( Fig. 30.27 ). In some dogs, it is possible to see the trachea being deviated focally toward the left on VD projections (see Fig. 30.25 ), and the normal left lateral margin of the aorta may not be evident. In a static barium esophagram, the narrowing of the esophagus at the heart base can be con ﬁ rmed (see Fig. 30.30 ). INFLAM MATORY DISEAS ES Esophagitis Esophagitis can result from infection, ingestion of hot or cor- rosive substances, vomiting, gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux, mega- esophagus, and foreign body obstructions. Survey radiography is usually unremarkable. Aspiration pneumonia can be identi- ﬁ ed, but the diagnosis of esophagitis usually requires endos- copy. The esophagus may have reduced motility and therefore be dilated with gas or ﬂ uid, but this is a nonspeci ﬁ c ﬁ nding. Ulcerations, motility disorders, or mechanical obstruction sec- ondary to in ﬂ ammation requires contrast procedures to be characterized further. If severe esophagitis is present, then segmental narrowing, irregular mucosal contours, indistinct folds of the esophageal wall, and thickening of the wall may be present in static barium contrast studies. Fluoroscopic contrast studies may be characterized by segmental spasticity and minor dilation. Gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux may be identi ﬁ ed with VFSS. Strictures Esophageal strictures usually result from foreign body or gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux. Esophageal strictures thought to be related to gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux during anesthesia are usually located at the caudal portion of the thoracic esophagus, caudal to the base of the heart. 46 Strictures of the esophagus typically have a smoothly bordered, tapered appearance caudally ( Fig. 30.30 ). Survey radiography may be unremarkable, or there may be segmental or generalized dilatation of the esophagus, depending on the site and extent of the stricture. Contrast esophagraphy is used to determine the location, size, and length of the stricture for treatment planning (see Fig. 30.30 ). Moreover, the contrast study helps to determine if the stricture is mural, extramural, or luminal. Smoothly bordered mucosal surfaces outlined with contrast medium and having a circum- ferential narrowing on lateral and VD projections are the typical appearance of a mural stenosis caused by chronic in ﬂ ammation or scarring. An irregularly bordered mucosal surface can be seen with neoplastic in ﬁ ltration of the wall or severe ulceration because of in ﬂ ammation. Extramural compressions have a smoothly bordered contrast column that is convex and tapering toward the narrowing in one projection with the narrowed portion appearing widened in the orthogonal projection. Thy- roid masses, enlarged lymph nodes, and cervical abscesses can impinge on or invade the cervical esophagus, causing obstruction. If liquid barium passes through the narrowed re- gion or no abnormality is seen, then barium-soaked kibble can be used to identify a stricture that allows ﬂ uid but not solids to pass. Esophageal neoplasms are rare in dogs and cats. Osteo- sarcoma and ﬁ brosarcoma of the esophagus are reported in areas endemic for Spirocerca lupi 47 Squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, branchioma, branchial cleft cysts, papilloma, angioleiomyosarcoma, and leiomyosarcoma have also been re- ported but are rare. 48 52 If the neoplasm is large enough, it may be recognized on survey radiographs as a soft tissue mass associated with the esophagus ( Fig. 30.31 eFig. 30.5 ). The esophagus may be dilatated cranial to the mass, but this is not always present. Differentiation of esophageal masses from an esophageal foreign body or a nonesophageal mass may require esophagraphy, CT, or endoscopy (see Fig. 30.31 ). Dystrophic mineralization of esophageal masses is rare, but its presence can be associated with neoplasia, Spirocerca infection, or oral administration of radiopaque medication. Esophageal dilation cranial to an esophageal mass may also be present. Tem- porary or persistent retention of barium may occur because of lack of secondary peristalsis where the wall is stiffened because of tumor in ﬁ ltration. Mural thickening, asymmetry of the lumen, absence of the mucosal folds, ulceration of the mucosa with barium retention, and a locally enlarged or dilated esophagus are suggestive of neoplasia. Infection of dogs and other carnivores with the nematode S. lupi occurs in tropical and subtropical regions throughout the world. 53 The parasite infects mainly the esophagus and aorta, leading to gastrointes- tinal, respiratory, and circulatory signs. 54 In survey radiographs, there may be a mediastinal mass in the region of the caudal thoracic esophagus because of granuloma formation ( Fig. 30.32 ). The in ﬂ ammatory esophageal mass can become neoplastic, with osteosarcoma and ﬁ brosarcoma being re- ported. There may be new bone formation on the ventral aspect of thoracic vertebrae dorsal to the mass and also enlargement of the descending aorta. 55 57 S. lupi has also caused spinal cord chondrosarcoma. 58 Radiographic abnor- malities of the aorta are rare, but dilatation of the proximal descending aorta and aortic mineralization have been re- ported. 59 In spirocercosis-endemic areas, dorsoventral and right lateral projections are recommended, because they also allow for better visualization of descending aortic aneurysms and prevent interpreting the potentially normally visible esophagus in left lateral images as a mass. 60 However, as noted in Chapter 28 , obtaining both left and right lateral views of the thorax should be routine procedure. Contrast studies of the esophagus con ﬁ rm the granuloma to be originating from the esophagus and are usually characterized by an irregular mucosal border with outpouchings and ﬁ lling defects. Endoscopy provides similar information, and the parasite may be visualized directly in some dogs. 14 Computed tomography (CT) provides infor- mation in con ﬁ rming nonesophageal or extraesophageal masses to be spirocercosis related because of earlier detection of aortic mineralization and spondylitis. 61 CT angiography perfusion analysis of esophageal nodules can be used to help differentiate nonneoplastic from neoplastic nodules associated with S. lupi S. lupi induced esophageal sarcomas are statistically signi ﬁ cantly less perfused than nonneoplastic granulomatous nodules. 62 DIVERTIC ULA, PE RFORA TION, AND FISTU LA FORMAT ION Esophageal diverticula are pouches of variable size that are either acquired or congenital. The acquired form is caused by a thinning of the esophageal wall that allows it to bulge. Causes include esophagitis, strictures, ulceration from a foreign body, vascular ring anomaly, hiatal hernia, parasites, and peri- esophageal in ﬂ ammation. Esophageal diverticula can be classi- ﬁ ed as either pulsion or traction types. Increased intraluminal pressure from a foreign body or chronic functional obstruction can cause a pulsion diverticulum. Pulsion diverticula are located most commonly between the heart and diaphragm. Traction diverticula are formed because of adhesions on the esophageal wall and are often located in the cranial and midthoracic esophagus. With an esophageal diverticulum, survey radiographs are characterized by a circumscribed soft tissue mass or out- pouching of the esophagus, impacted ingesta, or a mixed gas and soft tissue content ( Fig. 30.33 ). Following survey radiog- raphy, further imaging may include endoscopy, CT, or contrast esophagraphy. Contrast medium retention in the outpouching on serial radiographs helps to con ﬁ rm the diagnosis. Endoscopy is indicated to fully assess the mucosal lining and the size of the opening into the diverticulum for surgical planning. Esophageal ﬁ stulas can be congenital or acquired. 65 Congenital forms are typically bronchoesophageal communi- cations, but tracheoesophageal communications also occur. 66 Acquired forms are typically due to esophageal perforation resulting in communication with the airways of the trachea or lung. 67 Survey radiographs may be characterized by an ill- de ﬁ ned soft tissue or mixed pulmonary opacity. The diagnosis of an esophageal ﬁ stula relies upon demonstrating a commu- nication between the esophagus and the airway with contrast medium or bronchoscopy. A swallow with liquid barium will usually show communication from the esophagus into the airway via a ﬁ stulous tract. ESOPH AGEAL VAR ICES Esophageal and paraesophageal varices may result from portal hypertension that generates reversal of portal blood ﬂ ow, which diverts venous blood in a cranial direction through the left gastric vein to the venous plexus of the esophagus. 68 69 Obstructions of the cranial vena cava can also lead to the for- mation of esophageal and paraesophageal varices. The varices can drain into the azygous vein, the caudal vena cava, or into the portal system, depending on the site of the obstruction. Gallbladder and choledochal varices, omental varices, duodenal varices, phrenicoabdominal varices, colic varices, and abdom- inal wall varices drain into the caudal vena cava and result from portal hypertension. CT angiography is necessary for deter- mining the origin, course, and termination of these vessels, and their underlying cause ( Fig. 30.35 ). Of note is that bronchoe- sophageal artery hypertrophy should be included in the differ- ential diagnosis of esophageal and paraesophageal varices in dogs as the two diseases appear similarly on CT angiography. 70 Both portal hypertension causing varices and bronchoesopha- geal artery hypertrophy secondary to chronic pulmonary or thromboembolic disease can occur concomitantly and can make imaging interpretation challenging. High-quality CT- angiography scans together with knowledge of the anatomy and possible physiopathology changes are essential for the diagnosis of these complex vascular anomalies. AERODIG ESTIVE DISO RDERS Aerodigestive disorders are a group of diseases which arise as a result of the close link between the digestive and respira- tory tracts. Typically, animals with aerodigestive disease will present with symptoms of respiratory dysfunction (cough, recurring pneumonia) without typical gastrointestinal signs. However, with further exploration, gastrointestinal dysfunc- tion such as pharyngeal weakness, esophageal dysmotility, or re ﬂ ux emerges as the underlying pathology ultimately leading to laryngeal penetration-aspiration (P-A) and/or aspiration pneumonia. 4 71 As many as 81% of dogs with respiratory signs and with no evidence of gastrointestinal symptoms have been reported to have abnormalities on VFSS. 4 Therefore, VFSS is indicated in dogs with respiratory disease for which an underlying cause is nebulous. A grading scheme for laryngeal P-A of contrast material as visualized on VFSS has been developed so as to determine the prevalence and clinical signi ﬁ cance of this process. Pathologic P-A has been de ﬁ ned as a score 3 which indicates contrast medium entering or surpassing the supraepiglottic space during VFSS. Seiler T he thoracic wall is composed of rigid structures such as the spine, sternum ribs, and costal cartilages as well as the interconnecting soft tissue structures including the skin, subcutaneous fat, subcutaneous and intercostal muscula- ture, as well as the parietal pleura, blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics. The thoracic wall plays an important role in pro- tecting the thoracic soft tissue structures and is an integral part of pulmonary ventilation. Careful inspection of the thoracic wall structures is an important part of the interpretation of thoracic radiographs and other imaging modalities. Radio- graphs are typically indicated for initial evaluation of a thoracic wall lesion, and additional imaging methods are selected based on ﬁ ndings. Thoracic ultrasound is an excellent method to evaluate the layers of the thoracic wall, and investigate pe- ripheral thoracic masses to determine if they are pulmonary or extrapleural in origin. Ultrasound-guided ﬁ ne needle aspirates or biopsy of soft tissue or bone lesions may be obtained. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is often used to get a more global assessment of the thoracic cavity and thoracic wall, and for surgical or radiation therapy planning. THE NORM AL THORA CIC WA LL Dogs and cats both have 13 thoracic vertebrae and paired ribs, although transitional vertebrae are common anomalies. The appearance and orientation of the ribs are somewhat depen- dent on breed and thoracic conformation in dogs, whereas it is more consistent in cats. Typically, the ﬁ rst few ribs are posi- tioned vertically and perpendicular to the spine in the lateral and ventrodorsal (VD) projections, respectively. Towards the caudal thoracic spine, the ribs become progressively caudally oriented proximally with a more or less pronounced cranio- medial curvature of the costal cartilages. The orientation of the ribs depends on the phase of respiration and the depth of inspiration. At full inspiration the ribs are in a more perpen- dicular orientation to the spine, whereas they are more caudally oriented during expiration ( Fig. 31.1 ). In dogs, variations in thoracic wall conformation can be breed related. Costochon- dral conformation in chondrodystrophic breeds can lead to misdiagnosis of pneumothorax or pleural effusion as discussed in Chapter 34 ( Fig. 31.2 ). When interpreting thoracic radiographs, it is important to follow each rib from its costovertebral to its costochondral junction as rib lesions such as fractures or lysis can be subtle and are easily overlooked. In general, it is helpful to look for symmetry of the left and right ribs and intercostal spaces in the VD or dorsoventral (DV) projections, and look for abrupt changes in direction of the ribs in a lateral view as well as loss of parallel orientation of the contralateral ribs ( Fig. 31.3 ). The appearance of the costal cartilages depends on the age of the patient. In juvenile animals the cartilages are soft tissue opaque and poorly delineated from the rest of the thoracic structures. As animals progress in age, particularly dogs, costal cartilages often become mineralized and can exhibit exuberant, expansile areas of mineralization that can be confused with pathology such as lung nodules ( Fig. 31.4 ). The sternocostal junction is a synovial joint for the ﬁ rst eight to nine ribs and the remaining ribs are fused to each other and to the sternum to form the costal arch. The last one or two rib pairs are not fused to the costal arch. The sternum is composed of three parts, the ma- nubrium, body, and xiphoid. Degenerative changes of the sternum are common and are usually not clinically signi ﬁ cant ( Fig. 31.5 ). Fig. 31.2 Ventrodorsal (VD) thoracic radiograp h of a normal adult Bassetthound. The soft tissues of the thoracic wall should always be scru- tinized for soft tissue nodules such as nipples, skin nodules (papillomas, lipomas), engorged ticks, etc., that could mimic the appearance of a pulmonary nodule in orthogonal projection due to summation artifact. Application of radiopaque markers such as barium paste on an identi ﬁ ed thoracic wall nodule followed by repeat radiographs can be useful to localize a questionable opacity ( Fig. 31.6 ). As mentioned earlier for the evaluation of rib lesions, the soft tissues of the thoracic wall should be evaluated for symmetry, focal thickening, disrup- tions, and changes in opacity in all projections. Common arti- facts that need to be differentiated from pathology are overlying skin folds, and wet hair coat artifact. CONGE NITAL AND DEVELO PMENT AL ABNOR MALITIE S Transitional vertebrae may be present at the cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junction. The 13th vertebra is most commonly affected and can have unilateral or bilateral hypo- plastic or aplastic ribs, or anomalous transverse vertebrae ( Fig. 31.7 ). Anomalous rudimentary ribs are occasionally pre- sent on the seventh cervical vertebra. Fusion of the ﬁ rst ribs may also be observed ( Fig. 31.8 ). These ﬁ ndings are usually not clinically relevant; however, they should be documented to avoid mistakes in vertebral counts when surgical procedures are planned. Congenital sternal anomalies are characterized by reduction or increasing number of segments, or fusion of adjacent segments. THORA CIC WA LL TRAUMA Thoracic wall trauma caused by impact or bite wounds is not uncommon in small animals. 5 Soft tissue swelling is often the ﬁ rst sign of thoracic wall trauma; however, it may be dif ﬁ cult to identify in lateral radiographs. Slight obliquity in VD projections causing inherent asymmetry of the thoracic wall may also be a hindrance. Trauma with disruption of the skin surface results in subcutaneous emphysema with gas accumulation within the soft tissues of the thoracic wall ( Fig. 31.12 eFig. 31.1 ). Other causes for subcutaneous emphysema of the thoracic wall include trauma to the cervical soft tissues or large airways ( Fig. 31.13 ). Subcutaneous ﬂ uid administration will result in subcutaneous emphysema associated with a focal soft tissue thickening. Deeper trauma to the thoracic wall with disruption of the intercostal muscles manifests as separation of the ribs and asymmetry of the rib spaces ( Fig. 31.14 ). These changes are important to recognize as the mechanical function of ventila- tion may be impaired. If unilateral rib fractures are present, the resulting pain can cause the patient to take shallow breaths and minimize movement on this side and asymmetry of the left and right thoracic walls may be noticed. Acute rib fractures are recognized by their sharp margins, whereas rounding and remodeling of the fracture margins and smooth new bone formation are indicative of the healing process ( Fig. 31.15 eFigs. 31.2 and 31.3 ). Traumatic rib fractures have to be differentiated from pathologic fractures due to aggressive lesions. Aggressive rib lesions are discussed in more detail later. Ultrasound can be helpful in evaluating questionable rib fractures since soft tissue masses associated with aggressive lesions as well as irregular lysis can be easier to identify, and tissue sampling can be performed ( Fig. 31.16 ). Spontaneous rib fractures, without external trauma, may occur in cats with chronic respiratory disease. This is presumed to be due to mechanical failure (a form of pathologic fracture), perhaps combined with age-related osteopenia 7 ( Fig. 31.17 ). Typically, the midportion of the caudal ribs is affected. Flail chest is caused by segmental rib fractures of at least two adja- cent ribs at two different levels or ﬁ ve or more sequential single rib fractures which results in separation of a thoracic wall segment from the normal respiratory bellows. The resulting destabilized thoracic wall segment moves paradoxically to the normal thoracic wall with inlet displacement during inspiration and outward displacement during expiration 8 9 ( Fig. 31.18 ). Sternal trauma most commonly manifests as luxation rather than fracture and can be painful and associated with soft tissue swelling when acute ( Fig. 31.19 ). THORAC IC WALL MA SS LESIO NS The Extrapleural Sign The extrapleural sign relates to any mass arising outside the parietal pleural, for example in the ribs or soft tissues of the thoracic wall. All extrapleural masses are characterized by growth into rather than expansion within the thoracic cavity. As long as the parietal pleura is intact, the smooth surface of the mass is preserved, and there is often a draping appearance at the junction of the mass with the thoracic wall. Soft tissue masses such as soft tissue sarcomas and adenocar- cinomas are soft tissue opaque and often more irregular in outline, and may occur anywhere in the thoracic wall. Sec- ondary bone invasion or destruction is possible. CT imaging is needed to evaluate the full extent of these lesions and deter- mine the presence of bone lysis 11 ( Fig. 31.23 ). Thoracic wall infection and cellulitis of the thoracic wall are most commonly caused by penetrating trauma and migrating foreign bodies such as grass awns. Fistulography, using either radiography or CT imaging, may be helpful to determine the extent of a su- per ﬁ cial draining tract and the connection with intrathoracic structures 12 ( Fig. 31.24 ). Lesions of the Ribs and Sternum Mass lesions associated with the ribs or sternum can be benign or malignant in nature. The majority of primary rib tumors are osteosarcomas and chondrosarcomas with a smaller portion of other sarcomas ( ﬁ brosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma). 13 14 They usually arise near the costochondral junction, are aggressive in nature, and cause lysis and irregular periosteal reaction of the affected ribs. Amorphous mineralization of the associated soft tissue mass is common. The extent of the lesion is often underestimated radiographically and clinically, as most of the tumor mass is intrathoracic. CT gives a much more detailed assessment of the size and origin of a rib mass, effect on adja- cent structures, and presence of metastatic lesions ( Fig. 31.25 eFig. 31.4 ). The intrathoracic portion of a rib tumor may be misinterpreted as a pulmonary mass if the adjacent ribs are not examined for the presence of lysis or periosteal reactions ( Fig. 31.26 ) Primary rib tumors typically affect a single rib, although the adjacent ribs can be affected by the mass and have signs of periostitis, compression atrophy, or invasion ( eFigs. 31.5 and 31.6 ). Differential diagnoses for multiple aggressive rib lesions include metastatic neoplasia or marrow- associated tumors such as multiple myeloma ( Fig. 31.27 eFig. 31.7 ). Metastatic neoplasia is often more lytic or expansile than proliferative with variable degree of periosteal reaction ( eFig. 31.8 ).Cartilaginous exostoses or osteochondromas are benign bone perforations characterized by a cartilage cap and can be singular or multiple (multiple cartilaginous exostoses or osteo- chondromatosis) ( Fig. 31.28 ). Single osteochondromas most commonly occur in growing dogs and growth of the mass stops with skeletal maturation. Elissa K. Randall T he diaphragm is the musculotendinous partition be- tween the thoracic and abdominal cavities. Embryo- logically, the diaphragm is formed by the septum transversum ventrally and by the mesentery of the foregut and two pleuroperitoneal folds dorsally. Movement of the diaphragm provides approximately 75% of the change in intrathoracic volume during quiet respiration, with the intercostal muscles providing the remainder. 1 The diaphragm also acts as a mechanical partition between the thorax and the abdomen. Lymph vessels from the abdomen penetrate the diaphragm and drain into the thoracic lymph nodes and vessels. Thus, in ﬂ ammatory or neoplastic abdominal disease may spread to the mediastinum and pleural space. Lymph ﬂ ow from the abdomen is primarily cranially with the ﬁ nal destination being the thoracic trunks, but there are lymphatic vessels in the thorax that drain to the abdomen. 2 The diaphragm consists of a tendinous center and three thin peripheral muscles: (1) the pars lumbalis , (2) the pars costalis, and (3) the pars sternalis. The pars lumbal is consists of the right and left crura, which attach to the cranial ventral border of L4 and the body of L3. The attachment area on these vertebra e occa- sionally has a concave indistinct ventral margin that may be mistaken for bone lysis ( Fig. 32.1 ). The pars costalis attaches in an oblique direction to the 13th through 8th ribs, and the pars sternalis attaches to the xiphoid cartil age. 3 The diaphragm is convex and extends into the thorax from its attachm ents, creating the phrenicocos talis and phrenico lumbalis recesses . There are three openings through the diaphragm: (1) the dorsally located aortic hiatus encloses the aorta, azygos and hemiazygos veins, and the lumbar cistern of the thoracic duct; (2) the centrally located esophageal hiatus encloses the esophagus and vagus nerve trunks; and (3) the caudal vena cava foramen is located at the junction of the muscular and tendi- nous portions of the diaphragm. NORM AL RAD IOGRAPH IC ANAT OMY Radiographically, only a portion of the diaphragm can be seen on any one view. Radiographic visualization of the diaphragm depends on adjacent structures being of different opacity. Most of the thoracic diaphragmatic surface is visible because of the adjacent gas- ﬁ lled lungs. The phrenicocostalis and phrenico- lumbalis recesses are not in contact with the lungs and there- fore not outlined. A large portion of the abdominal diaphragmatic surface is not seen because it silhouettes the adjacent liver. The ventral abdominal diaphragmatic surface is visible on the lateral view when fat is present within the falci- form ligament. The dorsal aspect of the left diaphragmatic crus and the gastric wall appear as one linear structure when gas is present in the gastric cardia. Diaphragmatic structures that may be seen distinctly on a radiograph are the right and left crura and the cupula (body) ( Figs. 32.2 32.5 ). Associated structures that may also be seen are the caudal vena cava and the caudal ventral mediastinum. The radiographic appearance of the diaphragm in VD or DV projections varies with x-ray beam centering. The diaphragm may appear as two or three separate dome-shaped structures (see Fig. 32.4 ) or as a single dome-shaped structure (see Fig. 32.5 ). The three structures represent the cupula and two crura. A single domed diaphragm may be seen on a VD view when the x-ray beam is centered on the mid-abdomen or on a DV view when the x-ray beam is centered mid-thorax. Two or three separate domed structures are seen on a VD view with the x-ray beam is centered mid-thorax or on a DV view with the x-ray beam centered mid-abdomen. 4 Diaphragmatic position and shape vary with phase of respiration, and intra-abdominal pressure. The normal inter- section point of the diaphragm and spine is between T11 and T13 but may vary between T9 and L1. The diaphragm changes position with normal respiration from one-half to two vertebral lengths. On a lateral thoracic view made in extreme inspiration, the diaphragm is oriented more vertically; the shape changes from convex to straight ( Fig. 32.6 ). The diaphragm is displaced cranially by increased intra-abdominal pressure, which may be caused by obesity, ascites, gastric or intestinal distention, abdominal pain, or abdominal masses. Separate diaphragmatic structures are not seen as distinctly in the cat, probably because of the relatively small thoracic size ( Fig. 32.7 ). On extreme inspiration, particularly if the animal is in respiratory distress, of if there is a large volume of free pleural air as with a tension pneumothorax, small symmetric muscle projections are noted from the thoracic diaphragmatic surface in the VD or DV view ( Fig. 32.8 eFig. 32.1 ). This has been referred to as tenting of the diaphragm and is discussed in Chapter 36 in reference to pulmonary hyperin ﬂ ation. RADIOG RAPH IC SIGNS OF DIAPH RAGMA TIC DISE ASE The signs directly associated with the diaphragm are not as numerous and speci ﬁ c as those in many other organs. Radio- graphic changes observed most frequently with diaphragmatic disease include general or focal loss of the thoracic diaphrag- matic surface outline and changes in diaphragmatic shape and position ( Table 32.1 ). The thoracic diaphragmatic surface will not be visible radiographically if soft tissue or ﬂ uid contacts the surface. Normal variations in diaphragm shape occur most frequently on the cupula often caused by contact with the heart ( Fig. 32.9 ) or position of the animal during radiographic examination. The cupula may appear more convex and extending to a more cranial position in the thorax in some large-breed dogs. This may also be the result of a ﬂ accid tendinous membrane, or it may be associated with a peritoneopleural hernia, which often produces no clinical signs. Thoracic masses or lung disease silhouetting with the dia- phragm, hiatal and small traumatic diaphragmatic hernias, masses originating from the diaphragm, and chronic pleural in ﬂ ammatory reactions are the most frequent pathologic causes associated with diaphragmatic shape changes. An asymmetric diaphragmatic shape may occur with unilateral tension pneu- mothorax or hemiparalysis. Suspected hemiparalysis should be con ﬁ rmed by observing diaphragmatic movement during ﬂ uoroscopy. DIAPH RAGMAT IC DISEAS ES The most frequently observed diaphragmatic diseases in the dog and cat are hernias, which may be traumatic or congeni- tally predisposed. Motor or innervation disturbances occur less frequently. Tumors associated with the diaphragm are rare. Diaphragmatic Hernias A diaphragmatic hernia is a protrusion of abdominal viscera through the diaphragm into the thorax. Diaphragmatic hernias that may be recognized radiographically include traumatic, peritoneopericardial, hiatal, peritoneopleural, and those sec- ondary to congenital diaphragmatic defects. Trauma is the most common cause of diaphragmatic hernia, which may be more accurately called traumatic diaphragmatic hernia or diaphragmatic rupture. A high momentary increase in abdominal pressure when the glottis is open produces a high pleuroperitoneal pressure gradient that may result in a dia- phragmatic hernia. The high pleuroperitoneal gradient may produce a rent in the muscular portion of the diaphragm, or it may force abdominal viscera through congenitally weak or defective areas. Clinical signs that may be observed with dia- phragmatic hernias include dyspnea, pain, vomiting, regurgita- tion, muf ﬂ ed heart sounds, and a weak femoral pulse. 5 6 Some diaphragmatic hernias may not cause clinical signs and are detected incidentally. Herniated solid abdominal parenchymal organs are dif ﬁ cult to distinguish from localized pleural ﬂ uid, pulmonary opacity, or both. Omentum is the most dif ﬁ cult to detect unless it is herniated in association with other abdominal organs. In such instances, it helps outline abdominal visceral organs. In the absence of ﬁ nding abdominal organs in the thorax, cranial abdominal organ displacement or absence of abdominal organs from their normal location is an indirect sign of dia- phragmatic hernia. The liver, spleen, small bowel, and stomach must be assessed closely for displacement. Barium sulfate may also be administered to identify the stomach and help detect mild to moderate gastric displacement not observed on survey radiographs. Peritoneopericardial Diaphragmatic Hernias A PPDH occurs when abdominal viscera herniate into the pericardial sac through a congenital hiatus formed between the tendinous portion of the diaphragm and the pericardial sac. This has been reported to occur in littermates, 26 and a predis- posing trait may be carried on a simple autosomal recessive gene in cats, with a 1:500 to 1:1500 rate of incidence. 27 Do- mestic long-hair cats, Himalayans, and Maine Coon cats appear to be overrepresented, as do Weimaraner dogs. 28 29 The hernia may have been present from birth or is acquired. Mild increases in intra-abdominal pressure may cause abdominal organs to herniate through a congenital hiatus. Herniated abdominal organs in the pericardial sac are usually caudal, or caudal and lateral, to the heart. Gas- or ingesta- ﬁ lled hollow visceral organs are not dif ﬁ cult to identify within the pericardial sac, but the conspi- cuity of the gas-containing viscus may be a function of body position during radiography ( Fig. 32.16 eFig. 32.5 ). Radio- graphically, gas within the bowel is in abrupt contrast to the adjacent structures of soft tissue opacity. Solid parenchymal organs, unless surrounded by omentum, are dif ﬁ cult to distin- guish as separate structures within the pericardium. When abdominal organs are herniated into the pericardial sac, cranial and ventral organ displacement within the abdomen may be seen, but this displacement is usually not as pronounced as that noted with traumatic diaphragmatic hernias.A large, round cardiac silhouette and a cardiac silhouette with an abnormal convex projection on the caudal border are signs consistent with PPDHs. These two signs depend on the amount of abdominal viscera within the pericardial sac. Large amounts of viscera produce a large, round cardiac silhouette, whereas smaller amounts, such as a portion of the liver, falci- form fat, or stomach, may produce only an abnormal convex caudal cardiac border. A large, round silhouette must be differentiated from pericardial effusion, generalized heart enlargement, or both. An abnormally convex caudal cardiac border must be differentiated from neoplasia, pleural granu- lomas, or localized pleural ﬂ uid. An indistinguishable outline to the ventral diaphragmatic surface and the caudal ventral cardiac silhouette is produced by the communication between the two structures. This ﬁ nding must be differentiated from normal contact between the heart and diaphragm, pleural ﬂ uid, localized pleuritis, and pleural granulomas. On the lateral view, identi ﬁ cation of the dorsal peritoneopericardial mesothelial remnant between the heart and diaphragm is a consistent radiographic sign of peri- toneopericardial hernia in cats ( Fig. 32.17 eFig. 32.6 ). 37 Sternal abnormalities may also be present. 34 Additional radiographic studies that may be performed to con ﬁ rm a diagnosis include oral administration of barium sul- fate, nonselective angiography, 38 and peritoneography. Barium sulfate may be used to demonstrate gastrointestinal structures within the pericardial sac or cranial ventral displacement of abdominal structures ( Fig. 32.18 ). Ultrasonography has been successfully used to diagnose PPDHs. 16 19 Ultrasonography is a reliable imaging modality to use for documentation of a peritoneopericardial hernia in pa- tients where soft tissue opaque abdominal structures are in the pericardial sac and dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from the heart on radiographs. If available, an ultrasound examination should be considered before contrast examinations are performed to assist in the diagnosis of PPDH. CT can assist in determining which structures are herniated, and it can con ﬁ rm a PPDH in cases in which radiographs are not conclusive or when more information is desired prior to surgery. Hiatal Hernias Hiatal hernias occur when a portion of stomach enters the thorax through the esophageal hiatus and can be congenital or acquired. Two recognized types of hiatal hernias exist: sliding (or dynamic) and paraesophageal. 39 41 The gastroesophageal sphincter and a portion of the stomach, usually the cardia, are herniated into the thorax with sliding hiatal hernias. 42 Sliding hiatal hernias are usually congenital and found in younger ani- mals. 41 They are often associated with esophagitis from gastroesophageal re ﬂ ux. As the name implies, the caudal esophagus and the cardia slide intermittently from the abdomen into the thorax, causing temporary cranial displacement of the thoracic esophagus. Patients with nonsliding hiatal hernias have been reported, with the gastroesophageal sphincter and the gastric cardia displaced through the esoph- ageal hiatus and ﬁ xed within the thorax. 42 A paraesophageal hiatal hernia is produced when the cardia or cardia and fundus of the stomach or other soft tissue struc- tures herniate through, or alongside, the esophageal hiatus and become positioned adjacent to the esophagus. They are usually static and do not slide between the thorax and abdomen, and the gastroesophageal sphincter is in a normal position. 40 42 The herniated stomach may cause esophageal obstruction from external pressure on the caudal esophagus. Hiatal hernias have also been classi ﬁ ed as types I through IV. Type I represents a sliding hiatal hernia, type II represents a paraesophageal hernia, and type III represents a combination of type I and type II. Type IV has been described two ways: (1) as a type III hernia combined with herniation of another organ rather than the stomach or (2) as a gastroesophageal intussus- ception. Other complicated hernias, such as a hernia through the esophageal hiatus combined with a second, separate gastric herniation through a defect in the diaphragm have been reported. 41 Hiatal hernias occur in both the dog and the cat. 43 They can be associated with other esophageal conditions in shar-pei dogs. 43 There may be no clinical signs, or vomiting, regurgita- tion, excessive salivation, dysphagia, and dyspnea may be observed. 43 45 Hiatal hernias can be associated with esopha- geal dysmotility and are seen more frequently in brachycephalic dogs, especially French bulldogs. Decreased intrathoracic pressure associated with increased respiratory effort may be the cause of these hernias in brachycephalic dogs. 46 Hiatal hernia may be suspected from the clinical signs and survey radio- graphic ﬁ ndings but must be con ﬁ rmed by an esophagram. Radiographic signs of a sliding hiatal hernia are listed in Box 32.3 . The most consistent survey radiographic sign is stomach displacement. The cardia appears to be stretched to- ward the diaphragm or may extend into the thorax. This displacement produces an abnormal shape to the cardia and fundus remaining in the abdomen. The caudal esophagus may or may not be distended, and a soft tissue mass may be seen adjacent to the left diaphragmatic crus ( Fig. 32.19 eFig. 32.7 Video 32.1 ). The size and visibility of this mass depend on the amount of stomach that has herniated into the thorax. The soft tissue mass associated with a hiatal hernia must be differenti- ated from pulmonary or diaphragmatic masses. Diaphragmatic tumors occur but are rare. 47 A dilated caudal esophagus is usually best detected and evaluated with an esophagram. An esophagram is also helpful for differentiating the type of hiatal hernia. The caudal esoph- ageal sphincter and a portion of the cardia are cranial to the diaphragm with a sliding hiatal hernia. 48 The caudal esophageal sphincter can be identi ﬁ ed as a concentric, smooth, 1- to 2-cm narrowing in the caudal esophagus ( Fig. 32.20 ). Displacement and narrowing of the caudal esophagus by the cardia and fundus can be seen with paraesophageal hiatal hernias. Barium outlining the caudal esophagus can also be seen superimposed over the herniated paraesophageal soft tissue ( Fig. 32.21 eFig. 32.8 Video 32.2 ). These are also called true diaphragmatic hernias. 57 In human beings, diaphragmatic defects have a familial incidence with a multifactorial mode of inheritance. 58 Congenital defects in dogs have been reported in the muscular diaphragm, dorsolateral in position at the site of the pleuro- peritoneal canal, 55 and in the membranous diaphragm associ- ated with umbilical hernias. 5 52 Bochdalek hernias are common peritoneopleural hernias in children, but are rarely reported in veterinary medicine. These are hernias at the dorsolateral margins of the diaphragm through the lumbocostal trigone, due to a failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal in children. There is also a report of extension of a retroperitoneal lipoma through the lumbocostal trigone. 59 The radiographic signs of peritoneopleural hernias associ- ated with muscular diaphragmatic defects can be the same as for traumatic diaphragmatic hernias ( Fig. 32.23 eFig. 32.9 ), although pleural effusion typically only occurs with traumatic hernias. With membranous defects, however, the liver (in dogs) or the falciform fat (in cats) is displaced cranially, while remaining in the caudal ventral thorax, and is often con ﬁ ned to the mediastinum because the peritoneal membrane and pleura are intact ( Fig. 32.24 ). 60 Foraminal Hernias Herniations may occur through the aortic hiatus, esophageal hiatus, or caval foramen. These are rare in humans and veteri- nary patients. Caval foramen hernias can look like caudal pul- monary masses and may cause compression of the caudal vena cava. CT may be required for correct diagnosis. 20 21 Motor Disturbances of the Diaphragm The diaphragm is the principal muscle of respiration and is innervated by the phrenic nerve. Motor disturbances of the diaphragm consist of unilateral paralysis, bilateral paralysis, and diaphragmatic ﬂ utter. 1 Dia- phragmatic paralysis may result from pneumonia, trauma, my- opathies, and neuropathies, or the cause may be unidenti ﬁ ed. 1 Transient post-traumatic hemidiaphragmatic paralysis has been reported in cats. 61 Diaphragmatic paralysis should be suspected when one or both diaphragmatic crura are displaced cranially ( Fig. 32.25 ). Con ﬁ rmation of paralysis is best achieved with ﬂ uoroscopy. Unequal movement between the crura is seen with unilateral paralysis. With bilateral paralysis, minimal or no diaphragmatic movement or a paradoxic cranial displacement of the ﬂ accid diaphragm may occur during inspiration. 62 Bilat- eral paralysis may be more dif ﬁ cult to con ﬁ rm with ﬂ uoros- copy, because diaphragmatic movement is sometimes produced by compensatory abdominal muscle contraction during respiration. Diaphragmatic ﬂ utter is most often associated with con- tractions of the diaphragm synchronous with the heartbeat. It is usually transient in nature and can be easily diagnosed with ﬂ uoroscopy by observing contractions of the diaphragm in synchrony with the heartbeat. 63 Muscular Dystrophy Muscular dystrophy caused by dystrophin de ﬁ ciency occurs rarely in dogs 64 and cats. 65 66 In dogs with muscular dystrophy, radiographic abnormalities include diaphragmatic asymmetry, diaphragmatic undulation, and gastroesophageal hiatal hernia. 67 68 In cats an irregular, scalloped appearance of the diaphragm, particularly along the ventral margin, was a consistent ﬁ nding observed on radiographs after 7 months of age. 65 The scalloped margin, noted best on the lateral view, should not be confused with the normal scalloping observed on the VD view in cats on maximal inspiration (see Fig. 32.7 ). The scalloped appearance is caused by muscular hypertrophy, which can be con ﬁ rmed by ultrasound. 65 Muscular hypertro- phy produced with feline muscular dystrophy has also been reported to cause megaesophagus from extraluminal hiatal obstruction. De ﬁ nitive laboratory tests, such as immuno ﬂ uo- rescence or immunoblot tests, are necessary to establish the diagnosis of muscular dystrophy. Federica Morandi  Donald E. Thrall NORM AL ANA TOMY There is one pleural sac on each side of the thoracic cavity, and the mediastinum is the space between them ( Table 33.1 ). The pleural layer bounding the mediastinum on each side is termed mediastinal pleura. Other components of the pleural sac are the costal parietal pleura , which is attached to the thoracic wall; the diaphragmatic parietal pleura , which is attached to the diaphragm; and the visceral pleura , which covers the lung. All of these pleural layers are contiguous. The connection be- tween the mediastinal and visceral pleural layers occurs at the hilus of the lung, where the mediastinal pleura is re ﬂ ected onto the surface of the lung as visceral pleura ( Figs. 33.1 and 33.2 ). The mediastinum extends from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm and is located mainly in the midsagittal plane, thereby dividing the thoracic cavity into right and left halves (see Figs. 33.1 and 33.2 ). The mediastinum is arbitrarily sub- divided into a cranial portion, cranial to the heart; a middle portion at the level of, and containing the heart; and a caudal portion, caudal to the heart. The mediastinum is also divided into dorsal and ventral portions by a dorsal plane coursing through the tracheal bifurcation. The mediastinum is not a closed space. It communicates cranially with the fascial planes of the neck by way of the mediastinal structures passing through the thoracic inlet, such as the esophagus and trachea and some major vessels. Caudally, the mediastinum communi- cates with the retroperitoneal space through the aortic hiatus. These communications enable the spread of mediastinal disease to the neck and retroperitoneal space, and vice versa. The mediastinum does not normally communicate with the perito- neal cavity. In mos t dog s and cats , the med ia stina l ple ura l lay ers do not for m an anat omi c barr ier bet ween the left an d righ t ple ura l spa ces, bec aus e norm al med iast ina l pleu ra cont ain fen estr ati ons. Thus , unil ater al ple ura l ﬂ uid or gas is not usu ally co ntai ned to one side by the med iast inu m. Of all of the structures in the mediastinum (see Table 33.1 ), only the heart, trachea, caudal vena cava, aorta, and, in young animals, the thymus are visible normally. Occasionally, a portion of the normal esophagus may be seen (see Chapter 30 ). The other mediastinal structures are not seen normally, because they are either too small or there is insuf ﬁ cient interposed fat to provide contrast, leading to border effacement. The cranial mediastinum immediately ventral to the trachea normally is of homogeneous soft tissue opacity in a lateral radiograph. The structures in this portion of the mediastinum (left subclavian artery, brachiocephalic trunk, cranial vena cava mediastinal lymph nodes) are not visible individually because they are in contact with each other and there is insuf ﬁ cient interposed fat to provide contrast ( Fig. 33.3 ). In lateral radio- graphs, the mediastinum just ventral to the trachea is thicker and thus more radiopaque than the mediastinum just dorsal to the sternum ( Fig. 33.4 ). In ventrodorsal (VD) or dorsoventral (DV) thoracic radio- graphs, most of the cranial mediastinum is superimposed on the spine in the midsagittal plane ( Fig. 33.5 ). In obese patients, particularly brachycephalic patients, the cranial mediastinum is increased in width because of fat accumulation, and this can be misdiagnosed as a pathologic mass ( Fig. 33.6 ). Contrary to a mediastinal mass, the borders of the mediastinum tend to remain straight with mediastinal fat only, whereas they tend to be laterally convex in the presence of a mediastinal mass. Other imaging modalities, such as ultrasound or computed tomogra- phy (CT), may be necessary to con ﬁ rm that fat deposition is the cause of increased mediastinal width in obese patients. The mediastinum normally deviates from the midline in three locations: (1) the cranioventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection, (2) the caudoventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection, and (3) the vena caval mediastinal re ﬂ ection ( plica venae cavae ). The ﬁ rst two are visible in thoracic radiographs of many dogs and cats, although not universally. The plica venae cavae is not seen radiographi- cally in normal dogs or cats. The cranioventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection appears in VD or DV radiographs as a curving radiopaque line, just to the left of midline, extending from approximately T1 or T2 to the region of the main pulmonary artery. The concave side of the line is to the right (see Figs. 33.4 and 33.5 ). The cranioventral medias- tinal re ﬂ ection is caused by extension of the apex of the right cranial lobe across midline, pushing the mediastinum to the left (see Fig. 33.4 ). The thickness of the cranioventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection is affected by the amount of fat it contains (see Fig. 33.6 ). On the lateral view, the cranioventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection is often identi ﬁ ed approximately midway between the thoracic inlet and the heart (see Fig. 33.3 ). The thymus lies in the cranioventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection and can sometimes be identi ﬁ ed in VD or DV radiographs of young animals as a triangular soft tissue opacity ( Fig. 33.7 ). The normal thymus is in close contact with the cranial contour of the cardiac silhouette and may lead to a false impression of cardiomegaly when visible in a lateral projection. The internal thoracic ar- teries and veins are also located in the cranioventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection and are not visible radiographically. Dis- tinguishing normal atelectatic from diseased atelectatic lung is usually not possible radiographically. A contralateral medias- tinal shift occurs as a result of a unilateral increase in lung volume, the presence of an intrathoracic mass, or unilateral increased pleural pressure. A mediastinal shift is detected in VD or DV radiographs by noting a change in the position of visible mediastinal organs or the position of mediastinal re ﬂ ections. Displacement of the heart to the left or right is the most reliable sign of a mediastinal shift ( Fig. 33.10 ). Suboptimal patient positioning due to rotation causes deviation of the sternum to the right or left and the false impression of a mediastinal shift. Detection of a mediastinal shift is often the ﬁ rst clue of a thoracic abnormality ( Fig. 33.11 ). Mediastinal origin of a thoracic mass should be considered if the mass lies on, or adjacent to, the midline; if the mass location is consistent with the cranioventral or caudoventral mediastinal re ﬂ ections; or if the mass causes deviation of another medias- tinal structure. Mediastinal masses are rarely completely outlined by gas, as a lung mass would be, because a mediastinal mass is in contact with other soft tissue structures within the mediastinum. Dorsal Mediastinal Masses Dorsal mediastinal masses, whether in the cranial, middle, or caudal aspect of the mediastinum, cause widening of the mediastinum in the VD or DV view ( Figs. 33.18 and 33.19 ). The caudal mediastinum can be evaluated more thoroughly in a VD view, compared with a DV view, because cranial excursion of the diaphragm in the DV view leads to compression of the caudal mediastinum. 9 10 The most common cause of a dorsal mediastinal mass is enlargement of the esophagus, which can be generalized or segmental. Enlargement of the cranial aspect of the thoracic esophagus, such as from a vascular ring anomaly, typically causes a craniodorsal mediastinal mass with ventral displace- ment of the trachea in the lateral view, and widening of the cranial mediastinum in the VD or DV view. The presence of esophageal gas (see Fig. 33.18 ), or a heterogeneous opacity created by esophageal contents, differentiates esophageal enlargement from other dorsal mediastinal masses. If a dorsal mediastinal mass is homogeneous, it is usually impossible to determine the origin of the mass from survey radiographs alone ( Fig. 33.20 ). The presence of regurgitation is not necessarily helpful in establishing the origin of a dorsal mediastinal mass as esoph- agus, because any mass in this location can compress the esophagus and lead to regurgitation. Radiographic signs of esophageal enlargement are discussed more completely in Chapter 30 . If the esophagus is suspected as the origin of a dorsal mediastinal mass, an esophagram can be helpful for positive identi ﬁ cation. Craniodorsal Mediastinal Masses Craniodorsal mediastinal masses are rare (see Table 33.1 ). A craniodorsal mediastinal mass typically causes ventral and rightward displacement of the trachea (see Fig. 33.19 ). Hilar-Region Mediastinal Masses The main causes of a mediastinal mass in the hilar region are enlargement of the tracheobronchial lymph nodes or a mass arising from the base of the heart (see Table 33.2 ). The tracheobronchial lymphocenter is subdivided into the right, left, and middle tracheobronchial lymph nodes. The right and left lymph nodes lie on the lateral side of their respective bronchus and are also in contact with the trachea. The right lymph node is ventral to the azygos vein, and the left lymph node is ventral to the aorta. The middle tracheobronchial lymph node is the largest of the group, and it has the form of a V with the point lying in the angle formed by the tracheal bifurcation. Afferent lymphatics to the tracheobronchial lymph nodes come primarily from the lungs and bronchi, but they also come from the thoracic parts of the aorta, esophagus, trachea, heart, mediastinum, and diaphragm. 3 Enlargement of the tracheobronchial lymph nodes classi- cally results in a soft tissue mass located dorsocaudal to the tracheal bifurcation on the lateral view, which usually causes cranioventral displacement of a principal bronchus or tracheal bifurcation. If the enlarged lymph nodes reside primarily ventral to the tracheal bifurcation, dorsal displacement of the bifurcation will result instead, which can be confused with left atrial dilation; however, this is very uncommon. Both tracheo- bronchial lymph node enlargement and left atrial dilation can cause lateral divergence or splaying of the principal bronchi on the VD or DV view ( Fig. 33.21 ); therefore, a lateral view is required to differentiate lymphadenopathy from left atrial enlargement. The extent of the hilar mass effect and degree of splaying of the principal bronchi depend on the magnitude of enlargement of the tracheobronchial lymph nodes, or the extent of left atrial dilation. With progressive enlargement of the tracheobronchial lymph nodes, the mass effect becomes more pronounced and splaying of principal bronchi becomes evident in the VD or DV view ( Fig. 33.23 eFig. 33.5 ).Masses arising from the base of the heart tend to be rela- tively inconspicuous since much of the mass is surrounded by other soft tissue structures, resulting in border effacement. These lesions usually create an ill-de ﬁ ned mass effect, rather than a distinct mass, and may become very large before being detectable on survey radiographs. Heart base region masses typically cause rightward displacement of the trachea just cra- nial to the bifurcation, which may be the most conspicuous ﬁ nding ( Fig. 33.24 eFig. 33.6 ). As the heart base mass enlarges, the tracheal displacement becomes more pronounced, but the mass itself is still not likely to be seen ( Fig. 33.25 ). A heart base mass may represent a heart base tumor, a right atrial tumor, a tumor arising from ectopic thyroid tissue, or an enlarged main pulmonary artery. Caudoventral Mediastinal Masses Caudoventral mediastinal masses are uncommon, and most are associated with the diaphragm, such as a diaphragmatic even- tration, or a hernia (see Table 33.1 ; Fig. 33.26 ). Caval foramen hernia may also cause a caudoventral mediastinal mass effect. Caudoventral mediastinal masses may cause border effacement of the diaphragm and/or cardiac displacement. In VD or DV views, caudoventral mediastinal masses are often located to the left of midline because of the normal left-sided location of the caudoventral mediastinal re ﬂ ection (see Fig. 33.26 ). As the accessory lung lobe is located on midline, a mass arising from the accessory lobe can appear identical to a caudoventral mediastinal mass 11 ( Fig. 33.27 ). Large accessory lobe masses will cause border effacement of the caudal vena cava, because the accessory lobe surrounds this structure (see Fig. 33.27 ). However, border effacement of the caudal vena cava can occur with any large caudoventral mediastinal mass; therefore, this sign cannot be used to differentiate accessory lobe masses from caudoventral mediastinal masses. Visibility of the caudal vena cava may be preserved with small caudoventral mediastinal masses, even if of accessory lobe origin (see Fig. 33.26 ). CT is usually needed to differentiate caudoventral mediastinal masses from accessory lobe masses. Caudodorsal Mediastinal Masses The mediastinal serous cavity is a normal, mesothelium-lined anatomic space in the caudodorsal mediastinum. It is located to the right of the esophagus and extends from the diaphragm to the heart base. Purulent material can accumulate in this cavity forming paraesophageal empyema, possibly due to foreign material migration or extension of infectious disease from the adjacent accessory lung lobe ( Fig. 33.28 ). 12 Medias- tinal serous cavity mesothelioma has also been reported in dogs. 13 Esophageal foreign bodies can have the appearance of a caudodorsal mediastinal mass but are typically associated with a degree of esophageal gas dilation cranial to the foreign material (see Fig. 33.20 ). Some Facts About Mediastinal Lymph Nodes The drainage patterns of mediastinal lymph nodes were de ﬁ ned in the section dealing with mediastinal masses. Mediastinal lymph node enlargement can be associated with a variety of diseases, but the most common causes are primary lymphoid neoplasia and mycotic infection. Spread of peritoneal disease to the sternal lymph node was discussed earlier. In the cat, lymphoma is a common cause of enlargement of the cranial mediastinal lymph nodes. The thymus may also be affected. In the dog, lymphoma results in enlargement of the sternal lymph nodes in slightly over half of affected patients, but enlargement of cranial mediastinal or tracheobronchial lymph nodes is uncommon. 14 Other reticuloendothelial malignancies, such as pulmonary lymphomatoid granulomatosis 15 16 and disseminated histiocytic sarcoma, 17 are also characterized by a high frequency of lymph node enlargement, particularly the tracheobronchial lymph nodes. In pulmonary lymphomatoid granulomatosis and disseminated histiocytic sarcoma, there is usually accompanying pulmonary parenchymal disease, and isolated mediastinal lymph node enlargement is unusual. Pul- monary mycoses, especially blastomycosis and coccidioidomy- cosis, are associated with a high prevalence of mediastinal lymph node enlargement. Interestingly, there are a variety of diseases that one might expect to result in mediastinal lymph node enlargement but rarely do, at least to the extent that the enlarged lymph nodes are visible radiographically ( Box 33.1 ). Distinguishing a Mediastinal Mass From a Lung Mass Radiographic differentiation of a lung mass from a mediastinal mass is not always possible. Many lung masses can be distin- guished from mediastinal masses, because the lung mass is lateral to the mediastinum, surrounded by air- ﬁ lled lung, and is therefore more sharply marginated ( Fig. 33.29 ). Some medias- tinal masses, however, may protrude laterally ( Fig. 33.30 ), or be in a thin portion of the mediastinum ( Fig. 33.31 ) and be sur- rounded by air making them sharply margined and easily mistaken for a lung mass. In addition, lung masses located in the more medial part of the lung can contact the margin of the mediastinum, particularly in the cranioventral thorax, and not be completely surrounded by gas. For these reasons, de ﬁ nitive localization of many intrathoracic masses is not always possible based on radiographs alone. If thoracotomy is being consid- ered, and the location of the mass is not obvious from radio- graphs, a presurgical CT scan can assist in determining the origin, location, and extent of the mass and can guide the sur- gical approach (e.g., intercostal vs. median thoracotomy). Confounding Effects of Pleural and Mediastinal Fluid As previously noted, cranial mediastinal masses often cause elevation of the trachea. Elevation of the trachea may also result from a large amount of pleural ﬂ uid that results in lung displacement from buoyancy ( Fig. 33.32 ). 18 A small volume of pleural ﬂ uid does not result in tracheal elevation unless a mediastinal mass is also present. If pleural ﬂ uid is present, de ﬁ nitive radiographic identi ﬁ cation of a concurrent medias- tinal mass is usually not possible. However, if the mass is large enough to compress the trachea and/or displace the tracheal bifurcation caudally, the presence of a mass can be inferred. Mediastinal ﬂ uid can be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from pleural effusion that has accumulated in the cranial thorax along the mediastinum. Mediastinal effusion is most commonly caused by hemorrhage, either secondary to trauma with rupture of thymic vessels in young dogs, or secondary to coagulopathies such as rodenticide toxicity. If pleural ﬂ uid obscures the mediastinum, and a mediastinal mass is suspected, various interventions can be used. The easiest and often the most successful is to remove the pleural ﬂ uid and repeat the radiographs. Positioning the patient upright and using a horizontally directed x-ray beam to take advantage of gravity, which causes pleural ﬂ uid to move away from the area of the suspected mediastinal mass, is often not successful or informative. If available, ultrasound or CT can be used to evaluate for a mass in the mediastinum. 19 20 Pleural ﬂ uid pro- vides an excellent acoustic window for sonographic examina- tion, and ultrasound-guided aspiration or biopsy aid in achieving a de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Pneumomediastinum Pneumomediastinum denotes free gas in the mediastinum. The radiographic ﬁ ndings of pneumomediastinum depend on the volume of gas present. Regardless of the amount of gas present, pneumomediastinum is rarely visible in VD or DV views because the overall size of the mediastinum is not increased, and the mediastinal gas is superimposed on the midline and obscured by other structures. Lateral views are typically the most useful for detecting pneumomediastinum. Pneumomediastinum can result from a variety of causes. It is common for air to escape into the pulmonary interstitium from sites of intrapulmonary alveolar rupture that do not involve the visceral pleural surface of the lung. These intrapulmonary rup- tures can be microscopic, with air leaking into the mediastinum and tracking in a retrograde direction in the loose connective tissue adjacent to bronchi and vessels into the medias- tinum. 21 22 This phenomenon, called the Macklin effect , is a relatively frequent occurrence following blunt thoracic trauma, 23 24 such as a motor vehicle accident, and also after iatrogenic pulmonary hyperin ﬂ ation during anesthesia or resuscitation. 25 Pneumothorax is not present when pneumo- mediastinum results from the Macklin effect, unless the visceral pleura becomes torn, or the mediastinal air accumulation ex- tends to the pleural space. Another common cause of pneumomediastinum is dissec- tion of gas from the fascial planes of the neck into the medi- astinum. Gas in the neck commonly results from neck trauma, such as a bite wound. Intrafascial cervical gas can also result from a tracheal perforation. In cats, the trachea can easily be perforated inadvertently during jugular venipuncture, and this can lead to air leaks and pneumomediastinum, as gas tracks down the neck. If a tracheal tear is intrathoracic, air enters the mediastinum directly. Tracheal rupture in anesthetized cats associated with overdistention of the endotracheal tube cuff is a noteworthy cause of pneumomediastinum. 26 27 Cuff over- distention may cause rupture of the trachealis muscle at the point of attachment to the tracheal cartilages. Tracheal rupture may occur at a modest cuff volume and may not be immediately apparent to the anesthetist. Development of subcutaneous emphysema occurs quickly following tracheal rupture from cuff over distention, and the amount of subcutaneous gas is usually pronounced. If subcutaneous emphysema develops during a surgical procedure, the anesthetist must be aware of this potentially fatal complication. Other less common causes of pneumomediastinum are esophageal perforation as a result of trauma, foreign body, neoplasia, in ﬂ ammation, or malposition of a feeding tube 28 ; extension of retroperitoneal gas into the mediastinum; and presence of gas-producing organism in the mediastinum. Gabriela S. Seiler PLEURA L ANATOM Y AND PHY SIOLOGY The pleural space is the space between two pleural layers, the visceral and parietal pleura. The visceral pleura covers the lung, whereas the parietal pleura covers the mediastinum, dia- phragm, and thoracic wall. There are two distinct pleural sacs dividing the left and right thorax; however, mediastinal fenes- trations allow ﬂ uid and air to travel between the pleural sacs in the majority of dogs and cats ( Fig. 34.1 ) The pleural space normally contains a few milliliters of ﬂ uid which facilitates gliding of the lung surface against the thoracic wall during respiration and maintains negative pressure in the pleural space, which is thought to prevent or reduce atelectasis in normal animals. Pleural ﬂ uid is produced by the mesothelial cells of the pleural layer and is reabsorbed by the pleura and associated lymphatics. NORM AL RAD IOGRAPH IC APPEARA NCE OF PLEURA AND PL EURAL THICK ENING Normal pleura is usually not visible radiographically. Pleura is very thin and also silhouettes with adjacent soft tissue every- where except in interlobar ﬁ ssures, where two layers of visceral pleura are in contact only with lung. Thin pleural lines between lobes are sometimes visible radiographically, particu- larly in the caudoventral thorax. These thin pleural lines may be because of the x-ray beam striking normal interlobar pleura exactly head-on, resulting in absorption of a suf ﬁ cient number of x-rays for the pleura to be seen, or because of slightly thickened pleura or a trace pleural effusion ( Fig. 34.2 ). When pleural thickening is more advanced, wider pleural ﬁ ssure lines between lung lobes may be seen ( Fig. 34.3 ). PLEURA L FLUID Causes of Pleural Fluid Normal homeostasis of pleural ﬂ uid is maintained by the dif- ference of hydrostatic pressures between the systemic and pulmonary circulations and by drainage through the lymphatic vessels. Pleural effusion is therefore the result of either high production and/or increased vascular permeability, decreased reabsorption, decreased lymphatic drainage, or a combination of thereof. Fluid in the pleural space can be an exudate, tran- sudate, or modi ﬁ ed transudate, chyle, or hemorrhage and can result from many causes ( Table 34.1 ). The radiographic changes associated with pleural ﬂ uid depend on the volume of ﬂ uid, the position of the animal in relation to the x-ray beam, the distribution of the ﬂ uid, and whether the ﬂ uid is free or trapped, so-called loculated ﬂ uid. There are no radiographic criteria that allow differentiation of an exudate from a transu- date, although an exudate may be more asymmetrically distributed. Measurement of Houns ﬁ eld units in computed to- mography (CT) has a limited ability to predict the characteris- tics of pleural ﬂ uid in dogs. 2 It is often not possible to determine the cause of pleural effusion radiographically, particularly since even large intrathoracic lesions can be obscured, but radio- graphs should always be evaluated for the presence of addi- tional ﬁ ndings that may help in determining the most likely cause as outlined in Table 34.1 . Making additional radiographs after removal of the ﬂ uid may provide important information. Any amount of pleural ﬂ uid is clinically signi ﬁ cant, and attempts should be made to reach a de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Thoracocentesis with appropriate ﬂ uid analysis should be considered if pleural ﬂ uid is identi ﬁ ed. Ultrasound can be used to determine the presence of pleural effusion if radiographs are equivocal and to guide needle placement for diagnostic or therapeutic thor- acocentesis. This is especially helpful in patients with chronic effusion that may be loculated with ﬁ brin strands that tend to adhere to the needle. Ultrasound may also be able to identify mass lesions or cardiac changes which are obscured by the pleural effusion radiographically. The improved contrast reso- lution of CT imaging and lack of superimposition allow detec- tion of concurrent or causative lesions including mass lesions, lung lobe torsions, and traumatic lesions. Radiographic Appearance of Pleural Fluid Regardless of the cause, if the negative pressure in the pleural space is not maintained, elastic recoil leads to retraction of the lung lobe margins and separation of the lobar margins from each other, which is the main radiographic ﬁ nding associated with pleural space disease. 3 Pleural ﬂ uid distributes itself ac- cording to gravity and the ability of the lung to expand d that is, lung compliance. 4 It is important to realize that the radio- graphic appearance of pleural ﬂ uid in ventrodorsal (VD) versus dorsoventral (DV) radiographs is different. In DV radiographs, with the dog in sternal recumbency, ﬂ uid gravitates ventrally and causes border effacement of the heart. In VD radiographs, with the dog in dorsal recumbency, pleural ﬂ uid does not obscure the heart because the ﬂ uid gravitates to the dorsal aspect of the thorax, where it does not make contact with the heart and does not cause border effacement ( Fig. 34.4 ). Also, the overall opacity of the thorax will be greater in DV radio- graphs in patients with pleural ﬂ uid because the ﬂ uid depth is greater (see Fig. 34.4 ). Retraction of Lung Margins With moderate or pronounced pleural ﬂ uid, the number and width of interlobar ﬁ ssures increase, and ﬂ uid also collects be- tween the thoracic wall and the lung, resulting in lung retrac- tion ( Figs. 34.6 and 34.7 ). Pleural ﬂ uid may cause blunting of the costophrenic angle in VD radiographs if ﬂ uid is present between the dorsocaudal aspect of the lung and diaphragm. Rounding of the costo- phrenic angles will seldom be the only radiographic sign of pleural ﬂ uid. Retrosternal Soft Tissue Opacity and Silhouette Sign In lateral radiographs, pleural ﬂ uid can also result in a region of homogeneously increased opacity dorsal to the sternum ( Fig. 34.9 ; also see Figs. 34.6C and 34.7B ). This opacity results from ﬂ uid having collected in the ventral aspect of the thorax and layered against the mediastinum in the nondependent hemithorax. The margin of this retrosternal opacity often ap- pears scalloped because of adjacent, partially collapsed lung that alters the con ﬁ guration of the ﬂ uid. It is important to differentiate retrosternal pleural ﬂ uid from mediastinal fat. In presence of pleural ﬂ uid, the borders of the cardiac silhouette and diaphragm are effaced, whereas mediastinal fat will create contrast with the diaphragmatic and cardiac margins. Asymmetric Distribution of Pleural Fluid Pleural ﬂ uid is usually relatively equally distributed between the right and left pleural spaces. Some patients, however, have asymmetric ﬂ uid distribution. Causes of unilateral or asym- metric pleural ﬂ uid include a difference in compliance between lung lobes, the closing of mediastinal fenestrations from in ﬂ ammation or a mass, and an anatomically complete medi- astinum ( eFig. 34.3 ). Pyothorax is a common cause of unilateral or asymmetric pleural ﬂ uid because of the viscous nature of the exudate ( Fig. 34.10 ), but other types of ﬂ uid can also be asymmetric. Chronic pleural effusions, particularly with exudative, hemorrhagic, or chylous effusions, result in pleural thickening and entrapment of ﬂ uid in ﬁ brous capsules. Pleuritis causes the lung lobe margins to be markedly rounded or scal- loped (see Fig. 34.10B ). Lung reexpansion can be reduced in presence of pleuritis, and this can result in lung rupture and pneumothorax if the pleural ﬂ uid is rapidly removed during thoracocentesis ( eFig. 34.4 ). Parenchymal disease or bronchial obstruction of a single lung lobe can also result in focal unilat- eral accumulation of pleural ﬂ uid due to decreased ﬂ uid ab- sorption and decreased pleural pressure. If free pleural ﬂ uid is present, it gravitates dependently where the x-ray beam strikes it in a parallel fashion ( Fig. 34.11 ). Pitfalls in Pleural Fluid Diagnosis Various normal structures can be misinterpreted as pleural ﬂ uid. Thickened pleura may have an appearance identical to pleural ﬂ uid (see Fig. 34.3 ). A distinction may be made by using a horizontally directed x-ray beam or with sonography. 4 A mineralized costal cartilage is sometimes confused with an interlobar ﬁ ssure. The position of these two structures is similar, but their shape is different. Pleural ﬁ ssure lines are distinctly curving, with the concave surface on the caudal aspect of the ﬁ ssure line. Costal cartilages are more linear and can usually be seen to attach to the end of a rib ( Fig. 34.12 ). Thoracic wall deformities, as found in chondrodystrophic breeds, such as the Basset hound, may result in increased radiopacity at the margin of the lung ﬁ eld. Without knowledge of this fact, the opacity may be misinterpreted as retraction of the lung from the thoracic wall because of pleural ﬂ uid ( Fig. 34.13 ). Accumulation of pleural ﬂ uid along the cranial mediastinum can mimic presence of the mediastinal mass. Evaluation of tracheal shape and position of the carina is helpful for differentiating mediastinal masses from pleural effusion. Simultaneous Pleural and Peritoneal Fluid The detection of simultaneous pleural and peritoneal ﬂ uid is an important ﬁ nding. Of 48 dogs with simultaneous peritoneal and pleural ﬂ uid, 32 had either neoplastic or cardiovascular disease. Simultaneous pleural and peritoneal ﬂ uid is an indicator of se- vere disease with poor prognosis. 5 PNEU MOTHOR AX Causes of Pneumothorax Air or gas in the pleural space is termed pneumothorax . Air can enter the pleural space through a thoracic wall defect or from the lung or mediastinum ( Box 34.2 ). Radiographs should be evaluated for the presence of thoracic wall or mediastinal trauma, and for the presence of cavitary lung lesions. CT im- aging is more sensitive for detecting cavitary lesions, and pos- itive pressure ventilation during CT can improve detection of pulmonary bullae. 5 6 In most animals, pneumothorax is bilat- eral, and this relates either to a bilateral source of pleural air or to movement of air through the mediastinum. When unilateral pneumothorax was induced in 24 dogs, bilateral pneumothorax was observed immediately after air instillation in 22 dogs, indicating rapid movement of air through fenestrations in the mediastinum. 7 Unilateral pneumothorax, however, can occur for the same reasons as for unilateral pleural ﬂ uid. Radiographic Appearance of Pneumothorax The character of the radiographic changes resulting from air in the pleural space depends on the volume of air and the relative position of the patient and the x-ray beam. In general, lateral views are more sensitive for detection of pneumothorax than VD or DV views. 8 Roentgen signs of pneumothorax are listed in Box 34.3 Fig. 34.13 Ventrodors al (VD) view of the left caudolateral aspect of thethorax of a normal Basset hound. Lung Retraction From Pneumothorax With a small volume of pleural air, separation of the lung from the thoracic wall is small and appears as a thin radiolucent line ( Fig. 34.14 ). As in pleural ﬂ uid, air surrounds the lung but is most apparent radiographically when the air/lung interface is struck in a parallel fashion by the x-ray beam. The lack of pul- monary vascular markings within the pleural gas allows differ- entiation from normal air- ﬁ lled pulmonary parenchyma in many but not all cases. Air-containing interlobar ﬁ ssures are almost never seen with pneumothorax, because air does not dissect between lung lobes as ﬂ uid usually does. A mild pneumothorax may also result in air collection against the cardiac apex. This occurs when the air is trapped against the mediastinum, most often in the dependent hemithorax ( Fig. 34.15 ). With increasing amounts of pleural air, these changes become more pronounced in lateral views, but the changes in the VD or DV view may remain inconspicuous or minimal ( Fig. 34.16 eFigs. 34.5 and 34.6 ). With pronounced pneumothorax, lung collapse is visible in VD or DV radiographs as well, usually best seen in the caudal thorax ( Fig. 34.17 ). The secondary lung collapse leads to the lung becoming more opaque than normal. The degree of increased lung opacity is directly related to the degree of collapse. This increased opacity resulting from atel- ectasis can interfere with radiographic evaluation of the lung parenchyma. If the pneumothorax is open (i.e., with no valve at the site of air entrance), air may continue to enter the pleural space until pleural pressure equals atmospheric pressure. Tension Pneumothorax Tension pneumothorax occurs when pleural space pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure during both phases of respira- tion. Tension pneumothorax results from a check-valve mechanism at the origin of pleural space air. Air enters the thorax with each breath but cannot escape. In tension pneu- mothorax, increased pleural pressure causes the lung to collapse to a greater degree than even its maximal collapse in an open pneumothorax. Thus, it may no longer maintain the shape of a lung but may assume the appearance of an amor- phous opacity compressed against the midline ( Fig. 34.20 ). With unilateral tension pneumothorax, the increased pleural space pressure will cause a contralateral mediastinal shift ( Fig. 34.21 eFig. 34.7 ).
