In conventional pneumothorax, the cardiac silhouette is usually shifted toward the side of the tho- rax containing the most air, but in a tension pneumothorax, it is shifted to the opposite side because of the increased pleural space pressure. Tension pneumothorax is uncommon, but it is important to recognize because it is potentially fatal and re- quires immediate thoracocentesis. Horizontal-Beam Radiography As with a small amount of pleural ﬂ uid, a small amount of pleural air may not be apparent radiographically. The likelihood of diagnosing pneumothorax is increased by using a horizon- tally directed x-ray beam and placing the patient in lateral re- cumbency and directing the x-ray beam onto the sternum. By so doing, air will collect beneath the nondependent thoracic wall where the x-ray beam strikes it in a parallel fashion. Justi ﬁ cation for using horizontal-beam radiography should be based on the suspected underlying cause. For example, pneumothorax resulting from lung disease is a potentially serious event, whereas a small pneumothorax occurring after trauma with no associated clinical signs may not be signi ﬁ cant. Pitfalls in Pneumothorax Diagnosis The causes of elevation of the cardiac silhouette from the sternum in lateral views other than pneumothorax have already been discussed (see Fig. 34.19 ). In VD views, skin folds can result in a radiolucent area that is superimposed over the lateral aspect of the thorax. In many patients, it may not be possible to identify lung markings in the radiolucent area. In these in- stances, a correct diagnosis of skin-fold artifact can be made by noting that the opacity of the fold extends beyond the limits of the thorax ( Fig. 34.23 ). Elodie Huguet  Clifford Berry INTROD UCTIO N High-quality thoracic radiographs are essential for the inter- pretation of the cardiovascular system. The cardiovascular sys- tem in the dog and cat is complex, and basic patterns of recognition are critical for correct radiographic evaluation. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provide superior spatial and temporal resolution of car- diac structures but are less widely available and require anes- thesia or sedation in patients who may be at risk of cardiovascular compromise. Echocardiography is the most practical, safe, and widely used imaging modality for evaluation of cardiovascular morphology and function. While echocardi- ography is best for assessing the heart, radiographs provide other information, such as vascular status and presence of heart failure. Hence, a comprehensive evaluation of the cardiovas- cular structures is best routinely achieved with the comple- mentary use of thoracic radiographs and echocardiography. RADIOG RAPH IC PROJEC TIONS AND TECHN ICAL CONSI DERAT IONS Three-view thoracic radiographs including right lateral, left lateral, and dorsoventral (DV) and/or ventrodorsal (VD) projections are the standard. For assessment of cardiovascular structures, a DV projection may be preferred to the VD to minimize cardiac magni ﬁ cation and optimize aeration of the caudal lung lobes and caudal lobar pulmonary vasculature. When possible, radiographs should be obtained before echo- cardiography to avoid atelectasis from prolonged lateral re- cumbency and wet-hair artefacts due to the presence of gel or alcohol. When positioning the patient for thoracic radiographs, the primary x-ray beam should be centered on the heart to avoid distortion of the cardiovascular structures, and radio- graphs should be acquired during peak inspiration to avoid atelectasis being misinterpreted as pulmonary disease. EVALUA TION OF CAR DIAC SILH OUETT E SIZE Because ﬂ uid and soft tissue opacities are radiographically indistinguishable, the heart and pericardial sac are interpreted as a single unit, termed the cardiac silhouette . Vascular changes and pericardial disease may also affect cardiac silhou- ette size and margination. It is also important to keep in mind that absence of cardiomegaly does not exclude the presence of cardiac disease. When evaluating the cardiac silhouette for size, qualitative and quantitative methods are utilized. Comparisons of both methods did not ﬁ nd a signi ﬁ cant increase in inter- pretation accuracy when the quantitative method was used in conjunction with qualitative means of evaluating heart size. 1 A higher con ﬁ dence level and degree of accuracy may be ex- pected with increased experience and severity of car- diomegaly. 1 In all instances, inherent variations in cardiac silhouette size should be considered between different breeds of dogs. For example, the cardiac silhouette in deep-chested dogs may appear abnormally small, whereas the cardiac silhouette in barrel-chested dogs may look abnormally large ( Fig. 35.2A F ). Cats have a more uniform body conformation, which may facilitate the evaluation of feline cardiac silhouette size. 1 The cardiac silhouette in kittens may look enlarged in the absence of disease. Qualitative assessment of cardiac silhouette size is often facilitated by the recognition of speci ﬁ c cardiac chamber enlargement, described in the following section. Multiple techniques are proposed for the evaluation of car- diac silhouette size. The most common of these is the vertebral heart scale (VHS), which was instituted to take into account the in ﬂ uence of body conformation on the size of the cardiac silhouette. 2 The VHS is obtained by measuring the length of the long and short axes of the heart on a high-quality right lateral radiograph and scaling these measurements against the length of the vertebral bodies starting at T4 to quantify heart size in terms of corresponding vertebral number. Based on 100 clini- cally normal dogs, the normal mean VHS 2 SD was 9.7 1 vertebrae. To further reduce variation, VHS measurements speci ﬁ c to particular breeds of dogs have been established and are listed in eTable 35.1 . The in ﬂ uence of respiration and the cardiac cycle can affect obtained VHS measurements by up to 1.0 vertebral body length and should be kept in mind when assessing the cardiac silhouette using this method (Video 35.1). 3 Normal VHS measurements (7.5 0.3 vertebrae) are also available in cats. 4 While the VHS may be a useful adjunct method for the assessment of cardiac silhouette size, it is of particular use for the longitudinal assessment of cardiac disease progression and treatment within an individual patient.An alternative and more ef ﬁ cient method of assessing the cardiac silhouette size using a heart to single vertebra ratio (HSVR) was recently proposed, taking into account the poten- tial presence of vertebral anomalies, which may affect VHS measurements. Using a similar approach, the length and width of the cardiac silhouette are measured and added before sub- tracting from the length of a single morphologically normal vertebra at T4 T8, including the caudal intervertebral disc space. 5 Obtained measurements are comparable to reported normal VHS measurements, although a higher accuracy is re- ported with HSVR measurements calculated using T7 as a reference vertebra. 5 Other quantitative measurements of car- diac size are proposed and mostly anecdotal ( Table 35.1 ); therefore, these methods should be applied with caution given the lack of research to support their accuracy and unclear effect of patient conformation on obtained measurements. With advan ced age, the long axis of the cardia c silhoue tte in cats may gradual ly rotat e and be in a plane that is more hori- zonta l to the sternum . Cats with such variat ion to the orien ta- tion of their cardiac silho uette are said to have a “ lazy heart . ” When obtaini ng measure ments of the cardia c silho uette in older cats, the orienta tion of the cardia c silhoue tte shou ld be taken into cons iderati on. Addit ionall y, the aortic arch may be enlarge d and redund ant in older cats, as charac terize d by the prese nce of a bulge at the cran ial aspec t of the cardia c silhoue tte (e.g., aorti c knob ). While these ﬁ nding s comm only repres ent normal age vari ants, systemic hyper tension and hyper thyroid ism may also be contri buting factors. 6 Microcardia is sometimes identi ﬁ ed on thoracic radiographs in dogs and cats, and is rarely associated with primary cardiac disease. Rather, microcardia is primarily indicative of hypo- volemia with reduced circulating cardiovascular volume from dehydration, blood loss, or hypoadrenocorticism ( Fig. 35.3A,B ). 7 Radiographically, the cardiac silhouette becomes abnormally Fig. 35.2 Right lateral and ventrodorsal thoracic radiographs from anormal Bo rzoi (A and B) , a normal Labrador retriever (C and D) , and anormal pug (E and F) , illustrating the effect of body conformati on on theappearance of the cardiac silhouette. SPEC IFIC PATTERN S OF CARD IAC CHA MBER ENLARG EMEN T Because individual cardiac chambers, sites of great vessel emergence/convergence, and the pericardium are radiograph- ically indistinguishable, evaluation of the cardiac silhouette margins is essential to localize alterations to speci ﬁ c cardiac chambers or the great vessels in the dog based on their relative positioning. For this purpose, a “ clock face ” analogy is commonly used to correlate alterations to the cardiac silhouette at speci ﬁ c sites to corresponding anatomical cardiovascular structures on both lateral and VD/DV projections ( Fig. 35.4A,B ). The positioning of the feline heart and subtlety of speci ﬁ c cardiac chamber enlargement on thoracic radiographs limits the use of this approach in cats. Left Atrium Enlargement of the left atrium is the most frequently encoun- tered cardiac enlargement in the dog due to the high preva- lence of myxomatous mitral valve disease. On lateral projections, enlargement of the left atrium in the dog causes bulging of the dorsocaudal margin of the cardiac silhouette at the 12 2 o clock position. The caudal border is subsequently ﬂ attened to mildly concave, resulting in a loss of the caudal “ cardiac waist ” ( Fig. 35.5 ). On the VD/DV projection, this bulge corresponds to a rounded focal region of increased soft tissue opacity caudal to the tracheal bifurcation. Superimposition and summation of the enlarged left atrium over the cardiac silhou- ette can create the appearance of a double wall due to distinction of both the caudal border of the left atrium and cardiac silhouette ( Fig. 35.6A,B ). With left atrial enlargement, splaying of the principal bronchi may be observed on the VD/DV projections ( Figs. 35.7 and 35.8A,B ). Similar splaying of the principal bronchi may occur secondary to tracheobronchial lymphadenopathy but this typically causes ventral displacement of the tracheal bifurcation in lateral views (see Chapter 33 ). In contrast, left atrial enlargement typically causes dorsal displacement of the tracheal bifurcation. A compressive effect on the left and right principal bronchi has been described in the presence of left atrial enlargement due to the spatial relation- ship between the vertebral column, aorta, left principal bron- chus, and left atrium. 8 While the bronchial narrowing may be attributed to direct impingement from the adjacent enlarged left atrium, coexisting bronchomalacia may facilitate this pro- cess as a result of altered bronchial wall integrity and/or cause bronchial collapse (Video 35.2). 9 Coughing in dogs with left atrial enlargement is common and can be attributed to tracheal narrowing versus pulmonary edema. 9 10 The absence of cough receptors within the alveoli and interstitium is a likely expla- nation; however, in dogs, coughing is to be expected in the presence of large amounts of cardiogenic pulmonary edema in ﬁ ltrating into the larger bronchial structures. 9 Therefore, causes of a cough other than heart failure should always be considered in dogs with a heart murmur. In cats, coughing due to pulmonary edema is very uncommon. Enlargement of the left auricle is less readily identi ﬁ ed than left atrial enlargement and is most prevalent when a higher degree of left atrial enlargement is present. On the VD/DV projection, enlargement of the left auricle may create a focal bulge along the left cardiac border in the 2 3 o clock position (see Fig. 35.7 ). While left atrial enlargement is most commonly evaluated subjectively, the vertebral left atrial size (VLAS) can be used to quantify left atrial enlargement in dogs with good repeat- ability. 11 12 On either a left or right lateral projection, VLAS in- dexes are obtained by measuring the distance from the mid ventral aspect of the carina to the most caudal margin of the left atrium at the intersection with the dorsal border of the caudal vena cava. This measurement is transposed to the vertebral column, starting at the cranial margin of T4, to count the equivalent vertebral body number. 13 In 80 healthy dogs, the normal medial VLAS was 1.9 with a reference interval of 1.4 to 2.2. 12 A cutoff value of 2.3 may support a diagnosis of left atrial enlargement in dogs. 12 13 Left atrial enlargement in cats is much less conspicuous, and in many cats there are no radiographic changes. In some in- stances, a bulge may be observed along the caudodorsal margin of the cardiac silhouette and is associated with concavity of the caudal margin ( Fig. 35.9 ). Left atrial enlargement in the cat is also associated with an increase in width of the cardiac silhouette in the region of the cardiac base on the VD/DV projections. In the presence of marked left atrial enlargement, the cardiac silhouette may be “ valentine shaped ” ( Fig. 35.10 ). Right Ventricle Similar to the left ventricle, the right ventricle may enlarge as a result of both concentric and eccentric hypertrophy. Isolation of right ventricular enlargement in cats is very rare. The right ventricle undergoes concentric hypertrophy in response to pressure overload, as with pulmonic stenosis or pulmonary hypertension, as with heartworm disease. Hypertrophy mainly occurs at the expense of lumen volume and may lead to no or minimal change in the appearance of the cardiac silhouette. On lateral projections, rounding of the cardiac margin in the 5 8 o clock position may be seen and associated with dorsal displacement or elevation of the cardiac apex from the sternum ( Fig. 35.12B,C ). On the VD/DV projections, this is further supported by rounding of the cardiac silhouette in the 6 9 o clock position with an associated leftward apical shift, giving the cardiac silhouette a pronounced “ reversed-D ” shape (see Fig. 35.12A ). Care should be taken to not over-read the more rounded appearance of the cranial and right lateral margins of the car- diac silhouette as it may be artefactual on expiratory radio- graphs or may represent a normal variation in some breed of dogs, such as brachycephalic dogs. Additionally, the cranial and right lateral margins of the cardiac silhouette may be rounded in the presence of severe left-sided cardiomegaly due to morphological distortion of cardiac anatomy from the severe left atrial and ventricular enlargement. 15 A more rounded appearance of the right margin of the cardiac silhouette and leftward displacement of the cardiac silhouette may be seen on DV projections when compared to VD projections. SPEC IFIC PATTERN S OF GREAT VES SEL ENLARG EMEN T Caudal Vena Cava The caudal vena cava is variable in size depending on the phase of respiration and cardiac cycle. The caudal vena cava size is commonly assessed subjectively for size; however, the normal caudal vena cava should be less than 1.5 times the diameter of the descending aorta. 16 17 The caudal vena cava can enlarge in response to increased central venous pressure, but the size of the caudal vena cava is not an accurate way to evaluate central venous pressure. Valid inferences on cardiovascular disease cannot typically be made based on the size of the caudal vena cava only. Kinking of the caudal vena cava is occasionally observed on lateral projections in dogs and may represent a recumbency- dependent change due to a positional shift of the cardiovas- cular structures, or an association with trauma, cardiovascular disease, or neoplasia ( Fig. 35.14 ). 17 18 While kinking of the caudal vena cava may be a primary cause for postsinusoidal obstruction of venous ﬂ ow (e.g., Budd-Chiari syndrome), it may also represent a secondary change seen in response to crowd- ing of the caudal intrathoracic structures from cardiomegaly and/or an increase in intra-abdominal pressure, such as sec- ondary to peritoneal effusion or organomegaly/presence of a mass. 17 18 Narrowing of the caudal vena cava is primarily seen with hypovolemia and is commonly identi ﬁ ed in conjunction with microcardia. The caudal vena cava may be intermittently nar- rowed with the phase of the cardiac cycle; therefore, a diag- nosis is best supported by persistent narrowing of the caudal vena cava on both lateral projections (see Fig. 35.3A,B ). Aorta Widening of the cranial and middle mediastinum in proximity to the heart base can indicate dilation of the aortic arch in both dogs and cats. On the VD/DV projections, a focal bulge in the descending aorta is suggestive of aortic dilation, as seen in pa- tients with aortic stenosis and patent ductus arteriosus, and may correlate with an increase in soft tissue opacity at the cranial aspect of the cardiac silhouette on lateral projections ( Fig. 35.15A,B ). In older cats, redundancy of the aortic arch and tortuosity of the descending aorta are described to likely represent a normal age variant although systemic hypertension and hyperthyroidism may also contribute ( Fig. 35.16A ). 6 On the VD/DV projections, the aorta is occasionally projected end-on within the left side of the mediastinum and should not be misinterpreted as a pulmonary nodule (see Fig. 35.16B ). 6 Main Pulmonary Artery Under normal conditions, the main pulmonary artery cannot be delineated on evaluation of the cardiac silhouette. Additionally, the caudal lobar pulmonary vessels are more perpendicular to the diverging x-ray beam, resulting in less distortion. The lobar pulmonary arteries and veins are located on opposite sides of their corresponding lobar bronchus. On lateral projections, the cranial lobar arteries are dorsal and the veins are ventral to the bronchus, whereas the caudal lobar pulmonary arteries are lateral and veins are medial to their corresponding bronchus on the VD/DV projections. 19 As a simpli ﬁ ed means to recall the relative positioning of the lobar pulmonary arteries and veins to each other, the lobar pulmo- nary arteries may be expressed as being “ up and away, ” while the veins are “ ventral and central. ” Under normal conditions, the lobar pulmonary arteries and veins should be symmetrical in size. 19 Additionally, normal lobar pulmonary arteries and veins follow a generally straight path as they gradually taper in the periphery of the lung ﬁ eld. The size of the cranial lobar pulmonary vessels may be assessed by comparing vessel diameter to the width of the fourth rib just ventral to the vertebral column on lateral projections and the width of the ninth rib in the VD/DV projections. 19 20 Variable rib conformation and a wide range of normal values limit the clinical usefulness of these comparisons. Acquired Cardiovascular Diseases Acquired cardiovascular diseases are more prevalent than congenital heart diseases in dogs and cats, reported to repre- sent up to 94.05% of all cardiac abnormalities. 25 Of these, valvular disease is most common in dogs, whereas cats more often have myocardial failure. Factors, such as age, breed, and diet, may increase the risk of acquired heart disease in both dogs and cats. Early diagnosis of acquired disease is important to avoid irreversible cardiac damage. Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease Myxomatous mitral valve disease is the most common acquired heart disease in dogs, representing approximately 75% of all cardiac disease in small animal practice. 26 Myxomatous mitral valve disease is highly prevalent in older small breed dogs, re- ported in 85% of 13-year-old dogs at necropsy, and may be inherited in certain dog breeds, such as the Cavalier King Charles spaniel. 26 27 Valve leaf degeneration often leads to left-sided cardiac decompensation and heart failure. 28 Rupture of chordae ten- dineae and atrial rupture may result in a rapid clinical decline. 28 29 Radiographic signs of myxomatous mitral valve disease include ( eFigs. 35.7 and 35.8 ):  Left atrial, and sometimes auricular enlargement, as described earlier.  The sole or combined presence of left atrial and ventricu- lar enlargement will result in an increase in apical to basilar length of the cardiac silhouette.  Distention of lobar pulmonary veins can result from pul- monary venous hypertension.  Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from left-sided heart failure. This usually develops in the absence of lobar pulmonary venous enlargement.  Distention of the pulmonary arteries with an artery to vein ratio > 1.1 has been described as supportive of pulmonary hypertension in patients with myxomatous mitral valve disease. 30 Myxomatous Tricuspid Valve Disease Approximately 54% of patients with myxomatous mitral valve degeneration have concurrent myxomatous tricuspid valve degeneration. 31 Minor tricuspid valve regurgitation may be negligible; however, severe tricuspid valve degeneration can result in valvular insuf ﬁ ciency and right-sided volume overload. The right atrium and ventricle will become enlarged with associated eccentric hypertrophy. Backward congestion may decompensate into right-sided heart failure with pleural and abdominal effusion developing from the increased hydrostatic pressure. Radiographic signs of myxomatous tricuspid valve disease include ( Fig. 35.27A,B ):  Right atrial and ventricular enlargement is more likely to be radiographically recognized in the presence of at least moderate cardiac chamber enlargement.  Distention of the caudal vena cava and generalized hepato- megaly are indicative of systemic venous hypertension.  Peritoneal and/or pleural effusion will develop due to right-sided cardiac decompensation. Cardiomyopathies Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle and have variable etiologies and presentation in both dogs and cats. Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is most prevalent in large breed male dogs and is also seen in cats. Canine breeds pre- disposed to DCM include the Doberman Pinscher, Great Dane, Irish Wolfhound, and Boxer. Although the cause for myocardial failure is not fully understood, genetic mutation, systemic dis- ease, toxins, and nutritional de ﬁ ciencies (including a more recent correlation between DCM and grain-free diets) are possible etiologies. 32 Failure of the myocardium results in pro- gressive concentric dilation of the left right cardiac cham- bers. The heart becomes volume overloaded, and mitral valve dysfunction may result from a change in shape of the mitral annulus because of cardiac dilation. The myocardium of the right ventricle is affected primarily; however, involvement of the left ventricle and atria is also possible. The myocardium becomes in ﬂ amed (e.g., myocarditis) and replaced by fat ﬁ brosis, leading to the development of potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias. 35 With disease progression and not necessarily before the emergence of arrhythmias, the cardiac chambers may undergo eccentric hypertrophy and become volume overloaded. When in excess, the heart will decompensate into right-sided congestive heart failure. 36 Radiographic features of ARVC include:  Commonly, there are no thoracic radiographic abnormalities.  Right-sided cardiomegaly is seen with more advanced sys- tolic dysfunction and congestion.  Right-sided congestive heart failure is occasionally observed. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common acquired heart disease in cats and is familial in some breeds, such as the Maine Coon and Norwegian Forest cat. 37 HCM is seen occasionally in dogs with a much lower prevalence than in cats. Concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle causes a decrease in ventricular volume capacity and increase in left ventricular ﬁ lling pressure. 38 The decrease in stroke volume is counteracted by tachycardia, which in turn further limits ﬁ lling of the left ventricle. Therefore, the left atrium becomes over- loaded with further backward hypertension of the lobar pul- monary veins as the disease progresses. In some instances, the papillary muscles may become thickened and result in mitral valve insuf ﬁ ciency, further exacerbating dilation and hyper- tension of the left atrium. The mitral valve may have altered motion and deviate toward the left ventricular out ﬂ ow tract, causing dynamic out ﬂ ow obstruction of the left ventricle during systole. 39 Other diseases, such as systemic arterial hyperten- sion, hyperthyroidism, and aortic stenosis, should be ruled out as a cause for ventricular hypertrophy. The dorsocaudal margin of the cardiac silhouette may be rounded with concavity of the caudal margin. In the presence of moderate to severe left atrial enlargement, the cardiac silhouette may have a “ valentine-shaped ” heart on VD/DV projections. These cannot be differentiated on thoracic radiographs. The cause of restrictive cardiomyopathies is not known. The left ventricular wall is restricted by the presence of ﬁ brosis in lieu of hyper- trophy, resulting in similar systolic dysfunction and congestion of the left atrium. 41 42 Cats with myocardial abnormalities which are not typical for hypertrophic or restrictive cardio- myopathies are considered “ unclassi ﬁ ed. ” 42 Pulmonary Hypertension Pulmonary hypertension results in reduced blood ﬂ ow and oxygen delivery to the lungs, as well as a backward increase in pressure within the right cardiac chambers. The right ventricle and atrium enlarge due to pressure overload, and concentric thickening of the cardiac chamber walls develops with chro- nicity from the increased cardiac workload. When in excess, the caudal vena cava and liver may also become enlarged, and the emergence of peritoneal pleural effusion indicates right- sided cardiac decompensation. 43 While a diagnosis of pulmo- nary hypertension is best made with echocardiography, changes to the cardiovascular structures on thoracic radio- graphs can support a diagnosis and direct the need of further diagnostic imaging to con ﬁ rm a diagnosis. 43 44 Thoracic radio- graphs may also help identify an underlying cause, which may vary from pulmonary cardiovascular disease, or primary pul- monary or systemic disease. 44 The American College of Veter- inary Internal Medicine (ACVIM) recently published a consensus statement classifying the etiologies of pulmonary hypertension in dogs as follows: 43 1. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, drug and toxin induced, congenital cardiac shunts, pulmo- nary vasculitis, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease or pul- monary capillary hemangiomatosis) 2. Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (left ven- tricular dysfunction, canine DCM, myocarditis, and ac- quired/congenital valvular disease) 3. Pulmonary hypertension secondary to respiratory disease, hypoxia, or both (chronic obstructive airway disorders, tracheal or mainstem bronchial collapse, primary pulmo- nary parenchymal disease, obstructive sleep apnea/sleep disordered breathing, chronic exposure to high altitudes, and developmental lung disease) 4. Pulmonary emboli/thrombi/thromboemboli 5. Parasitic disease ( Diro ﬁ laria or Angiostrongylus infection) 6. Pulmonary hypertension with multifactorial or unclear mechanisms Pulmonary hypertension is less prevalent in cats and possibly underdiagnosed. It may be associated with similar etiologies as dogs but predominant with diseases of higher prevalence in cats, such as chronic lower airway disease (e.g., feline asthma), left-sided heart failure, or upper respira- tory obstructions (e.g., nasopharyngeal polyp). 45 Depending on the underlying etiology and severity, pulmonary hypertension may be reversible in both dogs and cats. Therefore, an early diagnosis and prompt medical management are important to prevent irreversible changes and progression, which may ulti- mately carry a poor prognosis. 43 45 Radiographic features of pulmonary hypertension include the following ( Fig. 35.30A,B ): 1. The main pulmonary artery becomes enlarged from turbulence of blood ﬂ ow and increased pressure. In dogs and cats with heartworm disease, enlargement of the main pulmonary artery may be due to the physical presence of heartworms and/or thrombi within the main pulmonary artery. Jugular vein distention is seen in response to the increased pressure, and caudal vena cava and hepatic enlarge- ment may also be observed and followed by the development of peritoneal and pleural effusion due to cardiac decompensa- tion into right-sided heart failure. 46 47 Radiographic features of pericardial effusion include the following ( Fig. 35.31A,B eFig. 35.10 ):  Enlargement and rounding of the cardiac silhouette are seen with larger amounts of pericardial effusion, creating a globoid contour. Cardiomegaly and rounding of the cardiac silhouette on thoracic radiographs are poorly sensitive and speci ﬁ c for the presence of cardiac tamponade. 49  Distention of the caudal vena cava and hepatomegaly are signs of increased central venous pressure if pericardial tamponade is severe enough to prevent diastolic ﬁ lling of the right atrium and ventricle. The concurrent presence of peritoneal pleural effusion is suggestive of right-sided congestive heart failure. Neoplasia Cardiac tumors have a low incidence in dogs, representing 0.121% and 4.33% of all tumor types, and an even lower inci- dence is reported in cats. 50 The most common cardiac tumor reported in dogs is hemangiosarcoma (69% prevalence), fol- lowed by aortic body tumors (chemodectoma and para- ganglioma) and lymphoma. Lymphoma is the most common neoplastic disease of the feline heart. Both dogs and cats can have metastatic lesions to the heart from tumors of other tissue origin. 50 51 While most cardiac tumors are diagnosed in middle- aged to older patients, lymphoma can affect dogs and cats of any age. 50 Hemangiosarcoma most commonly originates from the right atrium/auricle and is highly metastatic. On the other hand, heart base tumors are less aggressive and are primarily identi ﬁ ed at the aortic root. 50 51 Brachycephalic dogs are pre- disposed to heart base tumors, and it is speculated that chronic hypoxia may be an inciting etiology. 50 Hemangiosarcoma may also be identi ﬁ ed at the aortic root, and lymphoma may affect any part of the heart. When larger in size, right atrial/auricular and heart base masses can obstruct the right cardiac chambers and cause vena caval and hepatic hypertension with risks of right-sided cardiac decompensation. Pericardial effusion may develop in some cases and result in cardiac tamponade. Cardiac tumors may be dif ﬁ cult to identify on thoracic radiographs, and echocardiography and advanced imaging (CT or MRI) are su- perior for the diagnosis and characterization of cardiac neo- plasms in dogs and cats. 50 51 However, radiographs remain a good screening tool and should be scrutinized for the presence of a mass even in asymptomatic cases as they may often be found incidentally. Radiographic features of cardiac neoplasia include the following ( Fig. 35.32A,B ):  Heart base and right atrial/auricular tumors cannot be differentiated on thoracic radiographs. When larger in size, a soft tissue opaque mass may be seen at the base of the cardiac silhouette, causing dorsal and rightward displace- ment of the trachea.  Cardiomegaly with rounding (globoid appearance) is indic- ative of pericardial effusion.  Distention of the caudal vena cava and hepatomegaly are seen secondary to obstruction of venous return to the right heart.  Peritoneal pleural effusion is suggestive of right-sided heart failure. In comparison, blood follows the path of least resistance with larger cardiac defects and is shunted from the left ventricle into the lower pressure right ventricle during systole; therefore, these defects are characterized as being nonresistive. Blood is commonly shun- ted directly into the right out ﬂ ow tract; hence, right-sided car- diomegaly is usually not seen with these lesions. Overcirculation of the pulmonary vasculature will result in backward overloading of the left heart. Left-sided cardiomegaly with eccentric hypertrophy may be observed in more advanced cases. When in excess, cardiogenic edema associated with left- sided congestive heart failure will ensue. The persistent shunting of blood into the pulmonary arterial vasculature re- sults in a progressive increase in pulmonary arterial pressure, which may be exacerbated by the development of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. A subsequent increased pressure overload on the right cardiac chambers predisposes to shunt reversal (right-to-left shunting), consistent with Eisenmenger syndrome. While small ventricular septal defects may have a good prog- nosis, larger defects have a poorer prognosis which is guarded once shunt reversal is observed. 62 Radiographic features of ventricular septal defects include ( eFigs. 35.14A,B,E and 35.15 ):  No abnormalities may be radiographically apparent in the presence of a small defect.  Enlargement of the left atrium and ventricle is seen in response to pulmonary overcirculation. ATRIAL SEPT AL DEFECT Atrial septal defects are embryological anomalies resulting in an abnormal communication between the atria. 65 Such defects are rare in dogs and cats, representing 0.7% to 3.7% and up to 10% of canine and feline congenital heart diseases, respectively. 58 65 However, the prevalence may be higher than previously re- ported, with access to higher-quality Doppler technology allowing for the recognition of smaller defects. 65 Boxers may be overrepresented. 65 66 Atrial septal defects can be divided into three categories, ostium secundum, ostium primum, and sinus venosus defects, based on their location. 65 Ostium secundum defects are most prevalent in dogs and are located at the level of the foramen ovale, dorsal to the atrioventricular valves. Similar to ventricular septal defects, small communications within the septal wall may not alter cardiovascular hemody- namics and remain clinically silent. 57 With larger defects, shunting of blood from the higher pressure left atrium to the right atrium results in volume overload and eccentric hyper- trophy of the right cardiac chambers. With progression, the caudal vena cava and liver become enlarged, and the subse- quent development of peritoneal pleural effusion indicate right-sided congestive heart failure. 67 The increased pressure within the right cardiac chambers, possibly exacerbated by concurrent pulmonic valve insuf ﬁ ciency and pulmonary hy- pertension, can result in reversed direction of blood ﬂ ow through the atrial septal defect (left-to-right shunting) when in excess to the left atrial pressure. 67 Radiographic features of ventricular septal defects include (see eFig. 35.15A,B ):  No abnormalities may be radiographically apparent in the presence of a small defect.  Right-sided cardiomegaly is the most common abnormality identi ﬁ ed with larger septal defects due to volume over- load with left-to-right shunting. 67  Enlargement of the main and lobar pulmonary arteries is suggestive of pulmonary hypertension.  Enlargement of the caudal vena cava and liver may be fol- lowed by the emergence of pleural and peritoneal effusion in patients with right-sided heart failure. PULM ONIC STENO SIS Pulmonic stenosis has a higher prevalence in dogs than cats. Depending on the location of the stenosis, supravalvular, valvular, or subvalvular morphologies have been described, with valvular stenosis being most common in dogs. 68 69 Pul- monic stenosis is de ﬁ ned as a narrowing of the pulmonic valve due to an abnormal development of the valve lea ﬂ ets. 68 70 Blood ﬂ ow through the right ventricular out ﬂ ow tract is sub- sequently obstructed, resulting in right ventricular pressure overload and concentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle. 68 69 While there is an overall decrease in blood ﬂ ow through the right ventricular out ﬂ ow tract, ejection of a high-velocity jet through the stenosis and poststenotic turbulence of blood ﬂ ow result in focal dilation of the main pulmonary artery. 69 Pressure overload of the right cardiac chambers may result in enlarge- ment of the caudal vena cava and liver with progressive emergence of peritoneal pleural effusion from right-sided congestive heart failure. 68 70 In brachycephalic dogs, pul- monic stenosis can be associated with aberrant coronary artery, which may affect treatment options. 71 Radiographic features of pulmonic stenosis include ( eFig. 35.16 ):  Dilation of the main pulmonary artery. While mild pul- monic stenosis may not cause any radiographically detect- able abnormalities, the main pulmonary artery may be so markedly enlarged in more severe cases that concurrent focal right-sided deviation of the trachea is occasionally seen and may be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from a heart base or right atrial/auricular mass.  Normal to decreased size of the lobar pulmonary vascula- ture is associated with pulmonary undercirculation.  Enlargement of the right ventricle is seen in response to pressure overload and ventricular hypertrophy may not be radiographically apparent if mild in severity.  Enlargement of the caudal vena cava and liver may be fol- lowed by the emergence of pleural and peritoneal effusion in patients with right-sided heart failure. TRICUSP ID VALVE DYSP LASIA Tricuspid valve dysplasia is most prevalent in large dog breeds and represents the second most common congenital heart dis- ease in cats. 59 60 65 76 Congenital malformation and thickening of the tricuspid valve result in tricuspid valve insuf ﬁ ciency and systolic dysfunction. Shortening of the chordae tendineae may further restrict closure of the tricuspid valve and exacerbate valvular dysfunction. 76 77 Although rare in dogs and cats, an Ebstein anomaly represents a form of tricuspid valve dysplasia, in which there is abnormal ventral positioning of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, often also associated with systolic dysfunction. 76 77 In all instances, the right atrium becomes volume overloaded due to the presence of tricuspid valve regurgitation. Eccentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle is also seen in more severe cases. With excessive volume overload of the right ventricle, increased pressure within the caudal vena and liver may be observed. The emergence of peritoneal  pleural effusion supports a diagnosis of right-sided congestive heart failure. 76 77 Radiographic features of tricuspid valve dysplasia include:  Right-sided cardiomegaly may be radiographically apparent in more severe cases of tricuspid valve insuf ﬁ ciency, vol- ume overload, and right atrial and ventricular enlargement. In cats, a nonspeci ﬁ c generalized enlargement of the car- diac silhouette is more commonly observed.  Enlargement of the caudal vena cava and hepatomegaly may precede right-sided congestive heart failure, as evi- denced by the development of peritoneal and/or pleural effusion. MITRA L VALVE DYSPLA SIA Mitral valve dysplasia is de ﬁ ned as a congenital malformation and thickening of the mitral valve lea ﬂ ets, which is infrequently identi ﬁ ed in dogs and cats. 59 78 Mitral valve function may be further impaired by thickening and/or shortening of the chor- dae tendineae. Mitral valve insuf ﬁ ciency during systole results in regurgitation of blood into the left atrium and volume over- load. Eccentric hypertrophy of the left ventricle is seen with increased chronicity and severity. With excessive left-sided volume overload, backward pulmonary venous hypertension and left-sided congestive heart failure may ensue. 78 Although rarely reported in both dogs and cats, mitral valve dysplasia may be associated with stenosis of the mitral valve annulus. 59 78 Radiographic features of mitral valve dysplasia include:  Left-sided cardiomegaly is commonly identi ﬁ ed.  Pulmonary venous distention may be observed in some cases due to pulmonary venous hypertension.  Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is indicative of left-sided congestive heart failure. MITRA L VALVE STENO SIS Mitral valve stenosis may represent a form of mitral valve dysplasia and is de ﬁ ned as a reduced size of the mitral valve annulus due to embryological malformation (e.g., thickening and fusion) of the mitral valve lea ﬂ ets. Subsequent obstruction of the mitral valve results in an increase in left atrial pressure. Pulmonary venous hypertension and left-sided congestive heart failure are seen in more severe cases. Although uncommon, both dogs and cats may be affected. Radiographic features of mitral valve stenosis include:  L e f t a t r i a l e n l a r ge m e n t d u e to a n i n c r e a s e i n t r a n s m i t r a l r e s i s t a n c e i s t h e m a i n r a d io gr a p h ic f e a t u r e r e p o r t e d . 7 9 I n c a t s , c a r d i o m e ga l y w i t h c o nv e x i t y o f t h e c a u d a l c a r d i a c ma r gi n m a y b e s u gg e s t iv e o f l e f t a t r i a l e n l a r g e me n t . 8 0  Development of cardiogenic pulmonary edema with or without lobar pulmonary vein enlargement due to left- sided heart failure represents a frequent sequela in dogs within 1 year of diagnosis and is also commonly identi ﬁ ed in cats. 79 80 TETRALO GY OF FALLOT Tetralogy of Fallot is an uncommon but highly fatal complex of cardiac abnormalities in dogs and cats. It is a result of abnormal ventricular septation during embryogenesis and is comprised of a combination of four congenital anomalies, consisting of a ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, obstruction of the right ventricular out ﬂ ow tract, and right ventricular hypertro- phy. 81 82 Cardiac function is most affected by the size of the ventricular septal defect and severity of the pulmonic stenosis. With mild pulmonic stenosis, blood is shunted through the ventricular septal defect from the higher pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle (left-to-right shunting). However, the pulmonic stenosis is often so severe that there is pressure overload of the right ventricle in excess to the systolic pressure of the left ventricle, resulting in shunt reversal (right-to- left). 81 82 Bidirectional shunting is reported in half of dogs and cats with tetralogy of Fallot at the time of diagnosis. 81 With shunt reversal, the pulmonary vasculature is subsequently undercirculated. Right-sided congestive heart failure represents a rare complication. 81 82 Radiographic features of tetralogy of Fallot include ( eFig. 35.19A,B ):  Right-sided cardiomegaly is most commonly observed due to the high prevalence of right-to-left shunting. In dogs, the cardiac silhouette will have rounded cranial and right lateral margins with leftward displacement of the cardiac apex and a “ reversed-D ” appearance. In milder cases, left- sided cardiomegaly may predominate. In cats, nonspeci ﬁ c generalized cardiomegaly may be seen.  Decreased size of the lobar pulmonary vasculature is seen with right-to-left shunting of blood through the ventricular septal defect due to arterial and venous undercirculation. The main pulmonary artery may be reduced in size, result- ing in a focal concavity of the cardiac silhouette in the VD/DV projection. Additional opacity is pro- vided by the musculoskeletal structures of the thorax, sum- mating with the lungs ( eFig. 36.1 ). The location of lung lobes is fairly constant among dogs and cats and their expected location can be extrapolated on standard three-view thoracic radiog- raphy, keeping in mind that lung lobes overlap considerably. The left lung is separated into cranial and caudal lung lobes ( Fig. 36.2A ). The left cranial lung lobe is further subdivided in cranial and caudal segments, connected to each other dorsally. The right lung is separated into cranial, middle, caudal, and accessory lung lobes (see Fig. 36.2B , inset, and C ). The acces- sory lung lobe occupies a midline position, caudal to the heart, as seen on a ventrodorsal (VD) image of the thorax (see Fig. 36.2C , right bottom panel) and overlaps with the right caudal lung lobe on the left lateral view (see Fig. 36.2B ). Airways A ﬂ owchart indicates the travel of air through the conduit air- ways up to the pulmonary parenchyma, where gas exchange occurs ( Fig. 36.3 ). In general, the bronchial walls are too thin to be seen on radiography, unless they are mineralized or abnor- mally thick ( Fig. 36.4 ). 1 Dogs > 10 years old are more likely to have bronchial cartilage calci ﬁ cation, which may not be of clinical signi ﬁ cance. 1 When the thickness allows their detec- tion, the bronchial walls tend to taper as the bronchus courses away from its origin. This unit includes everything beyond the terminal bronchiole, that is, in the order of the incoming air ﬂ ow, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli (see Fig. 36.3 ). THE BREATH ING CYCLE APPLI ED TO THORAC IC RADIOG RAPHY Exposure factors tailored to the lungs will favor a wide range of shades of gray (low mAs, high kVp) to maximize detection of lung lesions. A short exposure time (e.g., 1/60 seconds or 1/120 seconds) minimizes motion artifact associated with respiration. Full in ﬂ ation of the lungs promotes the visibility of the bron- chial and vascular structures, and is more likely to depict lung lesions ( Fig. 36.5 ). 3 Overin ﬂ ation results in more radiolucency than normally expected. Exhalation is passive during quiet breathing. Relaxing mus- cles and diaphragm return to their normal position, allowing carbon dioxide containing air to be exhaled, and thus, gener- ating increased pulmonary opacity and decreased contrast be- tween bronchial and vascular structures and pulmonary parenchyma, and pulmonary lesions (see Fig. 36.5 ). 3 Factors Affecting Lung Volume A dog s or cat s ability to in ﬂ ate and then de ﬂ ate their lungs depends on many factors, some of which are discussed in further detail later.  Sedated dogs and cats with shallow breathing may not achieve maximal lung in ﬂ ation.  Placing healthy, conscious dogs in left or right lateral re- cumbency for 10 minutes leads to lung volume loss, even faster if sedated or anesthetized ( Fig. 36.6 eFig. 36.2 ). 4 6 Keeping patients in lateral recumbency for as little time as possible prior to and during radiography acquisition best limits the effects of recumbency on lung volume ( eFig. 36.3 ). Mechanical ventilation and adequate species- speci ﬁ c airway pressure during breath-hold technique and positive end-expiratory pressure may also help maintain better lung aeration while the animal is under general anesthesia. 7 11  Impaired caudal displacement of the diaphragm by, for example, excess abdominal content reduces the size of the thoracic cavity and is often compensated by increasing the width and depth leading to a barrel-chested appearance. 12  Any mechanism preventing ventilation of the alveoli, whether as a result of airway occlusion by tissue, ﬂ uid, or solid material, or as a result of compression by an extrapul- monary mass, will result in a reduction in volume. Airways have to remain open during exhalation to expel air out of the lung parenchyma. Abnormal closure of the airways on exhalation traps air. Standard Examination: Three Recumbent View Study (R, L, and VD/DV) Lung assessment is best performed on thoracic radiographs captured during the inspiratory phase of respiration. Acquiring additional expiratory views can be useful for highlighting dy- namic airway collapse. 14 17 Right and left lateral recumbent views are mandatory for radiographic assessment of lung disease to mitigate the negative effect of recumbency on lung volume and aeration ( Fig. 36.7 ). Omission of one (left or right) of the lateral recumbent views may result in misdiagnosis. 18 A VD view is usually best for assessment of the accessory lung lobe, whereas a dorsoventral (DV) view may be indicated for dorsally located lesions or to evaluate the caudodorsal pulmonary vasculature. Description of Lung Lesions Interpretation of lung disease on thoracic radiography is chal- lenging and there are several reasons for this. 1. The lungs are surrounded by numerous soft tissue and osseous structures that become superimposed over the lungs and add opacity on radiographs. 2. The different conformations of dog breeds challenge what is considered normal for one breed while abnormal for another. 3. The degree of lung expansion in ﬂ uences its radiographic appearance. Subtle lung lesions may be missed in expira- tory radiographs. 4. Very few diseases, if any, have a pathognomonic radio- graphic appearance. It is common for diseases to share a few or even many radiographic ﬁ ndings. 5. The Use of Roentgen SignsNumber A single lesion is called focal or solitary . When two or more lesions are visible surrounded by unaffected areas in the lung, the term multifocal is used. Multifocal lesions can be found in different lung lobes or in a single lung lobe. Lesions involving the majority of a lung lobe/segment, with no evidence of unaffected areas, or with very little unremark- able lung, are ultimately diffuse . Although diffuse lesions often involve two or more lung lobes or segments, they can apply to lesions involving a single lung lobe or segment. Location/Position The position of a lesion should be described based on lung lobation. Anatomical landmarks such as the heart base, caudal vena cava, and trachea can also be used to describe the position of a lesion relative to another structure. The location of lesions has also been categorized according to three concentric zones relative to the hilum of each lung, the central or perihilar, middle and peripheral regions. There are a few diseases that tend to be more often associ- ated with speci ﬁ c lung lobes or a location. Pulmonary edema of cardiogenic or noncardiogenic origin tends to have a bilateral symmetrical or asymmetrical appearance localizing ﬁ rst to the hilar region, and more pronounced in the caudal lung lobes, although other locations and distributions, especially in cats, are possible ( Fig. 36.8 ). 19 Bronchopneumonia or aspiration pneumonia often localizes to the cranial or right middle lung lobes ( Fig. 36.9 ). The caudal lung lobes are a common site for primary lung tumors ( Fig. 36.10 ), while histiocytic sarcoma most commonly occurs in the left cranial and right middle lung lobes ( Fig. 36.11 ). 20 21 Size Circular or oval lesions are commonly reported according to their diameter. Circular or oval lesions with a diameter of < 3 cm are called nodules , while a lesion of or exceeding 3 cm is termed a mass ( Fig. 36.12 ). 13 20 22 The presence of numerous small punctate soft tissue nodules throughout the lungs has been described as miliary nodules ( Fig. 36.13 ). 23 Mineral opacity lesions and metallic objects can be detected even if they are very small ( w 1 mm). Digital radiography can today reliably depict soft tissue nodules of 2 to 3 mm in diameter. 24 26 However, some nodules may be dif ﬁ cult to identify or completely missed on radiography compared to computed tomography (CT), even if their size exceeds the minimum detection threshold. 24 26 Pulmonary vessels can sometimes be confused with pulmonary nodules when viewed in cross-section or, in other words, end on ( Fig. 36.14A ). End-on vessels are superimposed over a parent vessel, usually linearly oriented, of the same or greater diameter, and located next to an end-on bronchus. End-on vessels are larger near the hilar region and smaller as they move away towards the periphery. When in doubt, oblique views can help to compensate for a possible overlap with a vascular shadow and to con ﬁ rm the identi ﬁ cation of a nodule. Cellular in ﬁ ltration, connective tissue deposition, and ﬂ uid collection in the lungs will generally result in increased soft tissue opacity. Mineral or metallic opacity can be caused by deposition of mineral concretions, dystrophic or metastatic mineralization of lung tissue, or inhalation of foreign material of metallic or mineral. Differential diagnoses for mineralization of the airways or pulmonary parenchyma are listed in Table 36.1 It is not uncommon to see small ( w 1 2 mm), circular to oval, well-circumscribed, mineralized nodules in the lungs of dogs, especially the cranial lung lobes (see Fig. 36.14B ). 1 These opacities re ﬂ ect osseous metaplasia (synonyms: heterotopic bone formation, pulmonary osteomas) and, in this instance, are not clinically signi ﬁ cant. Broncholithiasis ( Fig. 36.15 ) and pulmonary alveolar micro- lithiasis represent additional conditions in which small mineral opacities are seen in the lungs. These rare disorders occur when calcium phosphate microliths collect in the airways or alveoli, respectively. The aggregates of micronodular calci ﬁ ca- tions in the alveoli may be more pronounced in the cranial lung lobes. 27 28 Mineralization of the bronchial walls, bronchial lumen (i.e., broncholithiasis ), pulmonary vasculature, or of unspeci ﬁ ed location has also been found in cats with mycobacterial in- fections, at diagnosis or during treatment follow-up. 29 Prior infection (i.e., inactive) associated with Histoplasma spp may result in pulmonary nodule(s) with mineralized foci and should not be mistaken for pulmonary metastases. 30 Rarely, metastatic neoplasia can result in mineralized lung lesions. 31 Differentiating osseous metaplasia nodules from metastatic nodules is of major clinical importance. In doubt, follow-up radiographs or CT examination are recommended. A metallic opacity found within the airways or in the pul- monary parenchyma is in all instances foreign. Aspiration of liquid barium sulfate or iodine-based contrast agents has the potential to ﬂ ow along the trachea and move downstream in the bronchial tree, after which it can collect in the parenchyma, if the amount is adequate. Serious complications associated with aspiration of large amounts of barium sulfate have been reported in dogs. 32 Metallic clips from prior lobectomy may also result in a small cluster of metallic opacities. Contour A lesion whose edges are sharp allowing easy distinction be- tween unremarkable and affected lung is said to be well cir- cumscribed with well-de ﬁ ned edges or clear margins. When it is dif ﬁ cult to outline a lesion, the edges of this lesion are poorly or ill-de ﬁ ned or blurred. 21 Distinction between benign and malignant lesions or between various types of lung tumors cannot be solely based on margin de ﬁ nition. 21 Lesions Localized to the Airways Involvement of large and medium-sized airways usually results in bronchial wall thickening , bronchial plugging, or bronchial dilation (i.e., bronchiectasis) Bronchial Pattern Bronchial wall thickening occurs as a result of edema, epithelial hypertrophy, glandular hyperplasia, smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, adventitial thickening, mucus coating the surface of the airway lumen, or cellular invasion by in ﬂ ammatory or neoplastic cells, or a combination of thereof. When viewed in a longitudinal plane, airway wall thickening may appear as tramlines or train tracks ( Fig. 36.16 , bottom left). When viewed end on, bronchial wall thickening will result in a “ ring-like ” appearance, or more commonly referred to as “ doughnut-like ” appearance (see Fig. 36.16 , bottom right). A clear demarcation of the bronchial wall is only possible if air surrounds both the external and internal wall outlines, providing contrast with the soft tissue component of the wall. Recognition of many thick-walled bronchi, whether located on one or more lung lobes/segments, is termed bronchial pattern ( Fig. 36.17 eFigs. 36.9 36.12 ). Lesions Localized to the Pulmonary Parenchyma Parenchymal lesions include abnormalities of the terminal res- piratory units including the alveoli (speci ﬁ cally the lumen of the alveoli), the interstitium (the septa bordering the alveolus), and the small vessels. Lesions affecting the pulmonary parenchyma may share a similar radiographic appearance regardless of eti- ology, chronicity, or anatomic structure affected. Several hy- potheses can be put forward to explain this ﬁ nding: 1. Radiography cannot distinguish between different types of cellular in ﬁ ltration, ﬂ uid collection, ﬁ brin and collagen de- posits, formation of small thrombi, or emboli. 2. There is a close spatial relationship between the alveolar lumen and the septa. 3. Many diseases affect all three components of the paren- chyma to varying degrees. Despite their names, interstitial and alveolar patterns may not always correlate to the same histopathological location of disease. 37 Diseases affecting small airways, small pulmonary veins (e.g., pulmonary veno-occlusive disease), or pulmonary capillaries may lead to recognition of a structured or unstruc- tured interstitial pattern on radiography. 38 39 As a precaution, it is therefore desirable to use the alveolar and interstitial patterns for descriptive terminology of lesions affecting the lung pa- renchyma, rather than true histological correlates. The Paradox of Aging Lungs Increased nonvascular linear markings in the lungs in associa- tion with pleural thickening and bronchial cartilage calci ﬁ ca- tion in dogs has previously been attributed to aging. 1 At the time, the authors attributed these markings to increased con- nective tissue, mainly focal alveolar ﬁ brosis, in lungs of old dogs associated with prior in ﬂ ammation. 1 Two recent studies found no differences in pulmonary lesions scores between young and old dogs on radiography or CT, although older dogs were shown to have increased bronchial mucosal irregularity, prominent vessels, and bronchiectasis on bronchoscopy. 43 It remains unclear whether these discordant ﬁ ndings are associ- ated with different environmental contexts, digitization of radiographic systems, or with the modality. It appears reason- able to suspect that as dogs live longer, they have a higher likelihood of accumulating structural lesions over time, possibly resulting in a subtle increase in nonvascular pulmonary mark- ings. It may then become dif ﬁ cult to differentiate these struc- tural lesions from clinically relevant active lesions. In these instances, advanced imaging (i.e., CT, bronchoscopy, positron emission tomography [PET]) and ancillary tests may be bene ﬁ cial. Alveolar Pattern The alveolar pattern is characterized by increased pulmonary opacity with effacement of vascular markings, air- bronchograms, and a lobar sign. Increased opacity is of no particular shape, showing ill-de ﬁ ned or wispy margins in com- parison to the surrounding parenchyma, rendering the pulmo- nary vessels within the affected area indistinct ( Fig. 36.27 ). These areas do not appear as discrete circular or oval shaped lesions, as these would often be categorized as belonging to a structured interstitial pattern. Affected parenchymal areas silhouette (i.e., border effacement) with adjacent soft tissue lesions or structures (i.e., cardiac silhouette, diaphragm, cranial me d ia st in um , pl eu ra l ﬂ u id ). Hypoperfusion Occlusion of a pulmonary artery by a thrombus, embolus, or both can result in perfusion de ﬁ cits of the terminal respiratory units beyond the blockage. Radiographic ﬁ ndings include an area of decreased opacity, or hypovascular pattern, in a pe- ripheral, middle, or central region, relative to the rest of the lung ( Fig. 36.30 ). 48 49 Abrupt truncation of a pulmonary artery may occasionally be detected. 48 Other radiographic paren- chymal manifestations include interstitial pattern, mixed interstitial-alveolar pattern, and an alveolar pattern, with the right lung being more affected than the left, and the caudal lung lobes being more commonly favored. Cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, and pneumothorax can also be seen. 50 Emphysema The term emphysema implies a destruction of alveolar septa with air freely escaping from alveoli, and dilated airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole as a consequence of in ﬂ ammation. 22 It has been reported histologically in lungs of dogs with inter- stitial ﬁ brosis, 1 pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, 27 and bron- cholithiasis. The amount of emphysema necessary for its radiographic detection is unknown. It is rarely observed in ca- nines and felines, but more frequent in cattle and humans. 1 Hyperin ﬂ ation and Air Trapping Hyperin ﬂ ation refers to an increase in lung volume exceeding that of a normal inspiration. In a conscious animal, it may be a fear response. In an animal under general anesthesia, increased lung volume may be a sequela of overin ﬂ ation. In both in- stances, the opacity of the lungs is associated with a homoge- neous decrease in radiopacity. Extension of the caudal boundaries of the lungs, ﬂ attening of the diaphragm, and cranial expansion of the rib cage may also be seen with hyperin ﬂ ation. Hyperin ﬂ ation may also occur as a compensatory mechanism when the ventilation of a lung lobe or segment is compromised or as a sequela of lobectomy. Air trapping refers to an excessive retention of air in the airspaces (i.e., respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs) and alveoli without destruction of the alveolar septa (see eFig. 36.4 ). 13 Severe lung hyperin ﬂ ation on radiography captured in inspiration and expiration in an animal showing expiratory efforts may be suggestive of air trapping ( Fig. 36.31 eFig. 36.20 ). Dogs who have aspirated in other positions than standing or sternal may have a different distri- bution of lung lesions. An alveolar pattern with air broncho- grams, a mixed interstitial-alveolar pattern, an interstitial pattern, or a mixed bronchial-interstitial-alveolar pattern is often seen with aspiration pneumonia (see Fig. 36.9 eFigs. 36.21 and 36.22 ). The number of lobes or segments affected is often limited, preferentially involving one or two lung lobes or seg- ments. Aspiration pneumonia may be complicated by second- ary bacterial pneumonia. Bacterial Pneumonia Bacterial pneumonia may occur secondary to impaired respi- ratory defenses, secondary to aspiration, respiratory viral infections, comorbid diseases, environmental stresses, and drug-induced immunosuppression or neutropenia. Bacterial pathogens responsible for community-acquired pneumonia in dogs are often opportunistic, whereas nosocomial pneumonia commonly involves multidrug-resistant and pathogenic bacte- ria. Bacterial pneumonia may be the result of canine infectious respiratory disease complex, in which multiple factors play a role. Lesions of bacterial pneumonia are often found in the cranioventral regions of the lungs, similar to aspiration pneu- monia, and characterized by a multifocal or focal alveolar pattern, or less commonly a mixed patchy unstructured inter- stitial and bronchial pattern ( Fig. 36.32 ). Of note, radiographic lesions may lag behind clinical and hematologic resolution of disease. Colonization of lungs by bacteria spreading from the blood circulation may have a different distribution of lesions with multifocal alveolar pattern or multifocal areas of consoli- dation or nodules that are not limited to the cranioventral re- gions of the lungs (see Fig. 36.24 ). Feline Asthma Hallmark features of asthma in cats include airway in ﬂ amma- tion, excessive mucus production, intermittent reversible airway obstruction, nonspeci ﬁ c airway hyperreactivity, and airway remodeling. The lack of airway or lung parenchymal radiographic changes does not rule out asthma. Cats with asthma may show a bronchial pattern (see Fig. 36.17 ). Exces- sive mucus production can lead to bronchial luminal plugging, which can lead to lung collapse and resorptive atelectasis (see Fig. 36.20 ). Chronic Bronchitis Chronic bronchitis is a common noninfectious in ﬂ ammatory disorder of middle-aged to older dogs of various breeds asso- ciated with a chronic cough ( > 2 months of duration), neutro- philic and/or eosinophilic airway in ﬂ ammation, mucus hypersecretion, and loss of ciliated epithelial cells. It is not uncommon for the underlying cause not to be identi ﬁ ed. Thoracic radiography and CT may be unremarkable in dogs with chronic bronchitis. When detected, lesions may include mild to severe thickening of the large and medium-sized airway walls, with or without bronchiectasis, resulting in a bronchial pattern ( Fig. 36.33A ). common. Epithelial lung tumors can be benign (papilloma and adenoma) or malignant. Various types of carcinomas (e.g., bronchial gland carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, etc.) have been described in the canine and feline lung, leading to a wide range of appearances on imaging. A single soft tissue opaque mass with or without smaller nod- ules or masses representing metastases are often identi ﬁ ed. Primary lung tumors in cats are often cavitated with a radiolu- cent center. Although any lung lobe can be affected, the larger pulmonary masses tend to occupy the caudal lung lobes (see Fig. 36.10 ). Central or perihilar masses are often of bronchial origin, whereas peripheral masses tend to arise from distal bronchiolar or alveolar epithelium. 2 Tracheobronchial lym- phadenomegaly may also be present concurrently. 55 Primary pulmonary histiocytic sarcoma (see Fig. 36.11 ) and neuroen- docrine tumors among other types can also be encountered. Histiocytic sarcoma tends to be more ventrally located than pulmonary carcinoma. In cats, pulmonary adenocarcinomas may spread to the digits, causing lameness, and leading to the so-called feline “ lung-digit syndrome. ” Osteolysis of the distal phalanx with potential extension to the distal interphalangeal joint and mid- dle phalanx with osteolysis and/or periosteal proliferation and soft tissue thickening are often seen. Pulmonary Edema Pulmonary edema consists in the abnormal accumulation of transudate ﬂ uid in the alveoli and interstitium as a consequence of elevated hydrostatic pressure, increased permeability of the alveolar wall, impaired lymphatic drainage, or other miscella- neous causes. It impedes lung function, obstructing gas ex- change at the alveolar level, among other processes. Left-sided heart disease and excessive intravenous ﬂ uid administration are common causes of pulmonary edema from elevated hydrostatic pressure and are described in Chapter 35 ( Fig. 36.36 eFig. 36.25 ). Pulmonary edema can occur secondarily to noncardiac causes, including anaphylactoid reactions, endotoxemia, diffuse alveolar damage, and within bacterial pneumonia lesions. Acute upper-airway obstruction (e.g., strangulation, foreign objects, airway collapse, laryngeal pathology), increased intracranial pressure from central nervous system derived trauma (e.g., cranial trauma, electric shock, seizures), hypo- proteinemia, impaired lymphatic drainage, and high altitudes can also cause pulmonary edema. 2 Bilateral symmetric or asymmetric interstitial, alveolar, or mixed interstitial-alveolar patterns, without increases in the caliber of the pulmonary vasculature, are commonly found with noncardiogenic pulmo- nary edema (see Fig. 36.8 ). 56 Lesions can be focal, multifocal, or diffuse, the latter less common, and the peripheral region of the lungs superseding the central lung region in terms of common distribution. 56 Radiographic changes do not appear to be correlated with survival. 56 Eosinophilic Lung Diseases Eosinophilic lung diseases represent a vast group of diseases of known (e.g., heartworm, fungal, bacterial, viral, drug reaction) and unknown (i.e., idiopathic) etiologies, affecting airways, parenchyma, or both. 2 In dogs, disease can be con ﬁ ned to the airways ( “ eosinophilic bronchitis ” ), to the parenchyma ( “ eosinophilic pneumonia ” ), or a combination of both ( “ eosin- ophilic bronchopneumopathy ” ). Eosinophilic lung diseases may have a wide spectrum of manifestations on radiography or CT, including the lack of detectable pulmonary lesions on radiography ( Fig. 36.37 ). Involvement of airways often leads to a bronchial pattern. Bronchial plugging with soft tissue opaci- ties may also be seen. 34 57 P a r e nc h y m a l i n v o l v e m e n t m a y m a n i f e s t a s p u l mo na r y n o d u l e s a n d / o r p u l m o n a r y ma s s e s , o f v a r i o u s s i ze s a n d l o ca - t i o n s , w i t h p r e f e r e n c e t o t h e c a u d a l l u n g l o b e s , a n d c a n c a u s e d i s p l a c e m e n t , o r p a r t ia l o r c o mp l e t e c o m p r e s s i o n o f n e a r b y b r o n c h i. 5 8 S o l i t a r y p u l m o n a r y ma s s e s w it h id io p a t h i c e o s i n o - p h i l i c l u n g d i s e a s e h a v e b e e n d e s c r ib e d . The absence of pulmonary contusions on radiographs taken immediately after trauma or progression of pulmonary dysfunction despite mild radiographic changes on the initial study may require repeating radiography as detectable imaging changes can be delayed. Cavities which can contain gas and/or ﬂ uid can also be seen ( Fig. 36.39 ). Radiography has a tendency to overestimate the severity of pulmonary contusions, and may not accurately re ﬂ ect the severity of pulmonary dysfunction. 60 Radiographs should also be carefully examined for concurrent traumatic injuries such as pneumothorax, hemothorax, fractures, luxation and subluxation, and hemoperitoneum. Pulmonary hemorrhage may also occur following non- traumatic causes such as bleeding disorders, rodenticide poisoning or other intoxication (e.g., copper sulfate powder), infection (e.g., leptospirosis, plague caused by Yersinia pestis, Angiostrongylus vasorum ), drugs including anticoagulants, thrombosis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, or neoplasia. Stephanie G. Nykamp RADIOG RAPH IC TECHN IQUE Technical aspects of radiographing the equine thorax are covered in Chapter 28 , but important principles are reiterated here. Radiographing the entire thorax of an adult horse requires a grid and large stationary x-ray tubes that are generally avail- able only at referral centers. Portable radiographic tubes require an excessively long exposure time to penetrate the adult tho- rax; this usually results in motion artifact, rendering the images nondiagnostic. The advantages of digital imaging are covered in Chapter 2 . The improved contrast of digital imaging is advan- tageous but the various processing algorithms from different systems can also increase the conspicuity of normal lung markings resulting in overinterpretation of the images. Digital images can have scatter correction in the processing algorithm but an antiscatter grid is still recommended for adult horses. 1 Four overlapping 14-inch 17-inch views are usually required to image the entire thorax of an adult horse. They are acquired in the craniodorsal, caudodorsal, caudoventral, and cranioventral aspects of the thorax ( Fig. 37.1 ). In addition to these standard views, radiographs centered over any identi ﬁ ed lesions may also be useful. Lateral radiographs of the foal thorax may be made with a single 14-inch 17-inch cassette and some portable x-ray tubes. Dorsoventral (DV) or ventrodorsal (VD) radiographs should also be acquired on foals whenever possible. The horse should be positioned with the thoracic limbs slightly forward to reduce the amount of muscle mass super- imposed on the cranial aspect of the thorax. Radiographs should be obtained during peak inspiration. In some instances, radiographs should also be obtained during expiration because a comparison of the degree of lung in ﬂ ation between inspiratory and expiratory radiographs may be helpful in the diagnosis of air trapping from chronic pulmonary disease. When thoracic radiographs are obtained in a standing horse, the lung closest to the cassette is seen most clearly. This occurs because the large width of the equine thorax results in the lung farthest from the cassette being magni ﬁ ed and blurred to the extent that even large lesions can be obscured. This is opposite to the situation in lateral radiographs of dogs and cats where lesions in the nondependent lung (i.e., farthest from the cassette) are seen most clearly because of the atelectasis that occurs in the dependent lung. In the horse, therefore, left-right and right-left radiographs are necessary to assess both the left and right lungs adequately in patients with pneumonia or neoplasia. Bilateral radiographs are less likely to impact the diagnosis in patients with diffuse or in ﬂ ammatory disease but as this is not known prior to imaging bilateral radiographs are recommended. 2 Radiographic exposure and degree of inspiration play an important role in the interpretation of thoracic radiographs and must be considered both for initial and serial radiographic ex- aminations. As the quality of the radiograph improves, the amount of perceived interstitial lung pattern decreases. 3 If a radiograph is underexposed or obtained during expiration, the lungs will appear diffusely more opaque than normal, mimicking a mild diffuse interstitial lung pattern often mistaken for disease. If the radiographs are overexposed, small or mild lung lesions may be obscured. Craniodorsal Projection The dorsal portion of the heart, descending aorta, caudal vena cava, hilar pulmonary arteries and veins, trachea, and carina are visible ( Fig. 37.2 ). The hilar portions of the lungs are visible but are dif ﬁ cult to evaluate because of the superimposition of the heart and blood vessels. Caudodorsal Projection This view provides the largest unobstructed view of the lungs ( Fig. 37.3 ). The normal equine lung has a mild diffuse bron- chointerstitial lung pattern when compared with canine and feline lungs. The pulmonary blood vessels should be seen clearly, tapering toward the periphery of the lung ﬁ eld. Caudoventral Projection The caudal borders of the heart, left atrium, caudal vena cava, pulmonary veins, and pulmonary arteries are evident on this view ( Fig. 37.4 ). A small triangle of lung bounded by the caudal vena cava, caudal border of the heart, and cranioventral aspect of the diaphragm is evident. Because of the cardiac notch, no pulmonary markings are present over the central portion of the heart. The absence of pulmonary blood vessels in this region should not be mistaken for lung consolidation. The ventral aspect of the caudal lung lobes is visible as a triangle of lung bordered by the caudal aspect of the heart, diaphragm, and caudal vena cava. ALTE RNATIV E IMAGING MODA LITIES Fluoroscopy is useful to evaluate esophageal disease, tracheal collapse, and the motion of thoracic masses. Unfortunately, ﬂ uoroscopy for equine evaluation is not available readily. 12 The use of ultrasound is common in equine practice. Air prevents the transmission of ultrasound waves, so the ultra- sound appearance of the normal lung is a bright interface with reverberation artifact characterized by equally spaced lines that parallel the surface of the lung ( Fig. 37.8 ). In real time, the normal lung slides along the body wall during respiration. Ul- trasound is more sensitive than radiographs in the detection of small pulmonary lesions as long as they extend to the pleural surface. 13 Ultrasound is the diagnostic test of choice for evalu- ating pleural disease in the horse because it is more sensitive to the detection of small amounts of ﬂ uid and provides informa- tion on the character of the ﬂ uid. 12 14 Ultrasound can also be used to assess the surface of the lung. A few areas of rough pulmonary surfaces that create a comet tail artifact can be seen in the ventral portions of the normal lung, but more extensive lesions will be present in horses with viral pneumonia and chronic pleural ﬁ brosis ( Fig. 37.9 ). 15 16 Ultrasound correlates well with radiographs and postmortem in cases of diffuse pul- monary disease such as acute interstitial pneumonia in foals. 17 Ultrasound is an inexpensive and accessible diagnostic test for serial monitoring for resolution or progression of disease. Point of care ultrasound as part of the routine physical examination is valuable in horses to detect pleural, pericardial, and peripheral pulmonary disease and is more readily available than radiographs.
