After the cranial pole of the right kidney is scanned in a sagittal plane, the transducer is moved medially to ﬁ nd the caudal vena cava. The right adrenal gland lies dorsolateral to the caudal vena cava and cranial to the renal vein. 46 The phrenicoabdominal veins cross the ventral surfaces of both adrenal glands and can occasionally be identi ﬁ ed with high-resolution transducers or by using color Doppler. The shape of the right adrenal gland of the dog is different from that of the left. The right has been described as having a comma- shaped or bent-arrow conformation. 110 Many large-breed dogs have adrenal glands with an elongated, thin shape. This is sus- pected to be a normal variant. Ultrasonographic determination of adrenal gland size has been used as an aid for evaluating dogs suspected of having hyperadrenocorticism and hypoadrenocorticism. A wide range of values (length, width, and thickness) have been reported in regards to normal adrenal gland size. The normal adrenal gland has been reported from 0.91 to 5.02 cm in length, from 0.19 to 1.74 cm in width, and from 0.17 to 1.07 cm in thickness. 33 111 114 Adrenal gland length is proportional to body weight, but the diameter (thickness or width) is not. 112 113 Therefore cross-sectional measurements are more valuable than length in the assessment of adrenal gland size. Adrenal gland thickness greater than 0.6 cm in small-breed and 0.74 cm on the left side and 0.81 cm on the right side in middle-aged to older large-breed dogs has been used as the criterion for maximum normal adrenal gland size. 104 115 However, adrenal gland mea- surements should not be used alone to diagnose abnormalities, because there is considerable overlap of adrenal size between normal versus abnormal dogs and variability of obtaining the measurements by observers. 116 The shape of the adrenal glands, the response of the patient to pituitary/adrenal axis testing, and the clinical signs must be correlated with the size of the adrenal glands when making a diagnosis. Computed Tomography of the Adrenal Glands CT is the most commonly used technique to evaluate the ad- renal glands in human patients. In dogs and cats, ultrasound is the most commonly used technique. In one study, incidental adrenal gland masses were identi ﬁ ed in 9.3% of dogs undergo- ing an abdominal CT examination, and these masses were more commonly noted in dogs older than 8 years of age. 117 The normal adrenal gland shape and size in CT images is similar to what has been reported in ultrasound studies. Normal adrenal glands have a homogeneous attenuation, which is similar in attenuation to the kidneys and similar in both adrenal glands. 118 119 The peak attenuation of adrenal glands in dogs after intravenous iodinated contrast medium injection is dependent on dose and timing. 119 The size and shape of the adrenal glands vary on CT images due to the position of the adrenal glands relative to the scan plane. Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Adrenal Glands The adrenal gland size and shape on magnetic resonance (MR) images are like that seen in ultrasound and CT images. The signal on fast-spin echo (FSE) sequences, including T2- weighted, T1-weighted, and T1-weighted after administration of a paramagnetic contrast medium, was homogeneous and hypointense to surrounding tissue or a corticomedullary type pattern with a hyperintense central area surrounded by a hypointense peripheral rim of tissue. The left adrenal gland was often easier to de ﬁ ne and more distinct. The demarcation of the right adrenal gland was more variable, especially if it was in contact with the liver or the caudal vena cava. 120 Abnormalities of the Adrenal Glands In cats and dogs, primary adrenal gland neoplasia causing clinical signs occurs rarely. Adrenal gland tumors comprise less than 1% to 2% of all canine tumors. Adrenal adenomas, ade- nocarcinomas, and pheochromocytomas are the most common lesions affecting the adrenal glands. 117 Hemangioma and mye- lolipomas have been described in the adrenal glands of dogs, but they occur rarely. 121 123 Malignant pheochromocytomas are the most aggressive adrenal gland tumors, with invasion of the adjacent vasculature noted in 20% to 93% of dogs and metastasis in up to 40% of dogs. 124 125 With the advancement of imaging techniques, adrenal masses are more commonly diagnosed incidentally, which can be a dilemma. 126 No current imaging modality can reliably differentiate benign from malignant adrenal gland lesions, and further evaluation of these patients for hypokalemia, hyper- tension, and loss of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal response to a low-dose dexamethasone stimulation test is recommended. 126 127 Increase in Size Radiography. Radiographically detectable adrenal gland enlargement may be caused by pheochromocytoma, cortical carcinoma, or adenoma. 128 An adrenal mass should be sus- pected when a soft tissue or partially mineralized mass is pre- sent craniomedial to a kidney ( eFig. 39.10 ). The kidney may be displaced caudolaterally by the mass. Large left adrenal masses may displace the fundus of the stomach cranially, the transverse colon caudoventrally, and the left kidney caudally ( eFig. 39.11 ). Masses of the right adrenal gland may be more dif ﬁ cult to detect radiographically than those of the left because of the position of the right adrenal gland near the liver. Functional adrenal car- cinomas and adenomas occur with equal frequency in the right and left adrenal glands; adrenal tumors occasionally occur bilaterally. 109 Functional adrenocortical carcinomas or ade- nomas are found in 10% to 20% of dogs with Cushing syndrome. 129 130 Dystrophic mineralization of adrenal tumors may occur ( Fig. 39.36 , see eFig. 39.10 ). 40 126 131 132 Radiographically visible adrenal calci ﬁ cation in dogs with Cushing syndrome is highly suggestive of neoplasia. In dogs with functional adrenal tumors, 92% and 54% of radiographically visible carcinomas and adenomas, respectively, were calci ﬁ ed. 109 In another study, adrenal calci ﬁ cation was found in 54% and 60% of carcinomas and adenomas, respectively. Carcinomas and pheochromocy- tomas may invade local tissues, including the caudal vena cava, and metastasize to the liver, lymph nodes, lungs, and kid- neys. 130 When adrenal carcinomas are advanced, it may not be possible to determine the origin of the primary mass lesion radiographically. In such an instance, the metastases may be the major radiographic ﬁ nding, although an ill-de ﬁ ned soft tissue mass may be present in the craniodorsal abdomen. Mineralization may occur in nonneoplastic adrenal glands ( Fig. 39.37 ), especially in cats. Adrenal gland dysfunction usually causes radiographically detectable changes. In patients with Cushing syndrome, this includes hepatomegaly, bronchopulmonary mineralization, dystrophic mineralization of the skin and other soft tissues, and adrenal gland enlargement with mineralization when functional tumors are present. Pulmonary arterial thrombosis also occurs in dogs with Cushing syndrome, but this is dif ﬁ cult to detect radiographically. 133 Ultrasound. The attenuation values of the adre- nal glands in normal dogs and dogs with PDH are similar. 119 In human patients, precontrast hypoattenuating nodular lesions were more likely to be adenomas, but the difference in atten- uation was less apparent in postcontrast images. Martha Moon Larson RADIOLO GY OF THE LIVER The liver is the largest solid organ in the abdomen. Changes in hepatic size, shape, location, and opacity are used to assess the liver for possible abnormality. 1 5 The liver is in the cranial aspect of the abdomen between the diaphragm, which delineates its cranial border, and the stomach, right kidney, and cranial portion of the duodenum, which de ﬁ ne the caudal extent. The liver is nearly entirely within the costal arch, with the caudal ventral border, composed of the left lateral liver lobe in the dog, extending just slightly beyond the costal arch. In dogs with a deep thoracic cavity, the liver lies more completely within the costal arch, whereas greater caudal hepatic extension is present in dogs with shallow, wide thoracic conformation. Abundant falciform fat, especially in cats, can result in dorsal displacement of the ventral aspect of the liver on lateral views ( Fig. 40.1 ). On ventrodorsal (VD) views, the liver is distributed symmetrically in dogs, but a larger portion is often right sided in cats ( Fig. 40.2 ). Hepatic shape may not be visible without suf ﬁ cient sur- rounding omental and falciform fat. The caudoventral hepatic margin protruding slightly from the costal arch should be rela- tively sharply marginated and triangular. It may protrude farther caudally in right lateral recumbent views, where it may merge with the spleen, blurring exact de ﬁ nition. If lateral views are slightly oblique, the liver can appear to have round margins, which should not be confused with hepatic enlargement. The gallbladder is located just to the right of midline, in the cranioventral portion of the liver, but is not visible normally because of silhouetting with the soft tissue of the liver ( Fig. 40.3 ). In some cats, the gallbladder can be seen on lateral abdominal radiographs as a curved structure protruding from the ventral liver margin (see Fig. 40.3C ). Hepatomegaly Hepatic enlargement can be detected radiographically, although mild size changes cannot be assessed accurately. The classic radiographic signs of generalized hepatomegaly are rounding or blunting of the caudoventral liver margins, along with extension beyond the costal arch, and caudal, and perhaps medial, displacement of the gastric axis ( Figs. 40.4 and 40.5 ). 5 7 Several nonpathologic conditions can result in extension of hepatic margins beyond the costal arch, including over- expansion of the thorax or deep inspiration ( Fig. 40.6 ). Older dogs and cats can have stretching or elongation of the triangular ligaments attaching the liver to the diaphragm, resulting in sagging and caudal extension of the liver. The same phenom- enon can occur in obese dogs with a pendulous abdomen. In the obese dog, the liver does not extend as far dorsally. Some brachycephalic and chondrodystrophic dogs have caudal extension of the liver because of it being aligned more hori- zontally compared with deep-chested breeds. In addition, neonatal and young dogs and cats have a larger liver size compared with body size, creating the appearance of hepato- megaly without a true hepatic abnormality ( Fig. 40.7 ). 1 8 Because of the numerous normal variations that can cause he- patic lobe extension beyond the costal arch, rounding or blunting of these lobes should also be present before hepato- megaly is concluded. Microhepatia As with subtle hepatomegaly, slight decreases in hepatic size are not identi ﬁ ed accurately radiographically. Marked micro- hepatia results in cranial displacement of the stomach and decreased distance between the diaphragm and gastric lumen ( Fig. 40.11 ). Hepatic atrophy due to a congenital portosystemic shunt and chronic hepatopathy such as ﬁ brosis or cirrhosis are the two most common causes of microhepatia. Diaphragmatic hernia with displacement of the liver cranial to the diaphragm can give the appearance of a small liver, but there will be intrathoracic abnormalities in this instance. Hepatic Opacity The normal liver is of soft tissue opacity. Mineral opacities can occur in the hepatic parenchyma or biliary system. 9 Choleliths should be considered when focal mineral opacities are visible in the area of the gallbladder ( Fig. 40.12 ). Linear trails of miner- alized opacities extending peripherally within the hepatic pa- renchyma are indicative of choledocholiths, or calculi within the bile ducts. 9 Biliary calculi are uncommon in dogs and cats but are visible radiographically if they contain suf ﬁ cient calcium (see Fig. 40.12 ). 10 13 Thes e are ofte n inci de ntal ﬁ ndi ngs , but cho led och oli ths can caus e bil iary obst ruct ion , espe cia lly in the cat . Mi nera liz atio n of the bil ia ry tree is seen occa si onal ly in dog s wi th bil e duc t carc ino ma. 14 Mi nera liza tio n of the gal lbl add er wal l has bee n asso cia ted with gal lbl add er carc ino ma, as well as cho lec yst itis or cys tic muc ino us hyp er plasi a (se e Fig. 40.3 A,B ). 13 Dystrophic calci ﬁ cation of hepatic granulomas, abscesses, hematomas, neoplastic masses, or areas of hepatic necrosis have been documented (see Fig. 40.9 ). Echinococcosis infec- tion can result in large hepatic soft tissue masses with miner- alization of varying patterns and should be considered in endemic areas. 15 Radiolucent areas within the liver are indicative of intra- hepatic gas, either in the biliary system, portal venous system, or hepatic parenchyma. Gas within portal vessels may occur because of severe necrotizing gastritis or enteritis, which is often associated with gastric dilation and volvulus complex. Gastrointestinal ulceration, distention, trauma, or interventional procedures may allow gas to ascend into the portovenous cir- culation ( Fig. 40.13A eFig. 40.3 ). 16 18 A linear, branching radiolucent appearance, similar to air bronchograms, may be visible. Gas in or around the gallbladder occurs with emphysema- tous cholecystitis, and this can be found in both diabetic and nondiabetic dogs. 19 20 Gas is seen initially in the gallbladder wall, followed by more complete ﬁ lling of the lumen (see Fig. 40.13B,C ). The gas eventually extends to the peri- cholecystic tissues. Gas bubbles conforming to the shape of the distended gallbladder can be seen within 24 to 48 hours of onset of disease. Obstruction of the cystic duct may be a common predisposing factor for emphysematous cholecystitis. Gas lucencies within the biliary system can also be seen after surgery of the duodenum or biliary system. COMPU TED TOMO GRAP HY OF THE L IVER Most common indications for computed tomography (CT) of the liver currently are vascular malformations and hepatic masses. Vascular Malformations Portosystemic shunts are congenital or acquired anomalies of the portal vasculature in which blood bypasses the liver and enters the systemic circulation directly. In the past, radio- graphic techniques have been used to identify and characterize the anomalous vessels, including cranial mesenteric portog- raphy, percutaneous splenoportography, and operative mesenteric portography. 23 26 CT angiography has largely replaced radiographic portography in the evaluation of porto- systemic shunts. 27 32 CT is minimally invasive and provides delineation of the portal vein and portal tributaries following intravenous injection of contrast medium ( Fig. 40.15 eFig. 40.4 ). Reformatted images in different planes or 3D ren- derings can be created to provide detailed evaluation of the vascular malformation, and aid in surgical planning. With dual- phase CT angiography, postcontrast images are acquired during calculated peak hepatic arterial and portal venous phases. Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT protocols have been used to evaluate patterns of contrast uptake of hepatic masses to help differentiate benign from malignant disease. 36 38 In triple-phase studies, postcontrast images are acquired at 13 to 20 seconds (hepatic arterial phase), 30 to 40 seconds (early portal venous phase), and 120 seconds (equilibrium or delayed phase) after injection. 36 37 In these studies, most hepatocellular carcinomas had heterogeneous enhancement in all phases, and were hypoattenuating compared to normal liver parenchyma in the portal and delayed phase ( Fig. 40.16 ). Metastatic lesions within the liver were homogeneous, with hypoattenuation compared to normal liver in all postcontrast phases. Benign hepatic adenomas had more diffuse enhancement in the he- patic arterial phase, with persistent enhancement in the portal venous phase. Finally, nodular hyperplastic lesions were ho- mogeneous, often with marked contrast enhancement in the hepatic arterial and portal venous phases, with isoattenuation compared to normal hepatic parenchyma in the delayed phase. In a similar study using dual-phase contrast imaging, with im- ages acquired within 30 seconds and at least 60 seconds post initiation of contrast administration, no CT features were signi ﬁ cantly associated with benign or malignant hepatic le- sions. 38 There appears to be enough overlap in the contrast enhancement pattern of benign and malignant lesions, that CT ﬁ ndings alone are not suf ﬁ cient to accurately predict the type of disease. ULTRA SOUND OF THE LIVER Ultrasound examination of the liver allows detailed evaluation of hepatic internal architecture, including the hepatic vascula- ture and biliary system. Ultrasound is also useful in guiding as- pirates and biopsies for nonsurgical, less invasive diagnoses. The liver can be imaged through a combination of subcostal, subxiphoid, and right and left intercostal windows. Intercostal windows may be the best way to evaluate the liver in a deep- chested dog, patients with gas-distended stomach, or in dogs with microhepatia. The right dorsal intercostal window allows excellent visibility of the porta hepatis, the caudate liver lobe, and the right kidney in many dogs. This window can also be used in cats but is not as often needed. Transducer frequencies ranging from 5 to 10MHz will accommodate most small animal patients. Transducers with smaller footprints are best for intercostal windows. Based on the individual scatter pattern, each abdominal or- gan has a characteristic texture and appearance. The liver has a moderately coarse texture and is usually hypoechoic to the spleen and, in cats, the falciform fat ( Fig. 40.17 ). 39 41 When using the right renal cortex for comparison to the caudate liver lobe, the liver may be isoechoic, or slightly hypoechoic or hyperechoic. The use of the renal cortex for comparison is therefore limited. The renal cortex of many normal cats is hyperechoic due to lipid deposition, and this should be considered before interpreting the liver as hypoechoic. 42 Assessment of echogenicity in any organ is subjective and any change should be correlated with the overall clinical picture. As with assessing echogenicity, the ultrasound assessment of liver size is subjective and based on operator experience, pa- tient conformation, and adjacent organs. A small liver is dif ﬁ cult to evaluate sonographically, because gas from a more cranial located stomach can obscure it. The gallbladder may appear large relative to overall hepatic size ( Fig. 40.19 ). Liver size may appear decreased in dogs with a deep thoracic cavity where liver location is more completely within the costal arch. Inter- costal ultrasound windows may be needed in these patients. The enlarged liver can be examined relatively easily with ul- trasound, because it extends well beyond the xiphoid cartilage and covers the right kidney more completely ( Fig. 40.20 ). Liver margins may appear rounded and may extend beyond the left lateral margin of the stomach. Hepatic and portal veins are visible routinely within hepatic parenchyma. Portal veins are smoothly tapering vessels char- acterized by bright, echogenic borders (see Fig. 40.17E ). 39 40 The larger left and smaller right branches originate from the main portal vein near the porta hepatis, although they branch in different imaging planes. Portal blood ﬂ ow courses normally from the hepatic hilus toward the periphery. Hepatic veins are anechoic linear structures extending through the parenchyma. Hepatic vein borders are not echogenic except at their con ﬂ uence with the caudal vena cava, immediately adjacent to the diaphragm. Hepatic venous ﬂ ow courses normally toward the hepatic hilus, into the caudal vena cava. In many dogs, the right lateral dorsal intercostal window provides an excellent window to the aorta, caudal vena cava, and main portal vein ( Fig. 40.21 ). Normal hepatic arteries are not visible without Doppler examination. The caudal vena cava courses through the liver in the right lateral abdominal quadrant. The hepatic artery is located between the caudal vena cava and portal vein, coursing cranially from the celiac artery. It may not be consis- tently identi ﬁ ed without Doppler ultrasound. The gallbladder is an oval, anechoic structure in the right cranioventral portion of the liver (see Fig. 40.17A ). Gallbladder size varies widely, and distention is normal in fasted or anorexic patients. Normal gallbladder volume in the dog is 1 mL/kg or less body weight, and it can be measured with the ellipsoid formula (length width height 0.52). 43 44 Cats may have a more uniform gallbladder volume of 2.4 mL, with no apparent association with body weight. 43 45 Intraluminal gallbladder contents are typically anechoic, although gallbladder sludge, which is dependent echogenic material without acoustic A S Fig. 40.14 Lateral abdominal radiograph of a dog with hepatic abscessa-tion. Abnormal Ultrasonographic Appearance of the Liver Ultrasound is helpful in differentiating between diffuse and focal hepatic disease in patients with hepatomegaly and/or elevated liver enzymes. Diffuse hepatic disease may cause no change in the ultrasound appearance of the liver. However, changes in hepatic echogenicity, increase or decrease in size, and irregular or rounded margins point to diffuse hepatopathy. 39 40 54 56 A hyperechoic liver is identi ﬁ ed by comparison with the echogenicity of an adjacent organ, such as being isoechoic or hyperechoic to spleen, or the in cats, the falciform fat. Loss or decreased conspicuity of the periportal echoes and abnormally increased attenuation of sound as it passes through the liver are indications of hyperechoic hepatic parenchyma ( Fig. 40.24 ). Several diffuse hepatopathies can potentially result in either a diffusely hyperechoic liver, or a mottled appearance (i.e., hyperechoic parenchymal back- ground with poorly de ﬁ ned hypoechoic nodules). 39 40 54 56 Vacuolar hepatopathies, including lipidosis and steroid hepat- opathy, are likely the most frequent diagnosis when this appearance is seen ( Fig. 40.25 ). However, a nonpathologic hyperechoic liver can be present in some obese cats, and ultrasound alone is likely insuf ﬁ cient for the diagnosis. 55 57 Chronic hepatitis with parenchymal ﬁ brosis can also cause increased echogenicity, although liver size is variable and may be normal, increased, or decreased. Hepatic cirrhosis typically results in a small, irregular, hyperechoic liver, often with numerous hypoechoic nodules ( Fig. 40.26 ). Ascites often accompanies cirrhosis secondary to portal hypertension. Other hepatic diseases that may result in increased/mottled parenchymal echogenicity include chronic hepatitis, lympho- sarcoma, amyloidosis, and cholangiohepatitis. In cats with cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis complex, the liver can appear normal, or hyperechoic, secondary to lipidosis; hypoechoic liver may also occur. 55 57 Mast cell in ﬁ ltration in the liver results in a variable appearance, from normal to increased echoge- nicity and size. Hypoechoic nodules may be present 58 59 ( Fig. 40.27 ). However, the sonographic appearance of the liver (and spleen) may be a poor predictor of cytologic mast cell in ﬁ ltration. 59 61 A decrease in hepatic echogenicity results in increased periportal echoes which is a somewhat subjective assessment. Decreased hepatic echogenicity may occur with hepatic congestion, lymphosarcoma, leukemia, amyloidosis, and chol- angitis/cholangiohepatitis. A dilated caudal vena cava and he- patic veins will accompany hepatic congestion. Acute suppurative hepatitis such as leptospirosis can cause hypo- echogenicity from in ﬂ ammation and edema. However, this may be uncommon, even with severe disease. 54 62 71 83 As noted previously, diffuse, even severe hepatic disease can appear normal ultrasonographically. Acoustic impedance of normal versus diseased tissue may simply be insuf ﬁ cient to permit visible change. 76 84 85 Any suspected hepatopathy should be compared with clinical signs and laboratory data, and a biopsy is necessary for de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. 63 66 Prebiopsy coagulation screening is a useful precaution when liver disease is suspected. Focal hepatic disease appears as a nodule or mass that differs in texture and echogenicity from surrounding normal liver pa- renchyma. They may interrupt the hepatic margin, resulting in change of shape or contour. Relatively small nodules can be detected, especially when using high-frequency transducers. Although ultrasound is sensitive for detecting hepatic nodules, it is not speci ﬁ c, and numerous considerations are possible for focal disease. Cysts, abscesses, primary or metastatic neoplasia, hematomas, granulomas, nodular hyperplasia, and focal extra- medullary hematopoiesis can all produce focal hepatic disease and may be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate on the basis of ultrasound appearance alone. 39 40 56 67 However, ultrasound is extremely useful in differentiating cystic versus solid masses; focal, multifocal, or diffuse distribution of masses; and the relation of the mass to adjacent structures, such as large blood vessels, diaphragm, or gallbladder. Hepatic neoplastic masses are variable in appearance, and they can be hyperechoic, hypoechoic, or of mixed echoge- nicity, solid, cystic, or cavitated ( Fig. 40.28 ). 68 80 The ultra- sound appearance is not speci ﬁ c for a particular tumor, and as in diffuse disease, there appears to be poor correlation to cytologic and histopathologic diagnosis. 39 40 55 56 58 60 67 81 83 A positive cytological diagnosis of neoplasia is often accurate, but a negative cytologic evaluation does not rule out neoplasia. 83 Primary hepatic tumors are classi ﬁ ed as massive (e.g., with a solitary mass affecting a single lobe), multifocal Fig. 40.26 Longitudinal ultrasound image of the liver in a dog withcirrhosis and ascites. Disease of the Biliary System Ultrasound is an important component in the diagnosis of gallbladder and bile duct disease, and in determining the cause of icterus. Abnormal wall thickness, luminal contents, obstruc- tion, and mass lesions may be diagnosed on ultrasound examination. Thickening of the gallbladder wall is a nonspeci ﬁ c sign found with primary gallbladder in ﬂ ammation or neoplasia, or nonbiliary diseases that have a secondary effect on the gall- bladder wall. 99 106 Wall thickening can appear double layered with a central hypoechoic layer between hyperechoic layers, or it may be diffusely thickened, irregular, and hyperechoic ( Fig. 40.35 ). Cholecystitis (in ﬂ ammation of the gallbladder) can be acute or chronic, and has nonspeci ﬁ c ultrasound changes, ranging from normal (no change) to hyperechoic, irregular thickening of the wall (see Fig. 40.35B ). 105 107 Sludge, both mobile and nonmobile, is often present. In one study, the ﬁ nding of immobile gallbladder sludge had a 70% sensitivity and 100% speci ﬁ city for the diagnosis of bactibilia and bacterial cholecystitis. 107 In a population of cats suspected to have hepatobiliary disease, cats with either/or a thickened gall- bladder wall or intraluminal sludge were 21 times more likely to have positive results of bacterial culture in bile. 108 Emphysematous cholecystitis, usually associated with a septic process and gas-forming bacteria, results in intraluminal echogenic foci and reverberation artifact. Percutaneous cholecystocentesis for culture and cytology of the intraluminal bile can be per- formed with care, although complications appear to be un- common. 108 109 Gallbladder wall thickening may be permanent because of in ﬂ ammation and ﬁ brosis despite resolution of the underlying disease process. 39 Cholecystoliths, or calculi within the gallbladder, are echo- genic focal structures, often with acoustic shadowing, and they may be single or multiple. 10 12 110 111 They are typically mobile, falling to the dependent portion of the gallbladder ( Fig. 40.36 ). Choledocholiths are stones within the bile duct, hepatic ducts, and interlobar ducts. 9 Although cholecystoliths and chol- edocholiths are frequently incidental, they have the potential to cause biliary obstruction. Choledocholiths located in the distal bile duct, in or around the duodenal papilla, are one of the more common causes of biliary obstruction in cats, and they are often associated with cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis as a co- morbidity. 111 112 In one study, a high prevalence of bacterial infection was noted in cats with cholelithiasis. 112 As noted earlier, intraluminal echogenic, nonshadowing, dependent, mobile biliary sludge is present in up to 66% of dogs undergoing routine ultrasound exam, and 35% to 48% of all dogs regardless of health status. 46 48 113 115 Canine dependent biliary sludge does not appear to change signi ﬁ cantly over time based on one study that followed asymptomatic canine patients for a 1-year period. 48 Another study noted that dogs with biliary sludge may have decreased gallbladder emptying compared to dogs without sludge. 47 It is hypothesized that decreased emptying may predispose to gallbladder mucocele formation secondary to biliary stasis, bile inspissation, and increased mucus accumulation. 47 48 Despite a high prevalence in asymp- tomatic dogs, biliary sludge may not be a completely benign process. 48 105 107 116 Nondependent biliary sludge may repre- sent a risk factor for development of a biliary mucocele, particularly in predisposed breeds. 117 Prevalence of biliary sludge in cats undergoing abdominal ultrasound ranges from 14% to 44%. 118 119 While one study indicated sludge was pre- dictive of increased liver enzymes and total bilirubin, a second study showed no increase, although gallbladder wall thickening was signi ﬁ cantly associated with gallbladder sludge. 118 119 Gallbladder emptying can be determined by measuring gallbladder volume pre and post feeding. Gallbladder distention may be minimal in the face of chronic in ﬂ ammation and ﬁ brosis. Progressive dilation of the common bile duct and hepatic ducts occurs during the next 3 to 4 days with dilation of lobar and interlobar ducts by 7 days. This results in multiple tortuous, irregularly branching anechoic linear tracks within the liver. These can be differen- tiated from hepatic vessels with Doppler interrogation (see Fig. 40.38B ). Pancreatitis is one of the most common causes of EHBO in the dog, with choledocholithiasis or neoplasia of the liver, bile duct, pancreas, or duodenum also capable of causing obstruction ( Fig. 40.39 ). 139 Tumors and in ﬂ ammation of the bile duct, pancreas, and duodenum, along with choledocholithiasis, are more commonly noted in the cat (see Fig. 40.39A,B,D ). 111 In 30 cats with EHBO, gallbladder disten- sion was present in only 43%, and it was not considered a reliable indicator of biliary obstruction. RADIOLO GY OF THE SPLEEN The spleen is a dynamic organ; and in the dog, the size and location of the spleen can vary widely. There are numerous variations on the radiographic appearance of the normal spleen in dogs and to a lesser extent in cats. 1 3 The spleen is divided into a dorsal extremity, termed the head of the spleen; a body; and a ventral extremity, termed the tail of the spleen. The dorsal extremity is relatively ﬁ xed in the left craniodorsal aspect of the abdomen. The ventral extremity is not ﬁ xed, and in the dog, the position of this portion of the spleen can vary considerably. On VD views of the canine abdomen, the dorsal extremity of the spleen is seen typically as a triangular soft tissue opacity caudolateral to the gastric fundus and cranio- lateral to the left kidney ( Fig. 40.43A ). The remainder of the spleen may extend caudally, adjacent to the left lateral abdominal wall, or more medially across the midline. When the spleen extends medially, the full length of the spleen is not visualized completely. On lateral views, the triangular soft tissue opacity of the dorsal extremity of the spleen is located dorsally, caudal to the stomach. The ventral extremity typically is a triangular soft tissue opacity immediately caudal and slightly ventral to the pylorus or liver (see Fig. 40.1A ). The ventral extremity of the spleen is often more conspicuous on right lateral views of the abdomen but may silhouette the caudal margin of the liver and be poorly delineated. The feline spleen is thinner and smaller compared with the canine spleen and less variable in size and position (see Fig. 40.43B ; also see Fig. 40.1C ). Like the dog, the dorsal ex- tremity of the spleen is seen on VD views in the left cranial abdomen, caudolateral to the stomach and craniolateral to the left kidney. On VD views, the ventral extremity usually extends caudally along the left lateral abdominal wall, but the amount of visible spleen varies with body fat, positioning, gastric contents, and splenic position. 151Fig. 40.42 Ventrodorsal (VD) radiograph of the abdomen of a cat in theregion caudal to the spleen. Splenic Size Radiographic assessment of splenic size in the dog is very subjective, because normal size varies widely. Feline splenic size appears to be more consistent. Splenomegaly in the cat should be considered if the ventral extremity is visible on the lateral projection of the abdomen. 151 In the dog, and to a lesser extent in the cat, generalized splenomegaly results in thick- ened, rounded, blunted margins, and dorsal and caudal displacement of the jejunum on lateral views ( Fig. 40.44 ). The jejunum may be displaced to the right or left, whereas an enlarged dorsal extremity results in cranial displacement of the stomach. Considerations for diffuse splenomegaly are numerous and include in ﬂ ammation caused by infection with toxoplasmosis, fungal organisms, Mycoplasma haemofelis, ehrlichiosis, hyperplasia (e.g., hemolytic disorders), systemic lupus erythe- matosus, chronic bacteremic disorders, congestion (e.g., from impaired venous drainage), portal hypertension, splenic tor- sion/infarction, anesthetic drugs, in ﬁ ltrative disease (e.g., primary and metastatic neoplasia), and extramedullary hematopoiesis. 152 155 Lymphosarcoma, leukemia, systemic mastocytosis, multiple myeloma, and malignant histiocytosis can all result in diffuse neoplastic splenic enlargement. ULTRA SOUND OF THE SPLEEN The spleen is well suited to ultrasound examination because of the super ﬁ cial location and lack of intervening gas-containing structures. Higher-frequency transducers may be used because of the super ﬁ cial location. Splenic location varies. The dorsal extremity of the spleen is in the left craniolateral abdominal quadrant and may be beneath the costal arch. Intercostal windows are sometimes necessary in deep-chested dogs. The canine splenic body and ventral extremity may extend caudally along the left lateral abdomen or move medially across the ventral midline. It often appears fol- ded on itself. The feline spleen is more consistent in location, along the left lateral abdominal wall, and rarely folds on itself unless enlarged. The splenic parenchyma has a uniform echotexture with a ﬁ ne, dense pattern. 167 168 Echogenicity of the canine spleen is slightly greater than the liver ( Fig. 40.48 ). Splenic margins are linear and smooth, with mild indentations noted along the mesenteric border where splenic veins exit. Splenic arteries are not usually seen without Doppler interrogation. Tissue sur- rounding splenic veins at the hilus may be highly echogenic normally because of capsular invagination and fat. 167 When enlarged, the spleen may extend caudally or more completely cover the ventral abdomen. Splenic borders become rounded or blunted, or appear to bulge from the capsule, compared with the normal sharp, linear appearance ( Fig. 40.49 ). The spleen has no absolute size limits in the dog. The normal feline spleen is less variable in size than the dog, and objective measurements have been determined. Mean splenic height, measured in the transverse plane, in the prox- imal third of the spleen, adjacent to a splenic vein, is 7.1 mm, with a range from 5.1 to 9.1 mm (see Fig. 40.48C ). 169 Similar splenic measurements were determined in a second study, where normal feline splenic height was 8.2 1.4 mm (range: 5.3 11.1 mm). 170 Abnormal Splenic Ultrasonographic Findings Diffuse Disease As in the liver, diffuse splenic disease potentially causes changes in size, shape, or echogenicity. Lymphoid hyperplasia can also have a diffuse mottled appearance. Splenic congestion as a result of a phenothiazine and pentobarbital drug group results in splenomegaly with no associated change in echogenicity in the dog. 170 Acepromazine has a similar appearance in the cat. 159 Congestion from portal hypertension appears similar, but dilated splenic veins may also be present. Echogenic areas with shadowing within the mass may indicate gas formation ( Fig. 40.56 ). Myelolipomas are fatty, hyperechoic nodules occasionally seen in the normal spleen, especially along the peripheral margin or adjacent to vessels ( Fig. 40.57 ). 179 180 Splenic myelolipomas are benign incidental ﬁ ndings but can be quite large. Rarely, mast cell tumors have been reported to cause hyperechoic nodules in the spleen. 157 The echogenicity of focal splenic infarction changes over time. Initially, infarcts are hypoechoic and may appear as a well- demarcated round or bulging mass or simple focal enlargement of the spleen ( Fig. 40.58 ). 162 With age, infarcts become increasingly echogenic and often are demarcated sharply from the normal splenic parenchyma. With color Doppler interro- gation, there is a lack of blood ﬂ ow in the infarcted area. Nodular lymphoid hyperplasia in the spleen has a similar appearance to that in the liver, and it is likely the most common abnormality of the spleen identi ﬁ ed on ultrasound. 39 The splenic border may simply be smoothly irregular or isoechoic; hypoechoic or hyperechoic nodules may be present. Hyper- plastic nodules can be quite large and complex. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can appear as hypoechoic, hyperechoic, or mixed echogenicity nodules and/or masses (see Fig. 40.52 ). As in the liver, splenic ultrasound is sensitive but not speci ﬁ c for both diffuse and focal splenic disease, with a large amount of overlap between normal and diseased spleen and between various splenic diseases. A normal ultrasound appearance does not rule out disease. Gabriela S. Seiler  Ryan Appleby R enal disease is common in dogs and cats, and imaging is an integral part of the diagnostic workup of these pa- tients. Multiple imaging modalities are available to evaluate the kidneys and ureters, and the modality to select depends on the type of information desired. In this chapter, the indications, technique, and normal imaging ﬁ ndings, as well as the imaging appearance of diseases of the upper urinary tract, are reviewed. NORM AL ANA TOMY AND IMAG ING PROC EDUR ES Radiography Indications Radiographs are often obtained in the diagnostic workup of patients with abdominal disease, and interpretation of the radiographic appearance of the kidneys is an important skill. Radiographs are useful to identify broad changes in the roent- gen signs (size, number, shape, opacity, location, margination) associated with the kidneys and ureters as well as to detect associated retroperitoneal or bone disease. Survey radiographs are indicated if there is a history of trauma to the abdomen or pelvis with possible involvement of the urinary tract or if a dorsal abdominal mass is suspected. Survey radiographs are an essential part of any abdominal radiographic procedure involving contrast medium. Technique A diagnostic radiographic study of the abdomen and kidneys should always include both left and right lateral as well as ventrodorsal (VD) views of the abdomen. Patient rotation should be minimized as even mild rotation may dorsally or medially displace one kidney and superimposition with the spine reduces visibility. Right lateral radiographs provide more longitudinal separation between the right and left kidney. 1 Suspected ureteral calculi can be separated from gastrointes- tinal content by use of oblique projections or compression techniques. Feces may have to be eliminated, by means of fasting or an enema, prior to a radiographic study to evaluate the distal ureters. Normal Radiographic Findings The kidneys are located in the retroperitoneal space and out- lined by surrounding fat. Canine kidneys are oval ( Fig. 41.1 ). The cranial pole of the right kidney is often poorly visible, because it abuts and sil- houettes with the caudate lobe of the liver. The left kidney is more mobile than the right, and it can be located relatively ventrally in animals with a large amount of retroperitoneal fat. In the VD projection, the right kidney is located at the level of the 13th rib but is often obscured by liver and other super- imposed abdominal organs, whereas the left kidney is normally visible caudal to the gastric fundus and caudomedial to the proximal extremity of the spleen at the level of L1-L3. Feline kidneys are more rounded and are located typically between L1 and L4, either at the same level or with the right kidney in a more cranial position ( Fig. 41.2 ). In lateral radio- graphs, the caudal pole of the right kidney may overlap the cranial pole of the left kidney and the summation of the two poles can give the false impression of a small rounded kidney or a retroperitoneal mass (see Fig. 41.2A ). An ectopic kidney or kidneys in a very caudal location occur sporadically. 2 Normal ureters are not visible radiographically. Small kidneys are indicative of chronic disease, whereas large kidneys are associated with more acute processes. In general, assessment of renal length is more reliable on VD projections because there is no overlap of the kidneys, and magni ﬁ cation of both kidneys is equal. Renal length in normal dogs ranges between 2.5 and 3.5 times the length of L2. 3 In cats, the normal renal length has been measured to be 2.4 to 3.0 times the length of L2. 4 Older cats without signs of renal disease can have smaller kidneys (1.9 2.6 times the length of L2); however, it is dif ﬁ cult to know whether subclinical renal dis- ease may have been present in these cats. 4 Hormonal in ﬂ uence depending on reproductive status alters renal length in cats, both in males and females. Intact cats tend to have larger kid- neys (range 2.1 3.2 times the length of L2) than neutered cats (1.9 2.6 times the length of L2). 5 It is important to realize that these normal relationships were determined from a relatively small number of cats and are only intended as guidelines. Normal kidneys are of uniform soft tissue opacity and smoothly marginated, although fat deposition in the renal pelvis in cats can lead to focal central radiolucency (see Fig. 41.2A ). Mineralization associated with the kidneys or ureters is always abnormal, although it may not necessarily be the cause of clinical signs. Ultrasonography Indications Ultrasonographic evaluation of the renal parenchyma is indi- cated if there is evidence of renal dysfunction. Speci ﬁ c in- dications include clinicopathologic abnormalities (azotemia, elevated symmetric dimethylarginine [SDMA], change in urine speci ﬁ c gravity), abnormal renal palpation or abdominal radio- graphic ﬁ ndings, and clinical signs such as hematuria, polyuria, oliguria, or anuria. Renal ultrasound may serve as a screening tool for congenital renal diseases such as aplasia, hypoplasia, dysplasia, and polycystic kidney disease. 2 6 7 Although ultraso und ﬁ ndings are usually not disease s pe- ci ﬁ c, they all ow diffe rentia ting acute and chro nic renal changes, mass le sions, cysts, miner alizatio ns, and alt erations of the collecti ng system and ureters. Nee dle aspi rates or biop sies can be ob tained under ultraso und gu idance. 8 9 Dopp ler ultra- sound is a useful addit ion to the grayscale ultraso und exam i- nation to evalu ate for abnor mal renal perfusio n cau sed by infarct ion, tra nsplant rejec tion, or mas s le sions. 10 Contrast - enhance d ultraso und allows more detaile d and more sens itive assessme nt of renal vasc ulature and per fusion, and normal perfusio n para meters have been described in dogs and cats. 11 12 Contrast -enhan ced ultraso un d of the can ine and feline kidney has potent ial for del ineation of renal parenchymal lesions s uch as mas ses or infar cts. 13 14 Technique Renal ultrasound should be performed with the highest fre- quency transducer that enables adequate penetration. In most dogs and cats, 7.5 to 15 MHz is appropriate; 5 MHz or lower frequency transducers should only be used in large dogs. Sub- costal or intercostal windows with the patient in lateral or dorsal recumbency allow access to the kidneys, depending on patient size and thoracic conformation. Standard image planes include dorsal ( Fig. 41.3A ), sagittal (see Fig. 41.3B ), and trans- verse (see Fig. 41.3C ) planes, always followed by fanning the transducer through the entire kidney. Renal length should be measured along its maximal pole-to-pole length in a sagittal or dorsal plane image, while avoiding obliquity which would result in arti ﬁ cial shortening of the kidney. The renal pelvis is best evaluated in dorsal and transverse planes. The ureters can be followed caudally from the renal pelvis if dilated. To verify patency and normal location of the ureterovesical junction, the bladder should be evaluated for presence of two urine jets from the dorsolateral bladder wall. If not seen with conventional grayscale imaging, Doppler ultrasound can be used to better delineate the jet. Addition of a diuretic markedly improves frequency and visibility of ureteral jets by increasing urine production and altering the speci ﬁ c gravity of the urine exiting the ureterovesicular junction compared with the urine already present in the bladder. 15 BA Fig. 41.2 Lateral (A) and ventrodorsal (VD; B ) radiographs of the abdomen of a normal cat. Excretory Urography and Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography Indications Intravenous administration of iodinated contrast medium, fol- lowed by imaging either with radiography (excretory urog- raphy [EU] or intravenous pyelography) or computed tomography (CT) allows assessment of renal structure and vascularity, patency of the collecting system, and to some de- gree, renal function. The use of EU has decreased but it can still provide useful information. CT has the advantage of imaging the urinary tract without superimposition of other soft tissue or osseous structures, with the option of multiplanar and three- dimensional reconstructions. Indications for EU or CT include urinary tract trauma, hematuria, suspected ureteral ectopia, assessment of retroperitoneal masses, and in some instances, ureteral obstruction. Dual-phase renal angiography can be performed to assess the arterial and venous blood supply of the kidneys separately. This is used mainly for presurgical assess- ment of feline kidney donors. 23 24 While both methods allow a crude estimation of renal functionality, it is possible to calculate glomerular ﬁ ltration rate in dogs and cats using contrast- enhanced CT imaging. 25 27 This has to be weighed against the fact that administration of contrast medium itself poses a risk in the presence of renal disease. Adverse reactions to the intravenous administration of iodinated contrast media include nausea, vomiting, hives, hy- potension, and importantly, contrast medium induced renal failure. Renal insuf ﬁ ciency is a risk factor for development of contrast medium induced nephropathy, together with the presence of hypovolemia. 10 11 28 29 Contraindications therefore include anuric renal failure, dehydration, hypotension, and known hypersensitivity to iodinated contrast media. Technique Patient preparation is a key to obtaining a diagnostic study. Food, but not water, should be withheld for at least 12 to 24 hours before the study. A cleansing enema can be used to evacuate the colon, preferably several hours before the study to allow fecal material and gas to pass. This is more important for EU where superimposition with a full colon may render the study nondiagnostic. The patient should be hydrated and have adequate renal function. Because iodinated contrast medium leads to increased urine-speci ﬁ c gravity and may also inhibit bacterial growth for at least 24 hours, urinalysis should be performed before contrast medium is administered. 30 Sedation or general anesthesia is recommended for both studies, and an intravenous catheter should be in place throughout the study to provide venous access if complications arise. Survey radiographs or CT images prior to contrast me- dium administration are an essential part of both studies as small urinary calculi and parenchymal mineralizations may be obscured by the contrast medium. Excretory urography : Iodinated contrast medium is admin- istered intravenously as a bolus injection at a dose of 600 to 700 mg iodine (I) per kg body weight. 13 14 VD and right lateral abdominal radiographs are acquired immediately after injection and are repeated typically after 5, 20, and 40 minutes or until a diagnosis is reached. Oblique projections for better visualiza- tion of the ureters can be added at 5 minutes and later time points. To evaluate the renal arteries, a VD radiograph should be acquired 5 to 7 seconds after bolus injection of contrast medium. Computed tomography : Iodinated contrast medium is administered intravenously as a bolus at a dose of 400 to 800 mg I/kg body weight. Image series are acquired to evaluate the different phases of contrast medium excretion as outlined later. Optimal ureteral opaci ﬁ cation occurs 3 minutes post injection and can persist for about 1 hour. 31 Image series may have to be repeated several times to visualize the entire course of both ureters because of ureteral peristalsis. Positioning the patient in sternal recumbency with the pelvis elevated is helpful in out- lining the ureterovesical junctions, because the contrast me- dium will accumulate in the bladder apex away from the neck, facilitating the distinction between the contrast medium ﬁ lled ureters and the bladder neck. Normal Imaging Findings For iodinated contrast medium to be excreted normally by the kidneys, normal arterial and venous ﬂ ow, an anatomically normal kidney, functioning nephrons, and unobstructed ﬂ ow of urine away from the kidneys into the urinary bladder are necessary. There are three phases of contrast medium excre- tion. The vascular phase starts approximately 5 to 7 seconds after intravenous bolus injection. In the nephrogram phase, contrast medium is present in the renal parenchyma through glomerular ﬁ ltration into the nephrons. The nephrogram phase begins after approximately 10 seconds and lasts up to 2 minutes until the pyelogram phase starts and the nephrogram begins to fade ( Fig. 41.4 ). Nephrogram opacity/attenuation should continue to decrease progressively; only approximately 25% of normal dogs still have a detectable nephrogram 2 hours after contrast medium injection. 32 In the pyelogram phase, contrast medium is ﬁ ltered into the collecting system without tubular reabsorption or secretion. Normal renal imaging on CT has been reported in dogs where the normal renal length to L2 vertebral body ratio in CT imaging was determined to be 2.7 (95% con ﬁ dence interval [CI], 2.5 2.9), and the renal length to aortic ratio was 7.4 (95% CI, 7.07 7.74). 33 42 If renal function is normal, the col- lecting system is consistently more opaque/attenuating than the renal parenchyma. The normal renal pelvis is curvilinear and less than 2 mm in width. The pelvic diverticula may be seen in some dogs and most cats and appear as thin (1 mm) spikes radiating from the pelvis toward the periphery. Neither the renal pelvis nor the diverticula should have blunted, rounded edges. The ureters tend not to be ﬁ lled with contrast medium uniformly throughout their length because of ureteral peri- stalsis. Imaging, therefore, may have to be repeated to assess the entire length of the ureters. Normal ureters are not more than 2 to 3 mm in width. They terminate at the dorsal aspect of the bladder neck, where they curve cranially for a short dis- tance before entering the wall. The duration and intensity of the opaci ﬁ cation of the kidney during an excretory urogram depend on the dose of contrast medium administered; renal perfusion; glomerular ﬁ ltration; tubular reabsorption of water; the patient s hydration status, which is important to maintain adequate renal perfusion; and patency of the renal out ﬂ ow tract. Antegrade Ultrasound-Guided Pyelography Indications Ultrasound-guided injection of contrast medium into the renal pelvis leads to excellent opaci ﬁ cation of the collecting system because the contrast medium is not diluted, and its concen- tration in the collecting system is not dependent on renal function. This procedure can be performed in azotemic pa- tients without loss of image quality. In addition, each renal pelvis and ureter can be assessed individually. Other advantages include the lack of systemic contrast medium reactions and collection of urine directly from the renal pelvis for urinalysis and microbiologic testing. The main indication for this pro- cedure is suspected ureteral obstruction. Contraindications include coagulopathies, because some hemorrhage may occur. Adverse effects may be signi ﬁ cant and include hemorrhage, focal damage of renal tissue, and spread of infection in the presence of pyelonephritis or pyonephrosis with perirenal sepsis and abscessation. Contrast medium may also leak into the retroperitoneal space. 34 Loss of renal function secondary to the 840 S E C T I O N V  Abdomi nal Cavity: Canine and Fe line

procedure is minimal but should be a consideration in patients with already severely compromised renal function. Technique Heavy sedation or general anesthesia is necessary. The skin is prepared aseptically, and a 22- to 25-gauge needle connected with an extension set and three-way stopcock is introduced into the renal pelvis under ultrasound or ﬂ uoroscopic guidance. Depending on the size of the renal pelvis, 1 to 2 mL of urine is removed for laboratory testing. Nonionic iodinated contrast medium equivalent to half of the volume of urine removed is then introduced slowly, and the size of the renal pelvis is monitored with ultrasound or ﬂ uoroscopy. 34 Overdistention of the renal pelvis should be avoided, because rupture may occur. Immediately after contrast medium injection, VD, oblique, and lateral abdominal radiographs are acquired. If bilateral abnor- malities are suspected, the procedure can be repeated on the contralateral side. Normal Imaging Findings The renal pelvis becomes distended with mild blunting of the pelvic diverticula, as contrast medium is introduced under mild pressure. If the ureter is patent, contrast medium should appear in the urinary bladder almost immediately ( Fig. 41.5 ). Narrow- ing of the ureter may be observed because of peristalsis; repeat images will be needed to differentiate between peristalsis and stricture. Magnetic Resonance Imaging Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used in people to assess renal diseases, perfusion, and function, but little work has been performed in small animals. Advantages and indications are similar to those described for CT, but use is limited by cost, availability, and duration of the imaging studies. Protocols for magnetic resonance angiography of the renal vasculature in renal transplant donors are available. 35 Scintigraphy Compared with other nonimaging renal function testing, renal scintigraphy using technetium-99m diethylenetriamine penta- acetic acid has the advantage of being able to determine the relative contribution of each kidney to total renal function. This is especially important in patients with impaired renal function before planned nephrectomy. Describing the technique of renal scintigraphy is beyond the scope of this chapter, and readers are referred to another source. 36 RENAL DISE ASES Abnormal Renal Size It is important to keep in mind that renal size and shape may be normal in the presence of renal disease. In particular, early chronic, acute toxic, in ﬂ ammatory, or infectious nephropa- thies, as well as amyloidosis, do not always lead to alteration of renal size or shape. 37 Small Kidneys Reduced renal size is most commonly caused by chronic ne- phropathy. Chronic renal disease is also associated with other radiographic ﬁ ndings that may include abnormal, irregular shape due to cortical infarcts, and renal mineralizations ( Fig. 41.6 eFig. 41.1 ). Other differentials of bilaterally reduced renal size include congenital anomalies such as dysplasia or hypoplasia. 7 Renal atrophy is seen with chronic, longstanding ureteral obstruction and is thus usually associated with hydro- nephrosis; the affected kidney (typically only one) can thus be reduced or relatively normal in size. Abnormal Renal Structure Diffuse Parenchymal Abnormalities Renal structure is evaluated best with ultrasound. Because of the large variability in normal renal size, architecture, and echogenicity, subtle changes in renal structure are not always detected. In fact, it is common for patients with acute kidney injury and glomerulonephritis to have normal appearing kid- neys on ultrasound. 40 Chronic Nephropathies. Chronic tubulointerstitial in ﬂ amma- tion and ﬁ brosis are the predominant histopathologic ﬁ ndings in chronic kidney disease, regardless of the underlying cause. On ultrasound, infarcts appear as wedge-shaped, hyperechoic areas in the cortex with an associated cortical defect. The appearance of infarcts has also been described on CT where they appear as a hypoattenuating region following contrast enhancement. They are often wedge shaped and are sometimes associated with ﬂ attening or depression of the adjacent cortical margin. 41 Parenchymal atrophy, infarction, and ﬁ brosis can result in distortion of the shape of the renal pelvis. Reduced cortical thickness has been associated with reduced renal function in cats. 42 The type of underlying renal disease cannot usually be determined at this stage. Renal dysplasia is usually diagnosed late in the disease process and changes in the kidneys resemble those from any other chronic renal disease. 43 61 Acute Nephropathies. Ultrasonographic ﬁ ndings associated with acute kidney injury leading to acute tubular necrosis, interstitial nephritis, or glomerulonephritis include renal enlargement, subcapsular or perirenal effusion, and cortical hyperechogenicity. In severe or advanced disease, the medul- lary echogenicity increases as well, leading to reduced corti- comedullary distinction. Acute kidney injury in dogs and cats has many causes, including toxins (e.g., ethylene glycol, lily in cats, and grapes in dogs), bacterial, protozoal, and rickettsial infections (e.g., leptospirosis, babesiosis, Lyme disease, pyelo- nephritis), drugs, hypercalcemia, sepsis, ischemia, multiple or- gan dysfunction syndrome, pancreatitis, and hyperviscosity. 44 It is usually not possible to determine the cause of acute kidney injury by ultrasound, and biopsy may be needed. The Doppler examination of renal vasculature with calculation of the resis- tive index may add some information. For example, elevation of the renal resistive index is seen with active tubulointerstitial or vascular disease; however, it remains a nonspeci ﬁ c param- eter. 45 Ethylene glycol toxicity leads to the most dramatic in- crease in cortical and medullary echogenicity with a hypoechoic rim at the corticomedullary junction and hypo- echoic central medullary regions ( Fig. 41.11 ). 46 The increased echogenicity is attributed to deposition of calcium oxalate crystals in the kidneys. 47 A hyperechoic medullary rim parallel to the cortico- medullary junction is observed commonly and may be seen in clinically normal dogs and cats 47 ( Fig. 41.12 ). A wide medullary band is more commonly associated with renal pathology than a thin rim. 48 49 It can be seen with mineralization, necrosis, and hemorrhage associated with many different disease processes, including acute tubular necrosis, leptospirosis, pyogranuloma- tous vasculitis in cats with FIP ( Fig. 41.13 ), and in hypercalce- mic nephropathy. 47 51 Hypercalcemic nephropathy is characterized by variable degrees of calci ﬁ cation and necrosis of renal tubules and collecting ducts. Perirenal Fluid. Perirenal or subcapsular ﬂ uid may be the result of acute renal failure, urine leakage, ureteral obstruction, hemorrhage, abscessation, perirenal pseudocysts, and neoplasia. If the ﬂ uid is subcapsular, renomegaly is seen on radiographs. EU, ultrasound, or contrast-enhanced CT is necessary to differentiate subcapsular ﬂ uid from renal parenchymal disease. Radiographically, ﬂ uid buildup outside the renal capsule leads to an increased opacity of the retroperitoneal space with a mottled or streaked appearance and loss of the outline of the kidneys or enlargement of the retroperitoneal space. Extracapsular ﬂ uid is characterized sonographically by triangular ﬂ uid accumulations adjacent to the kidney, predominantly on the dorsal aspect. Common causes include urinary tract rupture and acute renal failure ( Fig. 41.17 ). 56 64 Proposed mechanisms for the ﬂ uid accumulation in the absence of rupture include tubular back- leak of an ultra ﬁ ltrate into the renal interstitial space in excess of what the lymphatics can drain, either because of increased tubular permeability or obstructive disease. 56 Focal in ﬂ ammation of the retroperitoneal fat resulting in an increased echogenicity may be seen with renal abscessation and pyelonephritis. Pseudocyst formation is caused by a transudate and has been associated with underlying renal parenchymal disease, such as interstitial nephritis. The affected kidneys are often reduced in size and have signs of chronic renal disease ( Fig. 41.18 ). 57 Renal Mass Lesions. Renal mass lesions can be caused by hematoma, abscess, neoplasia, and granuloma. Primary renal tumors are usually unilateral and include renal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, papillary carcinoma, and nephro- blastoma. 58 Other tumors that may affect the kidneys are his- tiocytic sarcoma, plasma cell tumor, metastatic carcinoma, hemangiosarcoma, and lymphosarcoma. 59 Larger masses can be identi ﬁ ed radiographically as asymmetric renal enlargement. Renal masses have less contrast medium uptake on EU or CT compared to the surrounding or contralateral renal paren- chyma, because of lack of ﬁ ltration and concentration of the contrast medium. Heterogeneous contrast enhancement within the mass may be seen if the mass is necrotic or cavitated ( Fig. 41.19 ). There is a wide variability in the ultrasound appearance of renal tumors. Most primary renal tumors appear as complex or homogeneous, well-perfused masses obliterating the normal renal architecture ( Fig. 41.20 eFig. 41.7 ). Cavitated masses are seen with renal hemangiosarcoma. Diseases of the Collecting System Distention of the renal pelvis can be observed in dogs and cats with increased urine production caused by diuretic therapy or renal insuf ﬁ ciency, or it can be associated with congenital malformations of the ureters, such as ectopic ureter or ureter- ocele, infection, or lower urinary tract obstruction. 18 Pyelonephritis and Pyonephrosis Acute pyelonephritis can lead to mild renal enlargement, whereas renal size is reduced in chronic pyelonephritis. Typi- cally, there is mild to moderate pyelectasia. 64 The mean diam- eter of the renal pelvis with pyelonephritis is reported to be 3.6 mm in dogs and 4.0 mm in cats. However, this range is quite wide, with overlap with other nonobstructive or obstructive renal diseases, and even with normal animals. 18 More impor- tant, the shape of the renal pelvis is usually distorted with infection, resulting in blunted and asymmetric pelvic diver- ticula, seen both on EU and ultrasound ( Figs. 41.24 and 41.25 ). Additionally, on ultrasound imaging, echogenic debris may be observed in the renal pelvis and proximal ureter rather than anechoic urine, and the renal pelvis may be surrounded by an echogenic rim caused by ﬁ brotic change. 64 66 The echoge- nicity of the renal cortex may be uniformly or heterogeneously A B Fig. 41.22 Transverse (A) and dorsal (B) co mputed tomograp hy images of a dog with a right dorsal abdominalmass. In severe acute pyelonephritis, regional in ﬂ amma- tion of the perirenal fat results in a hyperechoic rim around the kidney and proximal ureter (see Fig. 41.25 ), often with a small amount of retroperitoneal effusion. Thickening of the proximal ureteral wall and mild ureteral dilation without evidence of intraluminal obstruction are common. Chronic pyelonephritis is dif ﬁ cult to distinguish from other chronic renal diseases, because it is characterized by small, irregularly shaped kidneys with mild pyelectasia. 64 Pyonephrosis is characterized by echogenic ﬂ uid in the renal pelvis with sediment settling to the dependent portion ( Fig. 41.26 ). 65 Hydronephrosis Hydronephrosis is de ﬁ ned as distention of the renal pelvis and pelvic diverticula, most commonly caused by urinary tract obstruction. 18 In severe hydronephrosis, the renal parenchyma is obliterated almost completely, and only a thin rim of cortex remains. Because renal vessels must still reach the cortex, elongated thin interlobar vessels may be seen forming radial streaks in the ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled cavity in the nephrogram phase of an excretory urogram ( Fig. 41.27 ). If the remaining renal paren- chyma is functional, contrast medium will outline the dilated renal pelvis in the pyelogram phase. Anechoic ﬂ uid distention of the renal pelvis and diverticula is seen on ultrasound, until the kidney essentially becomes one cystic structure with a thin cortical rim (see Fig. 41.26 ). Ureteral obstruction or aberrant termination of the ureters is a primary concern if hydro- nephrosis is present, and a detailed investigation of the ureters should be performed (discussed later). Acute renal failure is often associated with perirenal effusion, which is best seen with ultrasound imaging. Ureteral Obstruction Ureteral calculi, ureteral strictures, and masses associated with the urinary bladder neck are the most common causes of ure- teral obstruction. Preureteral vena cava (circumcaval ureter) is a common vascular anomaly in cats (prevalence of 22.4%) where the ureter courses dorsal to the caudal vena cava and displaces the vena cava ventrally. This anomaly has been asso- ciated with ureteral strictures in people and may predispose cats for urinary tract signs. 70 79 Ureteral dilation and varying degrees of hydronephrosis are consequences of ureteral obstruction that are apparent with most imaging modalities. A severely dilated ureter may be seen on survey radiographs as a tubular, tortuous structure in the retroperitoneal space extending from the kidneys to the dorsal aspect of the urinary bladder trigone, and ureteral calculi may be radiopaque and visible in the course of the ureter ( Fig. 41.30 eFig. 41.10 ). The presence, location, and degree of obstruction have to be veri- ﬁ ed using additional imaging modalities, such as ultrasound, antegrade pyelography, EU, or CT. On an EU or CT study with contrast medium, a ﬁ lling defect and lack of contrast medium distal to the ﬁ lling defect con ﬁ rm ureteral obstruction. Ultra- sonographically, a dilated ureter can usually be followed from the renal pelvis to an intraluminal obstruction, such as a cal- culus. Ureteral calculi appear as round or irregularly-shaped intraluminal hyperechoic structures with distal shadowing ( Fig. 41.31 ). A ureteral stricture can be recognized as focal narrowing surrounded by hyperechoic tissue, which is most commonly seen in the proximal ureter. 71 However, it should be noted that in some patients, the ureter is not dilated all the way to the obstruction, and in those instances, a small calculus or ureteral stricture may be missed. 72 Obstructions caused by soft tissue structures, such as hypoechoic mucous plugs and he- matomas, as well as strictures, can be dif ﬁ cult to identify ultrasonographically, because they are often not distinct from the retroperitoneal fat and ureteral wall. If in doubt, the ultra- sound examination can be repeated the next day to assess progression of ureteral or renal pelvic dilation, or contrast procedures (such as antegrade pyelography or CT) could be considered ( Fig. 41.32 ). Obstruction warrants decompression by stent or subcutaneous ureteral bypass placement. Degree of renal pelvic distension, although not useful as a prognostic in- dicator, can help in determining the presence of ureteral obstruction. Renal pelvis dilation greater than 13 mm has a high speci ﬁ city for ureteral obstruction. 18 The resistive index is ex- pected to increase in an obstructed kidney after administration of a diuretic. 73 81 EU is the least valuable method for detecting Box  41.1 Functi onal Aspe cts of the Ex cretory Urogram Good initial nephrogram followed by gradual decrease over 1 3 minutes, simultaneous with the appearance of the pyelogram  Normal Poor initial nephrogram that fades quickly  Insuf ﬁ cient dose of contrast medium  Primary polyuric renal failure Poor initial nephrogram followed by persistent opaci ﬁ cation  Severe generalized renal disease (primary glomerular dysfunction or severe generalized acute or chronic renal disease) Poor initial nephrogram followed by progressive increase in opaci ﬁ cation  Acute extrarenal obstruction  Systemic hypotension before contrast medium administration  Poor renal blood ﬂ ow Good initial nephrogram followed by persistent or increasing opacity  Sy st em ic hy po te ns io n (m ay b e co nt r as t me di um i nd uc ed )  Contrast medium induced renal failure  Acute tubular necrosis  Acute tubular obstruction Poor opaci ﬁ cation of the pyelogram phase  Renal failure d decreased concentrating ability Fig. 41.30 Lateral abdominal radiograph of a small-bre ed dog with cysticand ureteral calculi. Ureteroliths Ureteral calculi are often radiopaque and therefore visible on survey abdominal radiographs; they are best seen on lateral radiographic views (see Fig. 41.30 ). In cats, struvite calculi are more common than calcium oxalate calculi, whereas in dogs, both struvite and calcium oxalates are common. 74 Radiographic identi ﬁ cation of ureteral calculi can be hindered by superim- position of mineralized particles in the gastrointestinal tract, especially the colon. Compression views are a simple radio- graphic technique that allows displacement of overlying gastrointestinal structures. The round opacity created by the end-on view of the deep circum ﬂ ex iliac vessels seen on lateral radiographs should not be confused with ureteral calculi (see Fig. 41.29 ). The sensitivity for detection of ureteroliths when combining radiographs and ultrasound is approximately 90%. 72 Ultrasonographically, ureteral calculi appear as round to slightly irregular, hyperechoic structures with a strong distal acoustic shadow (see Fig. 41.31 ). A twinkling artifact may be seen when using color Doppler ultrasound. 75 Ectopic Ureters Ectopic ureters are congenital abnormalities of the ureteral junction with the bladder. One or both ureters may be affected. Ectopic ureters may terminate in the bladder neck, urethra ( Fig. 41.33 ), and in rare instances in the vagina. In the majority of cases, the distal portion of the abnormal ureter tunnels in the wall of the bladder neck and proximal urethra before opening into the urethral lumen (intramural ectopic ureter). In these instances, the ureter appears to terminate normally at the bladder neck but continues to tunnel caudally below the mu- cosa. 76 Extramural ectopic ureters insert directly in a caudal location. The differentiation can be dif ﬁ cult as both types of ectopic ureters tend to run parallel to the bladder trigone and urethra as they reach the pelvic inlet. Ectopic ureters can be normal in size but are often dilated and tortuous with associated hydronephrosis. The intrapelvic location of the terminal ureter in these patients creates dif ﬁ culties for evaluation with both EU and ultrasonography. Careful patient preparation (sedation, empty colon, and rectum) is important. Urethrography may have to be added to an excretory urogram if it is inconclusive. Vaginourethrography has been described as a diagnostic method; however, it should be avoided if possible due to complications such as vaginal rupture ( Fig. 41.34 ). Fluoroscopy may also be helpful to identify the ureteral opening and is often used in conjunction with cystoscopy during interventional procedures to address ureteral ectopia. 76 Administration of a diuretic is very helpful to enhance the ureteral jets during ul- trasound evaluation. 15 CT is increasingly used for diagnosis of ectopic ureter. 77 78 Lack of superimposition of skeletal and gastrointestinal structures is a major advantage of the use of CT for this purpose ( Fig. 41.35 ). Ureteroceles Ureteroceles are cystic dilations of the terminal ureter and are classi ﬁ ed as orthotopic or ectopic. Orthotopic ureteroceles are also called intravesicular ureteroceles and are dilatations of the submucosal portion of the distal ureter. Orthotopic ureter- oceles extend into the lumen of the urinary bladder and communicate with the urinary bladder lumen through an opening. Ectopic ureteroceles on the other hand are associated with ectopic ureters and located in the bladder neck or urethra ( Fig. 41.36 ). Ureteroceles may cause obstruction and secondary hydroureter and hydronephrosis which can be unilateral (grade 2) or bilateral (grade 3) if the ureterocele is large enough to affect the ureterovesicular junction on the contralateral side. 79 80 The appearance of ureteroceles on CT or EU depends on the timing. The ureterocele may ﬁ ll with contrast medium before the urinary bladder and present as radiopaque round structure but later in the study or in a cystogram it may present as ﬁ lling defect if the remainder of the urinary bladder is completely opaci ﬁ ed. Similarly, a round, anechoic cystic structure at the ureterovesical junction, usually within the bladder lumen, is visible ultrasonographically. 79 81 Ureteroceles are often associated with narrowing of the ureteral ori ﬁ ce and therefore have to be treated either surgically or with laser ablation. Ureteral Tumors Ureteral tumors are rare. Reported types include leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma, and urothelial carcinoma. Extension of a transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder neck into the distal ureter is common. Fibroepithelial polyps in the proximal aspect of the ureter have been described in dogs. 82 The etiol- ogy is unclear; they may be in ﬂ ammatory in origin, similar to polypoid cystitis, or hamartomatous or neoplastic, but they have a good prognosis when removed. In clinical practice, ultrasound is often the ﬁ rst advanced imaging method used when urinary tract trauma is suspected and survey radiographs are not conclusive, because it is noninvasive and can be performed in the awake patient. However, information gained with regard to urinary tract trauma is often limited, except in patients with complete disruption of the renal architecture or blood supply. More subtle urinary tract tears are dif ﬁ cult to detect with certainty, and the use of ultrasound is limited to guide sampling of retroperitoneal ﬂ uid pockets. Complete ureteral tears of some duration can be suspected if focal dilatation of the proximal ureter is seen, in addition to retroperitoneal effusion, because the site of rupture often contracts and adhesions form, essen- tially leading to ureteral obstruction. Doppler ultrasound can be used to verify both arterial supply and venous drainage of the kidney. Angela Marolf ANAT OMY The urinary bladder is divided grossly into three parts: the cranially located apex, the body in the middle, and the neck or trigone caudally ( Fig. 42.1 ). 1 2 Three ligaments formed from peritoneal re ﬂ ections hold the urinary bladder loosely in posi- tion. 2 The middle urinary bladder ligament extends along the ventral surface of the urinary bladder and two lateral ligaments extend along the lateral urinary bladder surfaces. These liga- ments often contain large fat deposits, facilitating radiographic visualization of the urinary bladder neck and body. The cranial and dorsal surfaces of the urinary bladder are visible radio- graphically because of adjacent fat within the omentum and mesentery ( Fig. 42.2 ). The urinary bladder is located cranial to the pubis, dorsal to the rectus abdominis muscle, caudal to the small bowel and omentum, and ventral to the large bowel. In females, the body of the uterus lies between the urinary bladder and colon/ rectum. The caudal portion of the normal urinary bladder may be cranial to the pubis or within the pelvic canal. 3 4 When distended, the caudal part of the urinary bladder is usually cranial to the pubis. 3 4 The normal urinary bladder in the cat is always intra-abdominal, being located 2 to 3 cm cranial to the pubis because of the long urinary bladder neck in this species ( Fig. 42.3 ). 5 Urinary bladder size varies with the amount of urine. After voiding, the urinary bladder may not be visible radiographically. With extreme distention, the apex may extend to the umbili- cus. Severe distention may occur normally owing to lack of opportunity to void or because of a strange or unfamiliar environment. The urinary bladder in the dog is usually oval, but with distention, it becomes more ellipsoid. The feline urinary bladder is almost always ellipsoid ( Fig. 42.4 ). The normal urinary bladder has a soft tissue radiographic opacity. Any opacity greater or less than soft tissue within the urinary bladder on survey radiographs is abnormal. The mus- culomembranous urinary bladder wall consists of mucosal, submucosal, and muscular layers. The peritoneum is adherent to the serosal surface, providing a separate fourth layer. The thickness of the urinary bladder wall or characteristics of the mucosa cannot be evaluated on survey radiographs because of border effacement by urine in the lumen. Radiographic visualization of the urinary bladder is reduced if there is insuf ﬁ cient abdominal fat, inadequate distention, and superimposed opacities. Intestinal content, pelvic limb muscu- lature, and adjacent osseous structures may obscure all or part of the urinary bladder. Focal superimposition may be created by ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled small bowel, nipples, the prepuce, and cutaneous masses. If necessary, some of these superimposition opacities can be eliminated or minimized by withholding food for 24 hours preceding the study, giving cleansing enemas, or using compression radiography, although these interventions are usually not necessary.
