RADIOG RAPH IC SIGNS OF URIN ARY BLADDE R DISE ASE There are few survey-radiographic signs of urinary bladder disease. Poor or nonexistent urinary bladder visualization and abnormal urinary bladder position, shape, size, and opacity indicate disease of the urinary bladder or, in many instances, disease of adjacent structures ( Table 42.1 ). Poor radiographic delineation of the urinary bladder may occur regardless of whether serosal contrast in the caudal abdomen is good or decreased. If serosal contrast is good and the urinary bladder is not seen, the urinary bladder is empty or has been displaced caudally or ventrally. If serosal contrast is decreased and the urinary bladder surface is not seen distinctly, free peritoneal ﬂ uid or inadequate peritoneal fat may be the cause ( Fig. 42.5 ). The urinary bladder may be displaced abnormally in various directions. 6 The cause of urinary bladder displacement may sometimes be determined by observation of surrounding structures or organs ( Fig. 42.6 ). With severe urinary bladder displacement, as with a hernia, cystography or ultrasonography may be needed for its identi ﬁ cation. Urinary bladder retro- ﬂ exion was observed in 24% (10/41) of dogs with a perineal hernia. 7 A urinary bladder partially within the pelvic canal ( Fig. 42.7 ) may be associated with congenital urinary tract anomalies. 8 A pelvic urinary bladder has also been reported as a normal variation, and this ﬁ nding should be correlated with clinical signs to determine its signi ﬁ cance. 4 9 Incontinent female dogs with a pelvic urinary bladder usually have a shorter ure- thra than continent dogs. 10 11 A change in shape of the urinary bladder is not common. Abdominal masses adjacent to the serosal surface of the urinary bladder may distort its shape. Tumors originating from the urinary bladder wall occasionally protrude from the serosal surface or cause thickening of the bladder trigone to produce a discernible change in shape of the urinary bladder but this is uncommon ( Fig. 42.8 ). 12 A pointed apex with an elongated urinary bladder may occur with a persistent urachal ligament. 13 An abnormally small or large urinary bladder is dif ﬁ cult to di- agnose radiographically because of the wide variation in normal size. In most instances, a consistently small or large urinary bladder with associated clinical signs is an indication that a contrast study or ultrasound examination should be performed to determine the cause of the suspected size change. Any change in radiographic opacity in the urinary bladder is abnormal and usually easy to detect. Gas in the urinary bladder may be introduced iatrogenically from catheterization or cys- tocentesis. Small luminal gas bubbles are usually located in the center of the urinary bladder on a recumbent lateral view ( Fig. 42.9 ). Gas in the urinary bladder lumen, urinary bladder wall, and occasionally the urinary bladder ligaments occurs with emphysematous cystitis ( Fig. 42.10 eFig. 42.1 ). Emphy- sematous cystitis is produced by glucose-fermenting organisms and may be seen in association with diabetes mellitus. 14 Emphysematous cystitis without diabetes mellitus can also occur. 15 16 Most increased opacities associated with the urinary bladder are calculi (see Fig. 42.6B Fig. 42.11 eFigs. 42.2 and 42.3 ). Opacities need to be con ﬁ rmed to be in the urinary bladder based on orthogonal radiographs. If doubt exists regarding the location or presence of cystic calculi, a compression view to displace adjacent structures overlapping or surrounding the urinary bladder ( Fig. 42.12 ) and ultrasonography are ways to con ﬁ rm the presence of calculi. The entire urinary tract from the kidneys to the terminus of the urethra should be examined for additional calculi. Not all calculi are radiopaque; thus, the absence of radiopacities within the urinary bladder does not rule out the presence of cystic calculi ( Table 42.2 ). In cats with suspected feline idiopathic cystitis, survey radiographs, cys- tography, or ultrasonography can be used to evaluate the uri- nary bladder. Radiographic signs that suggest a need for cystography include identi ﬁ cation of increased or decreased opacity in the urinary bladder, eval- uation of caudal abdominal masses that may be associated with the urinary bladder, nonvisualization of the urinary bladder af- ter abdominal trauma, and an abnormal shape or location of the urinary bladder. Cystography can be performed as negative-, positive-, or double-contrast procedure. Retrograde positive- and double-contrast procedures are often more useful to eval- uate the urinary bladder than is negative-contrast cystography alone. Positive-contrast cystography is the method of choice for identifying urinary bladder location, tears, hernias, and abnormal communication with adjacent structures. Double- contrast cystography is better than positive-contrast cystog- raphy for assessing urinary bladder wall lesions and intraluminal ﬁ lling defects. The selection of positive- or double-contrast cystography is based on clinical history, clinical signs, radio- graphic signs, and urinalysis ﬁ ndings ( Table 42.3 ). Cystography Technique If possible, food should be withheld for 12 to 24 hours and an enema may need to be given preceding cystography because fecal material superimposed over the urinary bladder may mask important information. All catheters and equipment should be sterilized, and the genitalia should be cleaned before the urinary bladder is catheterized. The equipment necessary for urinary bladder catheterization is illustrated in Fig. 42.13 . Various other types of catheters are available. Complications resulting from catheterization and cystog- raphy occur infrequently and are usually not detrimental. Radiographic Signs With Contrast Cystography Radiographic signs observed with urinary bladder disease include intramural thickening, an irregular mucosal border, ﬁ lling defects, and leakage ( Table 42.4 ). 27 These radiographic changes must be differentiated from artifacts such as air bub- bles and inadequate urinary bladder distention. Intramural Changes (Urinary Bladder Wall Thickening) The normal urinary bladder wall is approximately 1 mm thick regardless of the degree of distention. 9 Intramural changes are best demonstrated with double-contrast cystography and include focal or diffuse increased urinary bladder wall thickness ( Fig. 42.16 eFig. 42.4 ). Mild urinary bladder wall thickening may be missed if the urinary bladder is distended completely. 26 Urinary bladder wall thickening may be caused by ﬁ brous tissue proliferation or cellular in ﬁ ltration from in ﬂ ammation (cystitis), hemorrhage, or neoplasia. With chronic cystitis, subserosal leakage can occur due to necrosis of the urinary bladder mu- cosa (see Fig. 42.14 ). Intramural urinary bladder thickening causes decreased urinary bladder distensibility, which may be symmetric with diffuse intramural urinary bladder disease or asymmetric with focal intramural urinary bladder disease. Mucosal Changes The urinary bladder has a transitional epithelium, which ap- pears smooth on a normal cystogram. Mucosal proliferation appears as an irregular outline along the inside urinary bladder surface and may be accentuated with inadequate urinary bladder distention, and can be obliterated if the urinary bladder is maximally distended. 26 The irregular mucosa is usually focally distributed but may be diffuse; it may vary in severity from a slightly irregular brush-type surface to a severe cobblestone appearance ( Fig. 42.17 ). Contrast Leakage and Retention Patterns Retrograde positive-contrast cystography is the best technique to assess leakage of urine from the urinary bladder. Urine leakage may occur into the urinary tract, adjacent visceral soft tissue structures, or the peritoneal cavity. Vesicoureteral re ﬂ ux can lead to contrast medium ﬁ lling the ureters. Retention of urine contrast medium may occur in ura- chal anomalies (see Fig. 42.20 ), and traumatic urinary bladder diverticula ( Fig. 42.21 ). Urachal anomalies include congenital or acquired diverticula, cysts, and persistent patent urachus or urachal ligament. 36 39 Congenital urachal anomalies are char- acterized by smooth contrast medium margins; they may be identi ﬁ ed as an extension from the urinary bladder. Contrast medium leakage from the urinary bladder to adja- cent visceral structures may be seen with a congenital or ac- quired ﬁ stula. The organs most commonly involved are the rectum and the vagina. ULTRA SONOGRA PHY The ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled urinary bladder is easily evaluated ultrasono- graphically. The super ﬁ cial location of the urinary bladder en- ables high-resolution imaging, and urine provides high sonographic contrast, which results in good visibility of the urinary bladder wall and intraluminal abnormalities. Urolithia- sis, neoplasia, cystitis, urachal, and vesicoureteral junction ab- normalities can be identi ﬁ ed by using ultrasonography. 41 43 High-frequency transducers (7 15 MHz) are best for exam- ination of the urinary bladder. A 5-MHz transducer may be necessary to penetrate to the far wall of a distended urinary bladder in large dogs. Linear and curved wide-aperture format transducers are particularly useful. Acoustic power and near gain should be decreased to suppress reverberation echoes generated between the transducer, the skin, and abdominal wall structures. The ultrasonographic examination is best performed when the urinary bladder is moderately full. If a nearly empty urinary bladder is encountered, it should be reexamined when it is moderately distended after some hours of inside con ﬁ nement, after administration of a diuretic, or after catheterization and sterile saline injection. The wall of a ﬂ accid urinary bladder can be deviated inward by a distended colon, and the acoustic shadow artifacts generated by colonic contents can appear like the shadows generated by calculi. 44 A fully distended urinary bladder is also less desirable because subtle mural abnormalities may be more dif ﬁ cult to see. Normal urinary bladder wall thickness varies depending on the degree of urinary bladder distention and body weight, being 2.3 mm thick with minimal distention and 1.4 mm thick with moderate distention. 45 In normal adult cats, the mean urinary bladder wall thickness should not exceed 1.7 mm 0.6 mm. 46 Urinary bladder ultrasonography can be performed with the patient in either dorsal or lateral recumbency. The urinary bladder should be evaluated in a transverse plane and orthog- onally in either a sagittal or dorsal plane. Accurate assessment of urinary bladder wall thickness requires a perpendicular orientation of the ultrasound beam with the urinary bladder wall. Assessment of the cranial aspect of the urinary bladder wall is challenging because of the suboptimal beam alignment and the adjacent gas- ﬁ lled bowel. 47 Side and grating lobe arti- facts generated by the adjacent colon can give rise to an erro- neous display of echogenic material in the urinary bladder lumen, and the curved urinary bladder wall can create addi- tional echoes adjacent to the dorsal urinary bladder wall ( Fig. 42.25 ). 48 Transducer rotation of 90 degrees over such suspicious areas is often helpful to enable recognition of the proximity of the colon and determination of the nature of the artifact. Free intraluminal abnormalities such as calculi, sedi- ment, and blood clots gravitate to the most dependent aspect of the urinary bladder. In lateral recumbency, careful examination of the most dependent area of the urinary bladder is required so that small calculi are not overlooked. Additional imaging after the animal has been positioned in the opposite lateral recum- bent or standing position allows detection of sediment swirling or gravitation of free intraluminal objects to a dependent posi- tion within the urinary bladder. The normal urinary bladder is ovoid in shape with a slight elongation caudally at the neck. The ureters and urethra are not typically visible unless they become distended with urine. With high-resolution transducers, three distinct layers of the urinary bladder wall can be seen. The mucosa is a thin hyperechoic surface outlined against the urine, the middle muscle layer is hypoechoic, and the outer serosal layer is hyperechoic. 46 The cranioventral aspect of the wall may be slightly thinner than in other regions. Typically, normal urine is anechoic. However, suspended clumped hyperechoic foci can be identi ﬁ ed in the urine of clinically normal cats with urine lipid. 49 The turbulence created by discharge of urine through the ureteral openings may generate transient echo jets in the urinary bladder lumen adjacent to the trigone. 50 Intraluminal Changes Urinary calculi, cellular and crystalline debris, gas, hemorrhage, and blood clots are detected readily by ultrasonography ( Fig. 42.26A ). Calculi and blood clots gravitate dependently whereas gas bubbles rise. The location of cellular and crystal- line debris and fresh hemorrhage is more variable. Severe acute hemorrhage can ﬁ ll the urinary bladder and give rise to a lacy hyperechoic pattern, which may change little with ballotte- ment or animal repositioning (see Fig. 42.26B ). A similar appearance can be observed with severe proteinuria and fat droplets. 51 Crystalline and cellular sediments generate a var- iably echogenic pattern in more dependent urine. In cats, the crystalline deposits may become thick enough to form a hyperechoic layer con ﬂ uent with the urinary bladder wall that creates acoustic shadowing. Ballottement or changing patient position can differentiate the swirling sediment from calculi. Calculi The urine/calculus interface is intensely hyperechoic and usu- ally appears convex. Multiple calculi often aggregate together and give rise to an irregular, somewhat continuous surface, which makes distinguishing and measuring individual calculi dif ﬁ cult. Distinct acoustic shadows may be observed deep to calculi ( Fig. 42.27 ). Shadowing is related to size (height) of the calculus and transducer frequency, with increasing height of the calculus and increasing transducer frequency more likely to produce acoustic shadows. 52 The application of color Doppler to distinguish calculi based on the twinkling artifact occurring deep to the calculus can be used to discriminate mineralized from nonmineralized structures. 53 Smaller calculi may not generate the characteristic shadows if the focal zone is not optimized at the depth of the calculi. Urothelial carcinoma of the urinary bladder can be evaluated with CT to determine extent of tumor size for pretreatment staging and to assess tumor response to treatment via volumetric comparison measurements ( Fig. 42.33 ). 68 82 URETH RA Anatomy The male urethra comprises three major areas: the prostatic urethra, membranous urethra, and penile urethra ( Fig. 42.34 ). 83 Combined, the prostatic and membranous portions make up the pelvic part of the urethra. 84 The prostatic urethra is sur- rounded completely by the prostate gland in the dog, whereas only dorsolaterally in the cat. 85 The membranous urethra is enveloped by cavernous tissue and the urethralis muscle. 85 The penile urethra extends from the ischial arch to the tip of the penis. This part of the urethra is also known as the cavernous urethra because the majority of it is encased by erectile tissues of the penis. 84 The most distal part of the penile urethra is inserted in and protected by the ventral urethral groove of the os penis in the dog. The arrangement of urethral muscle and surrounding spongy tissues confers a diffuse sphincter mecha- nism to the urethra in male dogs. The female urethra is shorter and wider than in males and entirely pelvic in location. The external urethral ori ﬁ ce lies caudal to the vestibulovaginal junction, where a muscular ure- thral sphincter is present. 84 In the cat, the urinary bladder is typically intra-abdominal in position, and a relatively long prepelvic part of the urethra extends between the neck of the urinary bladder and the pelvic urethra. 85 RADIOG RAPHY AND URETH ROGRAP HY Radiography of the urethra must include orthogonal caudal abdominal and/or pelvic images to ensure that the urethra is fully included in the ﬁ eld of view. In male dogs, lateral pelvic radiographs with the pelvic limbs both hip-extended (pulled caudally) and hip- ﬂ exed (pulled cranially) are also recom- mended to avoid missing lesions of the penile urethra caused by superimposition of the pelvic limbs. Retrograde urethrography is a special radiographic tech- nique to examine the urethra using positive-contrast medium. Only water-soluble, iodinated contrast medium should be used. The contrast medium can be diluted with sterile saline to a ﬁ nal concentration of approximately 150 mg iodine [I]/mL. 83 86 Pa- tients generally require sedation, and evacuation of the colon and rectum through defecation or cleansing enemas is recom- mended to prevent superimposition of feces on the urethra. DISE ASES OF THE URETH RA Urethral Calculi Radiopaque urethral calculi may be seen on survey radiographs. In male dogs, calculi commonly occur at regions of luminal narrowing or restriction: the ischial arch and base of the os penis. There are several potential pitfalls in imaging of the urethra that can result in misdiagnosis of urethral calculi ( Fig. 42.42 ). In male dogs, nipples may be superimposed upon the penis on lateral views. This can be differentiated from a calculus ﬁ rst by inspection of the patient for the presence of nipples adjacent to the prepuce. Coating the nipple with barium paste or another type of metallic marker and repeating the radiograph can be performed for de ﬁ nitive assessment. Some male dogs have a separate center of ossi ﬁ cation of the os penis that results in a mineral body separate from the cranial tip of the os penis. This should be recognized as a normal anatomic variation and would be an unexpected location for a calculus. In some male cats, a small and faintly mineralized os penis is visible on radiographs and may be mistaken for urethrolithiasis. 97 Urethral Neoplasia and In ﬂ ammation Urethral mass lesions caused by neoplasia or in ﬂ ammation are generally indistinguishable. Neoplasia is more common and may originate from the urethra or extend into the urethra from the urinary bladder or prostate gland, as with urothelial carci- noma and prostatic carcinoma. 91 98 99 Granulomatous urethritis is a less common in ﬁ ltrative in ﬂ ammatory disease reported in female dogs. 99 Fibroepithelial polyps of the urethra have also been reported. 100 With urethrography, the mucosal margin of the urethra is markedly irregular, and ﬁ lling defects may be seen in the lumen ( Fig. 42.43 ). 101 Narrowing of the lumen with intramural disease is expected, but widening may be seen with mass extension into the lumen. The absolute normal size of the prostate is variable in the dog and is dependent on the age, size, and neuter status. 1 In many neutered dogs, the normal prostate is small ( < 2 cm) and not radiographically visible ( Fig. 43.1A ). When visible, the prostate is recognized radio- graphically by its round shape, soft tissue opacity, and its rela- tion to adjacent organs. Delineation of an enlarged prostate from the urinary bladder is evident from a triangular fat opacity ventral to and between them (see Fig. 43.1B ). The normal prostate in an intact dog should not be more than 70% of the height of the pelvic inlet on lateral views, measured as the distance between the ventral aspect of S1 and the cranial border of the dorsal pubis. 2 If seen on the ventrodorsal (VD) view, the normal prostate should not be more than 80% of the width of the pelvic canal. A full rectum may obscure the prostate on the VD view. If the shape or position of the prostate is altered, the gland may not be recognizable other than as an indistinct opacity between the bladder, rectum, and pelvis. The normal prostate gland is not visible in the cat because of its location on the dorsal lateral surfaces of the mid pelvic urethra and small size. The normal feline prostate measures up to 10 mm in diameter. 3 Prostatic diseases causing clinical signs in cats are very rare and will not be considered further in this chapter. The most com- mon organisms isolated include Escherichia coli Staphylo- coccus spp, Streptococcus spp, Pseudomonas Brucella canis Proteus , and Mycoplasma , among others. Usually, a mixed bacterial population is present. 6 The infection may arise within the prostate, or it may extend from other sources such as the urinary bladder or testicles. A normal prostate gland is more resistant to infection than is an enlarged or in ﬂ amed gland. Because many antibiotics do not penetrate the prostate readily, the gland may also be a reservoir for reinfection or extension to other organs. 4 There is improved penetration of antibiotics into an in ﬂ amed prostate due to disruption of the blood-prostate barrier. 6 Prostatic in ﬂ ammation may vary from a mild tran- sient process that causes minimal or no clinical signs to a fulminating hemorrhagic or emphysematous process that de- stroys the entire gland rapidly, resulting in severe systemic signs. 7 9 The latter may result in rupture of the capsule with secondary peritonitis and sepsis. Chronic, recurrent prostatitis may result in a scarred, ﬁ brotic gland that is typically normal in size or small. Chronic scarring may result in stricture of the urethra. 1 4 Such a stricture is dif ﬁ cult to recognize radiographically unless a urethrogram is performed. Prostatic abscesses may form as a sequela of prostatitis or primary cystic disease. Large abscesses distort the shape of the prostate gland and may also rupture, causing peritonitis and sepsis. 10 11 As previously stated, cysts form in advanced BPH and are usually contained within the gland. Squamous metaplasia can cause obstruction of the prostatic ducts, leading to retention cysts. Cysts protruding from the surface of the prostate or separate from the prostate are also referred to as paraprostatic cysts because they are no longer con ﬁ ned within the gland. They have been associated with cystic enlargement of the Müllerian ducts or remnants of the uterus masculinus. 12 14 Enlargement of the Müllerian ducts results in a bilateral tubular mass that resembles uterine enlargement. 15 16 These cysts may be sterile but often become infected, which may be the inciting cause for presentation to a veterinarian. 17 18 Cysts occasionally result from neoplasia, but this is rare. Formation of functional neoplastic secretory cells without an accompanying ductal system results in a cystic structure lined with neoplastic epithelium. Prostatic tumors are rare in dogs and very rare in cats. The majority of prostatic tumors are carcinomas (adenocarcinoma, urothelial carcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas, undifferenti- ated carcinomas). Very rarely, mesenchymal cell tumors are identi ﬁ ed. 19 20 Lymphoma may arise within the prostate but is more often involved secondarily and may serve as a sanctuary site for disease during treatment. 21 The incidence of all pros- tatic tumors is very low (0.35%). 22 Neutered male dogs have an odds ratio of approximately 2.84 in comparison to intact males. 23 Prostatic carcinoma is often advanced at presentation with metastasis to regional lymph nodes, the pelvis, lumbosa- cral spine, and distant sites such as the liver and lungs. 22 25 Patients may present with urinary signs as the tumor can invade or compress the urethra. Small in situ prostatic carcinomas are unusual but do occur; they are usually discovered as a result of metastasis rather than from their local effects. Large prostatic neoplasms are often infected or necrotic, and affected dogs may therefore have clinical signs of prostatitis. These tumors are often slow to be diagnosed, unless signs of metastasis are pre- sent, because of the tendency of clinical sign of cystitis or prostatitis to overshadow those of neoplasia. Clinical Signs The clinical signs of prostatic disease are usually localized to urinary or gastrointestinal signs. Stranguria, hematuria, and py- uria are seen commonly in cases of prostatitis and neoplasia. 1 4 5 24 In cases of marked prostatomegaly, patients may present with dyschezia and small or ribbon-like stools as the enlarged prostate gland displaces the colon and/or rectum dorsally, compressing the rectum ( Fig. 43.2 ). Patients are often systemically ill in cases of acute prostatitis and may present with anorexia, fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, and preputial discharge, whereas patients with chronic prostatitis are often asymptomatic or display mild clinical signs. Most commonly, patients with chronic prostatitis will have a history of recurrent urinary tract infections and bloody urethral discharge. The prostate is typically normal in size and nonpainful on rectal palpation. 1 5 A less common sign of prostatic disease is a pelvic limb gait abnormality manifesting as pelvic limb weakness and lumbar pain or myelopathy due to spinal metastasis or direct tumor extension into the vertebral canal. The animal may refuse to climb stairs and jump or may have a stiff gait. Owners often believe the animal has developed osteoarthritis, but such ani- mals may have severe, active septic prostatitis or metastatic disease. The pain caused by the prostatic infection is exacer- bated by walking, climbing, and jumping. Both pelvic limbs are usually affected. These animals are also usually sensitive to palpation of the caudal abdomen. Gait abnormalities are seen rarely in uncomplicated BPH. 22 25 Radiographic Changes Most common prostatic diseases cause enlargement. The enlargement may be symmetric (diffuse) or asymmetric (focal). Prostatic symmetry is usually judged by the shape of the pros- tate and the relative mass of the prostate gland with respect to the neck of the bladder and the pelvic inlet. Identi ﬁ cation of prostatomegaly depends on identi ﬁ cation of a soft tissue mass in the caudal aspect of the abdomen and on the relation of that mass to surrounding structures, principally the bladder, colon, and body wall. Prostatomegaly typically displaces the urinary bladder cranially. If prostatomegaly is uniform, bladder displacement is cranial along the ﬂ oor of the abdomen. If prostatomegaly is eccentric, as often occurs with large cysts and abscesses and occasionally with tumors, the direction of bladder displacement may be variable. A cyst or abscess occasionally may extend dorsal to the bladder ( Fig. 43.3 ). Alternatively, with ventral prostatomegaly, the bladder neck may be elevated. 1 5 Severe and irregular enlarge- ment may also result in obliteration of the normal triangle of fat formed by junction of the caudal ventral bladder and the prostate gland. 26 The other major radiographic sign of prostatomegaly is dorsal displacement of the colon (see Fig. 43.2 ). Prostatic enlargement, particularly if intrapelvic, may also cause nar- rowing of the lumen of the rectum and possible impaction of feces cranial to the site of rectal narrowing. This compression may be visible radiographically, or the colon may simply become con ﬂ uent with the prostate mass at the pelvic inlet. Very large prostatic lesions usually lie on the ﬂ oor of the abdomen, so some dorsal displacement of the caudal abdominal contents can occur. Prostatic and paraprostatic cysts may become so large that they reach almost to the costal arch. Masses of this magnitude cause organ displacement so severe that the actual source of the mass may be dif ﬁ cult to determine without using special radiographic procedures, sonography, or advanced imaging such as computed tomography (CT). Pros- tatic disease that results in urethral stricture or urethral inva- sion, as in the case of neoplasia, may result in severe urinary bladder distention from obstruction, which is then secondarily responsible for the displacement of the abdominal structures cranial and dorsal to it. A prostate that exceeds 90% of the distance from the pubis to the sacral promontory in an intact dog is considered pathologic. 2 Any enlargement ( > 2 cm) in a dog neutered more than a few months prior to imaging should be considered abnormal. 1 2 However, when a dog is neutered for treatment of prostatic disease, enlargement can persist for several months. 27 The actual degree of prostatic enlargement varies widely, however. For example, prostatic size may vary from slight enlargement to 10 times normal size for BPH, and the gland may actually decrease in size in chronic prostatitis due to ﬁ brosis. 1 5 Acute prostatitis and neoplasia alone do not usually cause se- vere enlargement, as seen with BPH. However, a combination of pathologies may be present resulting in enlargement. Pros- tatic pathology may be discovered incidentally during abdom- inal imaging with ultrasound, CT, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or on postmortem examination. Paraprostatic cysts and abscesses usually have well-de ﬁ ned, sometimes mineralized margins that are easily seen (see Fig. 43.3 eFigs. 43.1 and 43.2 ). 14 Abscesses are typically poorly marginated and are often surrounded by edema or ﬂ uid, resulting poor delineation of the prostate, reduced periprostatic serosal detail, and a heterogeneous appearance of the caudal abdominal fat. A cyst or abscess may occasionally extend caudally into the pelvic canal; such lesions may not be readily visible on survey radiographs and may not produce the usual displacement of the bladder. 18 These lesions do, however, often produce marked displacement and compression of the rectum and are therefore recognized as an intrapelvic mass and on occasion can even be within the contents of a perineal hernia. De ﬁ nitely distinguishing a cyst from an abscess on the basis of radiographic examination alone is impossible; howev- er, if the margins are smooth, the structure is uniform in soft tissue opacity, and there is no evidence of regional in ﬂ amma- tion ( ﬂ uid/edema), a cyst is more likely.Evaluation of prostatic margination is important. In the presence of emaciation, pelvic trauma, or abdominal effusion, the prostatic margins may be inconspicuous. If the prostate gland has smooth margins that are easily seen, the disease involving the gland is likely to be benign or is slowly pro- gressing, such as BPH or low-grade or chronic prostatitis. An irregular or indistinct margin in the presence of adequate abdominal fat is more likely to be caused by an acute or aggressive process such as neoplasia or acute prostatitis. 8 9 11 Most patients with aggressive prostatic disease have some evi- dence of secondary in ﬂ ammation affecting the surrounding tissues ( Fig. 43.4 eFig. 43.3 ).A change in the opacity of the prostate from its normal soft tissue opacity indicates severe or chronic disease. Areas of calci ﬁ cation within the gland are a sign either of longstanding prostatitis or of neoplasia. Wispy or indistinct calci ﬁ cation within the prostatic parenchyma has a strong positive predic- tive value (100%) for carcinoma in neutered dogs, whereas intact dogs are unlikely to have prostatic neoplasia if no mineralization is present ( Fig. 43.5 eFig. 43.4 ). 28 Therefore, although unusual, indistinct calci ﬁ cation in the prostate gland is a serious ﬁ nding that warrants biopsy. Prostate gland calci ﬁ ca- tion may be more easily seen with ultrasonography or CT because of improved soft tissue contrast resolution and elimi- nation of superimposed structures in comparison to standard radiography. The prostate does not normally communicate with any air- containing organ, so it should not contain gas. Intraprostatic gas is evidence of gas-forming bacterial prostatitis. This is extremely rare. 9 Severe prostatitis results in hemorrhagic ne- crosis of the gland, potentially causing a generalized peritonitis and septic shock. Because of the rapidly fatal course of these infections, identi ﬁ cation of noniatrogenic gas within the pros- tate carries an unfavorable prognosis. Rarely, the prostate may contain air because of re ﬂ ux from the bladder during a nega- tive- or double-contrast cystogram. It is also a sign that aggressive disease is present. 29 30 Evidence of either asymmetric prostatic enlargement or urethral abnormalities is an indication for prostatic cytology, which is best acquired by diagnostic urethral catheterization. Urethrography can be performed easily in the male dog, and several methods may be used. Urethrography provides indirect evidence of prostatic disease. If the urethra is deviated around a large mass or does not pass directly through the center of the prostate gland, the disease within the prostate is asymmetric, such as a cyst, abscess, or tumor. If the urethra passes directly through the middle of an enlarged prostate, the disease is more likely to be diffuse, such as hyperplasia or prostatitis (see Fig. 43.7A ). In addition, a urethrocystogram identi ﬁ es the true location of the urinary bladder. In some instances, abdominal masses, such as an omental tumor, a paraprostatic cyst, or an enlarged retained testicle, lie next to the bladder and the mass can be misinterpreted as the urinary bladder. Knowing the identity of each mass is important, and urethrocystography is useful for this, especially if ultrasound is not available. Signs of urethral disease of prostatic origin include urethral stricture, ulceration of the mucosa, and ﬁ lling defects within the urethra. Ulceration or stricture of the prostatic urethra should be regarded as highly suggestive of neoplasia. 29 Extravasation of contrast medium into the prostate should not be interpreted as abnormal as long as only the prostatic ducts ﬁ ll with contrast medium (see Fig. 43.7B ). 30 This appearance is often seen in animals with a normal prostate. However, pooling of the contrast medium within the prostate is abnormal. Large cavities with irregular walls that communicate with the urethra or cavitary smooth-walled lesions containing intraluminal masses are suggestive of neoplasia; aspiration may be indicated in these instances. 13 29 Conversely, if extravasation does not occur, the prostate gland is not necessarily normal or solid. Large cavitary lesions, such as cysts and abscesses, often attain their size because they do not communicate with the urethra. 1 18 If these lesions do ﬁ ll with contrast medium, they are usually ovoid with smooth walls. The normal prostatic urethra as seen on the urethrogram has a smooth mucosal border. The urethra is usually slightly greater in diameter near the center of the prostate and tapers slightly at the cranial and caudal borders. The degree of the central dila- tion depends somewhat on the size of the prostate, the disease present, the degree of bladder distention, and the amount of pressure applied during injection. 31 A small, smooth ﬁ lling defect in the dorsal wall of the urethra near the center of the prostate gland represents the colliculus seminalis and is a normal ﬁ nding ( Fig. 43.8 ). 30 The point at which the prostatic urethra joins the neck of the bladder should be evaluated carefully. Small ﬁ lling defects or mucosal ulcers that may be early lesions of urothelial carci- noma may be detected. These small lesions may not be detected on a cystogram or even ultrasonography because they are obscured by the internal urethral sphincter, which is actually encircled by the prostate. These associated structures may be affected secondarily in prostatic disease, or they may be the site of the primary disor- der resulting in secondary prostatic changes. A very small normal gland, such as seen in a neutered dog, may not be seen if pelvic in location, but an abnormal prostate is usually visible cranial to the pubis. Images should be acquired in the trans- verse, sagittal, and parasagittal planes. Alternatively, a cine loop capture can be made while scanning slowly through the gland in the transverse plane. This will ensure that the entire prostate is adequately represented in captured images. 35 The prostate is typically imaged most easily from the right side of the os penis with the dog in dorsal recumbency by tracing the trigone of the urinary bladder caudally. In some dogs, angling the probe caudally is necessary to see the caudal pole of the prostate gland where it lies just dorsal to the pubic brim. Sedation is sometimes required for thorough assessment in uncooperative patients. Ultrasonographic measurement of the prostate and its lesions is performed easily with ultrasonography and has been found to be accurate. 2 The normal prostate in a neutered male is uniformly rela- tively hypoechoic with a homogeneous, medium to ﬁ ne echo- texture relative to surrounding fat which has a coarser echotexture. The urethra is usually seen as a small hypoechoic region in the center of the gland surrounded by a narrow band of slightly hyperechoic tissue representing the urethral wall ( Fig. 43.9 ). BPH usually results in a uniformly enlarged gland that is hyperechoic and has smooth margins. The dorsal portion of the gland may be enlarged to a greater degree than the ventral portion, or vice versa, but the changes are generally symmetric from right to left ( Fig. 43.10 ). This symmetry may be lost as the hyperplasia increases in severity and cysts develop. As cysts form, some invariably become larger than others and distort the shape of the prostate but typically do not extend beyond the capsule. Commonly, small anechoic cystic regions are seen within the parenchyma of dogs with BPH ( Fig. 43.11 ). The ultrasonographic changes seen in prostatitis vary from mild hyperechogenicity of the parenchyma with variable enlargement to severe prostatic enlargement with a mottled hyperechoic to hypoechoic pattern ( Fig. 43.12 ). The shape of the prostate may be normal or markedly distorted. Distortion of the shape and margin is common when abscess formation is present in the gland. Some dogs may have a hypoechoic band of edema in the capsule outlining the prostate gland. Edema may also extend into the surrounding tissues, resulting in hyperechoic fat with hypoechoic striations adjacent to the prostate. In severe necrotizing prostatitis, delineation of the gland from the surrounding fat may be lost, and the prostate may appear as a dark structure with an irregular and indistinct margin. Generally speaking, the more acute and severe the in ﬂ ammation is, the more hypoechoic the prostatic paren- chyma becomes. In cases of chronic in ﬂ ammation, the prostate is typically more hyperechoic due to ﬁ brosis. Cysts and abscesses within and attached to the prostate appear as thin-walled structures with variably hypoechoic centers. They vary widely in size from a couple of millimeters to several centimeters. Their contents may be anechoic, or they may have variable amounts of cellular debris within the lumen. 18 The presence of septation or large amounts of debris within the lumen is typically more indicative of abscess, whereas anechoic contents are suggestive of a cyst; however, this is not a universally accurate distinction. The presence of through transmission deep to a highly echogenic structure is indicative of a ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled rather than a solid cellular mass. Color Doppler can be helpful for con ﬁ rming vascularization within a prostatic lesion. Both cysts and abscesses occasionally occur in conjunction with neoplasia. Cavitary lesions with irregular in- ternal margins or solid tissue masses within them are highly suggestive of neoplasia, whereas smooth margins are more indicative of cysts ( Fig. 43.13 ). Calci ﬁ cation within the prostate gland is recognized as bright echoes that cast shadows. Mineralization is generally considered a sign of malignancy, particularly in neutered males ( Fig. 43.14 ). However, in some instances, chronic prostatitis in intact males can cause slight calci ﬁ cation of the prostate, 26 which is detectable with ultrasonography, and, anecdotally, small urinary calculi have been observed to become displaced into prostatic ducts. Thus, a diagnosis of malignancy should not be made on the basis of ultrasonographic evidence of calci ﬁ cation alone, but calci ﬁ cation is a strong justi ﬁ cation for obtaining prostatic cytology or histopathology. Malignant tumors of the prostate in the dog are usually advanced at the time of detection. These are highly aggressive and may destroy the architecture of the gland, resulting in a mixed echogenic pattern, and often causes asymmetric enlargement. Contrast ultrasonography can be performed. In normal dogs, there is diffuse and uniform enhancement of the prostate. 36 37 Peak enhancement of the normal prostate occurs approxi- mately 30 seconds after intravenous injection of the contrast agent. Prostatitis and BPH exhibit no difference in enhance- ment whereas prostatic carcinoma exhibited a signi ﬁ cantly shorter time to enhancement and a greater level of enhance- ment than either normal dogs or dogs with benign disease. 37 A de ﬁ nitive diagnosis of the type of prostatic disease cannot be made on the basis of ultrasonographic ﬁ ndings alone. 38 An ultrasound-guided biopsy (preferably via diagnostic catheteri- zation) should be performed to support the ultrasonographic diagnosis. In dogs with suspected neoplasia, aspirates should be obtained of the primary lesion of interest as well as the other quadrants of the gland if the diagnosis cannot be made from diagnostic catheterization. Federica Rossi I ntact dogs and cats are commonly affected by diseases of the genital tract, especially infections and neoplasia. In spayed females, complications like ovarian/uterine stump infections or ovarian remnant syndrome may occur, and in cryptorchid males, retained testicles can be affected by torsion or neoplasia. All these are clinical situations where imaging is used as diagnostic workup and radiology and ultrasound are often combined. Radiographs are particularly helpful if there is signi ﬁ cant enlargement of the genital organs and if gas and mineralization are present. Ultrasound is essential to evaluate small structures like the ovary or to de ﬁ ne uterine content and wall structure. Cross-sectional imaging such as computed to- mography (CT) is indicated to investigate challenging cases or to complete presurgical staging or radiation treatment planning in cases of genital neoplasia. IMAG ING PRO CEDURE S AND NORM AL ANAT OMY OF THE FEMALE GEN ITAL TRACT RADIOG RAPH Y Technique A standard radiographic study includes three projections (left and right lateral and ventrodorsal) of the abdomen and the pelvis. A compression radiograph with the animal in lateral recumbency, as described in Chapter 38 , may be added to decrease the superimposition between the colon, uterus, and urinary bladder in the caudal abdomen 1 ( Fig. 44.1 ). However, this technique is usually replaced by ultrasonography. Retrograde Vaginography Positive contrast vaginography can be performed in dogs and cats under general anesthesia as part of the workup in case of vaginal diseases. 2 3 Because of technical challenges and re- ported high risks of vagina rupture if the tip of the catheter is placed too cranially in the vagina, this technique should be replaced by other diagnostic modalities (vaginoscopy or advanced cross-sectional imaging) whenever possible. If correctly performed ( Fig. 44.2 ), it can be successfully used in special circumstances, especially with diseases which impair a complete direct examination of the vagina lumen. 4 To avoid misinterpretation due to fecal content in the descending colon and rectum, an enema is necessary before the procedure. A Foley catheter pre ﬁ lled with contrast medium is placed at the vaginal vestibulum, caudal to the urethral ori ﬁ ce, and gently in ﬂ ated with saline. A tissue forceps is positioned at the vulva to prevent contrast medium leakage and the expulsion of the catheter. Under ﬂ uoroscopic guidance, approximately 1 mL/kg of diluted iodinated contrast medium (150 200 mg I/mL con- centration) is infused until moderate distention of the vagina and vestibulum is reached and the urethra is opaci ﬁ ed. A slight narrowing is normally visible between the vagina and the ves- tibulum in the lateral view. If the procedure is performed in estrus and the cervix is open, contrast medium can enter the uterus. Incomplete distention of the vestibulum and vagina produces mucosal irregularity mimicking vaginal diseases. Air bubbles can be confused with ﬁ lling defects caused by vaginal masses. Af te r m ul ti pl e pr eg n an ci es , th e ov ar ie s as su me a mo re ca ud ov en tr al po si ti on . 5 6 The uterine horns have variable length and uniform diam- eter in a nulliparous animal (0.5 1 cm in the bitch and 3 4 mm in the cat). In the proximal half, they assume a lateral position, in contact with the lumbar abdominal wall. Distally, they become more ventral and axially located, with variable contact with the descending colon and the small intestinal loops. In the caudal abdomen, the uterine horns converge dorsal to the uri- nary bladder. When enlarged because of pregnancy or ﬂ uid collection, the uterine horns bend upon themselves and displace ventrally. The short uterine body and neck ( cervix uteri ) lie dorsal to the urinary bladder and ventral to the descending colon to enter the pelvic inlet. The cervix is char- acterized by a thicker muscular layer; its lumen opens during estrus just before the luteinizing hormone (LH) peak. The va- gina is a long tubular structure (12 15 cm in the dog and 2 3 in the cat), highly dilatable due to the presence of longitudinal folds. The cranial part of the vagina is covered by peritoneal re ﬂ ection; the caudal part lies in the retroperitoneum. The most caudal portions of the female genital tract are the vestibulum and vulva. At the cranial vestibulum, the urethra opens ventrally with an elevated tubercle. ULTRAS OUND Technique Ultrasound provides information about size, shape, structure, and contents of the genital tract. 7 8 The ﬁ rst general approach is usually performed with a me- dium-/high-frequency microconvex probe (5 7.5 MHz, depending on the animal size); however, a complete and detailed exam of the small uterine horns and super ﬁ cial ovaries requires a linear high-frequency probe (10 18 MHz) especially in small-/medium-sized dogs and cats. To identify the ovaries, the caudal pole of the kidney is ﬁ rst imaged in longitudinal plane and the probe is translated caudally and slightly fanned laterally to scan the adipose area caudal to the kidney. With the animal in dorsal or lateral recumbency, the colon and the urinary bladder are identi ﬁ ed cranial to the pubis, and the uterus appears as a round/oval hypoechoic structure located between the two organs, often slightly displaced to the left or right. Moving the probe crani- ally, the bifurcation of the body into the two uterine horns is visible. The normal vagina is dif ﬁ cult to see through the abdominal approach because of the intrapelvic location. The perineal window might be useful to identify the vulva and the caudal vagina especially if enlarged by diseases like masses or if dis- tended by ﬂ uid. Normal Imaging Finding Table 44.1 and associated ﬁ gures summarize the ultrasound features of the normal genital tract in the different phases of the cycle. 9 12 During anestrus, the normal ovaries are oval hypoechoic structures compared to the hyperechoic fat of the ovarian bursa. Often, they are associated with edge shadowing, which helps in their identi ﬁ cation. The uterine horns are hypoechoic with a diameter similar to the jejunal loops but without the wall layering and peristalsis typical for intestines. Ovaries are easier to identify in the periovulatory period because they are larger and contain small cyst-like structures representing follicles or newly formed corpora lutea. Follicles have anechoic content and a thin wall (less than 1 mm). The number and size of follicles increase during proestrus until ovulation, when they become corpora lutea with a progres- sively more echogenic appearance and thicker wall. Corpora lutea identi ﬁ cation can be challenging or impossible when they become isoechoic with the surrounding ovary. 11 Since follicles and newly formed corpora lutea may have a similar appearance, B-mode ultrasound alone cannot be used to accurately deter- mine the ovulation time but must be interpreted in combina- tion with clinical ﬁ ndings and laboratory results. 9 10 Sequential (daily) scanning of the ovary during proestrus using color Doppler can accurately predict ovulation in the dog, by detecting increases of the blood ﬂ ow that correlate with LH peak. 11 Under hormonal in ﬂ uence during proestrus/estrus and diestrus, the uterine wall mildly thickens, and this can improve its visibility. A minimal amount of anechoic to hypoechoic ﬂ uid can be observed in the lumen in proestrus/estrus or immedi- ately after mating. The persistence of some ﬂ uid 5 to 14 days after ovulation suggests lack of pregnancy. 13 COMPU TED TOMO GRAP HY Technique Standard CT examination is performed with the animal in sternal recumbency under general anesthesia. Pre- and post- contrast series are obtained after injection of iodinated contrast medium at the dose of 400 to 700 mg I/kg body weight. Delayed sequences (3 minutes or later) may be useful to better outline the caudal ureters or the urinary bladder neck which can be affected by uterine or vaginal diseases (e.g., stump granuloma/abscess). Similar to retrograde vaginography, CT vagino-urethrogram can be performed using the same technique as previously described, with the only difference that the contrast medium concentration can be lowered to 100 mg I/mL. This technique can be useful in the diagnosis of vaginal masses and genitouri- nary congenital and acquires abnormalities like clefts, ﬁ stulae, stenoses, or strictures. 14 15 Normal Imaging Findings In anestrus, the ovaries are small, oval, and with homogeneous soft tissue attenuation ( Fig. 44.4A ). Follicles and corpora lutea are visible as small round hypoattenuating structures, often protruding from the ovarian surface. The uterus is a tubular organ, the uterine horns mix with the intestinal loops as they extend into the caudal abdomen to reach the dorsal aspect of the urinary bladder. 16 The uterine horns can be distinguished from the small bowel by its smaller diameter, different wall structure, and contrast enhancement (see Fig. 44.4B ). 17 The uterine body and cervix are recognized between the colon and the urinary bladder; the cervix may be thickened during estrus (see Fig. 44.4C ). The vagina is located in the pelvis. In post- contrast images, the urethral wall strongly enhances; this en- ables its identi ﬁ cation caudally to the bladder neck (see Fig. 44.4D ). The vestibulum is oriented caudoventrally and ends caudally with the vulva. Multiple methods and formulas have been proposed with some limitations due to variation in breed and size (especially in dogs), litter size (only for cats), gestational period in which the measurement is performed, and measuring technique. 20 26 28 These formulas allow to calculate the DBP. Accuracy is higher at week 5 of gestation and decreases after week 8. In large and giant dogs, the reported accuracy of measuring ICC is greater compared to the BD. 27 Table 44.4 summarizes reported formulas that can be used in dogs and cats to calculate the number of DBP. Early during pregnancy, a characteristic appearance of echogenic particles within the yolk sac, progressive loss of ﬂ uid volume, and hypoechogenicity of the adjacent uterus are observed. Gesta- tional sacs are more irregular in shape and smaller compared to normal ones ( Fig. 44.7A ). Some fetal malformations can be diagnosed during pregnancy, for example, hydrocephalus and hydrops fetalis, where subcu- taneous thickening due to edema, pleural, and pericardial ﬂ uid is reported. 30 Radiographic signs of fetal death may be observed approx- imately 24 hours after death and are less reliable than sono- graphic indicators. The presence of gas within or around the fetus, overlapping or misalignment of the bones of the cranium, a tightly curled fetus, and collapse of the fetal skeleton may be evident ( Fig. 44.8A,B ). After 14 days, the uterus diameter is less than 1 cm and distinct uterine layering is not visible by ultrasound. 34 ABNOR MAL RADIOG RAPH IC AND ULTRA SONOGRA PHIC FINDIN GS IN OVA RIAN DISE ASES Ovarian Remnant Syndrome This results from hormone production by ovarian remnant tis- sue, usually secondary to incomplete surgery. The right ovary is more frequently involved. Presurgical ultrasound is effective to identify the residual ovary especially during estrus; however, false-negative or false-positive studies are possible. The remnant presents as a hypoechoic structure often with cystic compo- nent located caudal to one of the kidneys. 35 Ovarian Cysts Functional (follicular or luteal) and nonfunctional ovarian cysts occur as solitary or multiple ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled structures of variable size that are unilateral or bilateral in the bitch. 36 Larger cysts can be recognized radiographically and should be considered as a differential diagnosis for ovarian masses ( Fig. 44.11A ). 3 Ultrasonographically, regardless of their origin, they appear as anechoic, well-de ﬁ ned structures with thin wall and distal acoustic enhancement that may deform the outer margin of the ovary (see Fig. 44.11B ). The size of the cyst does not correlate with the hormonal production, and follicular and luteal cysts often coexist in the same ovary. 36 Ovarian cysts may not be distinguishable from normal folliculi or corpora lutea during estrus; however, if the diameter is larger than 1 cm, a cyst is suspected. Correlation with clinical data (prolonged heat or anestrus, persistent diestrus, signs of hyperestrogenism) and hormonal status (increased estradiol or progesterone level) is needed to differentiate the two situations. Alternatively, ultra- sound can be used to monitor the cystic structure over time. Normal follicles and corpora lutea should not persist longer than 30 and 60 days, respectively. Functional ovarian cysts predispose the bitch to the development of cystic endometrial hyperplasia (CEH) pyometra complex. Minerali- zation or bone within teratomas and teratocarcinomas causes hyperechoic shadowing areas within the tumor. 39 The ultrasonographic appearance of ovarian tumors overlaps; therefore, cytology or histopathology is required for de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Determination of a mass as ovarian in origin is based on its location and association with an adjacent uterine horn. This can be challenging with unilateral large ovarian neoplasia, which can be dif ﬁ cult to differentiate from other peritoneal masses. 39 In these cases, CT is indicated (see Fig. 44.12E ). Peritoneal ﬂ uid is common in animals with ovarian tumors and is often seen with carcinomatosis or compression of lym- phatics by the mass itself. Ultrasound can be useful to evaluate the peritoneum and to search for nodules compatible with metastases. Hypoechoic nodules located in the connecting, visceral, or parietal peritoneum are detected especially if sur- rounded by ﬂ uid. Pyometra or CEH may be concurrent and is related to hormonal disturbances. ABNOR MAL RADIOG RAPH IC AND ULTRA SONOGRA PHIC FINDIN GS IN UTERIN E DISE ASES Generalized Uterine Diseases The most common cause of generalized uterine enlargement is uterine ﬂ uid collection. The type of accumulated ﬂ uid corre- lates with the systemic effects. Pyometra, particularly closed- cervix pyometra, can be a life-threatening condition that must be recognized and treated rapidly. Mucometra is an accumula- tion of sterile intraluminal mucoid ﬂ uid, hematometra is an accumulation of sterile, bloody ﬂ uid, and hydrometra is an accumulation of sterile, watery ﬂ uid. CEH frequently develops in old bitches under the effect of pregestational stimulation during the luteal phase and often evolves to luminal ﬂ uid collection. Even in the early phase of the disease, diffuse or focal thickening of the uterine wall can be detected with ultrasound, associated with intramural focal anechoic structures representing dilated glands or ducts and accumulation of a small amount of intraluminal ﬂ uid ( Fig. 44.14A,B eFig. 44.3 ). 7 Accumulation of sterile or infected material produces uter- ine horn enlargement. The echogenicity of the accumulated ﬂ uid cannot be used as de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Anechoic content can be observed both with pyometra and hydrometra. Uterine stump disease may occur after ovariohyster- ectomy due to early postsurgical bleeding or late infection/ granulomatous in ﬂ ammation of the caudal uterine stump. Stump pyometra is associated with residual functional ovarian tissue. Abscesses or granulomas can develop as reaction to surgical material, whereas severe bleeding may be secondary to coagulopathy. In radiographs, a focal area of increased radio- pacity may be observed between the colon and urinary bladder in the lateral view. This cannot be differentiated from neoplasia arising from the uterine stump. With ultrasound, thickening of the uterine stump of variable echogenicity is observed, often with a complex mass appearance. 7 One or multiple pockets of echogenic ﬂ uid may be present in case of recent bleeding or pus accumulation. Sometimes, surgical material in the granu- loma can be present as hyperechoic foci associated with shadowing. Complications in case of site infection include involvement of adjacent bladder neck or vesico-urethral junc- tion and peritonitis with ﬁ stulous tracts. Rarely, plant foreign bodies may migrate from the vagina to the uterine body and horns. They usually appear as linear, hyperechoic, spindle-shaped structures of variable length, possibly associated with shadowing ( Fig. 44.19 eFig. 44.8 ). Fluid accumulation, thickening of the uterine wall, and changes of the surrounding peritoneum can be observed. Uterine Neoplastic and Nonneoplastic Nodules and Masses Uterine neoplasia is considered rare in small animals, usually occurring in middle-aged to older animals; however, uterine adenocarcinoma has been reported in dogs and cats younger than 1 year of age. Leiomyoma is the most common tumor in dogs; this is a benign, slow-growing, noninvasive, and non- metastasizing neoplasia, often incidentally diagnosed. Malignant aggressive adenocarcinoma is more frequently observed in cats. Other types of benign and malignant neoplasia can be rarely found in both species. 37 Uterine nonneoplastic nodules and masses include granu- lomas, polyps, and focal or multifocal uterine wall hyperplasia. Polyps are focal growths of the uterine wall projecting into the lumen. They are variable in number and size, pedunculated or sessile, often associated with luminal ﬂ uid accumulation and rarely with torsion. 44 Masses arising from the uterus can be identi ﬁ ed radio- graphically depending on their size; however, even if large, they cannot be distinguished from segmental ﬂ uid. They pre- sent as soft tissue opacity, rarely mineralized. They are located in the midventral abdomen if originating from the uterine horns or in a more caudal position, between the colon and urinary bladder, if growing from the uterine body or cervix. 3 46 Dorsal displacement of the descending colon and cranial compression of the urinary bladder can be observed with large caudal masses. Differential diagnoses include extrauterine masses arising from the vagina, ovary, or mesentery. Ultrasound on the other hand provides detailed information about the abnormalities of the testicular parenchyma and of the adnexa (scrotum, epididymis, distal part of the spermatic cord with the ductus deferens, vessels, and nerves). 54 Due to their super ﬁ cial location, scrotal or inguinal testicles are best imaged with a high-frequency (8 13 MHz) linear probe. Longitudinal and transverse views of both testes are acquired and compared. Color, power, and pulsed-wave Doppler can be used to assess the arterial and venous ﬂ ow and to investigate parenchymal vascularization. 55 56 For the search of retained abdominal testicles, which are more deeply located, a convex probe with mid to high frequency is often necessary especially in large dogs. Hydrocele is the most common cause of extratesticular ﬂ uid collection, and can result from trauma, neoplasia, infarction, torsion, or infection or can be idiopathic. Extratesticular ﬂ uid collection is easily visualized as an anechoic to echogenic band surrounding the testicle, depending on the cellular con- tent. Other indications for ultrasound include tunica vaginalis diseases like malformations, infections, trauma, or neoplasia. However, in puppies and kittens until 6 months of age, the small and soft testes can move from the scrotum to the inguinal canal. In dogs, a genetic basis is suspected, with a reported incidence range from 1% to 15%, higher in small-size breed, most frequently unilateral and right sided. 68 Feline cryptorchidism is less frequent compared to dogs. Ultrasound has a high predictive value for the ﬁ nal, surgical location of a retained testicle. 69 The ultrasonographic search of the cryptorchid testicle is best performed with the animal in dorsal recumbency. First, the affected side is identi ﬁ ed by palpation of the scrotal testicle; this restricts the search to 50%. The scan starts in the subcutaneous inguinal region from the scrotum to the inguinal ring, then it continues in the abdomen just lateral to the urinary bladder neck cranially to the caudal pole of the ipsilateral kidney ( Fig. 44.25 ). The testicle must be differentiated from the inguinal or colic/jejunal lymph nodes based on the shape (oval for the testicle and more elongated for the lymph nodes), the absence of the hilus, and the presence of the testicle mediastinum. The retained testicle is usually smaller compared to the scrotal one but similar in echogenicity and structure. Even subtle changes in echogenicity or structure should be considered suspect for neoplastic transformation. Testicle agenesis is rare however possible. If a suspected testi- cle is not identi ﬁ ed, CT or MRI can be useful as further diag- nostic methods. Neoplasia Canine testicular neoplasia is common in old intact dogs, with a reported prevalence between 9% and 27%, and is mainly rep- resented by three types of tumors: interstitial cell (Leydig cell), Sertoli cell, and seminomas. Up to 20% of dogs diagnosed with testicular cancer have more than one primary testicular tumor; most of them are characterized by local invasion but rarely metastasize, with the highest metastatic rate (less than 15%) reported for Sertoli cell tumors and seminomas. 37 The risk of developing testicular neoplasia increases with a retained testis. Hyperestrogenism and femininization syndrome are commonly associated with Sertoli cell tumors. The main clinical signs include bilateral symmetric alopecia and hyperpigmentation, pendulous prepuce, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, atrophy of the penis, and squamous metaplasia of the prostate. Severe pancy- topenia can also develop. Independent of the tumor type, at- rophy of the contralateral testicle is common. As in ovarian neoplasia, the mass can be located between the caudal pole of the kidney and the inguinal canal. With large or mineralized masses, abdominal radiographs can show the lesion located in the mid to caudoventral abdomen ( Fig. 44.26 eFigs. 44.12 and 44.13 ). If caudally located, the enlarged testicle can be confused with the urinary bladder or with a large para-prostatic cyst. Susanne M. Stieger-Vanegas D iagnostic imaging is an important component in the clinical evaluation of animals with gastrointestinal disease. Survey radiographs are usually the ﬁ rst im- aging modality, often followed or sometimes replaced by an ultrasound examination. Contrast radiographic studies remain in use but they are laborious and time consuming and are often replaced by ultrasound. Nevertheless, contrast radiography re- mains important for evaluation of functional disorders of the stomach and obstructive processes. Computed tomography (CT) is used increasingly for evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract, especially when disease staging is required. While mag- netic resonance (MR) imaging is regularly used in human pa- tients, it is rarely used for the evaluation of the gastrointestinal tract in animals. NORM AL ANA TOMY The stomach is the relatively large muscular, hollow aspect of the digestive system, which ful ﬁ lls an important function in the transient storage and digestion of food. The stomach is caudal to the liver, and when empty normally lies cranial to the last pair of ribs or slightly caudal to the costal arch. 1 2 The empty stomach has a U shape, which disappears with ﬁ lling. In the ﬁ lled state, the position of the caudal aspect of the stomach is variable and can be located as far caudal as the third to fourth lumbar vertebrae. Independent of ﬁ lling stage, the stomach lies primarily to the left of midline in both the dog and cat. 2 T he st om ac h is ar bi tr ar i ly su bd iv i de d i nt o th e ca rd ia , fu n du s, bo dy , an d py lo ru s ( Fi g. 45 . 1 ) . 1 Th e ca rd ia i s a sm al l ar e a at th e es op ha g og as tr ic ju nc ti on i mm ed ia te ly ca ud al to th e di ap hr ag m. The greater omentum, which is a large, lacy, fat-containing double folded structure, attaches to the stomach and extends caudally to the urinary bladder, covering the intestines ventrally and laterally. The super ﬁ cial aspect of the greater omentum originates from the greater curvature of the stomach and con- tinues to the proximal part of the duodenum in alignment with the attachment of the lesser omentum to the duodenum. 1 3 The gastrosplenic ligament is part of the greater omentum and connects the hilus of the spleen to the greater curvature of the fundus and body of the stomach. 1 The lesser omentum is small and extends from the liver to lesser curvature of the stomach and the cranial part of the duodenum. 1 3 The largest aspect of the lesser omentum is the hepatogastric ligament connecting the liver with the lesser curvature of the stomach. 1 IMAG ING PROC EDUR ES Radiography Indications Radiography is used commonly to evaluate the stomach. Survey radiographs allow evaluation of the position and content of the C H A P T E R 45 Stomach Pylor ic sphinct er E sophagus Lesser cur v atur eC anal Antr um Angular incisur e Gr eat er cur v atur e C ar dia Body F undus Fig. 45.1 The division s of the stoma ch. 923

stomach. Sometimes, gastric wall thickening or gas within the gastric wall, called gastric pneumatosis, can be detected. Gastric dilation and volvulus (GDV), a frequently occurring life- threatening disease in dogs, can usually be diagnosed radio- graphically. Furthermore, mineral or metal attenuating foreign bodies are easily detected on survey radiographs. Additionally, survey radiographs are highly sensitive for evaluating the presence of peritoneal gas, if a gastric perforation is suspected. Survey radiographs are also an important baseline if a contrast radiographic study is planned. Radiographic Technique Three, or preferably four, views of the abdomen are required for a thorough evaluation. 4 Performing left lateral, right lateral, ventrodorsal (VD), and dorsoventral (DV) views of the abdomen is especially valuable for the evaluation of the stom- ach as the position of the patient affects the position of the luminal gas and ﬂ uid within the stomach. 5 Due to gravity, ﬂ uid settles dependently, and gas rises to the highest part of the lumen of the stomach. This was discussed in detail in Chapter 38 . These changes in appearance of the stomach help to eval- uate all aspects of the stomach. Oblique views may occasionally be of value to isolate or project certain areas of the stomach, such as the pylorus, especially when a foreign body or pyloric wall mass is suspected. Radiographic examination of the stomach in an animal that has fasted for 12 to 24 hours may be more informative than when the stomach is in the ambient state, as ingesta within the stomach may obscure some lesions or simulate other lesions. 6 8 However, this is not done routinely due to time constraints, and in some patients fasting may be contraindicated. Also, many drugs used for treatment of gastrointestinal disorders or for sedation to facilitate radiographic positioning, alter gastric motility and may cause gas distention of the stomach. Normal Radiographic Findings The stomach is usually easily recognized by its location, shape, and the content of gas, ingesta, or both. The entire stomach may not be discernible on survey radiographs if it is empty or if gastric ﬂ uid silhouettes with the liver or other abdominal structures. As a general guide, the axis of the stomach from the fundus through the body and pylorus on the lateral view is either perpendicular to the spine, parallel to the ribs, or somewhere between these angles ( Figs. 45.2A,B and 45.3A ). In VD radiographs, the long axis of the stomach is generally perpendicular to the spine with the stomach running transversely across the abdomen, making the angular notch dif ﬁ cult to identify (see Fig. 45.2C ). On the VD view of the dog, the cardia, fundus, and body of the stomach are located to the left of midline, and the pyloric portions are located to the right of midline ( Fig. 45.4A ). The pyloric sphincter in the dog usually is located in the right cra- nial abdominal quadrant at approximately the level of the 10th or 11th rib and is usually cranial to the pyloric canal. 9 In immature dogs the pylorus may be located closer to midline than in adults. 10 Variations in the appearance of the stomach in the dog based on breed conformation have been described. 9 On the VD view of the cat, the stomach is more acutely angled compared to the dog, with the pylorus located at or near the midline (see Figs. 45.3B and 45.4B ). To understand the radiographic appearance of the stomach and movement of the gastric content when the position of the patient is altered, the stomach should be visualized as lying in a transverse plane with the fundus positioned dorsally on the left, and the pylorus ventrally on the right ( eFig. 45.1 ). Thus, with a patient in ventral recumbency for a DV view, gas rises to the fundus, and ﬂ uid settles dependently to ﬁ ll the pyloric portions and part of the gastric body ( Fig. 45.5A , see eFig. 45.1A,B ), whereas with a patient in dorsal recumbency for a VD view, ﬂ uid within the lumen follows gravity and settles dependently to the fundus and body of the stomach. Gas rises to the up- permost portion, which will be the pyloric antrum and the gastric body near midline (see Fig. 45.5B eFig. 45.1C ). On the left recumbent (right-left) lateral view ( Figs. 45.5C and 45.6A ), gas rises to the pyloric portion of the stomach, and ﬂ uid settles dependently in the fundus and body. A gas pocket may be trapped occasionally in the fundus in a left lateral view. The fundus and/or body may be dif ﬁ cult to see in a left lateral view because of the intraluminal ﬂ uid silhouetting with adjacent structures (see Fig. 45.6A ). On the right recumbent (left-right) lateral view (see Figs. 45.5D and 45.6B ), gas rises to the fundus and body, and ﬂ uid settles dependently to ﬁ ll the pyloric por- tions and part of the body of the stomach.
