Christine L. Gremillion ANAT OMY The large intestine consists of the cecum, colon, rectum, and anal canal ( Fig. 47.1 ). The cecum is a diverticulum arising from the proximal colon, located in the right midabdomen, at approximately the level of L3 and L4. 1 The cecum can be quite variable in shape and size depending on its luminal contents. In dogs, the cecum tends to be larger and sigmoid or c-shaped, whereas in cats the cecum is shorter in length and more cone- shaped ( Fig. 47.2 ). 1 2 The mesentery of the colon (mesocolon) is present along its entire length, and is shorter than the mes- entery of the small intestine. The mesocolon is also attached to the mesoduodenum via the duodenocolic ligament. These fac- tors combine to make the large intestine overall less mobile than the small intestine, and thus, its normal position within the abdomen is more consistent. 1 The colon is divided into three parts: the ascending, transverse, and descending colon. The ascending colon is the most proximal portion of the colon, located in the cranial abdomen to the right of midline. The ascending colon is located near the descending duodenum, right lobe of the pancreas, and right kidney. The right colic ﬂ exure connects the ascending colon to the transverse colon. The transverse colon lives in the cranial abdomen, coursing from the right to left side, and is located adjacent to the greater curvature of the stomach and left lobe of the pancreas. The transverse colon communicates with the descending colon at the left colic ﬂ exure. The descending colon then courses caudally, parallel to the body wall, to the level of the pelvic inlet, where it transitions into the rectum without demarcation. The terminal portion of the descending colon and rectum are located dorsal to the urinary bladder, urethra, and prostate/ uterus. The rectum then continues caudally to the level of the second or third caudal vertebrae, where it communicates with the anal canal. 1 IMAG ING PROC EDUR ES Radiography Normal Radiographic Findings The colon is often readily visible on plain radiographs due to normal intraluminal gas and/or fecal contents, although areas devoid of contents may be indistinct. Fecal material often has a granular appearance with mixed soft tissue and gas opacity. The normal colon is shaped like a question mark or shepherd s crook, coursing from the ileocolic junction in the right mid- abdomen cranially, across midline, and then caudally along the left abdomen in the ventrodorsal view. Occasionally, the distal portion of the descending colon may partially extend to the right of midline in animals that have longer, redundant colons C H A P T E R 47 Large Bowel A B 3 2 1 4 1 4 5 3 2 4 1 1 4 5 Fig. 47.1 Survey lateral (A) and ventrodorsal (B) radiographs of demonstrat ing normal large intest ine anatom y. or distention of the urinary bladder ( Fig. 47.3 ). 3 In the lateral views, the entirety of the colon is typically located in the dorsal third of the abdomen, running approximately parallel to the vertebral column. 3 The diameter of the normal colon can be variable depending on the luminal contents, but in dogs, a general rule of thumb is that the colon diameter should be less than the length of the L7 vertebral body. 4 In cats, normal colon diameter should be less than 1.28 times the length of the L5 vertebral body. 5 The cecum is variably visible in dogs depend- ing on the degree of distention. Due to the smaller size of the cecum in cats, it is often not seen radiographically. Gas is occasionally present in the anal sacs, which can appear as either unilateral or bilateral well-circumscribed lucencies sum- mating with the ischia in the ventrodorsal view ( Fig. 47.4 ). It is important not to confuse this ﬁ nding with geographic bone lysis. Contrast Radiography Contrast radiography of the large intestine may be utilized when the diagnosis or appropriate treatment for a patient cannot be determined by survey radiographs and other imaging modalities are not available or desirable. The use of ultrasound and direct inspection of the large intestine via endoscopy have largely replaced many radiographic contrast studies of the co- lon 2 ; however, contrast studies are still helpful for speci ﬁ c indications. Pneumocolonography Pneumocolonography, or negative contrast studies of the co- lon, are typically performed in patients to determine the posi- tion of the colon on radiographs and to differentiate it from distended small intestines. 3 6 Pneumocolonography has also been described in aiding the diagnosis of colonic torsion. 7 Survey radiographs should always be acquired ﬁ rst. With the patient positioned in lateral recumbency, approximately 1 to 3 mL/kg of air is introduced into a red-rubber catheter that is placed in the rectum and then lateral and ventrodorsal pro- jections are obtained. 6 The ﬁ nal volume of air required to suf- ﬁ ciently ﬁ ll the entirety of the colon is patient dependent, and often small increments of air are introduced, radiographs are acquired, and if there is an insuf ﬁ cient volume, the process is repeated. In most patients, it is desirable to ﬁ ll the entirety of the colon with air to the level of the cecum. Survey radiographs should always be obtained prior to initiation of the study. Unless performed as an emergency procedure, preparation including a 12- to 24-hour fast, laxa- tives, and cleansing enemas is preferred. 9 The volume of contrast medium utilized depends on the indication for the study. A dose of approximately 10 to 15 mL/kg of body weight of barium suspension can be expected to ﬁ ll the entirety of the colon 3 9 ; however, this full volume is not required for diagnosis of all disease processes. A diagnosis of colonic torsion has been made using dosages of as little as 3 mL/kg of body weight. 10 Barium is usually administered via an in ﬂ atable Foley catheter placed in the distal rectum. 4 8 9 To minimize risk of perforation, the colon should either be ﬁ lled slowly by gravity or infused in small increments until the desired effect is seen radiographi- cally. Both lateral and ventrodorsal projections should be ac- quired following introduction of barium. If back pressure is present on the syringe, infusion of barium should be dis- continued. If colonic perforation is suspected prior to initiation of the study, iodinated contrast medium should be used instead of barium due to the risk of granulomatous peritonitis with extravasation of barium. 9 Ultrasound of the Large Bowel Ultrasound allows assessment of large intestinal wall thickness, layering, and evidence of mass lesions, and also provides the ability to assess the surrounding mesentery and regional lymph nodes. Ultrasound-guided tissue sampling ( ﬁ ne needle aspirate or biopsy) can also be performed. 11 The primary limitation of ultrasound of the large bowel is the presence of feces and gas with distal acoustic shadowing and reverberation artifacts, respectively, which result in limited visibility of the bowel wall in the far- ﬁ eld of the image. The wall of the large intestine is thinner than that of the small intestine, measuring only 1 to 2 mm in thickness on ul- trasound. 12 Similar to the stomach and small intestine, distinct wall layers of the large intestine are visible: a hyperechoic luminal surface, hypoechoic mucosa, hyperechoic submucosa, hypoechoic muscularis, and hyperechoic outer serosa ( Fig. 47.5 ). When the colon is empty, the wall can have an irregular appearance due to infolding and should not be confused with wall thickening. Occasionally, a thin hyper- echoic line can be seen in the muscularis layer of the colon that parallels the serosal surface. Histologically, this correlates with ﬁ brous tissue in the myenteric plexus. As this is seen in dogs without a history of diarrhea, this ﬁ nding is considered a normal variant. 13 The descending colon can be easily recognized when imaging in a transverse plane in the caudal abdomen, where it lies dorsal to the urinary bladder at the pelvic inlet. The typical appearance of the colon is a thin-walled tubular structure with a curved hyperechoic luminal interface. When identi ﬁ ed near the urinary bladder, the descending colon can then be traced cranially through the remainder of the large bowel. The ileo- colic junction ( Fig. 47.6 ), cecum, and ascending colon are located medial to the right kidney, which can serve as a land- mark as well if unable to trace the entirety of the colon from distal to proximal. Computed Tomography of the Large Bowel Computed tomography (CT) provides a three-dimensional view of the large bowel and surrounding structures and is particu- larly helpful for assessing abnormalities within the pelvic canal compared to radiographs and ultrasound ( Fig. 47.7 ). 14 When nonionic iodinated contrast medium is administered intrave- nously, the colonic mucosa strongly enhances, but discrete wall layers are not visible on CT. 15 Water, barium, and air have been described as luminal contrast agents. 16 17 Bowel preparation protocols may be utilized for bowel cleansing to optimize im- age quality and aid in interpretation. 18 LARGE BO WEL DISEAS ES Large Intestinal Displacement From Mass Effect Abnormalities of the organs adjacent to the large intestine can result in displacement, and sometimes compression, of the colon and rectum depending on the severity ( Figs. 47.8 and 47.9 ). Moderate to severe enlargement of the iliosacral lymph center will result in ventral displacement of the colon and/or rectum on lateral radiographs ( Fig. 47.10A ). Ventral displace- ment of the colon will also occur secondary to renomegaly and other causes of mass effects from the retroperitoneal space such as retroperitoneal effusion. Dorsal displacement of the colon and/or rectum commonly occurs secondary to enlarge- ment of the prostate gland, uterus, vagina, or urinary bladder (see Fig. 47.10B ). Alterations in Large Bowel Diameter Constipation/Obstipation/Megacolon Constipation is de ﬁ ned as reversible, infrequent, or dif ﬁ cult defecation with associated retention of fecal material. 2 Recur- rent constipation that is refractory to treatment is termed obstipation , and implies a permanent loss of function. 2 Mega- colon is a descriptive term, used when there is irreversible dilation of the colon, and represents end-stage colonic dysfunction in patients with obstipation. 2 5 ( Fig. 47.18 ; eFig. 47.5A,B ) Differentials for patients with chronic constipation, obstipation, and megacolon can be split into functional and mechanical causes. Functional causes include neuromuscular dysfunction; spinal cord diseases, including lumbosacral, cauda equina, and sacral spinal cord deformities (such as that seen in the Manx cat); hypogastric or pelvic nerve disorders; submu- cosal or myenteric plexus neuropathy; aganglionosis of the large bowel; and feline dysautonomia. 2 30 32 Metabolic and endocrine diseases can also be a functional cause of chronic constipation, with young cats with congenital hypothyroidism being particularly predisposed. 2 33 34 Mechanical causes of chronic constipation include luminal obstruction secondary to mural lesions of the large intestine (such as masses or stric- tures), h ern iat io n of la r ge bo we l w it h a s s oci a te d o bs tr uc ti on , an d co ng en it al d ef or mi ti e s s u ch a s at res ia ani a nd a tr es ia c ol i. MURAL ABN ORMALITI ES OF THE LARG E BOWEL Focal Wall Thickening Focal wall thickening and mass lesions of the large intestine occur secondary to in ﬁ ltration of the wall with cells, most commonly secondary to neoplasia, in ﬂ ammation, and/or infec- tious disease. Mass lesions of the large intestine may be visible on radiographs if they are large in size; small lesions are better visualized with ultrasound. Ultrasound ﬁ ndings include focal thickening of the intestinal wall and/or discrete nodules/masses arising from the intestinal wall with alteration or loss of wall layering. While neoplasia is a common cause of these changes, these ﬁ ndings are not speci ﬁ c and there is overlap between neoplastic and in ﬂ ammatory lesions. Patient signalment, his- tory, clinical signs, and lesion location can sometimes aid in prioritizing differential diagnoses, but ultimately, tissue sam- pling must be performed for de ﬁ nitive diagnosis. Focal Wall Thickening From Infectious/ In ﬂ ammatory Disease A variety of infectious and in ﬂ ammatory diseases can result in focal wall thickening or mass lesions of the large intestine with alteration or complete loss of wall layering. In dogs, conditions reported to cause focal masses with loss of wall layering of the colon include pythiosis, fungal disease, and protothecosis. 39 42 Granulomatous colitis can also cause focal wall thickening and masses. 43 Submucosal thickening and mineralization of the co- lon wall have been reported in dogs secondary to Hetero- bilharzia americana infection, although these changes are often less pronounced than that seen in the small intestine. 44 45 In cats, feline infectious peritonitis, fungal disease, and eosin- ophilic sclerosing ﬁ broplasia can result in mass lesions and focal thickening of the large intestine. 46 47 In both dogs and cats, bacterial etiologies, such as disseminated mycobacteriosis, can result in focal or multifocal intestinal lesions. 48 Benign Mass Lesions of the Large Intestine Benign polyps have been reported in the large intestine of both dogs and cats, and have rarely been associated with intussus- ception. 21 38 49 Adenomas and leiomyomas are benign neo- plasms that can occur within the large intestine, although these are less common than their malignant counterparts (adenocar- cinoma and leiomyosarcoma, respectively). Hemorrhage and/or hematoma formation within the wall can also result in focal mass lesions of the large bowel, 50 and cecal mucoceles are a cause of intraluminal mass-like lesions which could be confused for a soft tissue mass. 51 Diffuse Wall Thickening Colitis/Typhlitis With colitis, a gas- or ﬂ uid- ﬁ lled colon may be seen radio- graphically. On ultrasound, mild diffuse thickening of the wall may be present ( Fig. 47.22 ), usually with preservation of wall layers, in conjunction with echogenic intraluminal ﬂ uid. Opacity Changes Pneumatosis Coli Pneumatosis coli is the presence of gas within the colon wall. This can occur secondary to a defect in the intestinal mucosa, such as an ulcer, or an increase in intraluminal pressure that allows luminal gas to pass into the bowel wall. Increased intraluminal pressure could occur secondary to large bowel obstruction, as with colonic torsion, 27 or iatrogenically from recent endoscopy. 55 Underlying gastrointestinal necrosis from ischemia or in ﬂ ammatory disease can also result in introduction of luminal gas into the bowel wall. 55 Anaerobic bacterial infection of the colonic mucosa has also been implicated in the development of pneumatosis coli, namely infection with Clos- tridium species. 55 Radiographically, pneumatosis coli appears as a heterogeneous gas pattern within the wall of the colon. When a large volume of gas is present, it can present as a band of gas that follows the course of the wall ( Fig. 47.24 ). With smaller volumes of gas, it can be dif ﬁ cult to distinguish between intramural gas and intraluminal gas trapped between periph- erally located fecal material and the wall.
